children.translated_text: 1. <s>Prabhāsajātaka</s>
To rescue the world from the abyss of the flood of existence, from the serpent of manifold afflictions (<s>kleśas</s>) —

children.text: buddhatvāya viśālo na bhavaty amahātmanāṃ praṇidhiḥ //
children.translated_text: the aspiration (<s>praṇidhi</s>) toward Buddhahood, vast [in scope], does not arise in those who are not great-souled.

children.text:
tadyathānuśrūyate 'tīte 'dhvanisadākusumitopavanaramaṇīyaparyantāparyantajanasamūhasaṃbādhavīthīcatvarāpaṇamaṇikanakastambhapaṅktimanoharabhavanāntarālā śaradadhikavimalatārāpatitārakāgaṇābhyalaṃkṛtā dyaur iva prabhāvatī prabhāvatī nāma rājadhānī babhūva |
tasyāṃ ca sakalavasudhāvadhūhārayaṣṭibhūtāyāṃ maṇir ivāmalaprabhāsaḥ prabhāso nāma rājā babhūva |
children.translated_text: Thus it is heard in tradition: In former times, there was a royal capital named <s>Prabhāvatī</s>, whose boundaries were beautified by gardens ever in bloom, whose broad streets were thronged with crowds, whose marketplaces, squares, and shop-interiors were made enchanting by rows of pillars of gems and gold — like the sky adorned with multitudes of bright stars fallen in an autumn clearer than usual. And in that city, which was like the necklace-cord of the bride that is the entire earth, there was a king named <s>Prabhāsa</s>, resplendent with spotless radiance like a jewel.
In his palace, upon the walls of spotless crystal,
the women who served as ear-ornaments and forehead-marks [i.e., the most beautiful attendants],
their delicate hands, while performing their toilette,
did not bear the fatigue and trouble of holding a mirror.
Him, whose seeds of merit had been nourished by the waters of generosity,
his kinsmen beheld as one who had become a rain-cloud;
even powerful enemies could not withstand his wrath,
[which was] like lightning-fire falling [upon them] in a single day.

children.text: tasyaivaṃvidhavibhūtiparākramodayasya kadācid udayabhūdharaśikharam iva savitur amalamaṇisahasravicchuritobhayapārśvaṃ siṃhāsanam adhitasthuṣaḥ kṣitipater yathāsthāpanam upaviṣṭabrāhmaṇarājasāmantāmātyadūtavargāṃ dauvārikaniṣidhyamānapariśaṅkitetarajanāṃ bahirnibaddhahastyaśvarathavarām āsthānīm ālokayataḥ samutpatyānujñātapraveśair vanacarakair avanitalavinihitajānubhiḥ prakṛtilaghumānasatvād āgatasādhvasagadgadaskhalitavacanair niveditam |
children.translated_text: Once, as that king of such magnificent splendor and prowess was seated upon his lion-throne — like the sun upon the peak of the eastern mountain, its two sides sparkling with thousands of spotless gems — surveying his court-hall, where brāhmaṇas, vassal kings, ministers, and envoys were seated in their proper places, where other persons were kept in check by the doorkeepers and made apprehensive, where horses, elephants, and chariots of the finest kind were stationed outside — forest-rangers, having been granted entry, arrived and, having placed their knees upon the ground, with voices faltering and stammering from the awe natural to those of humble mind, reported:
'In the mountain depths, amidst a herd of elephants,
we have seen a lordly elephant, white as a heap of white lotuses,
at the foot of the Himalayan peak
which was obscured by masses of fresh clouds — resembling it in form.'

children.text: idānīṃ tu grahaṇe devaḥ pramāṇam ity atha sa rājā saṃprāptāyāṃ śaradi karigrahaṇābhivṛddhakutūhalo halayotronmūlyamānamustadarbhamūlasaṃbhūtataṭataṭāśabdāṃ kvacit kṣetragopikāhastatāladhvanivimiśracchoṭkāraśabdasaṃtrāsasamutpatitaśukapakṣākṣepavicalitapariṇatakapiśakalamaśuṅkajālāṃ bhaktahārīpariveṣyamāṇakṛṣīvalāntikanilīnacakitavāyasāṃ kaluṣapalvalajalāvasthitaromanthāyamānamahiṣīyūthasavadanāvaghūrṇanavinivāritadaṃśapātāṃ śrūyamāṇapravicaritagogaṇacalitakiṅkiṇīvikvaṇāṃ kedāratāmarasanālaskhalitaśarārikādambacakravākamithunāṃ nagaragrāmasaṃbaddhāṃ kṣetrabhuvam atikramya sainyasaṃtrāsavibhidyamānahariṇakulākulam aśvakṣuracchidyamānaśaṣpāṅkuraṃ rathavarādhirohī sitātapatravinivāritadivasakarakiraṇasaṃtāpas tad acalavanāntaraṃ praviveśa ||
children.translated_text: 'Now, regarding its capture, the lord [the king] is the authority.' Thereupon, King <s>Prabhāsa</s>, his curiosity greatly aroused at the approach of autumn for elephant-capture, passing through the agricultural lands connected to the city and villages — where the sound of crackling came from mustard and <s>darbha</s> grass roots being uprooted by ploughs, where parrots, startled by the clapping sounds mixed with shouts from the hands of field-guardswomen, flew up and their wing-beats shook the nets of ripened tawny rice-husks, where frightened crows lurked near the field-laborers being served their meal-portions, where herds of buffaloes stood in muddy pools chewing their cud with faces swaying to ward off gadfly-bites, where the tinkling of bells from wandering herds of cows could be heard, where pairs of <s>cakravāka</s> birds and <s>śārārikā</s> cranes slipped upon the lotus-stalks of the paddy-field pools — mounting an excellent chariot, sheltered from the sun's scorching rays by a white parasol, he entered that mountain-forest region, where herds of deer were scattered in alarm by the army, and where the sprouts of grass were cut by horses' hooves.

children.text: atha gajapatim ārāt taṃ sthitaṃ yūthamadhye surabhiviśadagandhāṃ śallakīṃ khaṇḍayantam /
children.translated_text: Then the king beheld that lord of elephants standing close by in the midst of his herd, breaking a fragrant, bright <s>śallakī</s> tree,

children.text: avanipatir apaśyad dānalekhopakaṇṭhabhramadalikulam īṣat karṇatālaiḥ kṣipantam //
children.translated_text: with swarms of bees buzzing near the streaks of his ichor, gently flapping his ears at them.

children.text:
paśyāmas tāvad asya gajapater asya cāsmanmattahastino yuddham iti vicintya prabhāsaḥ saṃyātaṃ nāma hastyāroham uvāca |
protkṣiptamukha paṭam imaṃ kṛtvā kuñjaravaraṃ saṃcodayaitena vanadantinā saha yuddhāyeti |
yad deva ājñāpayatīti hastāsphālanajanitayuddhotsāhaṃ tadabhimukhaṃ tam ādhoraṇaḥ parasainyanivāraṇaṃ vāraṇam akarot |
atha parasparālokanakrodhād adhikatarasamabhivṛddhamadakaṇapaṅktisaṃsiktasurabhīkṛtabhūrajasoḥ parighaguruviṣāṇasaṃghaṭṭadhvanibhīṣaṇam ayaṃ bhagno 'yaṃ bhagna iti senājanenāvalokyamānayoś ciram abhavad yuddham ||
children.translated_text: 'Let us see the battle between this lord of elephants and our own rutting elephant!' — thinking thus, <s>Prabhāsa</s> addressed the elephant-rider named <s>Saṃyāta</s>: 'Raise the face-cloth and urge this excellent elephant forward to fight with that wild tusker!' 'As the lord commands!' — and the rider, mounting, drove the war-elephant, whose battle-enthusiasm was aroused by the slapping of hands, toward [the wild one] as a barrier against the opposing force. Then, as the two [elephants], whose wrath was mutually increased by seeing each other, with rows of rut-drops profusely flowing and perfuming the dust of the earth, made fearsome sounds from the collision of their tusks heavy as iron bars — watched by the soldiers [thinking] 'This one is broken! That one is broken!' — the battle lasted long.
Of the two elephants, with faces split by mutual blows, with rolling tawny eyes,
their ears flapping wildly in agitation, one white and one dark like clouds,

children.text: krodhād utkṣipatoḥ karau dviradayoḥ sthūlau calatpuṣkarau
children.translated_text: raising their thick trunks with swaying tips in fury, the two great tuskers —

children.text: kiṃ cit pallavapāṭale gatavatī vyaktiṃ tayos tālunī
children.translated_text: their palates, slightly pinkish like flower-petals, became visible.
Then, from the collision with the tusks of the lord of white elephants,
speckled with sparks of fire that arose,
the iron bands encircling the tusks
of that royal elephant became loosened.
When the king's elephant was defeated by that [wild] elephant,
the rider became ashamed, his face downcast;
and when the lord of elephants rejoined its herd,
even the king, though profound, was filled with wonder.

children.text:
tataḥ prabhāsaṃ mahāmātrāḥ samupagamyocuḥ |
deva duḥsādhyo 'yam ebhiḥ samastair api karibhir mantraparijaptair oṣadhibalair ayam anekapo vaśīkartavya iti |
tatheti ca sa rājābhidhāya punas tāṃ rājadhānīm ājagāma |
te 'pi tenopāyena taṃ gandhahastinaṃ kariṇībhiḥ parivṛtam ānīya hastiśālāṃ praveśyālāne nibadhya rājño nivedayām āsur ānītaḥ sa gaja iti |
tato rājā saṃyātaṃ hastidamakam uvāca |
bhadra tathāyam ibharājo damayitavyo yathā madvāhanayogyo bhavatīti |
sa ca saśiraḥpraṇāmaṃ gṛhītarājāvavādas taṃ dantinaṃ damayām āsa ||
children.translated_text: Then the great ministers approached <s>Prabhāsa</s> and said: 'Sire, this one is impossible to subdue even by all these elephants; he must be brought under control by means of mantras and herbal potions — this unrivaled one.' And the king, saying 'So be it,' returned to that royal capital. They, by that stratagem, bringing that scent-elephant surrounded by she-elephants, leading him into the elephant-stable, tying him to a post, reported to the king: 'That elephant has been brought.' Then the king addressed the elephant-trainer named <s>Saṃyāta</s>: 'Good sir, this lord of elephants must be tamed in such a way that he becomes fit to be my mount.' And he, having received the king's instruction with a bow of his head, tamed that tusker.
Whatever training
the elephant-tamer taught him,
like an intelligent pupil,
that elephant grasped each one.
Then, having brought forward the great lordly elephant,
the one who crushes the pride and rut of other elephants,
with head bowed in humility, hands joined in respect,
the rider spoke thus to the king:
'This elephant is tamed, O lord of the earth,
fully [capable of] warding off other kings' elephants;
having now completed the training of a lordly elephant,
even rut does not make him act improperly.'
'Even without a goad, even without a bamboo-staff,
even without a rider, he does not misbehave;'
'urged again by me to "Accept these!" —
this elephant today [swallowed] burning iron balls.'
'Therefore, having mounted this lordly elephant
who has conquered the enemy's pride, resembling the Himalaya —'
'surely, being yourself competent in testing jewels,
may your lordship, whose curiosity is aroused, examine him!'

children.text: atha prabhāsas taṃ kuñjaravaraṃ śaratkāladhavalam iva divākaro balāhakam adhiruhya sāntaḥpuraparivāraḥ pramadavanakrīḍām anubhavituṃ prātiṣṭhata ||
children.translated_text: Thereupon <s>Prabhāsa</s>, mounting that excellent elephant, white as the sun [mounting] an autumn cloud, set forth, accompanied by his retinue of the inner palace, to enjoy sport in the pleasure-garden.

children.text: atha sarasi salīlaṃ toyam aṅge kṣipantīṃ
children.translated_text: Then the lord of elephants saw, in the lake, a she-elephant playfully splashing water upon her body,
breaking a lotus stalk with a snap of her bright fetters,
he, the gentle-gaited one, saw that she-elephant
touching her split lotus with her trunk.
Seeing that she-elephant in the midst of the lotus thicket,
the lord of elephants was struck in his heart by the arrow of passion;
though restrained by the driver with stumbling harsh words,
he ran ever more swiftly — and she too, frightened, departed.
As the bull-elephant pursued the departing she-elephant,
tracing as if a white line with his body,
the servants, standing on the bank, swiftly following on horses

children.text: vahanam iva taṭasthāḥ kiṃ cid aikṣyanta bhṛtyāḥ
children.translated_text: [which seemed like] a wind-driven conveyance, could see them only for a moment.

children.text: na kadā cid ahaṃ tvayā nirastā kim idaṃ niṣkaruṇatvam īdṛśaṃ te /
children.translated_text: 'Never have I rejected you — why this such pitilessness of yours?'

children.text: iti ṣaṭcaraṇāvalī muhūrtaṃ rudatīvānujagāma tasya mārgam //
children.translated_text: Thus a line of bees, as if weeping, followed his path for a while.
The rider could not restrain that elephant,

children.text: sa niyantā na śaśāka taṃ niroddhum
children.translated_text: whose frontal boss was split by goad-blows;
even a man cannot be controlled [when maddened by desire] —
how much less an animal, blinded by lust and dull of mind?

children.text: kṣipram eva ca gavalamalinadāvāgnidhūmadhūsaragirigahvarāntam ativiṣamabhūbhāgam ibhakulonmūlitataruśikharaparyastaśakunikulāyapatitabhagnāṇḍakapālaśabalitaikadeśaṃ vyāghropayuktojjhitamṛgakaḍevarapiśitavighasāvalīnagṛdhravāyasajaṃbukam atiparuṣacīrīvirāvabhīṣaṇam aruṇasārathikiraṇasaṃtāpitabhūdharaśikharopalajālam asatsaṅgatam ivānabhirāmaṃ sā hastinī bhītā yat praviveśa so 'pi ca rāgavaśāt kaṇṭakivaṃśataruśākhāskhalanābhighātakṣatorujaṅghabhujavakṣaḥsthalaprasṛtaśoṇitam avanipatim udvahann agaṇayaṃs tān aṅkuśaprahārāṃs tad evāraṇyaṃ prapede ||
children.translated_text: And swiftly, the frightened she-elephant entered the mountain-cave interior, gray with the smoke of forest-fires fed by dry buffalo-dung, over extremely uneven terrain, where in places eggshell fragments from nests of birds dislodged from treetops uprooted by elephant-herds were scattered about, where vultures, crows, and jackals lurked near the flesh-remnants of deer carcasses left by tigers after feeding, fearsome with the harsh cries of crickets, where the rocks on the mountain-peaks were heated by the sun's rays — unlovely like bad company. And the [bull-elephant] too, driven by passion, heedless of the goad-blows, bearing the king whose thighs, shanks, arms, and chest were wounded and bleeding from being struck and scraped by the branches of thorny bamboo trees, entered that very wilderness.
Observed for a moment by tree-dwelling monkeys, motionless,
whose face-shadows were pinkish like ripe <s>udumbara</s> figs, curious about the bell's sound,
the elephant, its goad fallen, leaving the ground dark with <s>kuśa</s> grass,

children.text: udgrīvaiś ca gṛhītaśaṣpakavalair dṛṣṭo muhūrtaṃ mṛgaiḥ
children.translated_text: was gazed upon briefly by deer with raised necks, holding tufts of grass in their mouths.

children.text:
tataḥ sa hastidamakaḥ taṃ rājānam uvāca |
deva gajapatir ayam idānīm anaṅkuśatayā durjana iva lajjāvirahāt sutarām avidheyaḥ |
yadi kathaṃ cid ayaṃ duṣṭahastī kasya cit taror adhastād yāyāt tat tasya śākhām avalambya devenātmā sthirayitavya iti |
sa rājā patitakirīṭakeyūrahārāṃśukaḥ śukāsvāditasindūrānurañjitapramadādharānurūpaphalām aniṣphalajīvitāśaḥ katham api nyagrodhaśākhinaḥ śākhāṃ ciravirahaparyutsukām iva dayitāṃ ghanam āślikṣata |
avatasthe ca taruvarasya skandhe ||
children.translated_text: Then that elephant-trainer addressed the king: 'Sire, this lord of elephants, now being without a goad, is utterly uncontrollable, like a wicked man without shame. If somehow this rogue elephant should pass beneath some tree, then your majesty should seize a branch and steady yourself.' The king — his crown, armlets, necklace, and garments fallen — like a fruit tasted by parrots with its vermillion coloring resembling the reddened lips of a maiden, not despairing of life — clasped tightly a branch of a banyan tree, as if clasping a beloved long separated and eagerly awaited. And he stood upon the trunk of that noble tree.
As the lord of elephants departed, its ear-fans brushed
by the branch-tips of the trees,
from its great distance, having passed beyond the range of sight,
the king could no longer hear the loud sound of its bell.

children.text: atha tasya nṛpateḥ śuddhāntasīmantinyo bāṣpapariplutekṣaṇāḥ praviśya bhavanaṃ bhuvanapatiśokavaśād avanitalagatāḥ punaḥ punar iti paridevanāṃ kartum ārebhire |
children.translated_text: Then the women of the king's inner chambers, with eyes overflowing with tears, entering the palace, casting themselves upon the ground from grief over the lord of the earth, began to lament again and again thus:
'Fallen somewhere in the mountain-cave,
harsh with the dust of the earth, rough with great boulders,
he, the lord of the earth, today without weapons —
how will he return from the fearsome forest?'
'With shoulders and arms loosened and broken from his fall,
or exhausted by overpowering thirst,
with the soft soles of his feet pierced by <s>kuśa</s>-grass needles —
how will he, thirsty, drink water today?'
'He has been carried by the elephant into an unanticipated
calamity, though surrounded by his people;
but then, the path of fate whose fruits are happiness and sorrow —
who indeed can transcend it?'

children.text: yadi tasya kiṃ cid aśivaṃ nṛpater
children.translated_text: 'If some ill should befall that king,
we too shall certainly desire death;
a herd of she-elephants whose bull has been slain by a lion
does not delight in the mountain forest.'
'If only the rider would come and say: "By good fortune,
the lord of the earth lives!"'
'If only we might see that king again,
with his moon-face charming with smiles, bearing the royal splendor!'

children.text: iti tāny avarodhanāni vilāpaparāṇi nayanajalakṣalitapatralekhāni samāśvāsyāmātyajanaḥ saparijanaḥ karṇīrathān adhiruhya krameṇa gatvā tāṃ tasya gajapateś caraṇavinyāsaparimṛditaloṣṭadarbhāṃ madalavanipātādhivāsitatṛṇāṅkuraparyantāṃ paribhramanmadhukaragaṇāṃ padavīm anusasāra ||
children.translated_text: Having consoled those women of the inner chambers, whose laments were supreme and whose leaf-ornament-paintings were washed away by tears, the ministers with their attendants mounted <s>karṇī</s>-chariots and, proceeding gradually, followed the trail of that lord of elephants — the path where clods and <s>darbha</s> grass were crushed by his footsteps, where the edges of the grass-sprouts were perfumed by the dripping of his rut-drops, and where swarms of bees circled about.
Near the mountain, they then saw a necklace — fallen, with its loosened, severed strings, its weighty gems slipping away,
its soft grass-blades covered by strands of pearls pale with fragrance —

children.text: upagiri hāram aikṣata tataḥ sa narapatijanaḥ
children.translated_text: that retinue of the king saw the necklace,
which all around stole the luster of a bright, motionless, startled serpent.

children.text:
hāradarśanāc ca niyatam āsanno deva iti manyamānās te 'mātyāḥ stokam antaraṃ gatvā tasya nyagrodhasyādhastāt taṃ rājānaṃ pipāsākṣāmaparipāṇḍuśarīram ālulitamaulim atitīkṣṇakaṇṭakataruviṭapābhipātajanitavedanam apaśyan |
avatīrya ca karṇīrathebhyas turagebhyaś ca pramuditamanaso bisavivaraviniḥsṛtam iva sacīpatiṃ divaukasaḥ sādaram upāsāṃ cakrire |
sa ca narapatir aśeṣaṃ tam eva vṛttāntaṃ tebhyo 'kathayat |
atha te 'mātyāḥ prītās taṃ daśarathatanayam iva rathavaram āropya tasmād araṇyapradeśāt punas tannagaraṃ aninyuḥ |
āgate ca tasminn avanibhuji prabhāvatīṃ rājadhānīṃ pratītahṛdayāḥ paurās toraṇāvabadhyamānasurabhivividhakusumamālānilīyamānadvirephām utkṣiptadhvajapatākāṃ gandhodakādhivāsitarathyāntarāṃ pravṛttacitranṛttotsavām akurvan |
so 'pi ca hastī tasyāṃ vāsitāyāṃ kṛtamadanakutūhalaḥ samadahaladharalīlām ivābhyasyan punas tena hastipakena bhayalajjāvimūḍhamanasā tasya rājñaḥ sakāśam aninye ||
children.translated_text:
And seeing the necklace, the ministers, thinking 'the king is certainly nearby,' went a short distance and beneath that banyan tree beheld that king — his body emaciated, pale, and parched with thirst, his crown disheveled, suffering pain from the scratches of the extremely thorny tree-branches upon which he had fallen.
Descending from their carriages and horses, the ministers, their minds delighted, reverently attended upon him like the celestials attending <s>Śacī</s>'s lord [<s>Indra</s>] emerging from the hollow of a lotus stalk.
And that king narrated to them the entire account of what had happened.
Then those ministers, overjoyed, mounted him upon an excellent chariot — like the sons of <s>Daśaratha</s> — and brought him back from that forest region to his city.
And when that sovereign arrived, the citizens of <s>Prabhāvatī</s>, the capital, their hearts reassured, made the royal city [festive] — with fragrant garlands of various flowers hung on arched gateways, among which bees concealed themselves, with raised flags and banners, with streets perfumed by scented water, and with celebrations of colorful dance performances.
And that elephant too, in that city in rut, practicing as if the sport of a rutting elephant shaking the earth, was again brought by that elephant-keeper — whose mind was bewildered with fear and shame — into the presence of that king.
Then, seeing the trembling elephant-keeper
quaking with terror before the king,
his eyes instantly became, from anger,
red like unsheathed red lotuses in hue.

children.text:
krodharāhukaluṣīkṛtavadanenduś cāvocad rājā |
are durātman hastipakādhama kiṃ bhavān upakṣiptaḥ kena cid yad enam adāntaṃ duṣṭahastinaṃ mām āropitavān asi |
nanu proktavāṃś ca bhavān yathāyaṃ kuñjaravaro mamājñayā jvalitān apy ayoguḍān aśnīyād iti paśyāma idānīṃ te satyam ||
children.translated_text: And the king, his moon-like face darkened by the <s>Rāhu</s> of anger, spoke: 'You vile wretch, lowest of elephant-keepers! Were you put up to this by someone, that you mounted me upon this untamed, wicked elephant? Did you not declare that this excellent elephant would, at my command, eat even red-hot iron balls? Let us now see your truth!'
Then, before the elephant,
resembling a fresh summer sun,
drawing them from the midst of fire,
he placed iron balls.
And he said to the chief minister,
surrounded by alarmed counselors:
'Dismount the elephant! Take up
these blazing iron balls!'
He, having assented 'So be it,'
took a goad before [the elephant],
saying 'Take!' to the elephant —
and it did not show defiance.
Seeing the elephant about to take
that iron ball, the king,
his composure restored, said:
'Let the elephant be restrained!'
When the elephant was restrained
by that elephant-tamer, the king then said:
'He is capable of subduing the body alone,
but not of subduing the restless mind.'

children.text:
atha śuddhāvāso devo vihāyasi sthitvā yady ayam avanipatir buddhānāṃ bhagavatāṃ guṇaparaṃparāṃ śṛṇuyāt tato niḥsaṃśayena buddhatvāya praṇidhānaṃ kuryād iti |
tad idam atra prāptakālam imam eva mahāmātram anupraviśāmīti vicintya kṣaṇād eva taccharīram anupraviveśa |
tataḥ saṃyātas taṃ rājānam uvāca
children.translated_text:
Then a deity of the Pure Abodes (<s>Śuddhāvāsa</s>), standing in the sky, [thought]: 'If this king were to hear of the chain of virtues of the blessed <s>Buddhas</s>, then he would undoubtedly make a vow for the attainment of Buddhahood.' [Thinking] 'This is the opportune moment; I shall enter this very chief minister,' in an instant he entered that body.
Then the possessed one spoke to the king:
'Even sages, their bodies emaciated by austerity, living on fruits,
have been led to distraction by desire (<s>Smara</s>).',

children.text: manodamas tair api cen na śakyate
children.translated_text: 'If even they cannot accomplish the taming of the mind,
how shall it be done by another?'

children.text:
rājovāca
kaḥ khalu cittadamane śaktaḥ syāt |
children.translated_text:
The king said: 'Who indeed would be capable of taming the mind?'
The possessed one replied:
'Those called <s>Buddhas</s>, lords of the world,
who have been, and who are yet to come —
they indeed are able
to tame both their own and others' minds!'
Hearing the word '<s>Buddha</s>'
from that inhabitant [of the Pure Abodes],
the king's serene joy seemed to multiply,
as shown by the arising of horripilation.

children.text:
rājovāca |
bhadra nanu kathyatāṃ tāvat kiṃprabhāvā buddhā iti |
children.translated_text:
The king said: 'Good sir, pray tell — what is the power of the <s>Buddhas</s>?'
The possessed one replied:
'For those blinded by the darkness of ignorance,
for the cessation of repeated rebirth —
that peaceful state which is to be awakened to,
that has been [realized as] <s>Buddha</s> by those <s>Tathāgatas</s>.'

children.text:
tataḥ sa rājā pramuditamanāḥ punar uvāca |
nanv ākhyāyatāṃ tāvat kathaṃ buddhatvam adhigamyata iti |
saṃyāta uvāca |
children.translated_text:
Then the king, his mind delighted, spoke again: 'Pray tell, how is Buddhahood attained?'
The possessed one replied:
'Through generosity (<s>dāna</s>), moral conduct (<s>śīla</s>), patience (<s>kṣamā</s>), vigor (<s>vīrya</s>),
meditation (<s>dhyāna</s>), and wisdom (<s>prajñā</s>) —
by those who strive diligently,
Buddhahood is attained by human beings.'

children.text: atha sa rājā buddhatvādhigamamārgam upalabhya praṇidhim iti cakāra ||
children.translated_text: Then that king, having understood the path to the attainment of Buddhahood, made a vow (<s>praṇidhi</s>):
'May I swiftly become,
for the pacification of beings again and again,
endowed with virtues such as generosity,
a <s>Buddha</s>, skilled in what is to be awakened to!'
When the <s>Bodhisattva</s>, pure in resolve, made this great vow,
the wise rejoiced.
Trapped in the snare of thoughts about the destruction of his own forces,
the Flower-bannered one [<s>Māra</s>], like a deer struck by an arrow, trembled.
The tree of his vow, planted in the field of his mind, delighting people,
with the first blossoms of compassion about to appear,
gradually, with the great water of generosity born of the wealth of unbroken resolve,

children.text: phalārthī bhūpālaḥ pratidinam asiñcat tarum iva
children.translated_text: the king daily watered [it] like a tree, desiring its fruit.
Of him who adorned the conduct of kings as vast as the sky,
who sought to pierce the impenetrable darkness of the world's ignorance —
the moonlight of generosity of that king-moon, radiant from the onset of his vow-autumn,
spread abundantly, causing joy to the night-lotuses of the affectionate.

children.text: bhṛtyān bhṛśaṃ ca kalabhān iva pālayantaṃ
children.translated_text: Protecting his servants greatly, as if they were young elephants,
delighting <s>Lakṣmī</s> (prosperity) like a she-elephant, for a long time —
those seeking gifts, affectionate, approached and surrounded
that king like bees around the lord of elephants.
He who was formerly unapproachable like fire,
with eyes crooked from fury,
that very king, his resolve fixed on enlightenment (<s>bodhi</s>),
became like a lake to the people.
When the darkness of envy is removed from beings,
the mind gradually transforms its nature;
the very smoke that irritates the eyes,
when accumulated, attains the state of a cloud.
Of the king who was supremely devoted to excessive generosity,
even his servants gave gifts;

children.text: ṛtur eva sa tādṛśo hi kaś cit
children.translated_text: for there is indeed such a season
in which even trees bear abundant fruit.
Seeing the king devoted to virtues,
even in the subjects a desire for virtue arises;
conforming to the light of the moon,
the moonstone yields pure water.
Who, being associated with virtuous people,
would not become well-disposed and fond of virtue?
Even the ferocious wild beast, having come into the range of sages,
abandons its savage nature.
Thus, hearing this speech describing
the virtues of the <s>Buddhas</s>, captivating the mind, from the elephant-keeper [now possessed],
this was the earlier vow of the son of the <s>Śākyas</s> [the <s>Buddha</s>],
which became the cause of breaking the bondage of existence.

children.text: tad evaṃ śrutasugataguṇamāhātmyāḥ puruṣaviśeṣāḥ śarīriṇāṃ saṃsāraduḥkhocchittaye buddhatvādhigamāya vīryasaṃnāham ābaddhavanta iti vicintya samyaksaṃbodhilābhāya ghaṭamānena dhīmatā prathamam eva dānapāramitāyāṃ yatnaḥ karaṇīya iti ||
children.translated_text: Thus, extraordinary persons, having heard the greatness of the qualities of the <s>Sugata</s> (the Well-Gone One), girded themselves with vigor for the attainment of Buddhahood in order to cut off the suffering of beings in <s>saṃsāra</s>. Reflecting thus, the wise one striving for the attainment of perfect enlightenment (<s>samyaksaṃbodhi</s>) should first of all make effort in the perfection of generosity (<s>dānapāramitā</s>).
The <s>Prabhāsa Jātaka</s> is complete.
2. <s>Badaradvīpa</s> (The Jujube Island)

children.text: yaḥ paraduḥkhair duḥkhī tadvicchittyai kṛtapratijñaś ca /
children.translated_text: He who suffers at the sufferings of others and has made a vow to eliminate them,

children.text: jagadartham īhamānaḥ sa eva sahate svaduḥkhāni //
children.translated_text: striving for the sake of the world — he alone endures his own sufferings.

children.text:
tadyathānuśrūyate
vibudhagaṇāśramabhūtāyāṃ nayapratāpavijitasarvasāmantena brahmadattena rājñādhiṣṭhitāyāṃ vārāṇasyāṃ rājadhānyām upacitavividhapuṇyasaṃbhāro 'nekaśāstrakalākauśalaprakhyātakīrtis tyāgadākṣiṇyakṣamādīnām adhiṣṭhānaṃ guṇānāṃ suhṛtpraṇayibandhujanapriyaḥ supriyo nāma bodhisattvaḥ sārthavāho babhūva |
children.translated_text:
Thus it is heard:
In <s>Vārāṇasī</s>, the royal capital, which had become a resort of hosts of divine sages, ruled by King <s>Brahmadatta</s> who had conquered all neighboring kings by statecraft and might, there lived a <s>Bodhisattva</s> named <s>Supriya</s>, a caravan-leader — one who had accumulated abundant varied merit, whose fame was renowned through skill in numerous arts and sciences, who was the abode of virtues such as generosity, graciousness, patience, and the like, and who was dear to friends, kinsmen, and loved ones.
'Everything is to be given
to all, always, and in every way' —
this was the vow
of that one who was compassionate toward all beings.
The vow of great beings, possessed of great soul,
who have utterly resolved
to destroy the afflictions of the world,
arises only in the great.
Generosity that delights people
spread in his mind
like the great rising of the moon in autumn,
which pierces the darkness.
'This one maintains enjoyments
acquired by the power of merit for our sake' —
thus the supplicants attached to [his] wealth
clung to a sense of ownership over him.
'Surely this wise one has sown the seed of his vow
in the soil of his mind, for the fruit of <s>Jina</s>-hood (victorious Buddhahood)!
Through the perfection of generosity first' — thus that doer of merit
eagerly embraced the dense [cloud of generosity], as if with longing.

children.text: ity upacitakuśalamūlasya mahāpradānapravṛttasya sattvārthaṃ prati karuṇāpratodasaṃcoditamanasturaṅgasya vyavasāyarathādhirohiṇo bodhisattvasya
children.translated_text: Of this <s>Bodhisattva</s>, who had accumulated the roots of virtue, who was engaged in great giving, whose mind-steed was spurred by the goad of compassion for the sake of beings, who had mounted the chariot of resolve —
'This one will not relinquish
the perfection of generosity soon!' — [thinking thus,]
the remaining perfections (<s>pāramitās</s>)
stood as if eager [for their turn].

children.text: atha sa mahātmā nidāghadinakarakiraṇair iva jalāśayam āpīyamānam anudivasam arthibhir alpāvaśeṣaṃ kośasāram ālokya yācanakajanāśāṃ viphalām aśaknuvan kartuṃ ratnadvīpagamanābhilāṣī vividhapaṇyaparipūritam ucchritaśītapaṭaskhalitamṛdupavanam atinipuṇakarṇadhārāvalambitakarṇam āptaparijanādhiṣṭhitam anekavaṇigjanaparivṛto vahanam āruhya
children.translated_text: Then that great-souled one, seeing the treasury — being daily drunk up by supplicants like a reservoir by the rays of the summer sun — reduced to a small remainder, unable to make vain the hopes of the begging folk, desiring to voyage to the Jewel Island (<s>Ratnadvīpa</s>), boarded a vessel filled with various merchandise, with gentle breezes slipping through raised white sails, with a helm held by a most skilled navigator, manned by trusted attendants, accompanied by many merchant-folk, and
resembling a bed strewn with blossoming flax flowers,
as if the sky had turned entirely to water all around,
with thousands of luminous serpent-gem lamps within,
he plunged into the ocean of deep, impassable waters.

children.text: vahanagativaśāc ca nimajjata iva velātaṭaśākhinaḥ kṣaṇam eva samavalokya pavanabalodīryamāṇamahātaraṅgaviṣamam agrato dhāvantam iva ca krameṇa mahāsamudram uttīrya ratnadvīpam āgamya vividhāni ratnāny ādāya saha tair vaṇigbhir avighnena supriyaḥ punaḥ pratinivṛtya sārthaṃ sthalapathena netum ārebhe |
children.translated_text: And by the motion of the vessel, as if the trees on the coastal bank were sinking, observing them for just a moment, and seeing the great ocean running ahead as if with waves uneven from the force of the rising wind — gradually crossing the great ocean, arriving at the Jewel Island, obtaining various gems, <s>Supriya</s> together with those merchants returned without obstacle and began to lead the caravan by the land route.
No group of supplicants who met him went away disappointed;
his mind treated even his son, who was hostile, with equanimity.
Thus, as his virtues were proclaimed, of him who was devoted to virtue,
not even a band of robbers plundered his caravan.
When a person is adorned with pure conduct
and their mind is devoted to the welfare of the world,
even people averse to <s>dharma</s>
approach benevolence as if becoming friends.

children.text: tataḥ sa mahātmā vārāṇasīm upagamya prītamanobhir bandhubhir ālokyamānaḥ svabhavanam anupraviśya tena ratnadvīpād upāttena svāpateyenārthijanasaṃmānanām anudivasam akarot |
children.translated_text: Then that great-souled one, arriving at <s>Vārāṇasī</s>, beheld by kinsmen of delighted minds, entering his own house, day after day he honored the supplicant-folk with the wealth obtained from the Jewel Island.
Of that great-souled one whose prosperity was for others' sake,
of that generous-hearted giver of gifts,
the door of [his] house was never empty of supplicants
who came with abundant, unfailing affection.

children.text: atha sa mahātmā kadācid varaśayanīyam upagataḥ kṣaṇadāyām idam acintayat | idam api na paryāptam evam arthijanapratipūjanāyāṃ draviṇam iti | kīdṛśaṃ punar yātrāphalaṃ sādhayeyaṃ yena me satatam avyavacchinnadānapratītamanaso 'rthinaḥ syur ity api nāmeyaṃ tvaritam apayāyān niśīthinī yato 'haṃ saṃmānayeyam arthivargam iti |
children.translated_text: Then that great-souled one, one evening, having gone to his excellent bed, thought during the night: 'Even this wealth is not sufficient for honoring the supplicant-folk in this way.' 'What kind of journey-fruit shall I accomplish, by which the supplicants, their minds ever delighted by uninterrupted generosity, might be [satisfied]?' And: 'Would that this night pass quickly, so that I may honor the supplicant-folk!'
'Every creature, at the time of weariness,
or when afflicted by exhaustion, desires sleep for the happiness of the mind;
this [sleep], since it creates an obstacle to the giver's giving,
was itself a source of suffering for that virtuous one.'

children.text: atha sa mahāsattvo nidrāvaśam upagataḥ svapne vimalakiraṇacakravālābhyudgatapariveṣanimagnamūrtim alikulābhinīlaśithilakeśapāśāvacchāditaikāṃsadeśāṃ kamalapalāśābhitāmrāyatākṣīṃ kanakakalaśānurūpapayodharoparikīrṇahāramaṇiprabhāsamuddyotitavakṣaḥsthalām abhinavabandhujīvakusumābhiraktādharāṃ trivalīsopānādhirohaṇavijihmīkṛtapratanuromarājikām indukāntim iva mūrtimatīṃ karṇābharaṇamaṇiprabhābhyaktakapolapattralekhāṃ tanudhavalottarīyasaṃvṛtāṅgīṃ śaraccandrikāprabhāparigatām iva kārtasvarapratimām apratirūpāṃ devatām apaśyat | sā cainam abhivyajyamānadaśanamaṇikiraṇāvabhāsitānanā sphuṭamadhureṇa vacasedam abhyadhāt |
children.translated_text: Then that great being, having fallen under the power of sleep, beheld in a dream a peerless deity — her form immersed in a halo rising from a circle of pure rays, one shoulder covered by loose tresses of hair dark as a swarm of bees, her elongated eyes coppery-red like lotus petals, her bosom illuminated by the luster of pearl necklaces scattered upon breasts resembling golden water-pots, her lips reddened like fresh <s>bandhujīva</s> flowers, the slender line of body-hair curving as if ascending the staircase of the three folds of her belly, like moonlight embodied, her cheek-leaf-designs anointed by the luster of the gems of her ear-ornaments, her body clad in a thin white upper garment, like a golden image surrounded by the radiance of autumn moonlight. And she, her face illuminated by the radiating gem-like rays of her teeth, addressed him with clearly sweet words:
'This treasury-wealth of yours will gradually diminish
due to your excessive passion for giving,
like the ocean's tide receding
at the end of the night, when the beauty of the moon is waning.'
'Then, when your prosperity has departed,
the supplicants, having cast a glance, will turn away,
like peacocks whose beautiful crests have dropped, whose lovely moonlight has faded,
gazing long at an autumnal cloud that gives no rain.'
'Thus, when the treasury-wealth has gone to exhaustion,
you will reach sorrow upon encountering the supplicants.
But this desire to give of yours, being so vast,
will never undergo change, not even once.'
'When the fuel is exhausted, the radiance
of the flickering-flamed fire goes to exhaustion.
But the generosity of the great, ever growing with practice,

children.text: na caiva ditsā mahatāṃ vipatsv api
children.translated_text: never diminishes, not even in calamities.'
'"Even when his wealth is utterly exhausted, he does not make the supplicants
distressed by the shattering of their refuge in petition" —
a person whose resolve has been thus made manifest to people
does not abandon magnanimity even in distress.'
'Thus I speak the truth to you,
who seek the state that severs worldly existence.
Swiftly equipping yourself with the raft of resolve,
go to <s>Badaradvīpa</s> for the welfare of the world.'
'Hear from me the directions for the journey there,
a journey terrifying with mountains, serpents, and <s>Yakṣas</s>,
and blocked by many oceans,

children.text: yad alaṃ sādhayituṃ tvam eva śaktaḥ
children.translated_text: which you alone are able to accomplish.'
'There is a sacred herb called <s>Sudhā</s>, growing on Mount <s>Malaya</s>,
an herb of steadfast potency and holy fragrance.
Having cooked it with ghee and eaten it,
it serves for the destruction of fatigue, thirst, overpowering [of foes], and hunger.'

children.text: pañcadvīpaśatāny atītya saritas tās tāś ca bhīmāmbhasas
children.translated_text: 'Having crossed five hundred islands and various rivers of fearsome waters,

children.text: tīrtvā ca plavamadhyago jalanidhīn puṇyena vīryeṇa ca
children.translated_text: and having traversed the oceans, going amidst rafts, by merit and valor,
upon a lofty mountain there is a great herb named <s>Mahaughauṣadhi</s> (Great Flood Herb) —
having taken that, you should proceed from there, for the destruction of the poison of great serpents.'

children.text: purastāc ca sūcibhedyaṃ vetravanam atikramya jaladhitīre bhūdharakandarāntarāvasthitaṃ tārākṣaṃ nāma rākṣasaṃ drakṣyasi |
children.translated_text: 'And first, having crossed a cane-thicket so dense it can only be pierced by a needle, you will see, on the ocean's shore, inside a mountain cavern, a <s>Rākṣasa</s> (demon) named <s>Tārākṣa</s>.'
'Of the sleeping one whose eyes blaze with the brightness of kindled fire, as if awake,
whose eyes have pupils equal to the orb of the sun,
whose eyelid-lines are encircled by tawny eyelashes,
and which, even when sleep departs, remain closed as if unmoving.'
'By the wind of his deep breathing while sleeping,
the trees become withered and their flowers turn pale;
and his tongue flashes out from the hollow of his mouth,
like a bolt of lightning from a thundercloud of terrifying roar.'

children.text: tato yakṣabhujagaśāntyartham atītabuddhabhāṣitāni sūtrapadāni paṭhatā bhavatā gantavyam | gatvā ca nātidūre rohitakaṃ nāma vividhodyānakusumasurabhipavanam anekaratnaprabhodbhāsitajaladhitaṭabhūdharāntaram uccāvacajanasaṃbādhavipaṇimārgam amarapurapratimaṃ puraṃ drakṣyasi | tatra ca paurṇamāsīniśākarapriyadarśano vividhaguṇaugho māghanāmā sārthavāhaḥ | sa te badaradvīpasya panthānam upadarśayiṣyati | sa ca mahāsārthavāho gāḍhaglānatayā siṃhaśārdūlabhīṣaṇācalavanāntarāṇi bahūni yojanāni gatvā kālakarmaṇā yokṣyate | na ca bhavatā tatrāpi viṣādaḥ karaṇīyaḥ |
children.translated_text: 'Then you must go forth, chanting the <s>sūtra</s>-verses spoken by past Buddhas for the pacification of <s>Yakṣas</s> and serpents. And having gone not far, you will see a city called <s>Rohitaka</s>, with breezes fragrant from the flowers of various gardens, mountains near the ocean-shore illuminated by the radiance of many gems, marketplace-roads crowded with people of every station — a city rivaling the city of the gods. There dwells a caravan-leader named <s>Māgha</s>, handsome as the full-moon's luminary, endowed with a flood of various virtues. He will show you the path to <s>Badaradvīpa</s>. And that great caravan-leader, after traveling many leagues through mountain-forests terrifying with lions and tigers, will meet his fate through severe illness. But you must not despair even then.'
'Driven by compassion,
the steadfast, for the welfare of beings,
having donned the armor of zeal,
accomplish their goal.'

children.text: paścād devatānubhāvāt puṇyaprabhāvāc ca dūram atikramya himagiriśikharānukāriprākārapariveṣṭitaṃ rajatanagaraṃ pihitadvāraṃ drakṣyasīti | tatra ca bhavatā punas tāny eva sūtrapadāni paṭhitavyāni | tataḥ svayam eva tad dvāram apāvṛtakapāṭaṃ bhaviṣyati |
children.translated_text: 'Afterward, by the power of the deity and the influence of merit, having traveled far, you will see a Silver City, enclosed by ramparts resembling the peaks of the <s>Himālaya</s>, with its gates shut. And there you must again chant those very <s>sūtra</s>-verses. Then the gate will open its doors by itself.'
'Then there will emerge, heavy with the burden of their pitcher-like breasts,
thoroughly languid, their teeth gleaming bright from their smiles,
with curved brow-lines, eyes dark as blue lotus petals,
four <s>Kinnarī</s> maidens wearing thin, white, divine garments.'

children.text: tāsu ca mṛduhasitakaṭākṣabhrūvilāsaprakāśitamanmathāsv api bhavatā bhaginīsaṃjñā karaṇīyā | tāś ca bhavato badaradvīpasya panthānaṃ darśayiṣyanti | tato badaradvīpādhipatiḥ kinnararājo devatāprotsāhito bhavate cintāmaṇiṃ dāsyati | tatra ca vaiḍūryamayasya nagarasyāntikajātam upavanam āgatam akṛṣṭoptasya śāler atuṣaṃ phalam aśnantam uditam iva śaradvalāhakaṃ valāhakanāmānam aśvarājaṃ drakṣyasi | sa tvāṃ vihāyasā kṛtārthaṃ vārāṇasīm āneṣyatīty abhidhāya sā devatāntaradhīyata | bodhisattvo 'pi ca kalyāṇasvapnadarśanāt paraṃ pramodam udvahan niyamenāhaṃ badaradvīpayātrāphalam āsādayiṣyāmīti vicintya devatāḥ pūjayitvā śramaṇabrāhmaṇakṛpaṇebhyaś ca dānāni dattvā yathādevatopadiṣṭaṃ caturdaśabhiḥ saṃvatsarair badaradvīpam āgamya kinnarādhipatisakāśāt taṃ cintāmaṇim āsādya cintayāmāsa | api nāma sa turagapatir āgacched iti |
children.translated_text: 'And even though those Kinnarīs display Cupid's allure through gentle laughter, sidelong glances, and playful brow-movements, you must regard them as sisters. And they will show you the path to <s>Badaradvīpa</s>. Then the lord of <s>Badaradvīpa</s>, the <s>Kinnara</s> king, encouraged by the deity, will give you the wish-fulfilling gem (<s>Cintāmaṇi</s>). There, in a park near a city made of beryl, you will see a horse-king named <s>Valāhaka</s>, risen like an autumnal cloud, eating the huskless fruit of self-grown rice. He will carry you through the sky, having accomplished your purpose, back to <s>Vārāṇasī</s>.' Having said this, that deity disappeared. And the Bodhisattva too, bearing supreme joy from seeing the auspicious dream, thinking 'I will surely attain the fruit of the journey to <s>Badaradvīpa</s>,' worshipped the deities, gave gifts to ascetics, brahmins, and the poor, and following the deity's instructions, arrived at <s>Badaradvīpa</s> in fourteen years. Having obtained that wish-fulfilling gem from the <s>Kinnara</s> lord, he thought: 'May that lord of horses come!'
No sooner was it thought by that one of meritorious deeds,
whose mind was devoted to accomplishing others' welfare,
than, like a gleaming mass of moonbeams,
that horse-king swiftly arrived.
Having arrived, he spoke in human speech,
his mane thick and fine like threads of silk:
'From here, across the inaccessible seas and mountains —
to which land shall I carry you through the sky?'
Beloved <s>Supriya</s>, foremost among the virtuous, of cherished qualities,
addressed that excellent steed, bright as moonbeams:
'To <s>Vārāṇasī</s>, within whose garden-groves buzz intoxicated bees —
carry me there swiftly, O king of horses!'
Addressed by the horse-lord: 'O master, heroic one of steadfast nature,
mount this back of mine and hold your body firm,'
having tied the gem of pure luster to his garment,
he mounted that steed whose speed equaled the king of birds.
Cleaving with its hooves the scattered clouds here and there,
its body tinted tawny by the brightness of lightning-flashes,
leaping into the sky, dark-blue as the waters of a calm ocean,
that horse-king descended upon <s>Vārāṇasī</s>.

children.text: taṃ ca svabhavanasamīpe 'vatārya valāhakaḥ punar badaradvīpam eva pratyāyayau | bodhisattvo 'pi ca praviśya pramuditamanobhiḥ praṇayibhiḥ suhṛdbandhubhiḥ pratyudgataḥ svabhavanam anyasminn ahani bahir niṣkramya taṃ cintāmaṇiṃ dhvajāgram āropyedam uvāca |
children.translated_text: And having set him down near his own dwelling, <s>Valāhaka</s> returned again to <s>Badaradvīpa</s>. And the Bodhisattva, entering the city, was welcomed at his own dwelling by his joyful-hearted, loving friends and kinsmen. On another day, going outside and raising that wish-fulfilling gem atop a banner-staff, he said this:
'Whatever thing any person desires
that is hard for humans to obtain here —
this wish-fulfilling gem (<s>Cintāmaṇi</s>)
shall properly bestow it upon him.'

children.text: tadā ca tasmin deśe nirvyāpārakṛṣīvalajanam anudakatayā dhavalajaladaśakalaśabaladikkāntam uparatagokaḍevarāvasthitavāyasagaṇam atyākuladaridravargam aparyāptabhaikṣopahāraṃ mahad durbhikṣam āsīt | tataḥ sa janakāya upetya supriyam uvāca | dhānyam eva tāvad ayaṃ maṇivaraḥ pravarṣatv iti | tathāstv iti coktaṃ bodhisattvena vicintya vilokitaś cāsau mahāmaṇiḥ |
children.translated_text: At that time, there was a great famine in that land: the farming folk were without work; the sky was adorned with white clouds like water-pots marking the horizons but giving no rain; flocks of crows sat upon unmoving cattle and donkeys; the destitute multitudes were in great distress; and the alms-offerings were insufficient. Then he, approaching his father, said to <s>Supriya</s>: 'Let this excellent gem first rain down grain.' 'So be it,' was said, and the Bodhisattva, having meditated and gazed upon that great gem —
sometimes striking upon the leaves of trees,
tumbling as it fell from the sky,
the great shower of grain covered the earth
without interruption.
Then, gems of varied and sparkling radiance,
and ornaments of pure brilliance, again and again,
shaken by the rushing wind,
and fine garments fell from the sky.
Then, adorned with various ornaments, garments, and garlands,
with the sounds of diverse festive musical instruments resounding,
with wonder, the supplicants praised him who had compassion for all people,
honoring him, extolling him thus:
'Ah, how utterly wondrous is this endeavor
of one who has taken birth for the benefit of others!
Ah, with your glories, white as jasmine,
the earth seems to smile, being put to shame!'
'Surely there must exist for such a person
such a wealth of good fortune, one who relies on virtue,
for those like you who act for the world's welfare —
that such is the birth of those whose lives are not in vain.'
'Having banished great suffering,
having bestowed great fruit without toil,
like the ripening of merit,
you are the cause of happiness for the supplicants.'

children.text: tad evam ātmaduḥkham agaṇayitvā jagatsukhavidhāyino mahākāruṇikā na pratijñām avasādayanti mahātmāna iti svasukhanirapekṣeṇa parārthaniṣpādanapaṭunā bodhigāminā bhavitavyam iti ||
children.translated_text: Thus, great-souled ones of great compassion, who create the world's happiness without counting their own suffering, do not let their vow fail. One walking the path to enlightenment (<s>Bodhi</s>) must be skilled in accomplishing others' welfare, without regard for one's own happiness.
|| The <s>Badaradvīpa Jātaka</s>, the second. ||
|| 3. The <s>Dharmakāma Jātaka</s> ||
None other than the Bodhisattva is fit for dispelling the darkness of ignorance;
who else would purchase the gem of a well-spoken truth at the price of his own life?

children.text:
tadyathānuśrūyate
bodhisattvaḥ kila śrutaśīlādiguṇābhilakṣite kṣititalālaṅkārabhūte bhūtānukampini satatapravṛttabrahmaghoṣāgnihotrasamiddarbhakarmānte vinītaśiṣyaparivṛtādhyāpake brāhmaṇakule lokahitāya vyāyacchamāno vaśitvād udapādi | pratidivasam āpūryamāṇakāntiś ca sa mahātmā
children.translated_text: As it is heard in the tradition: The Bodhisattva, it is told, was born intentionally for the benefit of the world, in a brahmin family distinguished by virtues such as learning and moral conduct, serving as an ornament of the earth's surface, compassionate toward all beings, with the chanting of the <s>Veda</s>, the tending of the sacred fire, and the rituals of <s>darbha</s> grass ever active, surrounded by well-trained pupils in its school. Growing in radiance day by day, that great soul —
as that beloved of the world grew,
like the moon dispelling darkness with its rays,
so did that great family
attain great growth, like the water of the ocean.
Only a certain greatly fortunate one
is born, esteemed by the good,
upon whom, like a tree-creeper, the glory of the lineage
depends and flourishes.

children.text: tasya ca mahānubhāvasya kṛtopanayanasaṃskārasya pramādabahule yauvane vartamānasya vinivṛttavyasanadoṣasya parām avekṣya dharmakāmatāṃ dharmakāma ity eva jñātayo 'nurūpaṃ nāma cakruḥ |
children.translated_text: And seeing the supreme love for <s>Dharma</s> of that great-souled one, who had undergone the investiture ceremony, who even in youth — a time full of heedlessness — had turned away from the faults of vices, his kinsmen gave him the fitting name <s>Dharmakāma</s> ('Lover of <s>Dharma</s>').
Generally, for beings in this world,
whether of the virtuous person or of the virtue itself,
even the name, born of merit,
attains loveliness.
When that seeker of well-spoken truths,
that wise one, heard a well-spoken truth from somewhere,
producing extraordinary effects through supreme delight,
it caused horripilation and the flowing of tear-drops.
By the pure, illuminating the world all around,
by the beautiful, darkness-dispelling, of renowned tradition,
by the spotless — like the hare-marked moon —
whose heart is not gladdened by the well-spoken truth of a great person?
He heard a darkness-dispelling verse, he who was a destroyer of darkness,
from whom the well-spoken truth was received, that supreme connoisseur of wise sayings,
whose greatness of intellect was renowned in the assemblies of the great —

children.text: prītaḥ paraṃ śatasahasram adāt sa tasmai
children.translated_text: supremely pleased, he gave a hundred thousand coins to that person.

children.text:
sa ca mahātmā yatra yatra gacchati sma tatra tatra janena pratipūjyate sma | tataḥ kadā cid
anyatamo duṣṭacetās tadapakāracikīrṣayā brāhmaṇas tasya mahātmanas taṃ lābhasatkāraviśeṣam anudivasam abhivardhamānam asahamānaḥ sāmarṣaṃ tvaritapadaṃ tatsakāśam ājagāma |
children.translated_text: And that great-souled one, wherever he went, was honored by the people everywhere. Then, one day, a certain evil-minded <s>brāhmaṇa</s>, unable to endure the special gain and honor of that great-souled one which increased day by day, desiring to harm him, came swiftly with angry steps to his presence.
One who is ignoble, not having obtained honor from elsewhere —
honor that is gained through virtues —
bears envy toward another
who is being honored, a learned one.

children.text: sa ca durātmā rākṣasa iva brāhmaṇarūpadhārītam mahāsattvam upagamyedam abhyadhāt |
children.translated_text: And that wicked one, assuming the form of a <s>brāhmaṇa</s> like a <s>rākṣasa</s> (demon), approaching the great being, said this:
'I have heard that you, sir, are exceedingly fond of wise sayings (<s>subhāṣita</s>),
and that you are indeed a possessor of the wealth of special knowledge;
therefore, disregarding other people, I have come to your presence
bearing an offering of a wise saying.'
'A bee, wandering among fragrant [flowers],
leaving aside the blossoming mango clusters,
approaches an elephant thirsting for rut-fluid —
surely it perceives some superior quality there.'

children.text: atha bodhisattvaḥ subhāṣitopāyanavantaṃ taṃ brāhmaṇam ālokya praharṣaprodbhidyamānapulakaśobhaḥ samutthāya svāgataṃ subhāṣitamahāratnavaṇije brāhmaṇāya | vayaṃ subhāṣitamaṇīnāṃ kretāra ity uktvā taṃ dvijātim ātmīye mahaty āsane samupaveśya svayamavanau niṣasāda | tato dharmakāmaṃ suhṛdas savismayam evam ūcuḥ |
children.translated_text: Then the <s>Bodhisattva</s>, seeing that <s>brāhmaṇa</s> bearing the gift of a wise saying, his beauty enhanced by the horripilation that burst forth from joy, rose up and said: 'Welcome to the <s>brāhmaṇa</s>, the great merchant of the precious jewel of wise sayings! We are purchasers of the gems of wise sayings,' and having seated that twice-born one upon his own great seat, he himself sat upon the ground. Then the friends of <s>Dharmakāma</s> spoke thus with wonder:

children.text: śroṣyāmīti subhāṣitāni bhavato jātaṃ mukhaṃ sasmitaṃ
children.translated_text: 'Your face has become smiling, [thinking] "I shall hear wise sayings from you!"'

children.text: śrutvā yāsyati sāśru locanayugaṃ prītyā śriyaṃ kām api
children.translated_text: 'Having heard them, your pair of eyes will attain, with tears, some beauty born of delight.'

children.text: ahnaś chedavaśāt sugandhi kumudaṃ mandaṃ samunmīlati
children.translated_text: 'A sweet night-lotus slowly opens when the day ends;'

children.text: prāpyendoḥ kiraṇān apāstatamasaḥ śobhāṃ parāṃ puṣyati
children.translated_text: 'having received the moonbeams, free from darkness, it assumes supreme beauty.'

children.text: atha dharmakāmaḥ sabahumānam ālokayaṃs taṃ brāhmaṇam avocat | abhidhātum arhaty ācāryaḥ śuśrūṣamāṇāya śiṣyāyeti | atha sa pāpīyān enam uvāca | yadi bhavān mahati khāte nirdhūmajvalanaparipūrite subhāṣitaratnalobhād ātmānaṃ muñcet tato 'ham idaṃ subhāṣitam aśrutapūrvam atimanoharam abhidadhyām iti | atha bodhisattvaḥ sattvaparibṛṃhitamatir idam abhyadhāt | mahābrāhmaṇa | nedaṃ duṣkaram ātmaduḥkhānapekṣiṇām mādṛśānām | kiṃ tu |
children.translated_text: Then <s>Dharmakāma</s>, gazing at that <s>brāhmaṇa</s> with great esteem, said: 'The master should speak to the disciple who wishes to listen.' Then that sinful one said to him: 'If you, sir, out of greed for the jewel of a wise saying, would release yourself into a great pit filled with smokeless fire, then I would utter this wise saying — unprecedented and supremely delightful.' Then the <s>Bodhisattva</s>, his mind fortified by courage, said this: 'O great <s>brāhmaṇa</s>, this is not difficult for those like me who disregard their own suffering. However —'
'I gather wise sayings for the welfare of the world from good people,
as one gathers fruit from a tree;
once I have gone into the flaming great pit,

children.text: ayaṃ janaḥ katham iva tad grahīṣyati
children.translated_text: how will these people receive it?'

children.text: brāhmaṇa uvāca || śrāvayitvedam subhāṣitam akhilasya janakāyasya tato 'gnikhadāyām ātmānaṃ mokṣyasi | bodhisattva uvāca | yathā ācya rocate tathāstu |
children.translated_text: The <s>brāhmaṇa</s> said: 'Having made this wise saying heard by the entire assembly, then you will cast yourself into the fire-pit.' The <s>Bodhisattva</s> said: 'Let it be as pleases the master.'
'Without descending for a long time into the vast,
difficult-to-cross ocean of great resolution,
with the great darkness of delusion dispelled —
how would the jewel of <s>bodhi</s> (enlightenment) be easily obtained in the world?'
'Therefore I, eager for wise sayings,
enter the fire as if it were water;
the fire will not cause pain
to me whose mind is captivated by the discourse of <s>Dharma</s>.'

children.text: iti nigadya sukhātam akhānayaddahanavac ca nṛbhis tad akārayat /
children.translated_text: Having said this, he had a deep [pit] dug, and like fire had the people fill it with [burning coals];

children.text: niragamac ca bahirbhavanāntarāt sapadi tena saha dvijarakṣasā //
children.translated_text: and he emerged from within the house at once, together with that demon in <s>brāhmaṇa</s>'s guise.
When the fire blazed, the great-minded one,
his mind resolved to leap in,
was restrained by his friends with tear-filled eyes,
who embraced him with the affection of companions.

children.text:
atha dharmakāmaṃ suhṛdo jñātayaś ca viṣādāśrupūrṇanayanāḥ sagadgadam evam ūcuḥ |
kim idam iti subhāṣitarasenānapekṣitakkāryo duṣprāpam idam amalakulotpannam uḍupatikiraṇaviśuddhayaśo'dhiṣṭhānaṃ mānuṣyam avamanya jñātijanaṃ cātyantaduḥkhabhāginaṃ kṛtvātmānaṃ parityaktum icchasi | nanu vinivartyatām iyamamārgayāyinī buddhiḥ | paśyatu bhavān |
children.translated_text:
Then the friends and kinsmen of <s>Dharmakāma</s>, their eyes filled with tears of despair, spoke falteringly thus:
'What is this? Intoxicated by the flavor of wise sayings, disregarding your duties — do you wish to despise and abandon this human birth, which is difficult to obtain, born in a pure lineage, the abode of fame pure as moonbeams, and to make your kinsmen share in the utmost suffering? Surely, let this wayward resolve be turned back! Look, sir —'
'Those life-breaths that are dearer to people always
than a son who yields desired fruits, and than a beloved wife —
with those very life-breaths, disregarding your own happiness,
why do you, O supremely wise one, purchase a wise saying?'

children.text: atha bodhisattvastasya janakāyasya subhāṣitaguṇāviṣkaraṇena dharmadeśanām iti cakāra |
children.translated_text: Then the <s>Bodhisattva</s> preached the <s>Dharma</s> to that assembly of people by revealing the virtues of wise sayings:
'A wise saying (<s>subhāṣita</s>), when cultivated, illuminates knowledge, extends insight,
reveals the truth, and cuts off the wrong path;
ah! what benefit does it not confer —

children.text: kalyāṇamitram iva kiṃ na hitaṃ karoti
children.translated_text: like a virtuous friend (<s>kalyāṇa-mitra</s>)?'
'Where, as when the sun of pure radiance rises,
the understanding of people blossoms like a lotus —
that well-spoken word, which is utterly free from darkness,
[coming] from a superior, wise person — how should it not be received with all one's being?'
'Therefore I, not considering the burning of the fire,
wishing to follow the path of the <s>Tathāgata</s>,
joyfully worship wisdom — the weightiest guru — for the sake of a profound wise saying,
with the offering of my body as the weighty fee.'
'Humanhood or divinity —
these are attained through the support of merit;
but only rarely do people obtain
the elixir of wise sayings.'

children.text: tan na me kuśalapakṣāvalambino bhavanto vighnam utpādayitum arhantīti tān suhṛdo bāndhavāṃś ca sānunayaṃ vinivārya jvalanasātkartum ātmānaṃ taruskandham āruhya taṃ brāhmaṇam uvāca | ācārya procyatām adhunā tat subhāṣitam iti | brāhmaṇa uvāca |
children.translated_text: Then, saying 'You who lean on the side of virtue should not create an obstacle for me,' and gently restraining those friends and relatives, he, in order to offer himself to the fire, climbed a tree-trunk and said to that <s>brāhmaṇa</s>: 'Master, let that wise saying now be uttered.' The <s>brāhmaṇa</s> said:
'By those who are always generous in giving,
who are established in stainless moral conduct,
and who are equipped with the armor of utmost heroic energy —
the imperishable state is attained.'

children.text: atha bodhisattvaḥ pramuditamanās tāṃ gāthām udgṛhya tasmai janasamūhāya śrāvayām āsa | tatas te suhṛdas tam enam artham ūcuḥ |
children.translated_text: Then the <s>Bodhisattva</s>, his mind delighted, having committed that verse to memory, recited it for that assembly of people. Then those friends spoke to him thus:
'Your own wise saying would produce supreme delight, again and again,
O you who lean on virtue;
since it has become a cause of sorrow,
is not this [saying] an ill-spoken one (<s>duruktam</s>) for us?'

children.text: atha tatra prakṛtikaruṇārdrāśayo mātṛgrāmastasya sādhor asaṃbandho'pi śokavaśād evaṃ paridevanaparo babhūva |
children.translated_text: Then, in that place, the womenfolk, whose hearts were naturally moist with compassion, though unrelated to that good man, overcome by grief, began to lament thus:
'This glorious lotus-face, perfumed with the fragrant honey of speech,
with radiating tooth-ray filaments —
how will this merciless fire
burn it?'
'This body of his, golden-bright like pure gold,
being engulfed by fire, with eyes contracted —
alas, it will become
like a burnt log, black and soiled!'
'This body, within the fire,
making a hissing, crackling sound —
as it darkens,
who today will be able to behold it?'
'The sound of bamboos cracking
as they are split in two —
how will his kinsmen
bear to hear the sound of his bones bursting?'
'These trees, with leaf-hands waving
from contact with the wind,
seem to be warding off the fire, saying
"Do not burn him!"'
'It tears apart our minds —
the eyes of his kinsmen, dim with tears,
and the single syllable "Hā!"
uttered by those wretched ones.'
'Here he held gatherings,
here he gave wealth to suppliants —'
'thus will the friends of this good man
point out [the places], with tears flowing.'
'The grief of losing our kinsman
burns our minds without him;
how will his friends and kinsmen
sustain their life-breaths?'

children.text: tan nedam atikaruṇaṃ raudraṃ karmāsya duṣkarakāriṇaḥ śakyate draṣṭum ity abhidhāya sa strījano gṛhābhimukhaḥ pratasthe | tato bodhisattvaḥ praṇidhim evam āviścakāra |
children.translated_text: Saying 'This overly pitiful and terrible deed of this performer of difficult feats cannot be watched,' that group of women turned toward home. Then the <s>Bodhisattva</s> made this aspiration (<s>praṇidhi</s>):

children.text: na prārthaye padam ahaṃ śubhalabhyam aindraṃ
children.translated_text: 'I do not pray for the station of <s>Indra</s>, obtainable through merit,
nor for lordship over the <s>Vidyādharas</s>, nor for kingship;
may I, having attained the state of a <s>Sugata</s> (Buddha), become
a means for the destruction of suffering for this world, through this arising of merit!'

children.text: ity uktvā tena mahātmanā muktaś cātmā | sadya eva ca so 'gnir upaśāntajvālākalāpadhūmasaṃghātaḥ surabhikamalodbhedagandhādhivāsitadigantarālaṃ kamalinīpalāśasthitavimalasalilalavaṃ sphaṭikakaṇākīrṇamarakataśilānurūpam alikulacakravākamithunahaṃsakādambopaśobhitaṃ padmākaratvam agamat |
children.translated_text: Having said this, that great soul released himself [into the fire]. And immediately that fire, its mass of flames, sparks, and smoke subsided, its surroundings in all directions perfumed with the scent of bursting fresh lotuses, with drops of pure water resting on lotus petals, resembling an emerald stone strewn with crystal fragments, adorned by swarms of bees, pairs of <s>cakravāka</s> birds, and <s>haṃsa</s> (swans) — it became a lotus pond.
While the lotus, believing
it had fulfilled its purpose by becoming a lotus [pond],
he too, the best of the wise,
saw himself standing [upon it].
Intoxicated bees wandering near his feet,
serene, <s>Dharmakāma</s> spoke the <s>Dharma</s>,
and with his lotus-petal-long eyes, seated on a lotus,
he bore the beauty of the lotus-born one [<s>Brahmā</s>].

children.text: eṣa svapnaḥ syād iyaṃ kiṃ nu māyā
children.translated_text: 'Is this a dream? Is this some illusion?
Where is the fire? And what is this becoming a lotus?' —
thus, with minds struck by astonishment and wonder,

children.text: taṃ paśyantas te janā vācam ūcuḥ
children.translated_text: the people, gazing at him, spoke these words.
For those people beholding him
standing in the midst of lotuses, with noble desire,
in a moment, tears of joy — arising impossibly [fast] —
expelled, as if with anger, the tears of grief.
Then from the sky fell a flower-shower, fragrant with pollen,
accompanied by rows of bees;

children.text: abhavad api ca māraḥ pauṣpam ādhāyapārśve
children.translated_text: and <s>Māra</s> (the tempter), placing his flowery bow at his side,
stricken with grief, placed his hand upon his face.

children.text: atha sa brāhmaṇo jvalitāṅgāramadhyagatam ivātmānam ṣṇaniśvāsābhitaptamukhāntarālaḥ katham api dhārayann idam avocat |
children.translated_text: Then that <s>brāhmaṇa</s>, feeling as though he himself were in the midst of blazing coals, the interior of his mouth scorched by hot sighs, barely sustaining himself, spoke thus:
'In a deep chasm of the earth, blazing,
I see before me a great fire;
and this body of mine, tormented and afflicted
by fever, seems to sink into the earth.'
'O <s>Dharmakāma</s>, as I am about to fall into this hell of intense fire,
may you be my refuge here today;
those of lofty aspiration, great ones who are architects of others' welfare,
such as yourself, are equal in their attitude toward friend and foe.'
Then the <s>Bodhisattva</s>, out of compassion for him, made a truth-declaration (<s>satyādhiṣṭhāna</s>):
'By the truth by which, for the welfare of beings,
I practice the conduct of awakening (<s>bodhicaryā</s>) —
by that truth, may this <s>brāhmaṇa</s> not go
to the blazing hell-fire!'

children.text: iti bodhisattvenābhihitaḥsa brāhmaṇaḥ sadya eva haricandanānuliptam ivātmānaṃ pramumude |
children.translated_text: Having been thus addressed by the <s>Bodhisattva</s>, that <s>brāhmaṇa</s> immediately felt as if his body were anointed with <s>haricandana</s> (yellow sandalwood), and he rejoiced.
'Having encountered a virtuous friend (<s>kalyāṇa-mitra</s>),
skilled in the welfare of the world,
the sin of even sinners
instantly dissolves.'

children.text: atha bodhisattvaḥ pramuditamanobhiḥ suhṛdbandhupraṇayibhir ālokyamāno dānaśīlādisamuttejanāya dharmyāṃ kathāṃ cakāra |
children.translated_text: Then the <s>Bodhisattva</s>, being gazed upon by friends, kinsmen, and dear ones with delighted hearts, gave a discourse on <s>Dharma</s> to encourage generosity, moral conduct, and the like:
'From scripture (<s>āgama</s>) and from inference (<s>anumāna</s>),
which are the two causes of ascertainment —
since special certainty arises [from direct experience],
direct perception (<s>pratyakṣa</s>) is the more powerful.'
'Having beheld this great sacrifice with wonder
for a long time, this fire with flickering crest —'
'following each living being, this [fire]'
'has attained the state of a pond full of blooming lotuses!'
'Therefore, having observed this great and wonderful
potency of this vast action,
and having reflected that good and evil yield pleasant and unpleasant fruits —
may one abandon the wrong path!'
'For beings whose eyes are closed by the sleep of heedlessness,
awakening through skillful means is [appropriate];
but for the wise, whose eyes of clear understanding are open,
when already awakened, what more is to be taught?'
'Good people, with righteous speech,
greatly awaken even those who are already inclined toward good;
the speed of horses already galloping
increases with the urging of the goad.'
'The household life, which is maintained through many pretexts,
is not to be trusted even in the slightest by the wise;
it is not fit to sleep for one who has mounted
a fierce, intoxicated elephant without securing the goad.'
'The prattling of children, a prosperous home,
women adorned with grace, charm, and beauty —
all this, for the attached who lack wisdom,
is an obstruction to the path leading to tranquility.'

children.text: kathaṃ cid aṣṭābhir apoḍham akṣaṇair avāpya mānuṣyam idaṃ sudurlabham /
children.translated_text: Having somehow obtained, by the eight favorable conditions, this human birth so difficult to attain,

children.text: śamāya yo na tvarate pramādabhāg niyojanīyo 'naḍuhām asau dhuri //
children.translated_text: he who does not hasten toward tranquility, being heedless — he should be yoked to the pole of oxen!
'This has been obtained; that is to be obtained;
this has been done; that is to be done by men' —
thus, through the painting of the mind's house,
the brush-stroke of desires never reaches
its end.
Embracing the enjoyment of sense-objects, terrible in its conclusion,
like sandal-paste entwined by a serpent,
following the imagination of what is unreal, calling it 'happiness,'
people lie upon a great web of suffering.
Shame! Alas, the world is humiliated by ignorance,
entirely stained by the impurities born of desire!
For, having arrived within the range of the enemy called death,
it remains as if in the sleep of an elephant [oblivious to danger].
Robbed of the good path by the wicked enemies that are the hindrances,
without considering constantly the fear of impermanence,
casting aside the raft of Buddhist teaching,
the world sinks in the ocean of calamity.
Life, at every moment, approaches its end,
like the body of a dying fire fading away.
Therefore, at all times, turn this mind away from sense-objects,
and make it swift toward what is beneficial!
If this speech of mine, spoken with reasoned argument, is unfitting,
then experience as you please the attachment to sensual pleasures!

children.text: atha tu guṇavad etat sādhavaḥ cintayitvā
children.translated_text: But if, O virtuous ones, having reflected, you find this worthy,
then embrace the supreme peace that restrains the thirst for sense-objects!

children.text: iti dharmadeśanāṃ kṛtvā bodhisattvaḥsasuhṛjjano gṛhaṃ praviveśa |
children.translated_text: Having given this teaching of the <s>Dharma</s>, the <s>Bodhisattva</s>, together with his friends, entered his house.

children.text: tad evaṃ subhāṣitaratnaparīkṣāpaṭunā tena bhagavatā prāṇair api subhāṣitāni krītānīti vicintya satatam eva duḥkhocchedam icchatā prājñena dharmakathāśravaṇe mahān ādaraḥ karaṇīyaḥ | kalyāṇamitrasevā cābhilaṣitaphalaniṣpādinī bhavatīti tadanuvartinā bhavitavyam iti ||
children.translated_text: Thus, reflecting that by that Blessed One — who was expert in examining the jewels of well-spoken words — well-spoken teachings were purchased even at the cost of his life, one who constantly desires the cessation of suffering, being wise, should cultivate great reverence for hearing the discourses on <s>Dharma</s>. And the service of a spiritual friend (<s>kalyāṇa-mitra</s>) is productive of desired fruits — therefore one should follow such a one.
|| Thus ends the third [birth-story], named the <s>Dharmakāma Jātaka</s> (The One Who Desired the Dharma). ||
4. <s>Śaśa</s> (The Hare)

children.text: tiryagyonigatair api sadbhiḥ prāṇāḥ parārtham utsṛṣṭāḥ /
children.translated_text: Even by virtuous ones born in animal form, their lives have been sacrificed for the sake of others;

children.text: ko nāma puruṣabhūtaḥ saktiṃ dhanamātrake kuryāt //
children.translated_text: what person of [human] nature, then, would feel attached to mere wealth?

children.text:
tadyathānuśrūyate
stimitanilīnaśukasaṃghātaharitaśādvalopagūḍhabhūbhāge vividhaśikharitarucchāyopaviṣṭaromanthāyamānahariṇagaṇe bhramadalikulopagīyamānakusumitalatāsaṃparkasurabhipavanākampyamānanirjharavāridhautaśilātalaparyante munijanamano'nukūle kūlaviṭapilatākisalayāskhalitasarittaraṅgāhatakumudadhavalaphenaśekharālaṃkṛtasalile salilacaravihaṅgonnāditapadminīvane kvacid acalavanāntare bodhisattvaḥ śaśo bhavati sma | tasya ca tatra sahavāsaguṇād abhivṛddhasauhṛdaḥ praśamopacayaśāntendriyagrāmo grāmyopabhogaparāṅmukhamanāś cīrājināṣāḍhakamaṇḍalumātraparigrahaḥ kaṣṭatapās tāpasaḥ sahāyo babhūva |
children.translated_text: As it is traditionally heard: In a region whose ground was covered with green meadows concealing flocks of still, hidden parrots; where herds of deer sat chewing their cud in the shade of trees on various mountain peaks; at the edge of rocks washed by the waters of waterfalls, swayed by breezes fragrant from their contact with flowering creepers sung to by swarms of wandering bees; in a place agreeable to the minds of sages; where the water was adorned with crests of white foam from lotuses struck by river-waves stumbling against the leaf-shoots and creeper-sprouts of the bank-side trees; where lotus-groves were resounding with aquatic birds — in a certain mountain-forest, the <s>Bodhisattva</s> was [born as] a hare. And there, through the virtue of living together, a certain ascetic became his companion — one whose affection had grown, whose senses were calmed by the increase of tranquility, whose mind was turned away from worldly enjoyments, whose possessions consisted only of bark-garments, deer-hide, grass-mats, and a water-vessel, and who practiced severe austerities.
Equal in the <s>dharma</s> of tranquility,
equal in the arising of sorrow and joy —
those two best of friends, when not seeing each other,
took no delight.

children.text: bālye śaśena rahitaḥ kaṃcit kālaṃ bhavaty anuṣṇāṃśuḥ /
children.translated_text: At times, the moon may be without the hare for some time;

children.text: na tu tena śaśākṛtinā kadācid api sa vratī suhṛdā //
children.translated_text: but that one devoted to vows was never without that friend in the form of a hare.
For the pure-hearted virtuous, friendship forms after just seven steps;
how much more so for those whose affection is bound by the mutual narration of each other's virtues!

children.text: bhavati śamābhiratānāṃ puṃsāṃ dharmāya pāṭavaṃ buddheḥ /
children.translated_text: For men who delight in tranquility, keenness of intellect serves the <s>Dharma</s>;
but for animals, whose minds are feeble — whence arises the very notion of undertaking <s>Dharma</s>?

children.text: śaśajātir aho kveyaṃ kvedaṃ vāksauṣṭhavaṃ kva ca śamo 'yam /
children.translated_text: 'How can this hare-nature exist alongside this eloquence and this tranquility?' —

children.text: abhavad iti devatānāṃ śaśa eva savismayaṃ cetaḥ //
children.translated_text: thus, the hare himself was the object of wonder in the minds of the gods.

children.text: atha kadācid asalilatayā paripāṇḍuṣu sāsūyakṛṣīvalajanāvalokyamāneṣu viśrāntavidyullatāvilāseṣu pavanabalavicchinnasaṃghāteṣu jaladeṣu dinakarakiraṇāpītasāvaśeṣasalileṣu parimlānagarbhalaghuśālicchanneṣu kedāreṣu sakṛtpūravicchedapratanujalavimuktavipulatarapulinataṭāvasthitasphuṭitottānaśuktipuṭāsv saritsv āgharmaklamavinibaddhaśvāsapracalatkaṇṭheṣu madakāle 'pi vinivṛttanṛttavyāpāreṣu nīlakaṇṭheṣu nimnapravirūḍhaśuṣkaśaṣpāṅkurāyāṃ vasumatyām alabdhatṛṇāhāratayā parikṣāmakukṣiṣu mandagamanacalitaśithilasāsnāsu kṣīrakṣayalaghūdhnīṣu paridurbalavatsāsu vatsatarīṣu śākaprāyakadannābhyavahārakṛśaparuṣāṅgeṣu daridrajaneṣu durbhikṣadoṣaparāṅmukhīkṛtātithijanasatkāreṣu grāmeṣu kvacit kvacic chrūyamāṇamanthānaśabdeṣu gokuleṣu sa tāpasas taṃ śaśam avocat | aho kṛtopakāram api vipatsu nānuvartante prakṛtilaghavaḥ prāṇinaḥ | paśyatu bhavān ayaṃ hi |
children.translated_text: Now, once, when the clouds, their lightning-creeper-play exhausted, were scattered in fragments by the force of the wind, their water drunk up by the sun's rays with some remainder; when the fields were covered with rice whose ripening grains were withered and light; when the rivers, their single flooding broken, stood with broad, thinned sandbars with open upturned oyster shells; when the peacocks, panting with gasps of breath bound by the heat's exhaustion, had ceased their dance-activity even in the mating season; when on the earth, where only dry grass-shoots grew in the low places, the cows — unable to find grass for food — had emaciated bellies, walked slowly with their dewlaps swaying loosely, had udders light from the depletion of milk, and their calves were exceedingly weak; when the poor people had bodies thin and rough from eating wretched food consisting mostly of greens; when in the villages hospitality to guests had been abandoned due to the fault of famine; when in the cow-settlements the sound of churning was heard only occasionally — that ascetic said to the hare: 'Alas, beings who are frivolous by nature do not continue to support even one who has done them favors, when misfortune comes! Look, my lord —'
'The peacock, who formerly with delight spread his tail adorned with shattered moon-gem spots in the rainfall,

children.text: lāsyaṃ lāsakavat purā viracayan stautīva yaṃ kekayā
children.translated_text: performing a dance like a dancer, praising [the cloud] with his cries —

children.text: tasminn eva śikhī nirambhasi ghane cakṣuḥpradānālasaḥ
children.translated_text: that very peacock now, when the cloud is waterless, is too lazy even to open his eyes.
Generally, people serve only the prosperous one!'

children.text: nistoyā viralībhavanti jaladā vicchinnam aindraṃ dhanuḥ
children.translated_text: 'The clouds become waterless, grow sparse; the rainbow is broken;
no longer are heard the voices of the peacocks, long-drawn-out from their association with mountain caves.',

children.text: sarvaṃ vastu nisargabhaṅguram iti dhyātveva śokāc ciraṃ
children.translated_text: 'Meditating on the thought that all things are by nature fragile,
the lightning-dancer abandons her dance, sweet with playfulness, as if from sorrow.'

children.text: jātaṃ kṣīṇaphalaṃ phaladrumavanaṃ śoṣaṃ gatā vīrudhaḥ
children.translated_text: 'The fruit-tree grove has been born but its fruit is exhausted; the herbs have dried up;

children.text: pramlānāni śanair bisāni bisinīpaṅke kharatvaṃ gate
children.translated_text: the lotus-stems have slowly withered, the lotus-pond mud having become hard.',
'Even the small heap of <s>badara</s> and <s>iṅgudī</s> fruits in my hut

children.text: kṣīṇaḥ so 'pi suduṣkarāya tapase yātrāṃ kariṣye katham
children.translated_text: is depleted — how shall I sustain my journey of severe austerity?'

children.text: āhāreṇa vinā pratikṣaṇam ayaṃ dehaḥ klamaṃ gacchati
children.translated_text: 'Without food, this body at every moment falls into exhaustion;

children.text: klāntyā cetasi yoginaḥ pratihate sthairyaṃ samādheḥ kutaḥ
children.translated_text: when the mind of the yogin is obstructed by fatigue, whence comes the steadiness of meditation?'
'Even for a wise one whose mind lacks meditation, whence comes direct orientation toward truth?
Then, [his] darkness of delusion bound to non-seeing of truth, he labors in vain!'
'Therefore, abandoning the deer-hide, water-vessel, and bark-garments,
I shall dwell among my kinsmen in my own home.',
'Having driven away the fault of famine, again at the forest's end
I shall dwell with you here for a long time, O affectionate one!'

children.text: atha bodhisattvaś cirasaṃvāsābhivardhitapremārdrahṛdayas tam ṛṣim uvāca |
children.translated_text: Then the <s>Bodhisattva</s>, his heart tender with love that had grown through long companionship, said to that sage:
'An elephant who, desiring comfort, has uprooted his tethering-post
and somehow gone to the forest's end —
forgetting again the pain of the goad's blow,
the fool wishes only to go to the habitation of men!'
'By tranquility, by intelligence, by the merits of austerity,
and by learning that follows the path of what is to be known —
you surpass other sages,
as the sun surpasses lamps, far, with its rays!'
'Thus you, who have ascertained the conclusions of the scriptures,
with the eye of discrimination, free from darkness —
how is it that you are seen, as if deluded,
wishing to enter the domain of the enemy, the sense-objects?'
'One who is dull does not appreciate the well-spoken words of the wise —
which pierce the darkness, illuminate the paths,
and generate serenity of mind in embodied beings —
like one blind from birth [does not appreciate] the disc of the moon.'
'Not to mention that, without the lamp of one's own understanding,
one cannot abandon the dark attachment to pleasure!',
