'That those of pure <s>sattva</s> should delight their minds
in the householder's state — that is a great impropriety!'
'Adorned with hermitages sheltering within them <s>badara</s> and <s>iṅgudī</s> fruits,
fragrant with the scent of ghee-oblations at both twilights,
embraced by trees, with <s>sārasa</s> cranes, enemies of reeds,
nestled in the ponds —'
'With young saplings growing, watered
by water from pots drawn by the daughters of ascetics;',
'with rivers restrained by the shade of bank-side trees;
with breezes fragrant with the perfume of burgeoning flowers —'
'With shoots of <s>vīraṇa</s> grass nibbled by deer
that follow the roaming sons of ascetics;',
'with wealthy ascetics, their necks held still by beards trembling from chanting,
dwelling in mountain caves —'
'Alas, do not even these foothill-regions of the earth
create longing in the hearts of the passionate ones —',
'those whose minds are bound by firm attachment,
clinging to a morsel of the taste of unreal pleasures, devoid of wisdom?'
'Arriving, through delusion, at the wrong path frequented by the wicked,
the ignorant one, without releasing the bonds of attachment, inevitably stumbles.',
'That even one who knows the dustless path followed by the virtuous',

children.text: yad arajasi na tiṣṭhaty etad aprāptam atra
children.translated_text: 'does not remain on it — that is unprecedented here!'

children.text: bahuvyasanadoṣam api nāma gārhasthyam avetya katham imāṃ śamānukūlāṃ vimuktimārgaprakāśinīṃ pravrajyām apāsya sukhalavahetor mahat pratibhayaṃ duḥkhapātālaṃ praveṣṭum icchasi | yac ca bhavatābhidhīyate punar ahaṃ tapovanam āgamiṣyāmīti nedaṃ śraddhīyate | kutaḥ | pracuravighno hi gṛhavāsaḥ |
children.translated_text: 'Understanding that the householder's life, though possessing the fault of many calamities, and knowing this mendicant life (<s>pravrajyā</s>) — which is conducive to tranquility and illuminates the path to liberation — how can you wish to enter, for the sake of a morsel of pleasure, the great abyss of suffering that is fraught with danger? And as for what you say — "I shall come again to the ascetic forest" — this is not to be believed! Why? Because household life is full of obstacles!'
'For one who is subject to the sense-objects, beholding women
adorned with smiling graces —',
'even if in an ascetic forest yielding unbroken fruit,
will the heart of a passionate one remain [there]?'

children.text: api ca maharṣe viṣayānuvartino hi prāṇino mahānti vyasanāny anubhavanti | paśya |
children.translated_text: 'Moreover, O great sage, beings who follow the sense-objects experience great calamities. Behold!'
'The deer, by the song of [another] deer,
is led into the range of arrows.',
'For those greedy for the taste of sense-objects,
calamities inevitably arise.'
'The moth, falling into the fire,
attains death after experiencing the terrible suffering of being burned.',
'How then will calamity not befall again
those embodied beings whose minds are captivated by beautiful forms?'
'If the fish did not take the bait upon the hook,
who would lift him from the water?',
'A person greedy for pleasure, of foolish mind,
does not see the danger attached to what lies before him.'
'The bee, remaining in the lotus when it closes,
meets with distress, excessively greedy for fragrance.',
'The elephant, following the she-elephant decoy from the forest,
endures the pain of the sharpened goad and prod.'
'The abode of calamities, the delusion of the weak-minded,
avoided by the great-souled ones of firm intellect —',
'if you have a desire for eternal happiness,
then abandon the domain of the sense-serpents as you would poison!'

children.text:
ṛṣir uvāca | satyam anekeṣāṃ paribhavādīnāṃ
doṣaśarāṇāṃ śaravyabhūto gṛhavāsaḥ sukhalavāsvādamohitātmabhir na śakyate parityaktum | kiṃ tu |
children.translated_text: The sage said: 'It is true — the householder's life is the target for the arrows of many faults such as humiliation and the rest; it cannot be abandoned by those whose selves are deluded by the taste of morsels of pleasure. However —'
'O hare, best of friends, ocean of virtue and fame!
Your qualities are indeed of such a kind',
'that, my mind captivated by them, I, desiring tranquility,
shall return here again.'

children.text: bodhisattva uvāca | yady avaśyam eva gantum abhilaṣitaṃ tathāpy ekam imaṃ divasam ihoṣitvā śvaḥ svam abhiprāyam anuṣṭhātāsi | tataḥ sa munir evaṃ cintayāmāsa | niyatam ayaṃ māṃ nimantrayitukāmaḥ |
children.translated_text: The <s>Bodhisattva</s> said: 'If you are absolutely determined to go, then at least stay here for this one day and tomorrow carry out your intention.' Then that sage thought to himself: 'Surely he wishes to invite me [for a meal].'
'Perhaps a <s>jambū</s>-fruit forest, charming with its fruits, has been seen by him somewhere;

children.text: dṛṣṭaṃ bhavet kim athavā phalito 'tra cūtaḥ
children.translated_text: or perhaps a mango tree here has borne fruit;',
'or perhaps, in the interior of the mountain, a cluster of figs,
ripening, tender and softly reddening, has made its abode;
or perhaps an <s>udumbara</s> tree?'

children.text: atha śaśas tāṃ rajanīm ativāhya prabhātasamaye kṛtsnaṃ tad vanaṃ paribhramyālabdhamūlaphalaś cintayāmāsa |
children.translated_text: Then the hare, having passed that night, at dawn, after roaming the entire forest and finding no roots or fruits, reflected:
'While this sage, my good companion, devoted to equal tranquil happiness,
remains unfed, hungry, with weakened body —',

children.text: bhokṣye tṛṇaṃ katham ahaṃ haritaṃ vanānte
children.translated_text: 'how shall I eat green grass in the forest's edge?
How shall I drink the cool, clear water?'

children.text: athavā saty asminn arthijanasādhanakṣame śarīre kim aham aśakta iva viṣaṇṇamanās tiṣṭhāmi | tatas tam ṛṣim upagamyovāca | maharṣe pratipālyatāṃ tāvan muhūrtaṃ yāvad aham āhārajātaṃ kiṃcid upaharāmi | tataḥ sa munir acintayat | parikṣīṇakandamūlaphale 'smin vane kīdṛśī punar āhāropaharaṇaśaktir asya syāt | atha sa mahātmā jvalitāṅgārarāśim avalokya praṇidhim evam abhivardhayāmāsa |
children.translated_text: Or rather, while this body of mine is intact and capable of serving the supplicant-folk, why do I stand despondent like one powerless? Then, approaching that sage, he said: 'Great sage, wait just a moment while I bring some kind of food.' Then that sage thought: 'In this forest where roots, tubers, and fruits are exhausted, what capacity could he have to bring food?' Then that great-souled one, beholding the heap of blazing embers, strengthened his vow thus:
'As I fearlessly give up my life-breaths in the fire of flickering flames
for the appeasement of a supplicant's hunger,
so may I attain the supremely hard-to-reach
state of the Ten-Powered One [<s>Buddha</s>], which removes the afflictions of the world!'

children.text: muktaḥ svātmā parārthe pramuditamanasā cintayitveti tena
children.translated_text: 'My self is released for the sake of others!' — having thought thus with a delighted mind,

children.text: kleśacchedāya śāntaṃ padam abhilaṣatā prāṇināṃ bāndhavena
children.translated_text: by that kinsman of beings who desired the peaceful state for the cutting off of afflictions,

children.text: śāntajvālākalāpaḥ sa ca vanadahanas tasya puṇyānubhāvāt
children.translated_text: that forest-fire, its mass of flames quelled by his merit's power,
attained the state of a lotus-pond, with trembling water-wave lines and stirring bee-swarms.

children.text: atha sa muniḥ kaṣṭam ity uktvā dahananirvāpaṇāya gṛhītasalilakamaṇḍalus tvaritam upagamya taṃ mahātmānaṃ vikasitapuṇḍarīkamadhye 'vatiṣṭhamānaṃ dharmaṃ deśayantam apaśyat |
children.translated_text: Then that sage, saying 'How terrible!', taking a water-pot filled with water to extinguish the fire, hastened there and beheld the great-souled one standing amidst blooming white lotuses, teaching the <s>Dharma</s>.
That lotus in the water, greatly adorned
by that hare, shone
like the resplendent moon-disc
in the clear autumn sky, [a sign of] manifest glory.

children.text: tataḥ sa munis taṃ śaśaṃ puṇḍarīkāvasthitam ālokya vismitamanāḥ stutim imāṃ pravyājahāra |
children.translated_text: Then that sage, beholding the hare seated upon the lotus, his mind amazed, uttered this praise:
'Oh, this deed of yours, O treasure of fame,
skilled in accomplishing the welfare of others, is wondrous!
Resorting to the special greatness of the inconceivable,
you, O some great intellect, dwell in the form of a hare!'
'Where was this blazing fire propelled by the wind-charioteer,
and where is such a state of lotus-lake here?
When sustained by the power of merit of great souls,
even a poison-tree would attain the state of a healing-tree!'

children.text: tataḥ sa mahātmā tasmāt puṇḍarīkād avatīrya praviṣṭaś ca tena saha muninā parṇaśālām | viditabodhisattvavṛttāntena ca vismitamanasā maghavatā samantād añjanācalanīlajaladharapaṭalapihitadinakaram aciraprabhāprakāśaparipiñjaradigantaram ambaratalam akāri |
children.translated_text: Then that great-souled one descended from that lotus and entered the leaf-hut together with that sage. And <s>Maghavat</s> [<s>Indra</s>], his mind astonished upon learning the story of the <s>Bodhisattva</s>, made the vault of the sky [appear as follows]: the sun concealed by a canopy of clouds dark as the collyrium-mountain, the horizon-intervals reddish-yellow with the light of recently appeared radiance.
Then breezes blew from all directions, scattering water-spray,
splitting the <s>kuṭaja</s> blossoms.
The mountain mango-trees, sheltering parrots,
shone with rows of ripe fruits.
As the sound of bees arose like a flute,
and the waterfall resounded like a drum,
the peacock, seeing the fresh clouds, danced
standing upon the mountain-top, that dancer of dancers.
Having strung the enchanting bow of <s>Vajrin</s> [<s>Indra</s>],
the clouds released showers of many glistening droplets,
and spread [their glory], flashing with lightning-splendor,
as destroyers of the heat of summer.
Angered by the striking of wandering bees,
sheltering among the freshly blossoming <s>ketaka</s> plants,
hissing, with a body resembling an iron ring,
the serpent spread its hood again and again.
By travelers sheltering under trees on mountain paths,
eager and restless with longing for their beloved's absence,
the voices of the <s>cātaka</s> birds were heard,
moving among the streams of rainfall.
The women of the travelers beheld, with trembling eyes,
the lightning flashing in the rain-cloud,
[looking] like a saffron-dyed banner
tied to [the top of] an elephant, blown by the wind.
Mixed with peacock-feather and <s>kāśa</s> grass,
with <s>śilīndhra</s> mushrooms whirling in eddies here and there,
the water of the rivers became turbid,
its foam broken by the falling of <s>jambū</s> fruits from the banks.
Seeing the riverbanks variegated with <s>jambū</s> fruits,
and the lovely beauty of the earth's soft green turf,
the sage, standing in the leaf-hut resounding with the patter of rain-drops,

children.text: tiṣṭhan saha pramumude sa muniḥ śaśena
children.translated_text: together with the hare, rejoiced.
He then asked him [the hare]:
'With this supreme resolve of yours,
do you, desiring celestial happiness,
aspire to conquer the station of <s>Indra</s>?'
The hare, steadfast in mind, told
that ascetic:
'I desire Buddhahood
for the pacification of the suffering of beings.'
The sage then said to him:
'When you become a <s>Buddha</s>,
may I be your disciple!'
And he [the hare] assented.

children.text: tad evaṃ tiryaggato 'py asau bhagavān bodhisattvacaryāṃ caran prāṇair api paropakāraṃ kṛtavān iti buddhe bhagavati prasādaparāyaṇair bhavitavyam iti |
children.translated_text: Thus, even though born in an animal existence, the Blessed One, practicing the <s>Bodhisattva</s>-conduct, rendered service to others even at the cost of his own life — therefore one should be devoted to faith in the Blessed <s>Buddha</s>.
|| The <s>Śaśa Jātaka</s> (Hare Birth-Story), the fourth. ||
5. <s>Candraprabha</s> (Moon-Light)

children.text: ko vismayaṃ na nītaḥ śirasas tyāgena bodhisattvasya /
children.translated_text: Who is not led to wonder by the <s>Bodhisattva</s>'s gift of his own head?
Or rather, the undertakings of the great are generally proportionate to [their] fruit.

children.text:
tadyathānuśrūyate
hutavahasakhabalasamudīritamahātaraṅgasya kṣīrodajaladher anukāriṇā himagirihāreṇābhyalaṃkṛtāyāḥ kauberyā digvadhvāḥ pramanasā pattralekheva viśvakarmaṇā likhitā vividhajanasaṃbādhā pavanavidhūyamānopavanakusumagandhādhivāsitadigantarālā sadā subhikṣatvāt paripūrṇakoṣakoṣṭhāgārā śrīr iva nagararūpeṇāvasthitā bhadraśilā nāma rājadhānī yeyam adhunā takṣaśileti khyātim āgatā | tasyāṃ ca nītibhujabalaparājitānyarājasāmantaḥ samudra iva saritāṃ sarvasaṃpadām āśrayaḥ sarvavidyānāṃ pātrabhūto bhūtānukampī vimalavadanenduśobhāhrepitacandraprabhaś candraprabho nāma rājā babhūva |
children.translated_text:
Thus it is heard:
There was a royal capital called <s>Bhadraśilā</s> — now known as <s>Takṣaśilā</s> — drawn by <s>Viśvakarman</s> like a delighted sketch-painting for the joyful bride of the Northern Quarter [ruled by <s>Kubera</s>], adorned with the necklace of the Snow Mountain resembling the great waves of the Milk Ocean stirred by the ally of Fire [the wind], thronged with diverse peoples, its horizon-spaces perfumed by the fragrance of flowers from groves shaken by the wind, its treasuries and granaries always full due to perpetual abundance, standing as <s>Śrī</s> (Fortune) herself in the form of a city. And in it there was a king named <s>Candraprabha</s> — who had defeated all neighboring kings by the arm-strength of statecraft, who was the receptacle of all forms of learning, like an ocean is the receptacle of all rivers' waters, who was compassionate toward all beings, and whose radiant moon-like face put the moon's own light to shame.
Stealing the glory from the lotus-beds of enemy cities' women,
producing delight for the night-lotuses of friendly people,
at night, the bodily radiance of that king among men
dispelled the web of darkness and served as a lamp.

children.text: tasya ca rājño lokottareyam akhilajanavismayakāriṇī pratijñābhūt |
children.translated_text: And this king had a superhuman vow that caused wonder in all people:
'If any supplicant should seek from me
my eyes, the anchors of life, or my head,
[since I am] one who aspires to the state that breaks the cycle of existence —
I would not sever the bond of affection to that person.'

children.text: bodhisattvasya ca daśaśatavasor ivāruṇaḥ satatapuraḥsaro 'mātyagaṇapradhāno mahāprajño mahācandro nāmāmātyo babhūva |
children.translated_text: And the <s>Bodhisattva</s> had a chief minister named <s>Mahācandra</s> (Great Moon) — the foremost of the assembly of ministers, of great wisdom, like <s>Aruṇa</s> (the Dawn) who always precedes [the Sun] for ten hundred years.
Always speaking of each other's virtues,
always intent on each other's welfare,
those two were never
separated from each other.

children.text: atha kadācin mahācandro rātrau nidrāvaśam upagato dagdhapalāśarāśinīlaparuṣacchavibhir analajvālākalāpakapilakeśaśmaśrubhiḥ kesarinakharakuṭilatīkṣṇakararuhaiḥ salilādhmātagurujaladharabṛhatkukṣibhir ayaḥstambhapīvaratatabhujorubhiḥ śaśikalākuṭiladaṃṣṭrāvibhaktasṛkkāntaiḥ sphuradaciraprabhāvijihmabhrūbhaṅgaiḥ sarudhirapuruṣacarmāvacchāditakaupīnair yātudhānaiḥ svapne tasya nṛpater apahriyamāṇaṃ vigalitacūḍāmaṇiṃ maulim apaśyat | prativibudhya ca vimanaska evam acintayat | aho kaṭuvipāko 'yaṃ mayā svapno dṛṣṭaḥ | svāminaś ca naḥ pratijñā śarīram api yācitenārthine mayā dātavyam iti | tad yāvat tasya nṛpater na kaścic chiro mṛgayate tāvad anekāni ratnamayāni śirāṃsi śilpibhiḥ kārayāmīti | tair eva kaṃcic chiroyācakaṃ bahir eva pratipūjya visarjayiṣyāmīti |
children.translated_text: Then once, <s>Mahācandra</s>, having fallen under the power of sleep at night, saw in a dream the king's crown — its crest-jewel fallen — being carried off by <s>rākṣasas</s> (demons) with complexions dark and rough like heaps of burnt <s>palāśa</s> leaves, with hair and beards tawny like clusters of fire-flames, with nails curved, sharp, and fierce like a lion's claws, with bellies huge like great clouds swollen with water, with arms and thighs massive like iron pillars, with mouths split by fangs curved like digits of the moon, with brow-furrows crooked like flashing lightning, and with loincloths covered in bloody human skin. Upon awakening, he thought with a troubled mind: 'Alas, I have seen this dream of bitter consequence! And our master's vow is that I must give even my body to a supplicant who asks. Therefore, before anyone seeks the king's head, let me have artisans make many gem-studded [replica] heads. With those, I shall honor some head-seeker outside and dismiss him.'
'May the king, protecting this earth,
with his senses controlled,
self-realized, living long,
keep all people alive!'

children.text: atha mahācandro 'mātyamukhyaḥ śirāṃsi ratnamayāni kārayitvā bahir eva yācanakajanaṃ vicārayāmāsa kenārtha iti | tato gandhamādanaparvate vānarānūkamukhaḥ pariṇatanālikelavalkalaparuṣaviralakeśaśmaśrur akṛtabhrūkuṭir api kṛtabhrūkuṭir iva dagdhasthūṇāsitakarkaśacchaviḥ prasthitajalaukaḥkuṭilasthūlasirājālaviṣamajaṅghorubhujo bhujaga iva prakṛtiraudro raudrākṣo nāma brāhmaṇaḥ prativasati sma | tasya cintā samabhavat | candraprabhaḥ kila rājā sarvaṃdadas tad gacchāmi tāvat taṃ rājānaṃ śiroyācanena vyarthapratijñaṃ kariṣyāmīti | kasya nāmāsti śiraḥpradāne śaktir iti vicintya krameṇa bhadraśilām āyayau |
children.translated_text: Then <s>Mahācandra</s>, the chief minister, having had gem-studded heads made, inquired among the supplicant-folk outside: 'What do you seek?' Now, on Mount <s>Gandhamādana</s>, there dwelt a <s>brāhmaṇa</s> named <s>Raudrākṣa</s> (Terrible-eyed) — like a monkey-faced creature, with hair and beard coarse and sparse like the bark of a mature coconut, with brows naturally furrowed as if in a scowl, with skin black and rough like a charred pillar, with arms and thighs uneven with thick, twisted, worm-like veins like crawling leeches, fierce by nature like a serpent. He had thought: 'King <s>Candraprabha</s> is said to give everything; so I shall go and render his vow futile by asking for his head! For who has the power to give away his head?' Thinking thus, he gradually came to <s>Bhadraśilā</s>.
Then the earth with its mountains trembled;
the ocean was momentarily churned;
the rivers' waters rose, turbid,
with fish trembling and agitated within.
The moon and sun did not shine,
their appearance like dusty mirrors;
the quarters in every direction became
soiled, like women whose husbands had departed.
Even out of season, the trees bore
flowers with pale petals and saffron stamens;
winds blew, stirring up masses of dust,
as if followed by trails of fire.
The earth with its moving and stationary beings
became defiled, emaciated, with its people anxious and agitated;
the night with its smoke-dimmed stars [appeared]
like the moonlit night when [the moon] approaches setting.
Even the milk of cows eating tender grass in the forest
instantly went to exhaustion;
even when fanned by a chowrie, the sacrificial fire with its established embers
would not blaze for the sacrificers at their rites.

children.text: atha vividhāny ajanyāni vilokya bhadraśilānivāsī janaḥ kim idam iti samāśaṅkamānaḥ paryākulatām ājagāma | ye tu tatra nipuṇatarās te rājño vināśam āsannam utprekṣamāṇās tumulamanaso bhūtvā parasparam evam ūcuḥ |
children.translated_text: Then the people dwelling in <s>Bhadraśilā</s>, seeing various ill omens and wondering 'What is this?', became agitated. And those among them who were most discerning, surmising that the king's destruction was near, became tumultuous in mind and said to one another:
'May no calamity born of these portents
befall this sovereign,
in the shade of whose arms
embodied beings sleep in comfort!'

children.text: atha sāśrulocanā nagaradevatā mahācandrāyāmātyāya nivedayāmāsa | raudrākṣo nāmāyaṃ brāhmaṇo 'sya rājñaḥ śiro yācitum āgatas tan nivāryatāṃ kenacid upāyeneti | athāmātyas tāni ratnamayāni śirāṃsy ānīya raudrākṣam uvāca | mahābrāhmaṇa yenārthas tad aham eva te pratipādayāmi | kiṃ bhavato rājñā dṛṣṭena prayojanam iti ||
children.translated_text: Then the city-goddess, with tear-filled eyes, informed <s>Mahācandra</s> the minister: 'This <s>brāhmaṇa</s> named <s>Raudrākṣa</s> has come to beg for this king's head. Let him be deterred by some stratagem!' Then the minister, bringing those gem-studded heads, said to <s>Raudrākṣa</s>: 'O great <s>brāhmaṇa</s>, whatever you need, I myself shall provide it. What purpose do you have in seeing the king?'
'If the desired object can be obtained even from a person of small wealth,
what need is there of one of great wealth?
If water dug in the area of an elephant's footprint
removes thirst, tell me — what use is the ocean?'
The <s>brāhmaṇa</s> said:

children.text: na sthūlakṣīradhārāḥ sitajaladarucaḥ prārthaye gāḥ savatsāḥ
children.translated_text: 'I do not seek cows with calves, pouring thick streams of milk, with the radiance of white clouds;
nor lordly elephants in rut, whose ears flick away swarms of confused bees;
nor ornaments of clear, sparkling gem-rays, nor special garments —

children.text: yāce mūrdhānam asmād aham avanibhujaḥ sarvado 'yaṃ kileti
children.translated_text: I demand the head of this king! He is said to give everything.'
The minister said:
'O virtuous one, these gem-studded heads —
I give them to you with devoted affection.',

children.text: na ced amībhis tava kṛtyam asti
children.translated_text: 'If you have no use for these,
then take my own head this very day!'
'A servant of steadfast mind, who bears his life-breaths
for the sake of his master —
if those [life-breaths] become a means for that [master's] purpose,
is that not indeed the fulfillment [of the servant's life]?'

children.text: brāhmaṇa uvāca | kim anena punaruktena | abhicāruke karmaṇi pṛthivīpatiśirasā mama prayojanam | atha candraprabho divyena cakṣuṣā taṃ śiroyācanakaṃ bahir avasthitam ālokya priyasuhṛdam iva pratyudgamya tam amātyamukhyam abhihitavān | alam alam arthinaḥ praṇayam upahatya | saṃsārasāgarottaraṇāya setubhūtāḥ khalu bodhisattvānām arthinaḥ |
children.translated_text: The <s>brāhmaṇa</s> said: 'Enough of this repetition! For a sorcerous rite I need the head of the king himself.' Then <s>Candraprabha</s>, seeing with divine vision the head-seeker standing outside, went out to receive him like a dear friend and addressed the chief minister: 'Enough, enough! Do not repulse the supplicant's affection! For the supplicants are indeed a bridge for <s>Bodhisattvas</s> to cross the ocean of <s>saṃsāra</s>!'
'For one who wishes to cross the ocean [of existence],
whose far shore is distant and supremely difficult to cross —'
He who breaks the raft that has been bound —
how can he be called a friend?
Therefore, by a man who is an ally of <s>dharma</s>,
who follows the path of <s>dharma</s>,
effort alone should be made;
an obstacle to <s>dharma</s> is not fitting.
If there were no such supplicant,
who would be the cause of liberation —
how would the <s>Bodhisattva</s>'s
<s>dānapāramitā</s> (perfection of generosity) be fulfilled?
Having spoken thus, drawing out his sword
and presenting it to the brāhmaṇa, the king
said, unperturbed: 'Cut off my head,
O brāhmaṇa!'
How [to reconcile] a brāhmaṇa with a heart acquainted with compassion —
'I consider myself as if fallen into the company of an outcaste by this [deed]!'
Pondering thus for a long time, the sacred thread of that brāhmaṇa
rested upon his chest as if ashamed.

children.text:
atha sa brāhmaṇa uvāca |
nāham amātyasuhṛdbandhujanaparivṛtasya bhavataḥ śaknomi śiraś chettum | ekākī bhavān bhavitum arhatīti | tataḥ sa rājā saśapathaṃ vinivartya taṃ bāṣpasalilapariplutākṣaṃ janasamūhaṃ tena nistriṃśapāṇinā brāhmaṇenānugamyamāno ratnagarbhaṃ nāmodyānam agamat | atha mahācandro 'mātya iti paridevanāparidīnākṣaram uvāca |
children.translated_text: Then that brāhmaṇa said: 'I cannot cut off the head of your majesty who is surrounded by ministers, friends, and kinsmen. Your majesty should be alone.' Thereupon the king, dismissing with oaths that crowd of people whose eyes were flooded with tears, followed by that sword-bearing brāhmaṇa, went to the garden called <s>Ratnagarbha</s> (Jewel-womb). Then the minister <s>Mahācandra</s>, with words faltering from grief and lamentation, spoke:
'To behold the lord of men
with his head removed — alas, who today will be able?
Like a sacrifice whose patron's proper rites have been ruined,
overwhelmed by evil spirits!'
'Now without the lord of the earth,
this city, its people most wretched, will not shine —'
'like a lotus-pool from which the full-blown lotuses have been plucked
by elephants, [yet still] swarming with buzzing bees.'

children.text: tad yāvad asya nṛpater na śṛṇomi mṛtyuṃ
children.translated_text: 'Before I hear of this king's death,

children.text: prāṇān ahaṃ prathamam eva jahāmi tāvat
children.translated_text: I shall first abandon my own life-breaths!'
Having resolved thus, that wise one, by the power of meditation,
attained the self-born state [of <s>Brahmā</s>], abandoning his own body.

children.text: dhanyaḥ sa eva puruṣaḥ samavāpya saukhyaṃ
children.translated_text: Blessed indeed is that man who, having attained happiness,
whose conduct shines bright as the moon's rays upon the world,
seeing the great calamity that has befallen his friends,
first of all attains the dissolution of his own body.

children.text: atha ratnagarbham ākrīḍaṃ praviṣṭe rājani mahān ākrandaśabdo 'ntaḥpure samabhūt | praviśya ca tad udyānaṃ sa brāhmaṇas taṃ rājānam avocat | evam avasthitasya svastharūpasya bhavato nāham asiṃ kaṇṭhe pātayituṃ śaknomi | rājovāca | brāhmaṇa tato mām atra sadāpuṣpe campakatarau badhāna | sa ca tathā brāhmaṇaḥ kṛtavān | athodyānadevatās taṃ raudrakarmāṇam evam ūcuḥ |
children.translated_text: When the king had entered the pleasure-garden <s>Ratnagarbha</s>, a great cry of wailing arose in the inner palace. And entering that garden, the brāhmaṇa said to the king: 'I cannot bring the sword down upon the neck of your majesty who stands thus, composed in form.' The king said: 'Brāhmaṇa, then bind me here to this <s>campaka</s> tree that is ever in bloom.' And the brāhmaṇa did so. Then the garden-deities addressed that cruel-acting one thus:
'The sharp sword — upon the neck
of this guiltless lord of the earth,
who is a friend of the entire world —
will you really bring it down?'
'If you, with a mind made harsh by causeless cruelty,
will cut off the head of the lord of the earth —'
'by a thunderbolt blazing with sparks,
we shall shatter this head of yours!'

children.text: atha sa rājā tāḥ pramadavanadevatāḥ sānunayam iti vārayāmāsa | na khalu mama bhavatībhir anuttarāṃ saṃyaksaṃbodhiṃ jigamiṣor mahān antarāyaḥ karaṇīyaḥ | anumodanayā hi puṇyāptir bhavaty ato 'nyathā kuśalapakṣahānir eva |
children.translated_text: Then the king pacified those garden-deities with conciliation: 'Surely, your ladyships should not create a great obstacle for me who desires to attain the supreme, perfect enlightenment (<s>anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhi</s>). For through rejoicing [in merit], the acquisition of merit comes about; otherwise, there is only loss of the side of virtue.'
'Of the heads given by me
to supplicants who asked —'
'with this head today,
the thousandth is being completed!'

children.text: iti bodhisattvavacanam ākarṇya tā devatās tataḥ sthānāt pratijagmuḥ | atha sa rājā praṇidhim evam akarot |
children.translated_text: Hearing the words of the <s>Bodhisattva</s>, those deities withdrew from that place. Then the king made this aspiration (<s>praṇidhi</s>):
'From the merit arising from this gift of [my] head,
which has long astonished the entire world —'
'having attained enlightenment (<s>bodhi</s>), may my bones in [the state of] peace
become [as tiny as] sesame seeds!'
'In this city called <s>Bhadraśilā</s>,
at the place where my heads have been given —'
'may there be, in that delightful spot,
a great <s>stūpa</s> for the welfare of living beings!'
When the lord of the earth had made his aspiration,
that merciless one, [striking] the one of compassion-tender heart,
with the sword flashing like a serpent,
cut the lotus of his face like a lotus.
When the head of the king was severed in an instant,
the young maiden-creepers, wind-shaken,
trailing tear-drops of shed blossoms in full bloom,
struck themselves with their sprout-hands as if in anguish.
Wind-tossed, with foam-circles broken, with faces of lotuses
trembling from the arms of rolling waves,
in that garden the assembly of lotus-pond brides
appeared as if in grief, with the humming of bees.
When the king had met his fated end, the royal capital,
crowded with many people bereft of glory, did not shine —
like a lotus-pool whose <s>cakravāka</s> birds and <s>śārārikā</s> cranes are silent and still,
when the sun has set.
When that lord of the earth had gone to the state of <s>Brahman</s>,
as if the earth, with its wailing and lamenting ocean-tide,

children.text: ruditam iva pṛthivyā dūram utkṣipya tuṅgau
children.translated_text: were weeping, the tawny-white-gleaming
arms of <s>Meru</s> and <s>Kailāsa</s> were flung far upward.

children.text: sa ca brāhmaṇas tatkeśeṣu śiraḥ samavalambya tasmād upavanān nirgantum ārebhe | tato bhadraśilānivāsī janaḥ śokavaśād evam uvāca |
children.translated_text: And that brāhmaṇa, grasping the head by its hair, began to depart from that garden. Then the people dwelling in <s>Bhadraśilā</s>, overcome by grief, spoke thus:
'That which was seen by his servants with upturned faces
and overflowing joy when the king was seated on the throne —'
'that [head], like a wilted lotus, is now being carried away,
grasped by the hair by the brāhmaṇa.'
And furthermore:

children.text: yaḥ pūrvācalasaṃsthitasya śaśinaḥ śobhāṃ vahan bhūyasīṃ
children.translated_text: 'He who, bearing the surpassing beauty of the moon risen on the eastern mountain,
was reverently gazed upon by kings with upturned faces as he sat upon the back of a lordly elephant —'
'that very lord of the earth, his chest smeared with dense blood streaming from the neck-wound,

children.text: śyenaiḥ so 'yam adhomukhaiḥ kṣitipatir bhrāmyadbhir ālokyate
children.translated_text: is now beheld by circling hawks with downcast faces.'
The grieving ministers, weeping, having prepared a great funeral pyre
containing camphor, sandalwood, and <s>turuṣka</s> (frankincense),
placing the king upon it, with the wind from fans
and with mantras, they kindled the sacrificial fire.

children.text: atha tāṃ jvalantīṃ citām ālokya paridevamānaḥ sa janakāya evam avocat| aho bhagavaty anityatā nāma nirviśeṣā |
children.translated_text: Then, beholding that blazing pyre, lamenting, [a certain person] spoke thus to the common people: 'Alas, the blessed impermanence (<s>anityatā</s>) is indeed universal!'

children.text: mandaṃ dattavilepanā śaśabhṛtaḥ kāntiṃ harantī purā
children.translated_text: 'That body which formerly, softly anointed with cosmetics, stole the beauty of the moon,
which was touched by the tender bud-like fingers of women bearing saffron-paste —'
'that same body of the king, resembling the fallen banner of <s>Indra</s>'s wife, now resting in peace,
is caressed by the restless fingers of the fire's flames.'

children.text: tad evaṃ svaśiraḥparityāgo 'py askhalitamanasā bodhisattvabhūtena bhagavatā kṛta iti vicintya bodhim icchatānyenāpi tyāgaparāyaṇena sādhunā bhavitavyam iti |
children.translated_text: Thus, reflecting that the gift of one's own head was made with unwavering mind by the Blessed One who was a <s>Bodhisattva</s>, one who desires enlightenment should likewise be devoted to renunciation.
The Blessed One, best among the worthy ones,
related this
<s>jātaka</s>, he who has conquered <s>saṃsāra</s>,
the great succession of sufferings.
'At that time, I was the king
named <s>Candraprabha</s>;'
'<s>Śāriputra</s> was the minister,
and <s>Devadatta</s> was that brāhmaṇa.'
|| The <s>Candrprabhajātaka</s>, the Fifth ||
6. <s>Rūpyāvatī</s>

children.text: strītve 'pi bodhisattvaś chittvā māṃsaṃ dadau nijād dehāt /
children.translated_text: Even in womanhood, the <s>Bodhisattva</s> cut and gave flesh from her own body;
how much more so in manhood, when the power of being is greater and skill in others' welfare [is more]!

children.text:
tadyathānuśrūyate
vividhopavanaśyāmaparyantā dhanadāyamānavaṇigjanaparipūrṇavipaṇimārgā gāndhāraviṣayatilakabhūtā vibhūṣaṇam iva kṣiter utpalāvatī nāma rājadhānī yeyaṃ puṣkalāvatīty adhunā khyātā | tasyāṃ ca bodhisattvaḥ prathamayauvanopacīyamānakāntilāvaṇyaśobhā devateva svabhavanasya rūpyāvatī nāma strī babhūva |
children.translated_text: Thus it is heard in tradition: There was a royal capital named <s>Utpalāvatī</s>, adorned by borders of various dark groves, whose market-streets were filled with merchant-folk prosperous as <s>Dhanada</s> (Kubera), the forehead-ornament of the <s>Gāndhāra</s> region, like an ornament of the earth — which is now known as <s>Puṣkalāvatī</s>. In that city, the <s>Bodhisattva</s> became a woman named <s>Rūpyāvatī</s>, like a deity of her own dwelling, whose beauty, charm, and splendor were growing with the bloom of early youth.
Through her tranquility, her dedication to helping others,
and the sharpness of her mind,
arousing extreme wonder in people —
she appeared as if compassion itself embodied.

children.text: atha kadācit tatra deśe kuśalamūlakṣayāt parikṣīṇakośakoṣṭhāgārāvalokanaparidīnajanam aruṇasārathikiraṇasaṃtāpavilīnasāvaśeṣahimagirituhinam atuhinatayā pariśuṣyatsaritsalilam asalilatayā ca parimlānakedāraṃ tadavalokanaviṣaṇṇakṛṣīvalajanam aparipūrṇātithimanoratham atidurbalagopālānugamyamānaparetāvaśeṣaviralagogaṇam āhāraparāyaṇadaridrajanam asajjanasaṃgatam iva pīḍākaram atimahad durbhikṣam abhavat |
children.translated_text: Then once in that region, from the exhaustion of the roots of merit, there arose a very great famine — tormenting, like bad company — where the people were wretched from seeing the treasury and granaries depleted, where the remaining snow on the Himalaya was melting from the scorching rays of the sun, where the rivers were drying from the heat, where the paddy-fields wilted from lack of water, where the farmers were despondent from seeing that [state of affairs], where the wishes of guests remained unfulfilled, where the extremely weakened herdsmen followed the remaining sparse cattle-herds with some already dead, and where the impoverished people were devoted solely to [finding] food.
The heavy breasts of women,
with sunken beautiful nipples, resembling pure golden pitchers,
lost their firmness,
though [the women's] eyes were not blind [i.e., they could see the suffering].
Upon the arm-creepers of women with dejected eyes,
having lost their cleanliness, displaying increased thinness,
the bracelets
became loose.
The faces of women became
disordered with rough, disheveled hair, ashen as the moon on a broken night,
devoid of the charm of eyebrow-play
and the arising of smiles.
Having plastered the interior of the house with clay,
having given the child stale food,
the housewife did not grieve so much for herself
as she did upon seeing her husband collapsed from hunger.
A cow that had lost its calf, no longer grazing,
its dewlap trembling at the mention of a morsel [of food],
coming home from the forest,
made the housewife's eyes even more tearful.
Of the cows that had gradually become extremely weak,
slow-moving from having no grass to eat,
as their udders further loosened,
the milk diminished to exhaustion.
Biting his lower lip slightly, in extreme weakness,
grasping the base of the tail, in confusion,
a cowherd boy, his bone-joints visible, somehow
lifted up the aged, thin-bodied, noble cow.
With food and drink exhausted, with cattle dead,
with pale bodies wrapped in rags,
the people in that region, attached to [their] dwellings,
were unable to leave their homes.

children.text: atha rūpyāvatī kvacid avacarake prasūtivaśād adhikataraprajvalitakṣudagnisaṃtāpitaśarīrāṃ nimnatarakapolanayanakukṣirandhrām abhivyaktaparśukāpaṅktim atimalinajarjaravasanasaṃvṛtāṅgīm ātmasnehagauravād apetatanayasnehāṃ tad evāpatyaṃ jighāṃsantīṃ kāṃcit sairandhrīm apaśyat | ālokya ca tām uktavatī | bhagini kim idam atinṛśaṃsaṃ karma kartukāmāsīti | sā yoṣid evam acintayat | iyaṃ khalu rūpyāvatī dānaśīlā karuṇāvatī ca | tato yady aham asyāḥ kathayeyam imaṃ vṛttāntaṃ niyatam eṣā mama kṣutpratīkāraṃ kuryād iti vicintyovāca | bhagini bāḍham asmi prasavābhivṛddhena kṣudagninā parigataśarīrā | tad icchāmi putrakam imaṃ bhakṣayitum iti |
children.translated_text: Then <s>Rūpyāvatī</s> somewhere in a back-lane saw a certain serving-woman who, due to childbirth, with her body scorched by the ever-more-blazing fire of hunger, with sunken cheeks, eyes, and hollow belly, with visible rows of ribs, her body covered by an extremely dirty, tattered garment — who, from the weight of self-love with her affection for her child gone, was about to kill that very offspring of hers. And seeing her, [<s>Rūpyāvatī</s>] spoke: 'Sister, what is this extremely cruel deed you wish to do?' That woman thought: 'This <s>Rūpyāvatī</s> is indeed generous and compassionate. If I tell her this account, she will surely provide me a remedy for my hunger.' Having reflected thus, she said: 'Sister, indeed my body is consumed by the fire of hunger intensified by childbirth. Therefore I wish to eat this little son of mine.'
'One's own son, born of one's own body —
when seen as if [he were] an enemy,
self-love of beings indeed
does not see <s>dharma</s> or <s>adharma</s>.'

children.text: atha rūpyāvatī karuṇāpravartitabāṣpāvilalocanotpalā tāṃ striyam iti babhāṣe |
children.translated_text: Then <s>Rūpyāvatī</s>, her lotus-eyes clouded with tears set in motion by compassion, spoke thus to that woman:
'This child, whose suffering is understood only through the sound of pitiful weeping,
with tangled, disordered locks —'
'O merciless one, how will you eat this little one
whose eyes are as enchanting as a fawn's?'
'Even toward another's child, a little one
with swiftly running gait and high bobbing crest-tuft, with eyelashes rough from the dust of the earth —'
'tender-hearted women indeed
feel motherly affection.'
'This face of your son — with lips like sprouts that tremble in laughter,
with the forehead-mark drawn, with elongated eyes —'
'babbling with stumbling, confused speech —
do you not wish to behold it?'
'Performing the play of horse-riding in childish sport,
with the [hair-tuft called] "crow's wing" disheveled and soiled from riding a stick-horse —'
'radiant with rows of tooth-buds gleaming in laughter —

children.text: kā yoṣid icchati vilokayituṃ na putram
children.translated_text: what woman would not wish to see [such] a son?'
'A mother-crow, though herself afflicted by hunger,
tenderly feeds her chick — following [her], with open beak, gazing upward,
craving food, uttering harsh cries —

children.text: kākī kṣudhā parigatāpi satī kim u strī
children.translated_text: with care; how much more so a woman?'

children.text: api ca | kadācid ayaṃ janaḥ śrutvā kopavaśād iyaṃ sā putraghātinīti piśācīm iva bhavatīm asmād deśān nirvāsayet tato viramyatām asmāt sāhasād iti |
children.translated_text: Moreover — 'Someday this public, hearing [of it] in anger, may banish you from this land like a demoness, [saying] "This woman is a child-killer!" Therefore, desist from this recklessness!'
'Having devoured this infant',
'like a tigress [devouring] a deer-fawn,
how will you, O sinful one,
devour the blazing iron balls [in hell]?'

children.text: sā provāca | kiṃ karavāṇi bhagini yan na śaknomi soḍhum enaṃ sarvāṅgīṇaṃ kṣudagnim iti | atha rūpyāvatīttham acintayat | yadi nāmāham enaṃ bālakam ādāya yāsyāmi niyatam eṣā prāṇaviyogam eṣyati | athāsyāḥ kṣutpratīkārārtham annam aticirād āneṣyāmi tata eṣā putrakam imaṃ prāṇair viyojayiṣyati |
children.translated_text: She replied: 'What can I do, sister? I cannot endure this fire of hunger that pervades my entire body!' Then <s>Rūpyāvatī</s> reflected thus: 'If I take this child away, she will certainly die of separation from him. But if I go to bring food for her to remedy her hunger, it will take too long, and she will kill this child.'
'Performing an action after the time has passed, a person achieves nothing,
and merely comes to grief through delusion.',
'One should bear the parasol only so long
as the fierce sun has not set.'

children.text: tad idam atra prāptakālaṃ svamāṃsenaināṃ prīṇayiṣyāmīti ||
children.translated_text: 'Therefore, this is the appropriate thing here — I shall satisfy her with my own flesh!'
'The essential should be extracted from the inessential,
from this body that is bound to fall —',
'like fruit from a tree on the bank
whose roots are loosened by the current-cut [river].'

children.text: tataḥ sā yoṣit punar uvāca | bhagini gamyatāṃ nāhaṃ tava purastād imaṃ bālakaṃ pramāpayituṃ śaknomi | atha rūpyāvatī tām avocat | ānīyatāṃ tāvad yadi te kiṃcid atra śastram asti | sā ca rūpyāvatyāḥ śastram arpayāmāsa |
children.translated_text: Then that woman said again: 'Go, sister! I cannot kill this child before you!' Then <s>Rūpyāvatī</s> said to her: 'Bring me whatever weapon you have here.' And she handed over a weapon to <s>Rūpyāvatī</s>.
Then, with that sharp weapon, cutting off both her breasts,
shaped like golden water-pots, from which blood poured forth,
<s>Rūpyāvatī</s> gave them to that young woman, overwhelmed by hunger,
without any thought of the suffering of her own body.
Those who remove the suffering of beings
without regard for their own suffering —
they are afflicted by the suffering of others,
not by their own suffering.

children.text: tac ca stanayugaṃ tasyai yoṣite pradāya rūpyāvatī svabhavanāntaraṃ praviveśa |
children.translated_text: Having given that pair of breasts to that woman, <s>Rūpyāvatī</s> entered the interior of her own dwelling.
Her necklace, garment, and girdle-string smeared
with the blood flowing from the cutting of both breasts,
the beautiful woman appeared like a golden statue
anointed with red sandalwood.

children.text: atha rūpyāvatīṃ bhartā sasaṃbhramam utthāyāsanāt papraccha |
children.translated_text: Then <s>Rūpyāvatī</s>'s husband, rising in alarm from his seat, questioned her:
'By whom, O beautiful one, has this
inauspicious thing been done
to your auspicious body,
as if by a <s>rākṣasa</s> — cutting off your breasts?'

children.text: sā taṃ vṛttāntaṃ patye nivedya punar uvāca | śīghram āryaputras tasyai prasavābhivardhitakṣudagnaye yoṣite dātum arhaty annapānam iti | sa ca rūpyāvatībhartā vismitamanās tathety abhidhāya |
children.translated_text: She reported the whole matter to her husband and then said: 'Quickly, the noble son should give food and drink to that woman whose hunger-fire has been increased by childbirth!' And <s>Rūpyāvatī</s>'s husband, his mind amazed, assented saying 'so be it' —
and sent well-prepared food, fit for all vessels,
described by her who was herself
a vessel of compassion,
to that destitute woman.
Then that public, beholding
that wondrous [deed] of <s>Rūpyāvatī</s>,
from amazement, repeatedly waved
the sprout-tips of their fingers [in applause].
And the people declared this:
'By this act of yours,
surely even the hearts of the miserly
have been inspired toward generosity!'
'That <s>dāna-pāramitā</s> (perfection of giving)
which is heard of among those who desire enlightenment —',
'you are surely its embodiment,
standing here for the benefit of the world!'

children.text: strītvaṃ kvedaṃ buddhir eṣā kva tīkṣṇā
children.translated_text: 'Where is this womanhood, and where is this keen intellect?
Where is this self-sacrifice, and where is this tenderness?',
'By the generosity of this virtuous woman, which surpasses all giving,
other generous ones have been put to shame!'

children.text: atha rūpyāvatyā bhartā satyādhiṣṭhānam iti cakāra |
children.translated_text: Then <s>Rūpyāvatī</s>'s husband performed an act of truth (<s>satyādhiṣṭhāna</s>):
'Just as no such gift as this
is heard of even from any other man —',
'so, by that truth, may the breasts
of my wife swiftly be restored!'
When this was spoken by that householder
who performed the act of truth,
her chest, heavy-laden with the weight of [restored] breasts,
was reborn again.
Quenching the thirst of the world with the water of giving,
her face-lotus beautiful with the stamen of teeth, garment, and hair —
in that city, the lotus-pool that was <s>Rūpyāvatī</s>,
with the pair of <s>cakravāka</s> birds that were her full breasts, shone forth again.

children.text: atha surapatiḥ kiṃ punar anena sarvalokatyāgātiśāyinā tyāgena rūpyāvatī mām amarapurāt pracyāvya svayam eva devādhipatyaṃ kartukāmā syād iti vicintya sāśaṅkamanās tasyās taṃ bhāvaṃ jijñāsamānaḥ prasāritajaladharapaṭalābhinīlam antarīkṣam avagāhyotpalāvatīṃ rājadhānīm avatīrya mṛṇālasūtradhavalayajñopavītābhyalaṃkṛtavakṣaḥsthalaṃ kaṇṭheguṇīkṛtākṣamālam abalānayanaśabalakṛṣṇājinatiraskṛtaskandhaikadeśaṃ dakṣiṇakaravinyastapallavapuṭakaṃ dvijātirūpam abhinirmāya bhikṣārthī nāma rūpyāvatyā bhavanam āgamat | atha rūpyāvatī vividhaṃ bhakṣyabhojyam ādāya śakrāya dvijātimūrtaye prāyacchat | prastāvapūrvakaṃ caināṃ surapatir uvāca |
children.translated_text: Then <s>Indra</s>, the lord of the gods, thinking 'What if, by this generosity surpassing that of the entire world, <s>Rūpyāvatī</s> intends to dislodge me from the city of the immortals and herself become the lord of the gods?' — thus apprehensive, wishing to test her disposition, he descended through the sky made dark-blue by spread-out cloud-masses, arrived at the royal capital <s>Utpalāvatī</s>, fashioned the form of a twice-born [Brahmin] — his chest adorned with a sacred thread white as lotus-fiber strings, a rosary hung as a garland around his neck, one shoulder partly covered with a black deer-skin dappled like the eyes of young women, a lotus-leaf cup placed in his right hand — and came as a beggar to <s>Rūpyāvatī</s>'s dwelling. Then <s>Rūpyāvatī</s>, taking various foods, offered them to <s>Śakra</s> in his Brahmin form. And the lord of the gods, prefacing with a preamble, said to her:
'By the fame born of your sacrifice of your breasts —
spreading far,
white as a conch-shell's cut surface —
the world has been adorned!'
'Do you wish to conquer
the station of <s>Indra</s> by this austerity?',
'Out of curiosity, O blessed one,
I ask this of you.'
She then spoke rightly to the lord of the gods:
'I desire Buddhahood (<s>jinatva</s>) for the pacification of the three worlds!',
'By this truthful speech of mine, O twice-born, may I immediately
attain manhood in the world, an abode of virtues!'

children.text: ity ukte vacasi jagāma sā naratvaṃ
children.translated_text: When this speech was uttered, she attained the state of a man;
<s>Śakra</s> too returned to his own city, his mind assured.
And the world, learning that this wonder had been accomplished,
became all the more firm in its resolve.
Beholding then the emergence of a beard on that face-moon,
sparse and dark as crushed collyrium —
the pair of breasts, plump as elephant-frontal globes,
immediately vanished on that broad chest, as if from modesty.

children.text: bodhisattvasya ca rūpyāvata iti loke nāma prakhyātim agāt | athotpalāvatyāṃ rājadhānyāṃ kadācid aputro rājā pañcatvam upajagāma | kālagate ca tasmin rājani rāhugṛhītarajanikareva niśīthinī sā purī na rarāja | rājavināśābhivṛddhaśokāś cāmātyāḥ keṣucid ahaḥsv atīteṣu śuddhāntajanam āśvāsya pauravargam evam ūcuḥ | anāyakatvād ayaṃ deśaḥ kadācid arātibhir āgatya niḥsvāpateyaḥ kriyeta | pradīptagṛhanirvāpaṇāya kūpakhananam iva cātītakālam āyāsahetur eva ca naḥ samīhitaṃ syād iti | tad idam atra prāptakālam ayaṃ rūpyāvataḥ kumāraḥ sakalarājalakṣaṇopeta ābhigāmikaguṇasaṃpannaś ca tad imam evādhipatyāyābhiṣekṣyāma iti |
children.translated_text: And the <s>Bodhisattva</s> became known in the world by the name <s>Rūpyāvata</s>. Now, in the royal capital <s>Utpalāvatī</s>, once the king died without an heir. When that king passed away, the city, like a night whose moon is seized by <s>Rāhu</s>, lost its splendor. The ministers, their grief increased by the king's death, after some days had passed, consoled the inner-palace women and addressed the citizenry thus: 'Without a leader, this land may someday be plundered by enemies and stripped of its wealth. And our endeavor, like digging a well to extinguish a house already ablaze, would only be a cause of effort when the time has passed.' 'Therefore, this is the appropriate course — this prince <s>Rūpyāvata</s>, endowed with all the marks of royalty and possessing the qualities of personal charm, let us consecrate him as sovereign.' And so —
With overflowing joy, the citizens performed his consecration —
of him whose mind was intent upon the welfare of others;
and the attendants raised up the mind-delighting white parasol
together with a pair of <s>cāmara</s> whisks.
The citizens made the city equal to the abode of <s>Kubera</s> —
with garlands fastened to shop-arches, delightful with the performances of mountain-dancers,
its streets and roads made fragrant
by the sprinkling of scented water.
The clouds gave rain abundantly at the proper season;

children.text: ītiḥ kadācid api na vyasanaṃ cakāra
children.translated_text: calamity never once wrought havoc;
while that lord of the earth ruled the earth with wise policy,

children.text: śuśrāva duḥkham iti naiva janaḥ kadācit
children.translated_text: the people never once heard the word 'suffering.'
Rice grew abundant in fruit without cultivation;
trees were always full of flowers and abundant fruit.

children.text: tasmin surājani pṛthāv iva pāti rājyam
children.translated_text: While that good king ruled the kingdom, as if <s>Pṛthā</s>'s son [<s>Yudhiṣṭhira</s>] ruled —
the cows of themselves yielded copious streams of milk.
With unbroken generosity fulfilling all wishes,
endowed with the arising of the threefold power, his senses conquered,
his person adorned with the ornaments of various virtues —
the earth was endowed with a king, by that sovereign.
Then that lion among kings, ascending the gem-beautiful
lion-throne, his lotus-feet saluted by [other] kings,
his face resembling a lotus, devoted to the <s>dharma</s> of discrimination,
taught the <s>Dharma</s> of supreme truth to the people:
'Behold this greatness of the fruit of giving!
For it is [this very giving] that, removing my womanhood,
has produced this manhood, lovely with sovereignty over the world —
the famous threefold fruit of a [good] birth!'
'From the tree of giving, this is but a blossom that has been produced;
the vast fruit will come hereafter, in the next life.',
'Considering this, on this earth rich with suppliants,
store up treasuries of all kinds of giving, stainless in conduct!'
'If the grounds that are the fields of suppliants
were not irrigated with the water of virtues —',
'where would the giver, desiring the fruit of giving,
plant the seed of generosity?'
'Those [suppliants] who surpass even kinsmen,
bestowing fame and merit —',
'what wise person would frighten them
with the serpent of a frown?'

children.text: ekaḥ prāha giraṃ muhuḥ stutimatīm ekas tu rūkṣākṣarām
children.translated_text: 'One speaks words of praise repeatedly; another, harsh syllables;

children.text: ekaḥ sādaram īkṣate dhanamadāt sāvajñam evāparaḥ
children.translated_text: one looks with respect; another, from intoxication with wealth, with disdain.',

children.text: ekaḥ sādhu dadāti puṇyayaśasī vastv ekam evāparo
children.translated_text: 'One gives well, [gaining] merit and fame; another, the very same thing —',

children.text: dūraṃ māṃ prati yācitā vijayate dātāram ebhir guṇaiḥ
children.translated_text: 'to the one petitioned by me, the giver surpasses [the non-giver] by far through these qualities!'
'If the directions are to be made fragrant with garlands of virtue-flowers,

children.text: punar bhoktuṃ hṛdyaṃ phalam atanu vāñchāsti yadi vā
children.translated_text: or if there is a desire to enjoy again sweet, abundant fruit —',
'then let wealth-trees be planted daily in the soil of those dear to the heart,
[trees] that rise up with the shade of great fame!'
Then, having entered the world for sixty years,
constantly creating happiness for the virtuous and for suppliants,
having illuminated the directions with fame white as the water-lily,
that king of great power passed on to another birth.

children.text: tad evaṃ strītve 'pi tena bhagavatā svamāṃsāni dattāni ko nāma manuṣyabhūto bāhye vastuny apekṣāṃ kuryād iti tyāgijanaprotsāhanāya varṇanīyam iti |
children.translated_text: Thus, even in womanhood, that Blessed One gave his own flesh — what person born as a man, then, would feel attachment to external things? This should be narrated to encourage generous people.
|| Thus ends the sixth [birth-story], the <s>Rūpyāvatī Jātaka</s>. ||
7. <s>Śreṣṭhi Jātaka</s> (The Merchant)

children.text: bahiraṅgam api dravyaṃ kṛcchrād guṇine 'pi dīyate nīcaiḥ /
children.translated_text: Even external wealth, though given with difficulty, is given grudgingly by the lowly even to the virtuous;

children.text: priyam api dehaṃ santas tiryagbhyo pi prayacchanti //
children.translated_text: but the virtuous give even their own dear body to those born as animals.

children.text:
tadyathānuśrūyate
śrūyamāṇamanoharāyāṃ dṛśyamānavismayakarāyām uttarāpathasārabhūtāyāṃ vikasitakamalotpalavanābhyalaṅkṛtopavanāyāṃ pavanavidhūyamānasuragoṣṭhadhvajapatākāyāṃ utpalāvatyāṃ rājadhānyāṃ bodhisattvo 'nyatamad amarapuram iva pārijāta utpadyamānaḥ śreṣṭhikulam aśobhayat |
atha śreṣṭhī pradhānaputrajanmalabdhapramodaḥ pravṛttacitrotsavaviśeṣe vividhātodyadhvaniśravaṇapranṛttamayūrābhyalaṅkṛtājire balisakhamadhuparisravanmadābhirajyamānayuvatikapole maṇitoraṇāvabadhyamānavividhasurabhisraji priyākhyānapratītaparijane svabhavane samanvitasuhṛdbandhuvarge mahad arthibhyo viśrāṇanam adāt |
children.translated_text: As it is traditionally heard: In the royal capital <s>Utpalāvatī</s> — delightful to hear of, wonderful to behold, the essence of the northern road, adorned with parks of blooming lotuses and blue lotuses — where the banners and flags of the divine assembly-halls were being waved by the wind, the <s>Bodhisattva</s> was born, like <s>Pārijāta</s> [the divine tree] produced in the city of the immortals, and he graced a merchant family. Then the merchant, having obtained joy at the birth of his chief son, in his dwelling — where a special festive celebration was underway, where the courtyard was adorned with peacocks dancing at the sound of various musical instruments, where the cheeks of young women were stained with the intoxicating flow of dripping honey from the offerings, where various fragrant garlands were hung from gem-studded arches, where the household was delighted by the auspicious reports — amidst the assembly of friends and relatives, gave a great distribution to suppliants.
By the radiance of the merchant's son — spreading all around
and robbing the beauty of the cold-rayed [moon] —
his own people accordingly
gave him the name <s>Candraprabha</s> ('Moon-radiance').

children.text: taṃ ca pitā bālaśaśinam iva pratidivasam upacīyamānakāntiśobham anyatamasmai śrutaśīlādiguṇaprakāśanāmne śāstrakāvyakalāgrahaṇāya gurave nivedayām āsa |
children.translated_text: And his father entrusted him — like the young moon, growing in beauty-splendor day by day — to a certain teacher whose fame was proclaimed for his qualities of learning, virtue, and the like, for the study of scriptures, poetry, and arts.
He then conquered all his fellow-students
by intelligence and learning,
in no long time —
he whose senses were conquered.
Observing his intellect,
surpassing all other students,
the teacher, full of praise,
was filled with wonder at his questions.
Shattering the mass of darkness,
illuminating the right and wrong paths —
knowledge shone more brightly in him
like moonlight in a bed of water-lilies.
Having seen with divine sight
whatever treasure he found,
the auspicious one gave it away
completely to each suppliant.
Gifts were given by him so abundantly,
fitting to his own being,
that the words 'give [me]'
were no longer heard from suppliants.

children.text:
atha tasya guros tāni pañcamātrāṇi śiṣyaśatāni candraprabham evam ūcuḥ |
aho praṇayinām upari bhavato mahatīm anukampāṃ manyāmahe |
yadi kaś cid arthī bhavantam asūn api mṛgayate niyamena tān tasmin bhavān prayacched iti |
bodhisattva uvāca |
mā maivaṃ yācanaka eva dātāram anukampayā viśinaṣṭi kutaḥ |
children.translated_text:
Then those five hundred disciples of the guru spoke thus to <s>Candraprabha</s>:
'Ah, we consider your great compassion toward those who are dear to you! If some supplicant were to beg you even for your life-breaths, you would certainly give them to that person.'
The <s>Bodhisattva</s> said:
'Not so! It is the supplicant who, through compassion, honors the giver. Why?'
'One who, having made himself a worthy vessel,
desiring the welfare of the giver,
endures the suffering of being asked —
there is no one more compassionate than such a one.'
'Fame in this world and reward in the next —
these two the supplicant bestows;
[the giver] gives only wealth; therefore
the supplicant excels the giver.'
'A supplicant who says "Give!"
is called lowly;
but a giver who says "I have nothing" —
is he not even more lowly?'
'For the giver, the request becomes
a wish-fulfilling creeper, to his utmost benefit;
that [request], praiseworthy when its fruit is revealed —
how can it be [considered] lowly?'
'If there were not these rain-clouds of supplicants,
pouring forth the waters of merit for the world's prosperity everywhere,
the rain-clouds of givers would not come into being,
bearing within them the great pearl-fame of virtues.'

children.text:
tatas te śiṣyāḥ punar api bodhisattvaṃ papracchuḥ |
kathyatāṃ tāvat kim anena mahāpradānaphalena śātakratavīṃ śriyam icchati bhavān uta cakravartitvam iti |
bodhisattva uvāca |
na khalu me prakṛtibhaṅguraṃ padam abhilaṣati buddhiḥ |
paśyantu bhavantaḥ |
children.translated_text:
Then those disciples again asked the <s>Bodhisattva</s>:
'Tell us then — what does one desire as the fruit of this great giving? Does one wish for the glory of <s>Indra</s>'s realm, or universal sovereignty (<s>cakravartitva</s>)?'
The <s>Bodhisattva</s> said:
'Indeed, my mind does not aspire to any station that is by nature perishable. May you observe —'

children.text: yad yad bhavapaṭamadhye rūpaṃ saṃskāraśilpibhiḥ kriyate /
children.translated_text: 'Whatever form is created by the artisans of <s>saṃskāra</s> (conditioned formations) upon the canvas of existence,

children.text: unmārṣṭi tat tad eṣā kruddhevānityatā capalā //
children.translated_text: this fickle impermanence erases it all, as if in anger!'
'Even the summit of existence (<s>bhavāgra</s>),
attained by the virtuous who have turned away from desire and hatred,
is not beyond the reach
of the wicked Death (<s>Kṛtānta</s>).'
'The duration of beings' lifespan, even while being sustained,
diminishes moment by moment,
like a crayon applied to a painting,
[worn down] at every stroke.'
'Prosperity does not shine for long,
having encountered cruel impermanence;
[it is] like the flame of a lamp at a crossroads,
struck by the wind.'
'Some, deluded, look at impermanence with alarm,
as at a lioness;
others, whose minds are cultivated, [look at] that same [impermanence]
fearlessly, as at a she-jackal.'
'Death does not distress the mind
of the wise one who has accumulated merit,
[just as] the sun does not scorch a traveler
who is concealed in the shade of an umbrella.'
'These prosperities of beings, which are ever momentary,
always difficult to approach like angry serpents,
causing the darkness of pride, conceit, and delusion —
are like followers in the science of grammar [ever-changing in form].'
'Having understood this world with all its moving and unmoving beings
as a mass of foam struck by currents of water,
free from the net of pride, conceit, and delusion —
strive at once, O men, for the unborn [state, <s>nirvāṇa</s>]!'

children.text:
tato 'ham atyantam eva lokaduḥkhakṣayāyānuttarāṃ samyaksaṃbodhim icchāmīti |
atha te śiṣyāḥ pramuditamanasaḥ punar evam ūcuḥ |
kiṃ bahunābhihitena |
children.translated_text:
'Therefore I desire the supreme, perfect enlightenment (<s>anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi</s>) for the absolute destruction of worldly suffering.'
Then those disciples, with delighted minds, spoke again thus:
'What need for many words?'
'Bearing between your brows the moon of the <s>ūrṇā</s> (hair-tuft), blazing with rays,
spreading a circle of light that has conquered all darkness,

children.text: utpaśyāmas tava guṇamahat saugataṃ bhāvi rūpaṃ
children.translated_text: we foresee your future form as a <s>Sugata</s> (Buddha), great in virtues,
with the radiance of cut gold, illuminating the path of liberation for embodied beings!'

children.text:
sarvathā vayam api prāptasaṃbodhes tava śiṣyā bhavema iti |
bodhisatva uvāca ||
children.translated_text:
'In every way, may we also become disciples of you who will attain enlightenment!'
The <s>Bodhisattva</s> said:
'One who, with great effort, wishes to cross
a jungle full of many serpents,
desiring to reach a blessed place —
who indeed would not wish for fellow travelers?'

children.text:
prapanno 'smākam anena mahātmanāmṛtasaṃvibhāga iti vicintya jātaprītiṣu gateṣu śiṣyeṣu svān ālayān kadā cid upagahvaragato bodhisattva evaṃ cintayām āsa |
kṛtaḥ khalu mayālamartho 'rthijana idānīṃ svamāṃsaśoṇitena tiraścaḥ prīṇayāmīti vicintya śastram ādāya madhusarpiṣī ca bandhūnām akathayitvā māhārajanavasanānurūpasaṃdhyāyavanikātiraskṛtāyām aparasyām āśāyāṃ ghanībhavattimiratirodhīyamānāyāṃ jagatyāṃ bhavanāntarajvālyamānapradīpaprabhāsaṃparkād dviguṇamukhaśobheṣu taruṇījaneṣu gṛhītaviśeṣamaṇḍanāsu salalitabhrūlekhotkṣepāvalokanahasitavilāsabaḍiśākṛṣṭakāmijanahṛdayamīnāsu gaṇikāsu sakhījanadīyamānasaṃdeśaśravaṇāvahitaniścalanayanāsu śambhalīṣu priyajanasaṃketasamutsukāsu tilakāvalokanakutūhalād darpaṇatalavinyastadṛṣṭiṣu kāminīṣu ṭl̃śrūyamāṇakṣīradhārāśabdāsu gopinīruddhavatsollehanacalitakiṅkiṇīsāsnāsu vatsatarīṣu catvaropaviṣṭaromanthanasukhavinimīlitanayanair vipaṇivṛṣabhaiḥ saṃruddhamārgeṣu nagararathyāntareṣu samadahaladharakapolābhipāṭalarāge pūrvācalaśikharam adhitasthuṣi śaśalakṣmaṇi kumudavanaprabodhagandhādhivāsitapavane prāpte pradoṣasamaye 'dyatamaṅgatabhartṛkākeśapāśaparuṣadhūmadhūsarīkṛtavividhapādapam unmukhapāpajambukīvirāvavivṛtavadanavivaraviniḥsṛtahutavahāvabhāsaprakāśīkṛtaśūlaprotapuruṣaskandhanilīnapiśitādhmātaniścalagṛdhrabhāsakaṅkam atiraudralāmāgaṇāvakṛṣyamāṇārdhadagdhacitāmadhyasthitapuruṣakaḍevaraṃ kva cin niśācaropayujyamānamānuṣapiśitaśabdaśravaṇavigalitabhūtagaṇamukhalālālavam anyatra ḍākinīkarāvalambitakartanīvicchidyamānapuruṣasakthivigalitarudhiradhārāsaṃsiktabhūtalam anibhṛtahutavahajvālāṅgulīsaṃtarjanād ivāpasṛtamahāndhakāraṃ kva cid abhinavakumudāvadātaparipāṇḍuśiraḥkapālataralam anyatra śmāśānikabhikṣusamālokyamānapramadākaḍevarāvalagnagomāyugaṇaṃ kva cid divyāvādikālikhitamaṇḍalaparyantasthitadikpālavikośīkṛtavimalanistriṃśasaṃkrāntasphuritahutāśanapratibimbābhīladarśanaṃ mahāśmaśānam ājagāma |
maitrīmantrakṛtaśarīrarakṣaṃ ca bodhisattvaṃ na tatra rakṣo'ṅganājanaś chalayituṃ śaśāka |
sa ca mahātmā śmaśānaikadeśe mṛgadhūrtakākārṣaṇavicalitaprakāśodarāntrajālakravyavṛkkāparśukāsaṃdhim aniloddhūtacitābhasmakaṇaparipāṇḍurīkṛtavyākulakeśapāśāṃ śyenāpahṛtādharatayā vibhāvyamānavikṛtadaśanamālām uparatāṃ pramadām ālokya saṃvignamanās tadgatastimitadṛṣṭir idam avocat |
aho rāgiṇām adūradarśinī buddhir yeṣām īdṛśe 'pi vairāgyahetau strīkaḍevare rāgotpattir bhavatīti |
children.translated_text:
Thinking 'Our share of the nectar has been obtained through this great soul,' when the disciples had departed to their own abodes with hearts full of joy, the <s>Bodhisattva</s> one day, having gone to a secluded place, thought thus:
'I have indeed satisfied the supplicant community sufficiently; now I shall gratify animals with my own flesh and blood,' and thinking thus, taking a weapon and honey-ghee, without telling his kinsmen, when the western direction was concealed by a curtain of twilight resembling a <s>mahārajana</s>-colored garment, when the world was being hidden by the thickening darkness — [in the city] where the beauty of the faces of young women was doubled by the contact of the light of lamps burning within the houses, where courtesans had donned special ornaments, their hearts like fish drawn by the hook of playful glances, raised eyebrows, smiling graces and sidelong looks — where <s>śambhalī</s> women sat with motionless eyes attentive to messages being whispered by their friends — where amorous women eager for trysts with their beloved ones cast their gaze into the surface of mirrors out of curiosity to see the <s>tilaka</s> [on their foreheads] — where the sound of streaming milk could be heard from young cows whose bells tinkled from the movement of licking by calves held back by cowherd women — where the city streets were blocked by market-bulls, seated at the crossroads with eyes pleasantly closed from the pleasure of rumination — when the moon, bearing the mark of the hare, had mounted the peak of the eastern mountain, its cheeks reddened with splendid color like a plowshare of intoxication, and when the breeze, perfumed with the fragrance of awakening night-lotus groves, announced the evening — he came to the great cremation ground, fearsome with its manifold horrors: the smoke-pillared pyres, the corpse of a woman now deceased whose hair-tresses — rough with the disheveled hair darkened like smoke of those whose husbands had died that very day — were strewn about, whose exposed teeth revealed a distorted grin from the lips being snatched by a vulture, wild dogs tearing at the corpses, a half-burnt man standing amid pyres being dragged by terrifying <s>lāmā</s> (demoness) troops, streams of blood flowing from a man's thigh being severed by scissors held in a <s>ḍākinī</s>'s hand, great darkness pushed back as if threatened by the fingers of unsteady fire-flames, skulls pale-white like fresh jasmine scattered about, jackals clinging to the corpses of women being observed by cemetery-dwelling mendicants, and in one place the terrible sight of reflected fire-images flashing on the drawn gleaming swords of the guardians of the directions standing around a <s>maṇḍala</s> drawn by a divine musician.
The <s>Bodhisattva</s>, whose body was protected by a spell of loving-kindness (<s>maitrī-mantra</s>), could not be deceived by the <s>rākṣasa</s>-women there.
That great soul, in one part of the cremation ground, seeing a dead young woman — whose mesh of intestines was exposed and luminous due to the dragging by jackals, dogs, and crows, whose rib-bones were bare, whose scattered disheveled hair was whitened by ash-particles blown up from the pyre by the wind, and whose exposed set of teeth appeared distorted due to the lower lip having been snatched by a hawk — he, his mind filled with spiritual urgency (<s>saṃvega</s>), his gaze fixed upon her, said this:
'Ah! How short-sighted is the understanding of the passionate ones, in whom even at the sight of such a cause for dispassion — a woman's corpse — passion arises!'
'Upon that charming face with steady gaze
where the beloved once applied a mark of sindūra (vermillion) —
upon that very face of the coquette today
a jackal repeatedly places its paw!'
'Those teeth which, slightly revealed by a smile,
used to steal the mind of the passionate —
those very teeth, with lower lips torn away by dogs and crows,
have now attained disfigurement!'
'Those eyes, gazing upon which the beloved attained delight,
beautiful as lotus petals attended by bees —
those very eyes, now robbed of their flesh and blood by birds,
resemble the holes of a serpent!'
'Those cheeks of tender sprout-like softness and complexion,
upon which her friends once drew leaf-patterns —
where has that <s>madhūka</s>-flower pallor gone
from those two cheeks now reduced to mere bone?'
'Those breasts of the young woman, which, when touched by her beloved,
produced goosebumps as she closed her eyes in pleasure —
those very breasts today are being torn apart
by the blood-reddened teeth of dogs!'
'She whom the beloved used to embrace, her flower-adorned hair tumbling from her shoulder,
and happily slept beside her, with closed eyes —
does he not come rushing now to embrace
his most beloved, lying on the cremation ground's earth?'
'In this container made of sinews, bones, flesh, blood, and entrails,
designated "woman," filled with abundant faults like serpents —
this world, struck by the delusion of false imagination,
vainly develops passion toward what is actually an object of dispassion!'
'Those steadfast ones who are not pierced by the sharp arrows of cruel, wicked [desires] —

children.text: dhīrās ta eva śamasaukhyabhujas ta eva
children.translated_text: they alone are truly brave, they alone enjoy the happiness of tranquility,
who, having cleared away the dense thicket of the poison-creeper that is women,
abide in the austerity-groves that yield the fruit of peace!'

children.text: atha tatrābhyucchritadhūmarāśiyūpe mānuṣavasopāyanāhutinipātajanitajvālitāṅgāracchīkāraśabde prārabdhabhaṇḍakāvirāvābhicārukamantrakarmaṇi śmaśānādhvare niśitena śastreṇāṅgāni paritakṣya madhughṛtābhyām abhyajya
children.translated_text: Then, at that cremation-ground sacrifice — with its pillar of rising smoke-masses, its crackling sound of blazing embers produced by the falling of offerings of human flesh, and the ritual of incantation-spells with the chanting of <s>bhaṇḍaka</s> cries commenced — he carved his own limbs with a sharp blade and anointed them with honey and ghee.
Moist with flowing streams of blood,
being consumed by ants,
this master reduced himself
to the state of a sacrificial animal, by his own [will].

children.text: tatra ca kalaṅkaparuṣapiṇḍitasaṃnāhamalinacchaviḥ karirudhiropadigdhamṛgapatinakharakuṭilaraktatīkṣṇatuṇḍaḥ kupitabhujaganayanasadṛśavilocano lohakandhuvāparuṣanakharaḥ kharavirasadhvānasaṃtrāsitānyapakṣigaṇaḥ kaṭhinapakṣaśabdasaṃsūcyamānagatir uccaṅgamo nāma pakṣī |
children.translated_text: And there [appeared] a bird called <s>Uccaṅgama</s> — its hide a dirty complexion of hardened, rough, spotted armor, its beak curved, reddish and sharp like the claw of a lion's paw stained with elephant blood, its eyes resembling the eyes of an enraged serpent, its talons harsh like an iron brush, its approach announced by the sound of its hard wings that terrified all other flocks of birds, with a harsh, discordant cry —
That bird, suddenly mounting his shoulder
as if [mounting] a pillar, for his body stood tall and motionless like a mountain,
tore out his eye, equal to a lotus petal,
and released it again, streaked with blood-drenched eyelashes.
'[A mother bird] who, in her devotion to protect her young,
advances even against a tiger —
how could compassion, that tender mother, though loving,
obstruct the <s>Bodhisattva</s> in accomplishing the welfare of others?'

children.text:
atha sa vihaṅgamo bodhisattvaṃ papraccha |
niyatam ākṛṣyamāṇe 'smin mayā nayane mahatīm vedanām anubhavati bhavān iti |
bodhisattva uvāca |
yadi kena cid anupayuktam me śarīraṃ kṣayam agamiṣyat tato mamābhaviṣyat pīḍā |
saṃprati tv evam upayujyamānam anekaiḥ sattvair ālokya parāṃ prītim anubhavāmīti |
children.translated_text:
Then that bird asked the <s>Bodhisattva</s>:
'Surely, while I am pulling out this eye, you experience great pain.'
The <s>Bodhisattva</s> said:
'If my body were going to perish unused by anyone, then I would have felt distress. But now, seeing it being used by many beings, I experience supreme delight!'
'If this body, the abode of misfortune,
serves again and again as a means [of welfare] for embodied beings,
it is highly regarded by the great, like a jewel;
otherwise, it is like a serpent, full of many faults.'

children.text: atha bodhisattvo bhakṣayantu māṃ yathāsukhaṃ kravyāśina iti vicintya mṛgam ivātmānaṃ darśayām āsa ||
children.translated_text: Then the <s>Bodhisattva</s>, thinking 'Let the flesh-eaters consume me at their pleasure,' displayed himself as if he were a deer [offering himself].
Then, by the vultures that arrived,
terrifying with their unceasing harsh cries,
his flesh was consumed repeatedly,
but the steadfastness of his mind did not turn away.
Then the life-breaths from his body,
which was fragrant with the scent of virtue's flowers,
departed, as birds [depart] a fallen nesting-tree,
somehow, agitated with arising anguish.

children.text: tato staśikhariśirasaḥ suciraparibhogamalinam iva kundāvataṃsam uḍupatim apanīya gatāyāṃ kṣapāṅganāyāṃ javākusumaśekhara iva divasamukhahastenāvabadhyamāne pūrvācalaśirasi gharmāṃśau divasakarakiraṇahastasaṃsparśasukhābhivyajyamānakamalanālakaṇṭakaromāñcāsu vinidrāsu kamalinīvilāsinīṣu kuraravirutānukāriṣu vimucyamāneṣu nagaradvārakapāṭeṣu prativibudhya bodhisattvasya pitāniṣṭaśaṅkāvyathithamanāḥ sasuhṛtparijanabandhuvargas tanayānveṣanavyākulas tat tac cintayām āsa |
children.translated_text: Then, when the night-lady had departed — having removed the moon from the mountain-peak's head like a <s>kunda</s>-flower ear-ornament soiled by long wearing — when the sun was being fastened upon the peak of the eastern mountain by the hand of the day's face, like a <s>javā</s>-flower crest; when the lotuses, their nail-like stalk-prickles manifesting the pleasure of being touched by the sun's ray-hands, bloomed sleepless like beautiful lotus-women; when the city gate-panels were being opened with sounds resembling the cries of <s>kurara</s> birds — awakening at dawn, the father of the <s>Bodhisattva</s>, his mind afflicted with apprehension of misfortune, together with his retinue of friends, servants, and kinsmen, anxiously searching for his son, thought this and that:

children.text: niśi kim ahinā daṣṭaḥ syān me sutaḥ sa paribhramann
children.translated_text: 'Was my son perhaps bitten by a snake while wandering at night?

children.text: uta vikaruṇair bhūṣāṃ hṛtvā hataḥ pratirodhakaiḥ
children.translated_text: Or was he killed by merciless robbers who seized his ornaments?
Or was his chest crushed by the tusks of a king's elephant?'

children.text: kim atha gamita[ḥ] stambhaṃ bhaṅktvā puraṃ samavartinaḥ
children.translated_text: or was he taken, breaking through the pillar, to the city of the <s>Samavartin</s> [i.e., the realm of the righteous king]?

children.text:
krameṇa copagamya śmaśānaikadeśe gṛdhrair avalupyamānamāṃsaṃ bodhisattvaṃ katham api pratyabhijñāya sa janaḥ śreṣṭhine nivedayām āsa |
kaṣṭam ayam asau mahātmā pañcatvam upagato yathā tarkyate tathā niyatam anenātmā tiryagbhyo nivedita iti |
tac ca śrutvā sa śreṣṭhī paraśunikṛtta iva pādapo nipapāta |
cireṇa ca pratilabdhasaṃjña iti vilāpaparo babhūva |
children.translated_text:
Gradually approaching, in a corner of the cremation ground, [they found] the <s>Bodhisattva</s> whose flesh was being torn off by vultures. Somehow recognizing him, those people informed the merchant.
'Terrible! This great-souled one has passed away. As one would surmise, he has surely offered his body to the animals.'
Upon hearing this, the merchant fell like a tree felled by an axe.
And after a long time, having regained consciousness, he became consumed with lamentation:
'Seeing this my son in such a state,
his bone-joints loosened, being torn apart by vultures —
alas, by fate's excessive cruelty,
even so I live, hard-hearted that I am!'
'If such extraordinary compassion for animals
was demonstrated by the giving of your own body,
how then, abandoning me, your innocent father,
have you practiced such ruthlessness?'
'Having slept comfortably on a charming bed
with soft cushions and white coverlets,
how do you now lie here today on a bed
of cremation-ground earth, strewn with bones and ashes?'
'Now that you, my dear son, accompanied by compassion, have gone to heaven,
you who excited the longing of people, heedless of your own happiness —
in gatherings adorned with flowers of discourse on noble qualities,
whose captivating words shall I hear?'
'You who were imagined [by me] as one who would eagerly offer me
the water-offering mixed with tears —'
'that hope of mine, though held by one of pure mind moist with affection,

children.text: bhagnas tvayā kim iti vatsa manoratho me
children.translated_text: has been shattered by you — why, O child?'

children.text: iti śreṣṭhī ciram vilapya bodhisattvaśarīre 'gnisatkāraṃ kṛtvā prasrutanayanodakābhiṣiktamukhaḥ śūnya iva sākrandaśabdaṃ svabhavanam ājagāma |
children.translated_text: Thus the merchant, having lamented for a long time, performed the fire-obsequies for the <s>Bodhisattva</s>'s body, and with face bathed in flowing tears, returned to his own home as if bereft, with the sound of weeping.
Then the host of immortals, striking golden drum-cymbals and kettledrums
whose sound was widely spread from the groves of <s>Meru</s> in every direction,
released a shower of fragrant flowers
there upon the <s>Bodhisattva</s>'s bone-pile in the fire of <s>nirvāṇa</s>.

children.text: tad evaṃ tena bhagavatā bodhisattvacaryāṃ caratā parārtha ātmā bahuśaḥ parityakta iti vicintya buddhe bhagavati paraḥ prasādaḥ karaṇīya iti ||
children.translated_text: Thus, reflecting that while practicing the <s>Bodhisattva</s>-conduct, the Blessed One gave up his own self many times for the sake of others, one should place supreme faith in the Blessed <s>Buddha</s>.
|| The <s>Śreṣṭhi Jātaka</s> (Merchant Birth-Story), the seventh. ||
8. <s>Padmaka Jātaka</s> (The Lotus-King Birth-Story)

children.text: tatyāja bodhisattvas tṛṇam iva dehaṃ parārthasaṃsiddhyai /
children.translated_text: The <s>Bodhisattva</s> gave up his body like a blade of grass for the accomplishment of others' welfare.
The resolute who are devoted to procuring the happiness of others pay no heed to their own comfort.

children.text:
tadyathānuśrūyate
śaradapagatajaladharasaṃghātāyāṃ divīva candramāḥ |
sakalāśasimaṇḍalakiraṇāvabhāsitāyāṃ kṣapāyām iva kumudavanavikāsaḥ |
pramadavanabhūmāv iva ca kamalākaraḥ |
prathamayauvanasamṛddhāv iva vinayaḥ |
sphuṭamadhurākṣarapadāyāṃ vācīvārthaḥ |
śaraccandrikayeva dīrghatvam āgatayā vimalasalilayā spaṣṭamīnakulākulayā taṭatarukusumaparāgaparipiñjarīkṛtaphenapaṅktirasanākalāpayā varāṇasayā nimnagayālaṅkṛtāyāṃ prakṛtiramaṇīyāyāṃ vārāṇasyāṃ rājadhānyāṃ sphuritadaśanamaṇikiraṇāvabhāsābhyalaṅkṛtavadanapadmaḥ padmako nāma rājā bodhisattvo babhūva ||
children.translated_text:
Thus it is heard:
In the royal capital of <s>Vārāṇasī</s>, naturally lovely — like the moon in the sky of autumn when cloud-masses have departed; like the blossoming of a night-lily garden on a night illumined by the rays of the full moon's disc; like a lotus-pond on the ground of a pleasure-garden; like modesty in the fullness of first youth; like meaning in speech of clear, sweet syllables and words; adorned by the river <s>Varāṇasī</s> [<s>Varaṇā</s>], which, having attained length like autumn moonlight, with clear water, teeming with schools of visible fish, with garlands of foam-streaks yellowed by the pollen of flowers from trees on its banks — there was a king, a <s>Bodhisattva</s>, named <s>Padmaka</s> (Lotus-King), whose lotus-face was adorned with the illumination of radiant tooth-gem rays.

children.text: kāntyā ca rūpeṇa ca tejasā ca
children.translated_text: By his luster, beauty, and splendor,
he simultaneously conquered — contemptuously — the causes
of delight, enchantment, and burning:
the moon, the Flower-armed one [<s>Kāma</s>], and the sun.
Like the contentment of birds on a fruit-bearing tree,
like that of bees in a lotus-pond,
