like that of merchants in a world's sole kinsman —
such was the people's happiness in him, as if in a dear friend.
Into [the heart of] him whose soul was exerted for the welfare of the world,
whose mind was purified by the embrace of compassion —
envy did not enter,
as a serpent [does not enter] a house protected by a charm.
By his generosity — great-souled, renowned,
spreading through the quarters, free of envy —
the world never heard from the supplicant-folk
the word 'Give!' — those humble words — again.
He, who was devoted solely to the work of others' welfare,
worthy of reverence by the entire world,
plunged into the Ganges-stream of fame, pure as moonbeams —
flowing from the summit of generosity on the snow-mountain of [his] heart, having washed away all dust, bathing the whole world.
'Whose calamity is to be removed today?
Who is to be gratified with wealth?
Who is to be established on the auspicious path?' —
Such was his constant disposition.
For great souls who wish to place themselves
on the virtuous path for the destruction of existence,
there is no other occupation
apart from the welfare of others.
The forces of that conqueror of foes, whose arm-valor was unvanquished,
rushed into enemy territory
like the waters of the ocean, whose swelling, towering growth
reaches to the bank's edge.
His war-elephants, their rage extended by
the mutual sounds of each other's war-drums,
at the time of marching could barely be
brought under control by those holding goads.
With the rise of their rut quelled by fear,
their grips loosened on swords and bows,
the enemies could not endure his pride in battle,

children.text: yudhi gajā iva yasya na sehire
children.translated_text: like elephants [cannot endure] that of a lion.
In [the realm of] him whose splendor was renowned, the subjects,
their prosperity augmented by the happiness of mutual affection,
always rested in comfort,
like birds on a fruit-bearing tree.

children.text:
atha kadā cit tasya rājño deśe dhātuvaiṣamyād upacīyamānodarāgniḥ pratidivasam āpāṇḍudurbalaśarīro nirojasko janakāyo mahatā rogeṇa jagrase |
bodhisattvājñayā ca bhiṣajaḥ sādaram api cikitsāṃ kurvanto na taṃ vyādhim apahartuṃ tasya janasya śekuḥ |
atha sa rājā tān vaidyān uvāca |
kenopayenāyaṃ janasya vyādhir apahartuṃ śakyaḥ syād iti |
bhiṣaja ūcuḥ |
deva yadi rohītamatsyamāṃsaṃ syāt tataḥ śaknuyāmo vayam enaṃ janam anātaṅkaṃ kartum iti |
atha sa rājā param api prayatnaṃ kurvan na kutaś cid rohītamatsyam upalebhe ||
children.translated_text:
Then once, in that king's realm, due to an imbalance of the bodily humors (<s>dhātu</s>), the digestive fire within the people increased, and day by day their bodies grew pale, weak, and devoid of vigor, consumed by a great disease.
Despite the physicians, on the <s>Bodhisattva</s>'s orders, treating them with great care, they were unable to remove that illness from the people.
Then the king asked those physicians: 'By what means can this disease of the people be removed?'
The physicians said: 'O King, if there were the flesh of a <s>rohita</s> fish, then we would be able to render these people free of disease.'
But the king, despite making supreme effort, could not find a <s>rohita</s> fish anywhere.

children.text: tataḥ kadā cit sa bahir viniryayau
children.translated_text: Then one day the lord of the earth went out,
mounted on the shoulder of a great elephant,
his heat warded off by a white parasol,
his garment fluttering in the trembling motion of scattered flowers.
Then the afflicted ones, seeing the king followed by his retinue,
mounted on the lord of elephants,
suddenly raising their hands with pitiable faces,

children.text: trāyasva no nṛpa gadād iti vācam ūcuḥ
children.translated_text: cried out: 'Save us from the disease, O king!'

children.text:
atha bodhisattvas teṣāṃ vyādhimatāṃ tumulamanasāṃ karuṇam ākrandaśabdaṃ ākarṇya duḥkhāyamānahṛdayo dayāparicayād udgatabāṣpasalilatirohitākṣa idam acintayat |
kiṃ mama rājyasukhena yatra me viṣayanivāsinām iyam avasthitiḥ |
praviśya ca bhavanam āhūya sacivān idam avocat |
icchāmy ahaṃ jyāyastanayābhiṣekaṃ kartum iti |
athāmātyā ūcuḥ ||
children.translated_text:
Then the <s>Bodhisattva</s>, hearing the pitiful crying of those afflicted by disease, their minds in turmoil, his heart aching with sorrow, his eyes concealed by tears arising from habitual compassion, thought thus:
'What use is the pleasure of kingship to me, when this is the condition of my subjects?'
And entering the palace, summoning his ministers, he spoke thus:
'I wish to perform the consecration of my eldest son.'
Then the ministers said:
'When your body is in the vigor of fresh youth,
when your prowess crushes enemies,
and when your rise is for the cause of others' welfare —
why this untimely desire to go to the forest?'

children.text:
rājovāca |
na khalv evaṃ yathā bhavantas tarkayantīti |
amātyāḥ punar ūcuḥ |
ko 'bhiprāyo devasya |
rājovāca |
duḥsvapnadarśanād āgatāśaṅko 'ham evaṃ tarkayāmi |
kadā cid atarkitaiveyam anityatā samāgamya māṃ vināśayet |
ataḥ putram abhiṣiktaṃ draṣṭum icchāmīti |
amātyāḥ procuḥ |
yad ājñāpayati deva iti ||
children.translated_text: The king said: 'It is certainly not as you gentlemen surmise.' The ministers again said: 'What is the King's intention?' The king said: 'Seized by apprehension from having seen a bad dream, I reason thus: this impermanence may at some unexpected time come and destroy me. Therefore I wish to see my son consecrated.' The ministers said: 'As the King commands.'
Then in the excellent house with raised golden arched gateways,
resounding with the clear notes of fine instruments,
that king, affectionate toward his son,
revered by [other] earth-protectors, consecrated his son.

children.text:
atha sa kumāraḥ pitaram āgamyovāca |
ājñāpayatu tātaḥ kathaṃ mayā vyavahartavyam iti |
rājovāca |
śrūyatāṃ vatsa |
sarvathā na kadā cid āyuṣmatā praṇayiṇām upari nirādareṇa bhavitavyam iti |
paśya ||
children.translated_text: Then that prince approached his father and said: 'Let father command: how should I conduct myself?' The king said: 'Listen, my child. Under no circumstances should you, who should long live, ever be disrespectful toward those who are affectionate.'
'Envy is a cause of reproach, a blocker of good destinies,
an empty abode — a den of the she-demon <s>Jālinī</s>,
a flood that destroys the bridge to well-being —
hostile to those blinded by greed, envy has become an enemy!'
'Base people, formerly attached to their own possessions,
having burnt themselves with the fire of envy's snake-venom,
with harsh words like flames fierce from the fire-arch of furrowed brows,
in the end burn the supplicant by saying "There is nothing!"'
'Those are the wise ones, those are the nobly born —
who in their next lives do not see the lower realms,
who have not led this self, for the sake of suffering,
to become the anthill of the envy-serpent.'

children.text: ibhyo 'pi pratiṣedhapāṃsumalināṃ yo vakti dainyāṃ giraṃ
children.translated_text: 'He who, even to beggars, speaks a pitiful word, soiled with the dust of refusal —

children.text: dūrāt taṃ janam arthinaḥ pariharanty āśāvisaṃvādakam
children.translated_text: supplicants avoid from afar that person who disappoints their hopes.',
'Even travelers parched by thirst do not perform the acts of bathing and drinking
in the pure water of a well at the gate of a house inhabited by one who turns away [the needy].'
'Those water-seeking spirits with long beards, faces of darkness, and deeply sunken eyes,

children.text: vāryante puruṣair upāttalaguḍaiḥ pretā yad ambho'rthinaḥ
children.translated_text: who are warded off by men wielding raised clubs —'

children.text: tattvajñas tad uvāca matsaraphalaṃ bandhuḥ prajānām jinaḥ
children.translated_text: 'the <s>Jina</s>, the knower of truth, the kinsman of beings, declared that to be the fruit of envy.',

children.text: saṃcintyeti paropakāravimukhī puṃsā na k'; matiḥ
children.translated_text: 'Reflecting thus, one should not adopt a disposition averse to benefiting others.'

children.text:
api ca vatsa |
loke bahumānam icchatā tvayā satyatyāgaśramādākṣiṇyādibhir guṇamaṇibhir ātmābhyalaṅkartavyaḥ ||
children.translated_text: 'Moreover, my child: By you who desire to be honored in the world, the self should be adorned with the jewels of virtue — truthfulness, generosity, effort, graciousness, and the like.'
'The peaceful ones, esteemed for virtues, skilled in severing the world's harm,
with love grown for the virtuous, wise, speaking truthfully,

children.text: pariṣvaktā lakṣmyā na ca madakalaṅkena malinā
children.translated_text: embraced by <s>Lakṣmī</s>, not soiled by the stain of arrogance —
excellent men are placed by people at the forefront in the reckoning of men.'
'Those who bear the yoke of relieving the entire world's burden of suffering,

children.text: dhiyo yeṣāṃ svacchā ruca iva maṇīnāṃ vitamasaḥ
children.translated_text: whose minds are clear like the luster of gems, free of darkness,

children.text: priyaṃ kartuṃ vāñchanty asubhir api ye ca praṇayināṃ
children.translated_text: and who wish to do what is dear to the affectionate, even at the cost of their lives —
how should they not be placed foremost in the reckoning of the virtuous?'

children.text:
na ca bhavatā pracurapuruṣeṇeva guṇavatsv anādareṇa bhavitavyam |
paśya ||
children.translated_text: 'And you should not, as if a man of many resources, be disrespectful toward the virtuous. See:' —

children.text: anuṣṇāṃśuṃ dṛṣṭvā guṇinam iva saṃprāptam atithiṃ
children.translated_text: 'Seeing the cool-rayed moon, like a virtuous guest who has arrived,

children.text: payovṛddhyā sindhuḥ prathayati muhuḥ saṃbhramam iva
children.translated_text: the ocean, by the swelling of its waters, displays, as it were, its eagerness again and again.',

children.text: na vardhante toyāny udayavati tatraiva sarasāṃ
children.translated_text: 'But the waters of ponds do not swell when that very [moon] rises —
the manifestation of joy at the great occurs only in the great.'

children.text: atha prakāśībhavaduḍugaṇaśabale nabhasi racitaśaśiviśeṣakāyāṃ pūrvasyāṃ diśi śalabhakulapatanavicalitadīpaśikhāṅgulīsaṃtarjiteneva navajalanīlāvabhāsā tamasā vimuktāntareṣu bhavaneṣu vāsayaṣṭivilīnaniścaleṣu tāmracūleṣv agurudhūpāmodādhivāsiteṣu vilepanavyāpāracalitamukharavalayālaṅkṛtahastapadmābhir abalābhir adhyāsitamṛduśayanīyataleṣu vāsagṛheṣu praviralajanakrayavikrayāyāṃ kva cid api vīthīyamānāpaṇāvīthyāṃ bodhisattvas tanayam anuśiṣya dīpikālokāvabhāsyamānālekhyaśobhāṃ bhavanasyottamāṃ bhuvam āruhya visarjitasarvāntaḥpurajanas tasyāṃ varāṇasāyāṃ nadyām ātmānaṃ mumukṣur evam uvāca ||
children.translated_text: Then, when the sky was variegated with emerging clusters of stars, when the eastern quarter had fashioned the mark of the moon, when the darkness, dark-blue as fresh rain-clouds, [retreated] from the spaces between houses — where the motionless roosters perched on perching-poles had copper crests, perfumed by the fragrance of <s>aguru</s> incense, where women with lotus-hands adorned with jingling bracelets moving as they applied unguents occupied beds of soft mattresses in their bedchambers — when buying and selling by the scant people on the market-street had ceased — the <s>Bodhisattva</s>, having instructed his son, ascending to the uppermost level of his palace, its splendid painted murals illuminated by lamplight, having dismissed all the harem attendants, spoke thus, wishing to cast himself into that river <s>Varaṇāsī</s>:
'In this river, with waters pure as white gems,
may I become a great-bodied
<s>rohita</s> fish,
for the pacification of the people's disease!'
Thus, for the sake of his subjects, the lord of the earth
released that body — its rise nourished [for this purpose],
accompanied by a special compassion, slender with virtue —
into the river <s>Varaṇāsī</s>, while the sky trembled in agitation.
Then that king, falling into the water
from his own palace, shone
like a wish-fulfilling tree from the slope of <s>Sumeru</s>
struck by the great tusks of the elephant of the Lord of the Gods [<s>Indra</s>].
Then, as the king fell, the wind
stirred his white garment into agitation;
the water, with its schools of fish set in motion —
overflowing the bank with [its] moving <s>cakravāka</s> birds and lotuses.
Fallen into that river, which in an instant
had become fearsome with the roar of rising waters,
the king, of a body befitting the ridge of the snowy mountain,
became a <s>rohita</s> (red) fish.

children.text:
sa ca mahātmā sitasikatāmanoharaṃ pulinam uttīrya yadi mām ayaṃ janakāyaḥ prāṇebhyo viyojayet tato duṣkṛtaphalena yukto durgatiparāyaṇaḥ syād iti |
tad idam atra prāptakālaṃ svayam eva sarvendriyanirodhaṃ kṛtvā jīvitaṃ parityakṣyāmīti vicintya prāṇān atyākṣīt |
atha kaluṣasalilābhiṣiktasitadviradakumbhākṛtāv astagiriśikharāvalambini śiśirāṃśau pratanupāṃsūpadigdhasphaṭikamaṇinibhāsu praviralībhavantīṣu tārāsu |
saṃmīlatsu kumudagahaneṣu vinidrībhavatsu kamalākareṣu haritālaraseneva bālātapena paricchuriteṣu giriśikhareṣu narapatiśūnyaṃ śayanaṃ śayanapālikājanād upalabhyāmātyāḥ |
kva punā rājā gataḥ syād iti bhavanasamīpajātam upavanam ālokya samantataḥ paribhramanto dadṛśur varāṇasāyāḥ samudrapatyāḥ puline muktārāśim iva dīrghīkṛtaṃ rohītamatsyam |
te ca śuśruvur adṛśyavapuṣo gaganasthasya divaukaso gambhīrāṃ bhāratīm ||
children.translated_text: That great-souled one, having emerged upon a sandbank beautiful with white sand, [thought]: 'If these people were to separate me from my life-breaths, they would be endowed with the fruit of evil deeds and destined for a bad rebirth.' 'Therefore, what is appropriate here and now: having myself restrained all the senses, I shall relinquish my life.' Having resolved thus, he gave up his life-breaths. Then, when the cool-rayed moon was resting upon the western mountain-peak like the white temple-globe of an elephant bathed in turbid water, when the stars — resembling crystal gems lightly dusted with fine powder — were growing sparse, when the groves of night-lotuses were closing and the lotus-pools were awakening, when the mountain peaks were sprinkled by the early sunlight as if by orpiment-paste — the ministers, learning from the bedchamber attendants that the royal bed was empty [of the king, asked]: 'Where then has the king gone?' Searching everywhere, looking at the garden near the palace, they saw upon the sandbank of the river of <s>Vārāṇasī</s>, the bride of the ocean, a <s>rohita</s> fish stretched out long like a heap of pearls. And they heard the deep voice of an invisible celestial being stationed in the sky:
'To cut short the suffering and affliction
of these people, that king,
having cast himself into the river's water,
has taken the form of a <s>rohita</s> fish.'

children.text:
atha te 'mātyās tac chrutvā śokaduḥkhavyathitamanasa idam ūcuḥ |
aho karuṇayā rājānam ātmānaṃ sattvahitārtham eva parityājayantyā sakalā vasudheyam anāthīkṛteti bahuvidham iti vilapya śūnyamanasaḥ svān ālayān abhijagmuḥ ||
children.translated_text: Then those ministers, hearing that, their minds afflicted by grief and sorrow, said: 'Alas, compassion has made the king sacrifice himself solely for the welfare of beings — this entire earth has been made orphaned!' Having lamented thus in many ways, with empty minds they returned to their own dwellings.
Learning the account from the ministers,
the queen, agitated,
with eyes streaming tears,
lamented for that king:
'Even though hearing, O friend of the world,
that the king has gone to heaven of his own accord —'
'still, the desire to live does not wish
to abandon me, whose lot is the suffering of impermanence!'
'Your heart, tender with compassion,

children.text: na jātu rūkṣaṃ hṛdayaṃ dviṣaty api
children.translated_text: is never harsh even toward an enemy;'
'why have you gone, abandoning without cause
these people who are devoted [to you] and who followed [you]?'
'"O fierce one, relinquish your great anger!"',
'— saying thus, insistent with the women-folk,
who will now approach and appease me,
with downcast face, angered by groundless jealousy?'
'Having placed a blooming fresh blue lotus upon [my] ear,
and arranged the beautiful curling locks like waves —'
'who, standing at the toilette-place, will gradually
make for me a charming forehead-mark?'
'That <s>vallakī</s> (lute), lovingly fashioned and adorned,
which was like a passionate beloved [made] by my beloved —'
'without him now, for a long time
it will become like a peahen lost in meditation.'
'This mirror, which once rivaled the beauty of his moon-face —
the beauty of a still water with a single lotus —'

children.text: sa eva śokād iva hā bhaviṣyati
children.translated_text: 'that very [mirror] will now take on, as if from grief, alas,
the appearance of the moon at dawn.'
'Having given you, O parrot, dwelling in the cage, a charming
ripe <s>jāmbava</s> (rose-apple) fruit —'
'without my beloved, soft as the down of a <s>śirīṣa</s> flower,
who will train you?'
'My beloved has gone, parted from [me, his] companion;
there is no longer purpose for [my] tresses.'
'This braid of mine, foretelling the arrangement of widowhood —

children.text: mamādya veṇī kim iyaṃ na badhyate
children.translated_text: why is it not bound today at last?'
Then, in a moment, the beautiful women of the inner palace,
hearing the queen's lamentation thus,
abandoning their fondness for gazing into mirrors,
gave up the charming, [previously] delightful art of ornamentation.
One woman, eager for eye-collyrium, having abandoned
the applicator-stick lingering at the corner of her eye,
in her despair, with tears flowing,
washed away her half-completed forehead-mark.
Another, distraught, having removed from her hair
a garland of blooming <s>kesara</s> flowers,
another [woman] separated a fragrant mango-blossom cluster
golden from the opening of its buds.
Others, with garments disheveled by swaying garland-ornaments,
with locks tangled and curling,
fell — like beautiful wish-fulfilling creepers struck by the wind of dissolution,
with bees buzzing about — the women.
Some women, hearing of the king's death
from the attendants, their eyes filled with tears,
like evening lotuses tossed by the wind,
falling upon the ground, closed their eyes.
Another woman, having slowly drawn that king
whose glory conquered the moon, seen by the retinue,
weeping from despair, resting [the portrait] upon her lap,
abandoned the painting-board together with the pigments.
Some young women, pulling their fragrant hair

children.text: phullaiḥ kva cit praviralaiḥ kusumaiḥ parītān
children.translated_text: adorned with severed-threaded, scattered full-blooming flowers,
struck their chests repeatedly with hands
copper-red as lotuses, with broken bracelets.

children.text:
atha te 'mātyāḥ śokavaśād āgatabāṣpasalilabindunā karuṇavilāpena tena jyeṣṭhaputreṇa nivāpasalilāñjaliṃ dāpayitvā tad antaḥpuraṃ kathaṃ cid āśvāsya taṃ vyādhigrastaṃ janam ūcuḥ |
kriyatāṃ tasya rājño 'bhiprāyaḥ |
evaṃ hi sa pūjito bhaviṣyati |
atha sa janakāyaḥ śastraiś chittvā tasya rohītamatyasyasya māṃsam ānīya vaidyābhihitena krameṇopayujya tasmād vyādheḥ pramumuce ||
children.translated_text: Then those ministers, overcome by grief, having had the eldest son offer the libation-water with tearful drops and a compassionate lament, and having somehow consoled those inner-palace [women], addressed those afflicted people: 'Let the king's intention be carried out. Thus he will be honored.' Then those people, having cut the flesh of that <s>rohita</s> fish with blades, brought [it], and consuming it in the manner prescribed by physicians, were freed from that disease.

children.text: tad evaṃ sa bhagavān bodhisattvabhūtaḥ sattvārthaṃ duṣkarāṇi kṛtavān iti ko nāma tasmin mahākāruṇike bhagavati buddhe sacetā jano bhaktimān na syād iti ||
children.translated_text: Thus, reflecting that the Blessed One who was a <s>Bodhisattva</s> performed difficult deeds for the sake of beings — what conscious person would not be devoted to that greatly compassionate Blessed <s>Buddha</s>?
|| The <s>Padmakajātaka</s>, the Eighth ||
11. <s>Mṛga</s> (The Deer)

children.text: tṛṇam iva jīvitam iṣṭaṃ karuṇānugatāḥ parārtham ujjhantaḥ /
children.translated_text: The great-souled ones, who, guided by compassion, abandon even their dear life like a blade of grass for others' sake,

children.text: kaṭhinamanasām api mano nayanti mṛdutāṃ mahātmānaḥ //
children.translated_text: lead the minds of even those who are hard-hearted to tenderness.

children.text:
tadyathānuśrūyate
svacchasalilatayā candrikayeva dravībhūtayā mṛdupavanapreritataraṅgasaṃghātayā cakravākamithunopaśobhitapulinayā varāṇasayā nimnagayābhyalaṃkṛtācalāntare vividhatarucchāyāpihitajalāśayajale sukumāraśādvalaharitabhūbhāge kvacid araṇye bodhisattvo mṛgayūthādhipatir babhūva |
children.translated_text: Thus it is heard in tradition: In a mountain valley adorned by the river of <s>Vārāṇasī</s> — whose water had become liquid moonlight in its purity, whose wave-masses were stirred by a gentle breeze, whose sandbars were beautified by pairs of <s>cakravāka</s> birds — on a patch of ground green with tender, soft turf, in a forest where the water of the pools was concealed by the shade of various trees, the <s>Bodhisattva</s> became the lord of a deer-herd.
With a belly white as the foam of the milky ocean,
and a back dark as a mass of bees,
with the tips of his eyelashes sparkling, dappled like the play of stars —
he shone like a sidelong glance of the forest-interior itself.

children.text: tasyaivaṃvidhasya bodhisattvasya kiṃcid rūpalāvaṇyapramāṇānukārī devadattas tatsamīpacārī nātimahato mṛgayūthasyādhipatyaṃ cakāra ||
children.translated_text: Of this <s>Bodhisattva</s> of such a nature, <s>Devadatta</s>, who somewhat imitated his beauty, charm, and stature, and who moved in his vicinity, assumed the leadership of another deer-herd of no great size.
Under the protection of those two leaders,
feeding on grass, the two herds
roamed about, free from apprehension of separation,
confident.

children.text: atha kadācit sātmībhūtamṛgayāvyasano brahmadatto nāma rājā nirgamya vārāṇasyās tiryaguraḥsthalaviniveśitadhanvā vājivarādhirohī sadṛśānuyātras turagakhurasamuddhatapāṃsuparidhūsaranayanapakṣmā divasakarasaṃtāpajanitasvedakaṇākrāntalalāṭadeśaḥ sasainyadhvanisaṃtrāsotpatitamayūratittiricakoravanakṛkavākūni viṣamonnatāni nimnabhūmibhāgāni kvacitpadāticaraṇasaṃtrāsitahariṇakhuravinyāsacakitasphuritaśapharīkulavimuktasravantītaṭasalilāni mattagajapatikapolanikaṣaṇasaṃkrāntamadādhivāsitataruskandhasamīpabhrāntamadhukaragaṇāni taṭaviṭapiśākhāvalagnaśuṣkakakubhākṣaphalamadgubalākāpicchaparimiśrakāśakuśavaṃśataruparṇasaṃcayasūcyamānacirātikrāntagirisaritpūrāṇi palvalapaṅkavinimagnavyāghrapadāni pakvodumbaragandhādhivāsitagahvarāṇi pavanacalitatanupatākākuṭilabhujagasṛtibhir aṅkitamārgapāṃsūni vanāntarāṇi vilokayan kiṃcid atikramya tan mṛgayūthadvayaṃ viśrabdhasthitaṃ sainyena pariveṣṭayāmāsa |
children.translated_text: Then once, a king named <s>Brahmadatta</s>, whose addiction to hunting had become second nature, having set forth from <s>Vārāṇasī</s> — with his bow placed horizontally across his chest, mounted on an excellent horse, followed by suitable attendants, his eyelashes gray with dust raised by the horses' hooves, his forehead covered with drops of sweat born from the sun's scorching heat — passing through forest regions where peacocks, partridges, <s>cakora</s> birds, and wild roosters flew up in alarm at the noise of his troops, over uneven, elevated and low terrain, where in places the waters of rivulets on the banks were agitated by the frightened darting of schools of <s>śapharī</s> fish startled by the hoofprints of deer alarmed by the footfalls of the infantry, where swarms of bees wandered near the tree-trunks perfumed by the rut-ichor transferred from the temple-rubbing of lordly rutting elephants, where the accumulation of dry <s>kakubha</s> fruit, <s>akṣa</s> fruit, feathers of <s>madgu</s> and <s>balākā</s> birds, and leaves of <s>kāśa</s>, <s>kuśa</s>, and bamboo trees, clinging to branches of the trees on the banks, indicated the long-past flood of the mountain river, where tiger-paw prints were sunk in the mud of pools, where the caves were fragrant with the scent of ripe <s>udumbara</s> figs, where the dust of the paths was marked by the writhing tracks of slender serpents [disturbed by] thin pennants fluttering in the wind — observing [all this], advancing slightly beyond, he surrounded those two deer-herds standing at ease with his army.
Then, seeing the army bearing bows,
with the rattling of shifting bridles rising high,
the deer, shelterless, their groups broken apart,
ran about in every direction, overcome by fear.
Seeing the deer surrounded on all sides
by the king's army, that <s>Bodhisattva</s>,
approaching the king who was drawing an arrow from his quiver from afar,
addressed him:
'Why do you prepare this bow with arrows
for the simultaneous destruction of [all] the deer?
Day after day, to your kitchen,
I shall send one deer at a time.'
The king then spoke to him:

children.text: yadi satyaṃ mṛga tat tathā kariṣye
children.translated_text: 'If [you speak] the truth, O deer, I shall do so;
but if you do not carry out this arrangement,
then I shall strike the deer again.'
When the king had departed, having agreed,
sheltered from the sun's heat by a white parasol,
the <s>Bodhisattva</s>, approaching,
addressed those deer who had reassembled together:
'When destruction comes all at once,

children.text: yadi labhyeta punaḥ kramaḥ sa sādhuḥ
children.translated_text: if a gradual course can be obtained, that is good;'
'by gaining time, for the sake of eventual peace,
something else will surely come to pass someday.'
'Kings, who are enemies even of powerful lions
skilled in splitting the frontal globes of elephants,
destroy [their] life-breaths with arrows —'
'how much more so those of deer in the forest, who eat only tips of <s>darbha</s> grass?'
'The moon, splitting the darkness with its rays
pure as white gems, having illuminated the world,
falls from the western mountain with its beauty gone —'
'all things are but a momentary cessation of sound.'
'<s>Vainateya</s> [<s>Garuḍa</s>], churning the water of great waves with his speed,
seizes a serpent from the midst of the ocean;'
'no one, however skilled in actions, however greatly renowned in strength,
can transcend the ripening of previous [karmic] deeds.'
'Having understood thus the course of <s>karma</s>,
the wise, skilled in discernment,
even when life is threatened, do not fall into
despair, being firm-minded.'

children.text: atha yūthapatidvayasamādeśāt tābhyāṃ yūthābhyām ahany ahany ekaiko mṛgas tasya rājño bhojanapaktikāle mahānasam agāt | evaṃ ca katipayeṣv ahaḥsv atikrānteṣu devadattayūthavartinyāḥ samāpannasattvāyā hariṇyāḥ prāpto gamanavāraḥ | tataḥ sā svayūthapatim āgamyovāca | svāmin niyataṃ śvaḥ prasavitrī bhavitāsmi | tataḥ prasūya vane mṛgaśāvaṃ vinikṣipya gantāsmi | mayā khalu tatra yuktaṃ martum | naitena garbhasthena śāvakeneti | devadatto yūthapatir uvāca | tat katamo 'nyo mṛgas tava vāre prāpte gamiṣyati | sarvathā tvayaiva gantavyam anātmajñā bhavatī yā mamājñāṃ laṅghayatīti | tena yūthapatinā nirbhartsitā sāpasṛtya mṛgī cintayāmāsa | yo 'yaṃ dvitīyo yūthapatir ayam atikāruṇikas tasmād enam api tāvad abhyarthayiṣye | gatvā ca bodhisattvam uvāca |
children.translated_text: Then, by the command of the two herd-leaders, from both herds, day after day, one deer went to the king's kitchen at mealtime. And so, when some days had passed, the turn came to a doe belonging to <s>Devadatta</s>'s herd who was with young. She approached her own herd-leader and said: 'Lord, I shall certainly give birth tomorrow. Therefore, after giving birth and leaving the fawn in the forest, I shall go. It is proper that I die there, not this unborn fawn in my womb.' The herd-leader <s>Devadatta</s> said: 'Then what other deer will go when your turn has come? In any case, you yourself must go. You are self-ignorant, you who transgress my command!' Rebuked by that herd-leader, the doe withdrew and thought: 'This second herd-leader — he is exceedingly compassionate. Therefore let me entreat him as well.' And she went and said to the <s>Bodhisattva</s>:
'O lord of the herd, my turn has come
to go to the king's abode;
but I am near to giving birth —
therefore protect this fawn!'
'Just after birth, having licked [the fawn]
which nestles close, with [my] tongue,
and having nursed at the breast
the restless-eyed little fawn —'
'[Having seen it] touching the tips of the grass
with its tooth-buds white as fragments of conch-shell,
at the forest's edge,
and having seen it standing before me —'
'O lord of the herd, in the herd
there is a younger sister of mine;
having entrusted my little one to her,
I shall go, my purpose fulfilled.'

children.text: iti putralālasāṃ tāṃ hariṇīm abhidhāyinīṃ samālokya /
children.translated_text: Beholding that doe, who spoke thus with tender longing for her offspring,
the heart of the herd-leader was filled all the more with compassion.

children.text: aparicite 'py anukampā duḥkhini sutarāṃ vivardhate sādhoḥ /
children.translated_text: The compassion of a good person grows all the more toward one who is suffering, even if unfamiliar,
like a creeper whose roots have been watered — it clings to [and nourishes] the tree.
Whoever has compassion, seeing a wretched one
who has come for refuge,
makes the utmost effort
to become the cause of the destruction of that one's misfortune.
Then the lord of the deer-herd spoke thus to that doe:
'O gentle one, abandon the grief arising in your mind;

children.text: tvaṃ tiṣṭha nirvṛtim upetya vane carantī
children.translated_text: you remain here, roaming in the forest, having attained peace;

children.text: yāsyāmy ahaṃ narapateḥ svayam eva veśma
children.translated_text: I shall go of my own accord to the king's abode.'
'Behold for a long time your fawn — nibbling young, <s>śirīṣa</s>-green grass,
drinking water pure as a net of moonbeams,
playing here with other deer-fawns —
your restless-eyed little son.'

children.text: āśvāsya tām iti mṛgīṃ sa jagāda dhīras
children.translated_text: Having thus consoled that doe, the steadfast one declared:
'As I today save this doe from death,
so too may I deliver all beings
from the suffering caused by rebirth, having attained enlightenment that conquers <s>Māra</s>!'

children.text: ity uktvā sa yūthapatir udarākrāntibaddhoṣmaṇaḥ khurapuṭotkhātarajaskān mṛgaromanthanojjhitabadarāsthinicitaparyantād vasatisthānāt prāg eva samutthāya vimanasā yūthenānugamyamāno vārāṇasīm abhitaḥ pratasthe |
children.translated_text: Having said this, the herd-leader, rising early from the dwelling-place — whose periphery was heaped with jujube pits shed from the deer's rumination, dusty from the digging of hooves, and warmed by the heat trapped beneath their bellies — set forth toward <s>Vārāṇasī</s>, followed by the sorrowful herd.
Then the mountain trees, with blossoms opened wide, confused and agitated
by the melodious humming cries of the spreading bees,
their branch-tip hands waved by the wind,
seemed to try to make him turn back.
As if being released by a dear friend, the deer —
the forest, with wind-stirred trembling leaves,
with the <s>cīrī-cīrī</s> cry spreading all around,
seemed to weep, exceedingly agitated.

children.text: atha bodhisattvo vārāṇasīsamīpam āgamya kiṃcid vilambya tan mṛgayūtham ity uvāca | nivartyatām idānīm | sulabhaviyogāni hi lokasaṃgatāni | suciram api vasantakālaramaṇīyam aravindavanam upāsya himasamayaparimlānapalāśakesarakarṇikam apagatagandham apahāya gacchaty eva prakṛticañcalā śrīḥ | avabhāsya ca prāvṛṭkālajaladapaṭāvaguṇṭhitāni digvadhūmukhāni lāsyam iva ca darśayitvā viraktā iva veśyāṅganāḥ śaratkālavigalitasalilalaghūn apagatavibhavān kāmukān iva parityajanti jaladharān aciraprabhāḥ | kṣaṇadāmukhaviśeṣakaḥ śiśirāṃśur api prabhātasamaye parityajyate sahajayā kāntyā | sarvathā na tat kiṃcij jagati vidyate yan nānyonyaviyogi syād iti vicintya dharmaparāyaṇair yuṣmābhir bhūtvā samyag ātmā paripālanīya iti | tac ca mṛgayūthaṃ sthitvā bodhisattvam ā cakṣurviṣayād gacchantam avalokya pitṛviyogād iva śokaśalyakṣatahṛdayaṃ śūnyam iva tad vanaṃ pratyājagāma | bodhisattvo 'pi ca hariṇavarāhamahiṣājāsthinicaye lagnaśvagaṇakalahabhīṣaṇam utpatitāvalīnasaraghākulamāṃsapeśīkam upanihitaniśātakartanīkaṃ mṛgāgamanapratīkṣibhir aurabhrikair ākīrṇasūnāsthānam āgamyāvatasthe | te ca tadvadhādhikṛtāḥ puruṣā yūthapatim ādāya rājñe darśayāmāsuḥ |
children.translated_text: Then the <s>Bodhisattva</s>, having arrived near <s>Vārāṇasī</s>, pausing briefly, said to the deer-herd: 'Turn back now. For worldly associations are easy to part with. Just as prosperity, inherently fickle — having long enjoyed a lotus-forest delightful in the spring season — goes away, abandoning it when its petals, filaments, and seed-pods have withered in the frost season, devoid of fragrance; and just as lightning-flashes, like disenchanted courtesans — having illuminated the faces of the quarter-brides veiled behind rain-season cloud-garments, and having displayed a dance, as it were — abandon the rain-clouds, grown light from their waters draining in the autumn season, like lovers who have lost their wealth; and just as the moon, the ornamental mark on the face of the night, though cool-rayed, is abandoned at dawn along with its innate radiance — in every way there is nothing in this world that is not eventually parted from what it is joined with. Therefore, reflecting thus, you should protect yourselves well, being devoted to the <s>Dharma</s>.' And that deer-herd, having stood watching the <s>Bodhisattva</s> depart until he was beyond the range of sight, returned to that forest — which now seemed empty — with hearts wounded by the dart of grief as if by separation from a father. And the <s>Bodhisattva</s> arrived and stood at the slaughter-house, which was fearsome with packs of dogs clinging to heaps of bones of deer, wild boars, and buffalo, fighting [over them], with scattered lumps of flesh upon which swarms of flies alighted and departed, with sharpened knives placed ready, and which was filled with butchers awaiting the arrival of animals.
Then the king, doe-eyed himself, addressed
that deer:
'Your herd is not yet diminished —
tell me, why have you come of your own accord?'
The <s>Bodhisattva</s> said:
'O lord, a pregnant doe
has come to me for refuge;
as she yearns to see her offspring,
I have come in her turn.'
'Having fulfilled the heart's desire
of that doe who wishes to see her fawn,
I consider death a joyous festival,
being supremely pleased.'
'That grief which arose in me upon seeing
both a doe and a deer going to their death here —
that [grief] shall not exist today.'
'Therefore slay me now, O lord of men!
Tell the butchers, O king — why do you delay?
Bound by the exceedingly long armor of compassion,
the arrow of despair cannot pierce this heart of mine.'

children.text: atha sa rājā tasya tāṃ parārthapratipattipaṭīyasīm anukampāṃ vicintya vismitamatir upālabdha iva lajjayā bodhisattvam uvāca | sādhu sādhu yūthapate |
children.translated_text: Then that king, reflecting upon his compassion — so adept in devotion to the welfare of others — his mind struck with wonder, as if rebuked, said with embarrassment to the <s>Bodhisattva</s>: 'Well done, well done, O herd-leader!'
'With your mind intent on accomplishing the welfare of others,
you, in the form of a deer, are the foremost among persons;
we, whose efforts are bent toward harming others,
are indeed equal to wild beasts and serpents!'

children.text: atha bodhisattvo vipratisāravantaṃ rājānam avetya jātaviśrambhamukham ity uvāca |
children.translated_text: Then the <s>Bodhisattva</s>, perceiving the king was remorseful and had assumed a trusting demeanor, said:
'Even an enemy who has committed offenses,

children.text: ripum api pāsi kila vyudasya kopam
children.translated_text: if he comes for refuge, you reportedly protect him, casting aside anger;
tell me then, how do your sharp arrows
fall upon these innocent deer?'
'Even in battle, you do not strike
an enemy who has turned his back;
how then do you kill
deer who are fleeing, terrified?'
'Abandon the sport of hunting,
nourished by wicked intentions —
it will become an offering
to the flickering flame of hell-fire!'

children.text: atha sa rājā pramuditamanās taṃ yūthapatiṃ mahati siṃhāsana āropya savinayaṃ nīcairāsanam adhiṣṭhāya proktavān | aho subhāṣitaṃ kriyatāṃ me mohatimirāpanodinī dharmadeśaneti | tato bodhisattvaḥ sakalayā rājaparṣadāvalokyamānas taṃ rājānaṃ saṃrādhayann ity uvāca |
children.translated_text: Then that king, his mind delighted, having seated the herd-leader upon a great lion-throne and himself respectfully taking a lower seat, said: 'How wonderful is your wise speech! Bestow upon me a discourse on <s>Dharma</s> that dispels the darkness of delusion.' Then the <s>Bodhisattva</s>, being gazed upon by the entire royal assembly, gratifying that king, spoke thus:
'Delight in wise sayings, freedom from the pride of prosperity,
action adept in accomplishing the welfare of others,
insatiable desire for virtues, and respect for the virtuous —
this is the deeply rooted conduct of the great-souled.'
'The two insignia of a [true] human being, brightly displaying lofty brilliance,
are these two:'
'fearlessness even in calamities, through the dignity of mind,
and a sense of shame that illuminates the path of the noble.'
'The wicked, whose hearts are inherently soiled,
are vigilant in vain over the disgrace of others;
the wise, whose minds are fixed on purifying their own hearts,
are exceedingly compassionate toward even those [wicked ones].'
'Even among men of equal fortune and valor,
not everyone's action benefits others;
when the cloudless sky blazes with stars,
it is <s>Agastya</s> [the star Canopus] alone that renders the waters poison-free.'
'A good person, even when merely thought of, evokes wonder
through his far-reaching noble conduct;
but when he comes within the sight of embodied beings,
he sprinkles their minds as if with nectar.'
'One whose stream of water of benevolence toward others is never cut off,

children.text: dhīcakṣuś ca viyogi yasya tamasā dvāv eva tau jāgrataḥ
children.translated_text: and one whose eye of wisdom is never parted from light — only these two are truly awake;
for all others — those of animal-nature, whose minds are dull regarding the task of benefiting others,
whose minds are heedless, sunken in the sleep of ignorance — day and night are the same.'
'For a good person wandering in <s>saṃsāra</s>, in its great darkness, or standing firm —

children.text: sādhoḥ sādhuphale nitāntamahatī dve eva te māṃ prati
children.translated_text: two [occasions] alone, bearing noble fruit, are truly great for me:'

children.text: yatra projjhya gṛhaṃ tapovanam abhiprasthīyate śreyase
children.translated_text: 'when one abandons the household and sets forth to the ascetic forest for the highest good,

children.text: yasmin vā kriyate vivekapaṭubhiḥ sākaṃ kathā sūribhiḥ
children.translated_text: and when one holds discourse with sages skilled in discernment.'

children.text: bhujyante svagṛhasthitā iva sukhaṃ yasyārthibhiḥ saṃpadaḥ
children.translated_text: 'One whose riches are enjoyed by supplicants as comfortably as if they were in their own homes,

children.text: paṭvī yasya ca dhīs tamaḥprahataye dvāv eva tau prāṇitaḥ
children.translated_text: and one whose keen intellect destroys darkness — only these two are truly alive;

children.text: yas tv ātmaṃbharir unnate 'pi vibhave hīnaś ca vidvattayā
children.translated_text: but one who is self-serving, even though his wealth be exalted, and lacking in wisdom —
his very existence, like that of a figure bearing only the appearance of a painted gem, is really non-existence!'

children.text: kṛcchrāl labdham api krameṇa bhavati prabhraṃśi bhūyaḥ sukhaṃ
children.translated_text: 'Happiness, even when obtained with difficulty, gradually decays and is lost;

children.text: tadbhraṃśe paritāpam eti puruṣaś cittānalaṃ jvālayan
children.translated_text: upon its loss, a man suffers torment, kindling the fire of the mind;
the cause of this suffering is the cunning, net-bearing [craving] that generates the chain of existence —

children.text: te 'tyantaṃ sukhino manaḥsu nihitā yaiḥ samyag alpecchatā
children.translated_text: those who have properly implanted contentment (<s>alpecchatā</s>) in their minds are supremely happy!'

children.text: mohacchedi subhāṣitaṃ vinayati dravyaṃ vinaiva śramād
children.translated_text: 'A delusion-cutting wise saying generates wealth without any effort;

children.text: adravye tu bhavanty api sphuṭapadā vyarthopadeśā giraḥ
children.translated_text: but when there is no [corresponding] substance, even words of clearly articulated teaching are futile —
even by a most skillful blacksmith, from iron — rough with spots —
though forged into a bell, the splendor of a sapphire pregnant with glory cannot be produced.'

children.text: iti guṇāguṇāntaravidā mahārājena satpathāśrayiṇā bhavitavyam iti | atha sa rājā dharmakathāmṛtāsvādaprīṇitamanā dattamṛgābhayaḥ sabahumānam iti bodhisattvaṃ praśaśaṃsa |
children.translated_text: Thus, the great king, knowing the difference between virtue and fault, should take refuge in the righteous path. Then that king, his mind delighted by tasting the nectar of the <s>Dharma</s> discourse, having granted safety to the deer, praised the <s>Bodhisattva</s> respectfully, saying:

children.text: utpāde sati loka eṣa maraṇavyādhiśramair bādhyate
children.translated_text: 'Once born, this world is afflicted by death, disease, and fatigue;
for the world bound by the thread of craving, these very sorrows recur;
thus <s>saṃsāra</s>, with its unbroken terror of rebirth, until cessation [<s>nirvṛti</s>] —

children.text: yuṣmatsaṃgamahetur ity avamato nāyaṃ sadoṣo 'pi naḥ
children.translated_text: is not despised by us, because it is the cause of encountering [beings] like you, even though it is full of faults.'

children.text: atha bodhisattvaḥ siṃhāsanād avatīrya rājānam āpapracche |
children.translated_text: Then the <s>Bodhisattva</s>, descending from the lion-throne, took leave of the king:
'Without me, O best of men, the deer-herd
will be despondent and agitated;
rule this earth free from thorns for a long time —
I go swiftly to their side.'

children.text: tataḥ sa yūthapatiḥ kṣitipālānumatas tad eva vanam ājagāma |
children.translated_text: Then that herd-leader, with the king's permission, returned to that very forest.
Then, seeing the herd-leader from afar,
that joyful deer-herd, with eager eyes,
grasping tips of <s>darbha</s> grass in their front teeth,
came swiftly to greet him in a row.
The earth, which had been as if with closed eyes
when the herd-leader had departed from the forest,
when that steadfast one returned there,
became as if with opened eyes again.
Then that doe, having approached the foremost of deer,
spoke thus, joyful, with moving, long eyes:

children.text: prahlādayan mama manaḥ śiśur eṣa dāve
children.translated_text: 'Gladdening my heart, this little one of mine, in the meadow,
plays, O lord of deer, by your grace!'

children.text: bodhisattvo 'pi ca tan mṛgayūthadvayam āśvāsya parāṃ prītim upajagāma | tad evaṃ parahitaparāyaṇaḥ sa bhagavāṃs tiryagbhūto 'py āsīd iti vincintya tadupāropitaprasādā bhavata yūyam iti ||
children.translated_text: And the <s>Bodhisattva</s>, having consoled both deer-herds, attained supreme delight. Thus, the Blessed One was devoted to the welfare of others even when born as an animal — reflecting upon this, may you be filled with faith arising from that! ||
|| The Deer <s>Jātaka</s>, the first ||
12. Peacock
By the <s>Bodhisattva</s> who, in the form of a peacock, protected beings by guarding moral conduct (<s>śīla</s>) —

children.text: prāṇabhayād yena purā kas tatra na ropayed bhaktim //
children.translated_text: who, [saving others] from the fear of death, would not develop devotion toward him?

children.text:
tadyathānuśrūyate
surabhikamalavanacchannamahāvimalasalilena prahlāditasiddhajanamānasena mānasena mahāsarasā sakalaśaśimaṇḍalabimbenevālaṃkṛtaikadeśe tripathagāsalilanipātakṣobhitabhūrjadevadārunameruvane prasrutānekaprasravaṇe tuhinopacayasthūlataraśikharasahasratayā rajatastambhair ivoparisamākīrṇe kesarisaṃtrāsaprasthitacamarayūthasphuritavālasaṃghātopavījyamānanikuñje nirjharasalilaprakṣālyamānaśilātale kusumitalatāprāntabhrāntamukharamadhukaragaṇasaṃgīte sābhiṣeka iva rājamāne bhūdharavare himavati dhautendranīlavimaladaṇḍākṛtiśirodharaḥ śaṅkhacchedāvadātāpāṅgadeśaḥ sphuṭitapāribhadrakakusumābhiraktatuṇḍo vipulavicitrapakṣatir indīvarapalāśākīrṇataruṇaśirīṣakusumasaṃghātānurūpabṛhatkalāpaḥ suvarṇāvabhāso nāma bodhisattvo mayūrādhipatir babhūva |
children.translated_text:
Thus it is heard:
On the great mountain <s>Himavat</s> — which was resplendent as if crowned, adorned in one part by the great lake <s>Mānasa</s> with its great, pure waters concealed by forests of fragrant lotuses, which refreshed the minds of <s>Siddha</s>-folk, like the full disc of the moon; with its <s>Meru</s>-grove of birch and <s>devadāru</s> trees stirred by the impact of the <s>Gaṅgā</s>'s waters, with many flowing streams, its peak-summits thickened by the accumulation of snow into thousands [of points] seeming strewn above with silver pillars; with bowers fanned by the waving tails of herds of <s>camara</s> yaks startled by lions; with rock-surfaces washed by waterfall-waters; resonant with the song of swarms of buzzing bees wandering near the tips of blossoming creepers — there lived a <s>Bodhisattva</s> as king of the peacocks, named <s>Suvarṇāvabhāsa</s> (Golden Radiance). He had a neck like a staff of polished sapphire, corners of the eyes as white as a cut conch-shell, a beak reddened like a blossoming <s>pāribhadraka</s> flower, vast and variegated plumage, and a great tail resembling a mass of young <s>śirīṣa</s> blossoms strewn with blue-lotus petals.
Having produced that supreme peacock,
with wonderfully variegated plumage,
even the artisan-craftsmen [of karma]
seemed to gaze upon him with astonishment.
When the female peacocks watched that king of peacocks
who was seized by the passion for dancing at the onset of clouds,
the coquetries of the modestly blushing lightning-dancers
became only faintly radiant.
In the waterfall that resounded like a <s>mṛdaṅga</s> drum,
and amid the sweetly humming bee-<s>vīṇās</s>,
in the charming inner bower of the vine-forest,
he, the peacock-dancer, danced wondrously.
When he, with his circle of shimmering eye-spot jewels [in his train],
ascended the bank-edge and danced,
the <s>Himālaya</s>, its forest stirred by the breeze,
seemed to appear as if wearing a crown.
When his beloved [peahen] spreads her lovely tail-plumage on the earth —
as if a <s>tilaka</s> mark drawn by <s>Anaṅga</s>'s (Cupid's) bride on the canvas of the earth —
Standing there, the gaze of the <s>siddha</s>-women upon the peacock,
was not satisfied, due to their intense curiosity.
When the autumn season arrived, with the horizon-edges covered by pale cloud-masses,
and the water [clear as] a string of pearls —
that land on which he released his moon-gem [plumage-spots]
appeared as if [strewn] with fragments of sapphire.
When the beloved one moved slowly, his plumage without horripilation,
skilled in the singular manner of walking followed by his flock,
the earth around that best of mountains, [adorned by] the peacock-king,
shone as if dappled with rainbows.

children.text: atha kadācid anilabalavibhidyamānakusumagandhādhivāsitadiṅmukheṣu bhramadalikulaśabaleṣu kalabharadanaparipāṇḍuṣu rāmaṇīyakaṃ gateṣu ketakeṣu kuṭajakakubhanīpakadambakusumasurabhīkṛtanikuñjeṣv indragopakābhyalaṃkṛtamarakataharitaśādvalaśyāmavanabhūmiṣu nayanaramyeṣu mahīdhareṣu sphuritataḍidvalayalāñchitodareṣu darśitendrāyudheṣu dhārāśaranipātaprodvāsitanidāghavairiṣu nabhaḥpidhāyiṣu jaladhareṣu śiśiraśīkarasparśāpanītadivasakarasaṃtāpeṣu parityajatsu candanadrumān phaṇiṣu prathamapūrapriyatamataraṅgahastāvalucyamānaphenāvataṃsāsu kaluṣasalilavasanapidhīyamānavipulapulinajaghanāsu mattāsv iva prāgalbhyam upagatāsu saridaṅganāsu sabāṣpaproṣitabhartṛkājananayanāvalokyamāneṣu meghadhvanipramuditeṣu vimuktamadhurārāveṣu gṛhamayūreṣu navajaladasalilakaṇanipātajanitakaṇakaṇāśabdeṣu tālatālīnālikeravaneṣu sa mayūrarājaḥ prabhātasamaye tanujalakaṇagurukṛtakalāpaḥ śrutihṛdayahāriṇīṃ kekāṃ vimuñcan nabhaḥśobhārtham ivotpatya vārāṇasīsamīpena prāgāt | tasyāṃ ca puri brahmadattena rājñā saha suptaprativibuddhā parasparapariṣvaṅgāpahṛtavilepanā kiṃcitparipāṭalalocanotpalānupamā nāma tasya rājño devī papraccha |
children.translated_text: Now, once, when the horizon-edges were perfumed by the fragrance of flowers scattered by the force of the wind; when the <s>ketaka</s> flowers had attained their beauty — pale as the teeth of young elephants, mottled with swarms of roaming bees; when the groves were made fragrant by the blossoms of <s>kuṭaja</s>, <s>kubha</s>, <s>nīpa</s>, and <s>kadamba</s>; when the forest-grounds were green with emerald-colored meadows adorned with glow-worms; when the mountains were delightful to the eye; when the clouds — their bellies marked with flashing garlands of lightning, having displayed the rainbow, their rain-arrow-fall having driven away the enemy that was summer, concealing the sky — [had arrived]; when the burning of the sun's rays had been removed by the touch of cool drizzle; when the serpents were abandoning the sandalwood trees; when the river-women — their foam-crests being torn away by the waves, the beloved arms of the first flood, their broad sandbar-hips covered by the garment of turbid water — appeared intoxicated, having attained boldness; when the household peacocks — beheld by the tearful eyes of women whose husbands had gone abroad — were gladdened by the thunder of clouds and had released their sweet cries; when the palm-groves, <s>tālī</s>-groves, and coconut-groves resounded with the patter-sound of falling drops of fresh cloud-water — that peacock-king, at dawn, his train made heavy by fine water-droplets, releasing his cry that captivated the ear and heart, flew up as if to adorn the sky, and passed near <s>Vārāṇasī</s>. And in that city, the queen of King <s>Brahmadatta</s>, named <s>Anupamā</s> — having awoken from sleep alongside him, her ointments rubbed off by their mutual embrace, her eye-lotuses slightly reddened — asked:
'Tell me, whose is this sound —
clear, O moon-faced one —',
'by which, as it is being carried across [the sky],
my mind has been gladdened?'

children.text: rājovaca | devi suvarṇāvabhāso nāma mānuṣālāpo mayūrarājo himavati kṛtādhivāsas tasyaiṣa nabhasā saṃcaramāṇasya prakṛtimanoharaḥ kanakamarakatendranīlavaiḍūryarāśiprabhāsvarasya svaraḥ | punaḥ sakutūhalā devy uvāca | kutaḥ punar asau mayūrādhipatir devasya śrutipatham āgata iti | rājovāca |
children.translated_text: The king said: 'O queen, there is a peacock-king named <s>Suvarṇāvabhāsa</s> ('Golden Radiance'), who speaks human speech and resides on the <s>Himālaya</s>. This is his voice as he traverses the sky — naturally enchanting, radiant with the splendor of heaps of gold, emerald, sapphire, and <s>vaiḍūrya</s>.' The queen, further curious, said: 'How has that lord of the peacocks come to the hearing of my lord?' The king said:
'Of men or of animals,
it is indeed their virtues that make them known —',
'as rays [make known] gems,
piercing the mass of darkness.'
'Having assumed the form of a peacock,
some [being], for some reason,
abides as a festival for the eyes
in the forest of the father of <s>Gaurī</s> [<s>Himālaya</s>].'
'The <s>Himālaya</s>, its caves adorned
by that lord of peacock-flocks,
considers itself
as if possessing a master.'
'The clouds, as if giving applause
with their thunder,',
'gaze upon him as he dances,
with their flashing lightning-eyes.'
'Summoned by the peacock as stage-director at the commencement of the drama of the rainy season,

children.text: sahasā taḍid ātmānaṃ darśayati naṭīva savilāsam //
children.translated_text: lightning suddenly reveals herself, playfully, like an actress.'

children.text: athānupamā tena tasya mayūrādhipateḥ śrutihāriṇā svareṇākṣiptahṛdayā mṛduhasitabhrūlatākṣepaparāvartanāvalokanakrīḍāparibṛṃhitair vilāsais taṃ rājānaṃ vaśīkṛtyovāca | deva kriyatāṃ yatnas tasya mayūrādhipater grahaṇāya | krīḍanako 'smākam antaḥpure bhaviṣyati |
children.translated_text: Then <s>Anupamā</s>, her heart seized by that ear-captivating voice of the peacock-lord, having brought the king under her control through graceful charms — enhanced by gentle laughter, brow-creeper play, turning away, and sidelong glances — said: 'My lord, let effort be made for the capture of that peacock-lord! He shall be a plaything in our inner palace!'
'By a peacock bearing brilliant moon-gem spots,
placed amidst the inner palace —',
'let the ground of our house become
like [a surface adorned with] various gem ear-ornaments!'

children.text: rājovāca | devi na kilāsau śakyate grahītum | devy uvāca |
children.translated_text: The king said: 'O queen, that one simply cannot be captured!' The queen said:
'Men who possess shrewd valor and cunning devices
bring under control even powerful elephants
that exude fragrant drops of ichor —',
'how much more so birds whose strength is slight!'
'Even a fish, large-scaled, fallen from the path of the eyes,
is drawn from the midst of water by a hook!',
'What is impossible for the resourceful?
When there is determination, actions bear fruit!'
'Your intellect is exceptionally keen,
you have many wise helpers —',
'if my wish is not fulfilled by you,
then you are surely turned away from affection [for me]!'
'A she-pigeon, wishing to protect her nestlings in their nest,
repeatedly sprinkled water upon the forest fire,',
'carrying it with her thin wing-cups from the river.

children.text: snigdho jano na khalu cintayati svapīḍām
children.translated_text: A loving being does not consider its own pain!'

children.text: atha sa rājā mā devi krodhaṃ kārṣīr akāryam api tvadarthe kuryām | ataḥ karomy ahaṃ tadgrahaṇāya yatnam ity uvāca |
children.translated_text: Then the king said: 'O queen, do not be angry! I would do even an improper thing for your sake. Therefore, I shall make the effort for his capture.' And he said:
'With the noose of coquetry that is drawn by the passion
of alluring women, his mind bound,
his awareness asleep to the search for good and evil —',
'even a non-violent person proceeds toward the state of a killer.'
'She who, having obtained limbs made of divine splendor,
became celebrated as the celestial woman <s>Tilottamā</s> —',
'even the three-eyed lord of the three worlds [<s>Śiva</s>]',
'was made four-faced by her own beauty!'
'The treasure of austerity, the son of <s>Gādhi</s> [<s>Viśvāmitra</s>], in the austerity-grove,
of mighty intellect, his senses stolen by <s>Menakā</s> —',
'<s>Kāma</s>, pulling [his bow] with contempt, his bow of lotus-stalks,
pierced him with an arrow, laughing!'
'Whatever causes frivolity to increase, whatever causes the dust of humiliation to fall upon one's head,',
'whatever arrows of reproach touch the mind —',
'[all] that is done to embodied beings
by women!'
'Putting on the armor of determination, placing the army of craving ahead,',
'forcibly mounting the utterly hard bow of shamelessness,',
'entering the midst of the battle of solicitation — men, made helpless by women,',
'endure the wound of the arrow of a frown, even from the lowly!'

children.text: atha sa rājā śākunikān āhūyāvocat | asti suvarṇāvabhāso nāma himavati mayūrādhipatis taṃ bhavantaḥ śīghram ānayantu | na ced āneṣyatha tataḥ sarvān eva bhavatas tīkṣṇena daṇḍenāntakasakāśaṃ praheṣyāmīti | te ca maraṇabhītās tatheti pratiśrutya kaṃcin nipuṇataraṃ śākunikam abhyarthya visarjayāmāsuḥ | sa ca śākunikaḥ krameṇa himācalam āgamya vijñāya tasya mayūrādhipater gocarabhūmiṃ viracayya pāśān ekānte 'vatasthe |
children.translated_text: Then the king summoned the fowlers and said: 'There is a peacock-lord named <s>Suvarṇāvabhāsa</s> on the <s>Himālaya</s>. Let the gentlemen bring him quickly! If you do not bring him, I shall send all of you to the presence of Death with severe punishment!' And they, frightened of death, having assented with 'So be it,' requested a certain most skillful fowler and dispatched him. That fowler, gradually reaching the <s>Himālaya</s>, having ascertained the feeding-ground of that peacock-lord, having set snares, stood hidden in a secluded spot.
Whatever snare-net was placed by that fowler
near the high peaks of the snowy mountain,
all of it, merely upon being seen by that peacock,
was cut to pieces from afar.

children.text: atha himavati dūrasthā divyacakṣuṣo munayas taṃ bodhisattvaprabhāvam ālokya vismitamanasa evam ūcuḥ |
children.translated_text: Then the sages with divine sight who dwelt far away on the <s>Himālaya</s>, beholding that power of the <s>Bodhisattva</s>, with minds amazed, spoke thus:
'Just as these snares, tightly bound,
have been cut by this glorious one, an abode of merit, by his mere glance —',
'so too, the weapon of wisdom of this virtuous one, once he attains enlightenment,',
'will cut the bonds of the afflictions (<s>kleśa</s>)!'

children.text: atha sa śākunikaḥ pāśacchedaviṣaṇṇamanāḥ samupagamya kṛtāñjalis tasmai mayūrādhipataye tāṃ krūrāṃ rājājñām ākhyāyābravīt |
children.translated_text: Then that fowler, dejected at the cutting of the snares, approached with folded hands and told that peacock-lord the cruel royal command, and said:
'O refuge of those who seek refuge,
who fear the severance of their lives —',
'O lord of the white-cornered ones [peacocks],
you alone are indeed our shelter!'
'The snares were cut by you with your glance,
white-tipped like the cut surface of a conch —',
'being of such power,
how will you not protect us?'
Beholding him [the fowler], pitiable,
like a kinsman sunk in calamity —
the mind of that compassionate-souled one
was flooded with sorrow.
'How can this steadfast one not rescue beings
from calamity?' — thus,
the perfection of moral conduct (<s>śīla-pāramitā</s>)
seemed to stand in him beyond all doubt.

children.text: māṃ cen na saṃtyajasi bodhim avāptukāma
children.translated_text: 'If you do not abandon me, O desirer of enlightenment,
O best of peacocks, then protect these [fowlers] from the king's punishment!' —
thus, Compassion herself, the virtuous lady, as if made gracious by the perfection of his moral conduct,
spoke to the peacock.

children.text: atha bodhisattvas tān maraṇabhītān prati duḥkhāyamāna īdṛśam acintayat |
children.translated_text: Then the <s>Bodhisattva</s>, pained on behalf of those who feared death, reflected thus:
'If I, of sweet voice and beautiful plumage,
had not existed here in this forest —',
'then from the merciless king,',
'no fear would have come to the fowlers.'
'Therefore, lest this person, distressed of mind on my account,
should come to calamity —',
'driven by the king toward death,',
'I shall indeed protect him meanwhile!'
'When another perishes, whether with or without cause,
having come [into contact with oneself] —',
'what is the use of such a birth',
'for that person whose self is wounded by arrows of manifold reproach?'

children.text: iti bodhisattvaś cintayitvā tam uvāca | gacchatu bhavān agratas tasmai rājñe nivedayituṃ mamāgamanam iti | atha sa śākunikaḥ pramuditamanās tvaritam āgamya nyavedayad idānīm evāsmadanukampayā deva sa mayūrādhipatir āgacchatīti | tataḥ sa rājā saha devyā paurajanena ca kutūhalavaśāt tadāgamanapratīkṣī punaḥ punar antarīkṣam ālokayāmāsa | so 'pi ca mayūrarājaḥ samāśvāsya vinivartya cānugāminaṃ mayūragaṇam ambaratalam utpatya sahasaivopagamya prakṛtimadhurayā kekayā sakalaṃ vārāṇasījanam ānandayāmāsa | tatas tasya tāṃ kekām ākarṇya niyamena sa mayūrādhipatir āgacchatīti vicintya pramuditamanaso nūpuravirāvasaṃtrāsitakapotapālīnilīnapārāvatamithunāḥ drutataragamanavigalitakarṇāvataṃsakāḥ kāścid anavasitaviśeṣakāṅkitalalāṭamadhyāḥ sindūrābhitāmrāṅgulayo drutagamanavighnakāriṇe gurunitambabharāyātyasūyantyaḥ kiṃcid gatvā cāparā gurujanāvalokanavrīḍitāḥ punas tvaritāṃ gatim avarundhānāḥ praharṣavikasannayanakuvalayapalāśaprāntaspṛṣṭaśravaṇāntāś ca kāścid aparāḥ punar ardhālikhitaṃ citraphalakam apāsya kṣīṇaprāṇaprāyaprāntavartikāḥ karaṇḍakeṣu vinikṣipya sitajaladatuhinakundamṛṇālasphaṭikarajatadhavalāni saudhatalāny āruruhur aparāś ca striyo vātāyanāny abhijagmuḥ |
children.translated_text: Having reflected thus, the <s>Bodhisattva</s> said to him: 'Let the gentleman go ahead to announce my arrival to the king.' Then that fowler, his mind delighted, quickly came and reported: 'Just now, out of compassion for us, O lord, that peacock-king is coming!' Then the king, together with the queen and the citizens, out of curiosity, eager for his arrival, gazed again and again at the sky. And that peacock-king, having reassured and turned back his following flock of peacocks, flying up into the vault of the sky, suddenly approaching, gladdened the entire populace of <s>Vārāṇasī</s> with his naturally sweet cry. Then, hearing his cry and thinking 'That peacock-lord is certainly coming!' — with delighted minds, some women [rushed out], their pigeon-pairs in the dovecotes startled and hiding at the tinkling of their anklets; some with garlands fallen from their ears in their hasty going; some with the forehead-marks of <s>viśeṣaka</s> half-drawn in the center of their foreheads; their fingers reddened with vermilion; some cursing the heavy burden of their ample hips as an obstacle to their rapid movement; and others, having gone some distance, then restraining their hurried pace out of modesty before their elders, the lotus-petal edges of their eyes expanded with joy touching the rim of their ears; and still others, setting aside a half-painted picture-panel, placing their nearly exhausted brushes into their boxes — ascended the white palace-terraces, white as fresh clouds, snow, <s>kunda</s> flowers, lotus-fiber, crystal, and silver; and other women went to the latticed windows.
Then, with the wide-eyed faces of the women
standing at the latticed windows,
agitated with excitement at beholding the peacock —
the city shone greatly, as if with many moons.
Out of curiosity, their crow-wing [side-locks] tossed by the wind,
swift, with eyes charming as [those of] fawns,
gazed upon with delighted minds by their mothers —
children emerged from their houses with upturned faces.
Abandoning their play of delightful ball-tossing,
their lovely forehead-regions bound with fine drops of perspiration,
their upper garments slightly raised by their budding breasts —
the maidens came out, with slender arm-creepers.
'Here he is! Here he is!' — thus, by the royal women, rising [on tiptoe] for a view of the peacock,
with the radiance of their manifest nail-gems, [fingers] red as lotus petals —
the faces of the smiling, beautiful royal women —
that city appeared as if sprouting [with leaf-tips of their fingers].

children.text: kṣaṇāc ca surāsurasaṃgrāmāt kṣurapranikṛttadaṇḍaḥ ketur iva vividhamaṇivicitras tasya rājño bhavanāntarālam alaṃkurvan sa mayūrarājo nipapāta |
children.translated_text: And in an instant, like a banner from a battle of gods and demons, its pole cut by a razor — variegated with diverse gems, adorning the interior of that king's palace, the peacock-king alighted.
Then simultaneously, the gazes of the people fell
upon that peacock with his coral-colored beak and weighty train,

children.text: dadati dhanam udāre kṣipram āśāḥ samantād
children.translated_text: as hopes from all directions quickly fall
upon a generous giver of wealth, a bestower of desired fruits upon suppliants.
The king and queen, beholding
that peacock-king, were delighted, having obtained their wish.

children.text: lokasya durlabham avāpya hi vastu kiṃcit
children.translated_text: For having obtained something rare for the world,
the weary mind seems to bear the joy of delight.

children.text: tataḥ pramuditamanāḥ sa rājā taṃ mayūrarājaṃ rājārhe radanapāde samupaveśyāsane paścād āsanam adhyatiṣṭhat | atha bodhisattvo madhuragambhīreṇa svareṇa taṃ rājānam ity ābabhāṣe |
children.translated_text: Then that king, with a delighted mind, seated the peacock-king upon a royal ivory throne, and afterward took his own seat. Then the Bodhisattva addressed that king in a sweet and deep voice:
'Having conquered the powerful senses by the force of intellect,
constantly rewarding the affection of the devoted with fruit,
casting aside vices from this ocean-girdled earth,
O protector of the earth, protect the world long with wise governance.'
'Are your bridges made of <s>Dharma</s>
flourishing well —
those bridges upon which you will cross
the fathomless ocean of suffering?'
'By the cruel sense-pleasures that watch for an opening,
like badly caught serpents,
whose great faults have been recognized —
you are not overly tormented by them, I trust?'
'Is all well with your disciplined servants,
your wives, and your sons?
Is all well with you, O king,
in body, and in this treasury of fame?'
The king spoke:
'There is indeed distress for embodied beings,
O lord of peacocks,
as long as there is no encounter with one
skilled in others' welfare, such as yourself.'
'Resounding with the thunder of <s>muraja</s> drums and clouds,
its interior adorned with the lightning of dancing women —
having obtained you, O peacock-king, my palace
has become like the rainy season.'
'The moon is the ornamental mark of the face of the lovely sky;
a pure gem is the adornment of a bright ornament.',
'O lord of peacocks, long desired, you have become
the adornment of this great palace of mine.'

children.text: ity abhisaṃrādhya sa rājā dīpaprabhāvabhāsitabhavanāntarāle prācīvadhūgṛhītaśaśidarpaṇe vibhāvyamānatārakākumudavanābhyalaṃkṛtanabhaḥsarasi prāpte ca kṣaṇadāmukhe surabhikusumapallavāstīrṇaṃ mayūrādhipataye mṛdu śayanīyam ādideśa | divase divase ca paripākasurabhimṛdūni phalāni prāyacchat | atha kadācit kāle gacchati sa rājā kiṃcit karaṇīyam uddiśya bodhisattvam anupamāyā devyā haste nikṣipya nātimahatā sainyenānugamyamānas turagakhurapuṭotkhātamārgapāṃsuparidhūsarakisalayakusumamañjarīkāṇi vanāntarāṇi kurvann amalasalilavāhinītaṭavetasacchāyānilīnaniścalabakabalākāvalokyamānacakitaśapharīkulākulataṭapayaskāḥ tvaritarathacaraṇadhvanisaṃtrāsarasitacakravākamithunaparityajyamānasitapulinās tās tāḥ samudrapatnīr ālokayaṃs trastasāraṅgotpatanasācīkṛtāni caṭulabahunayanānīva digantarāṇi paśyan prasṛtagokuladaśanacchidyamānaśaṣpāṅkurān ikṣuvaṇoparuddhān anekāṃś ca grāmasīmno 'tikramya kiṃcid deśāntaraṃ jagāma |
children.translated_text: Having thus pleased the Bodhisattva, that king, in the palace interior illuminated by lamplight — when the evening had arrived, the eastern quarter like a bride holding the mirror of the moon, the lake of the sky adorned by the water-lily garden of visible stars — ordered a soft bed, strewn with fragrant flowers and shoots, for the lord of peacocks. And day after day he offered him ripe, fragrant, and soft fruits. Then, in time, the king, intending some business, entrusted the Bodhisattva to the hands of Queen <s>Anupamā</s>, and followed by a modest army, making the forest interiors have their shoots and blossom-clusters dusted with road-dirt churned up by horse-hooves, gazing at those rivers — wives of the ocean — whose banks teemed with startled schools of fish watched by motionless herons and cranes sheltering in the shade of willows along pure flowing waters, whose white sandbanks were abandoned by pairs of <s>cakravāka</s> birds crying out in alarm at the sound of the swift chariot-wheels — seeing the horizons appearing to dart about with many restless eyes, like startled <s>sāraṅga</s> deer taking flight — crossing many village-boundaries where pastures of sprouting grass, cropped by grazing herds of cattle, were hemmed in by sugarcane fields — he departed to a certain other region.
Then that queen of the king, her face confused
by smoky tresses, her body very pale,
fixed her long-lashed eye, extended through the window,
for a long time upon a passing cunning rake.
And seeing that beautiful-eyed one, a delight to the eyes,
that chief of rakes approached the wall.

children.text: pārśvāni vīkṣya cakitā ca punaḥ punaḥ sā
children.translated_text: And she, looking nervously to the sides again and again,
released a fragrant ear-lotus upon his body.
Having taken up that blue lotus with opening petals,

children.text: āghrāya mūrdhni ca niveśya sa jṛmbhamāṇaḥ
children.translated_text: smelling it and placing it on his head, he, stretching with delight,
when the sun had set, helplessly, somehow,
guided by her gaze, slowly departed.
Going then to a courtesan's house, that pleasure-seeker,
with his heart deeply distressed, lying upon the bed,
his sighs betraying the strikes of Cupid's arrows,
yearned intensely for her, having lost all composure.
The courtesan spoke to the rake in jest:
'I see the noble gentleman as if empty now.'
Then that trickster spoke, hiding his feelings:

children.text: dyūte jito 'ham iti tena vitānatā me
children.translated_text: 'I was defeated at dice, hence my distress.'

children.text: atha sa viṭas tāṃ varṣaśatopamāṃ rajanīṃ manyamānas tadgatamanāḥ samutthāya rahasi kasmaicit suhṛde taṃ vṛttāntam āvedayāmāsa | śrūyatāṃ vayasya hyo mayā yad anubhūtam iti | yeyaṃ rājño 'gramahiṣī nimeṣamātreṇa mānuṣīti loke varṇyate salīlam ālokayantyā karṇād ādāya |
children.translated_text: Then that rake, considering that night to be like a hundred years, his mind absorbed in her, arose and in private informed a certain friend of the incident: 'Hear, O friend, what I experienced yesterday. She who is the king's chief queen, described in the world as human only for the blink of an eye [i.e., like a goddess] — while playfully gazing, taking from her ear —'
'Leaning upon the window, that graceful one,
gleaming with the rays of her jewel-like teeth flashing in her smile,
she, <s>Anupamā</s> ('Peerless') by name, the lotus-eyed one,
peerless in beauty — released a lotus upon me.'
'Her moon-like face joined with the window's opening,
stealing the moonlight with the luster of her jewel-like teeth,
with the bow of her eyebrow playfully raised,
she, of slender body, released the arrow of her glance upon me.'

children.text: tac cintyatāṃ tāvat saṃgamopāya iti | atha suhṛd vihasyovāca | kadācit kākatālīyam idaṃ bhavet tvaṃ ca nṛpatibhavanabhittisamīpam anuprāptas tasyāś ca katham api kim apy ālokayantyāḥ | svayam eva tavopari karṇotpalaṃ patitaṃ syād ato mā bhavān gaṇikāviṭajanamadhyam āgamyātmānaṃ hāsyavastu kārṣīt | tat parityajyatām ayam asadvikalpaḥ | yady api ca kāmayamānayā rājamahiṣyā tavopari karṇotpalaṃ pātitaṃ syāt tathāpi na yujyata eveyam utkaṇṭhā | durlabhakāminījanasamāgamopāyacintā hi puruṣasya mahatīm aratim utpādayati | nidrām apaharaty aṅgāni durbalayati bhojanarucim apāsyati | hitavādinām api suhṛdām upadeśaṃ nābhinandati pravṛddhanavasalilaughasarid iva taṭalatāṃ dharmasthitim unmūlayati ramyāṇy api dveṣṭi | sajjanaguṇakathābhyasūyinī sarvathā pratisaṃkhyānabaleneyam abhāvaṃ śakyate netum iti | viṭa uvāca | anekadehalīlaṅghanā jaghanasaṃparkaniṣṇātabuddhayo mādṛśā dhūrtapuruṣāḥ kathaṃ sakāmām akāmāṃ vā sīmantinīṃ na jñāsyanti | śrūyatāṃ vayasya | śravaṇakaṇḍūyanastanaprakāśanalajjāparāvṛttāvalokanahasitādayo hi bhāvāḥ strīṇāṃ sakāmaṃ hṛdayam āviṣkurvantīti | kim atra saṃdehena | suhṛd uvāca | yady evaṃ khagapatir iva prākāram api laṅghayitvā bhavān nṛpatibhavanaṃ rātrau praviśet | kiṃ nv akṛtasaṃketā tatrabhavatī rājamahiṣī pratibodhyamānā tvayā |
children.translated_text: 'So let us think about the means of meeting.' Then the friend, laughing, said: 'Perhaps this is a mere coincidence — you happened to be near the palace wall and her ear-lotus simply fell upon you of its own accord. Therefore abandon this improper notion. Even if the queen did drop the ear-lotus upon you out of desire, still this yearning is not appropriate. For thinking about the means of meeting an unattainable woman produces great distress in a man — it steals sleep, weakens the body, removes the appetite for food. It does not welcome even the advice of well-meaning friends. Like a river swollen by a fresh flood of water, it uproots the creeper of righteous conduct from its bank. It hates even what is delightful. Envious of the tales of virtuous people's qualities — by all means, this can be destroyed only by the force of discriminating reflection.' The rake said: 'How would cunning men like me, whose intelligence is well-versed in amorous affairs across many encounters, not recognize whether a married woman is willing or not? Hear, O friend: the gestures of women — scratching the ear, displaying the breast, looking away with embarrassment, laughing — reveal a desiring heart. What doubt is there?' The friend said: 'If so, then like a bird you might scale even the palace wall and enter the royal compound at night. But what if the queen, without a prior assignation, is awakened by you?'
'With her lotus eyes confused by disturbed sleep,
her body trembling, garment slipping from her hips,
speaking fearfully: "Who is this?" —
she will be like a doe frightened by a tiger.'

children.text: tataḥ parijanakolāhalaprabuddhakāñcukīye rājakule nāyatikṣamam etat karma paśyāmi | evaṃ ca tayor mitho vicārayator eva mṛdugamanacalitamukharanūpuramanoharacaraṇakamalayugalavinyāsenārcayantīva vasudhātalam abhinayagatim iva darśayantī cakitahariṇanayanaspardhinā savilāsāvalokanadviguṇaśobhena karṇasuhṛdā cakṣuṣā hrepitam iva kiṃcid avanataṃ karṇotpalaṃ niyacchantī sthūlamuktāhāramaṇiprabhoddyotitagurupayodharā payodharavirahaprakāśaniśākarā niśeva mūrtimatī kiṃcid ātapajanitasvedakaṇajālakākrāntaviśeṣakāntā viśeṣakāntabakulamālikāparipūritakeśahastā hastāvalambitaśithilamekhalākalāpā kalāpicandrakamadhyanīlam uttarīyam udvahantī pratanumecakayā romarājyā vipulagambhīranābhinimnatām iva didṛkṣamāṇayopaśobhitatrivalītaraṅgaviṣamamadhyā madhyāhnasamayadivasakarakiraṇāliṅgiteva kamalamālā gamanapariśramavaśād īṣatparimlānasukumāraśarīrayaṣṭiḥ karpūrasurabhitāmbūlarāgāruṇādharā pariṇatalavalīphalābhipāṇḍukapolatalālikhitapattralekhā vigrahavatīva lakṣmīr lakṣmīvatī nāmānupamarūpānupamayā devyā prahitā vacanakuśalā kuśalaśilpighaṭiteva kanakapratimā dūtī | samāgamyābhivādya ca tad viṭadvayam upaviśya vijñāya ca tayor niryantraṇasuhṛttāṃ viśrabdham eva rājamahiṣīvṛttāntam ācaṣṭe |
children.translated_text: 'Then, with the attendants roused by the commotion and the chamberlains alerted in the royal household, I see this deed as not feasible.' And while the two were thus deliberating, there appeared a messenger — as if worshipping the earth's surface with the placement of her pair of charming lotus-feet set to music by the tinkling anklets of her gentle gait, displaying as it were an actress's walk, with eyes rivaling those of a startled doe whose beauty was doubled by playful sidelong glances, who slightly lowered her ear-lotus as if abashed — her heavy breasts illuminated by the luster of a necklace of large pearls, like a moonlit night revealing the moon from behind the clouds, slightly beautiful with the perspiration-droplets born of the sun's heat upon her forehead-mark, her tresses adorned with fragrant <s>bakula</s> garlands arranged like hair-ornaments, her loosened girdle-tassel dangling from her hand, wearing a dark-blue upper garment with the color of a peacock-eye feather, her slender line of body-hair adorning the three folds above the deep and expansive navel as if gazing into its depth, like a garland of lotuses embraced by the rays of the midday sun, her delicate body slightly wilted from the exertion of walking, her lips reddened by the crimson of <s>tāmbūla</s> (betel) fragrant with camphor, her cheek-surface pale as ripe <s>lavalī</s> fruit with painted leaf-designs — an embodiment of <s>Lakṣmī</s> herself — a skillful speaker named <s>Lakṣmīvatī</s>, a messenger sent by Queen <s>Anupamā</s> of peerless form, fashioned as if by a skilled artisan like a golden image. Having approached, greeted the pair of rakes, sat down, and perceiving their unreserved friendship, she confidently related the queen's story:
'O representative of the Flower-weaponed one (Cupid), when you were seen
passing within the palace by <s>Anupamā</s>, the king's wife,
she, my friend, placing her lotus-face upon her palm,
from that time bears emaciation and pallor.'
'Now bearing a body thinner,
pale as lotus-stalk mud, having lost composure,
<s>Manmatha</s> (Cupid) ceaselessly shoots all his arrows
into the mind of my friend, O companion.'
'From the heat born of her body,
her flower-bed wilts daily, she whose body is emaciated by Love;
even gazing upon the beautiful garden,
she does not delight, like a doe separated from the herd.'
'Therefore, this one whose body is struck by the arrows of the flower-bowed one,
whose cheeks quiver with unceasing sighs,
whose beautiful face is downcast with shame —
console my friend at least with words today.'

children.text: athāvasitavacanāyāṃ tasyāṃ dūtyāṃ sa tasya vayasyo vihasyāvocat | avaśyam eva sphuṭitasahakāramañjarīko vasantasamayaḥ kokilayā saha yujyate | siddhās te manorathā iti | viṭa uvāca | sarvathā kṛtārtho 'smi sakhi kathyatāṃ tāvat katamasmin pradeśe kasyāṃ vā velāyāṃ mayānupamā draṣṭavyeti | dūty uvāca | kiṃcid āsanne prasuptajane niśīthe yo 'sau bahiḥprākārasamīparohī nyagrodhas tam adhiruhya tasyaiva nṛpatibhavanabhittisaṃśliṣṭapramadavanopariprasṛtaśākhayāvatīrya vayasyena tatra suvarṇāvabhāsāya mayūrādhipataye dīrghikātaṭacitraśālāvasthitāhārasalilopanayanacchalenānupamā ciram ātmānaṃ vinodayantī samabhigamanīyeti | viṭa uvāca | sakhi madvacanād evam anupamā vaktavyā |
children.translated_text: When that messenger had finished speaking, his friend laughed and said: 'Inevitably, spring-time with its blossoming mango clusters is joined with the cuckoo. Your wishes are fulfilled.' The rake said: 'I am utterly fulfilled, O friend! Just tell me — in which place and at what hour shall I see <s>Anupamā</s>?' The messenger said: 'When midnight approaches and people are asleep, there is a banyan tree growing near the outer wall — climb that, and descend by its branch touching the royal pleasure garden. The friend should wait for his return. My friend <s>Anupamā</s>, on pretext of bringing food and water to the golden-colored lord of peacocks, will be waiting for a long time at the painted pavilion beside the pool in the pleasure garden — she is to be approached there.' The rake said: 'Friend, convey these words of mine to <s>Anupamā</s>:'

children.text: upari mamotpalam asitaṃ karṇād ādāya yat tvayā muktam /
children.translated_text: 'The dark lotus that you released from your ear upon me —

children.text: jīvitam iva tad dayitaṃ mlānam api na saṃtyajāmy etat //
children.translated_text: like my very life, that beloved thing, even though wilted, I do not abandon.'

children.text: tathāstv iti ca praṇamya gatāyāṃ tasyāṃ vacanahāryāṃ bahulapakṣāndhakāratiraskaraṇadurālakṣyeṣu pathiṣu śrūyamāṇasuptagajaniśvāseṣv ālānasthāneṣu prathamayāmikajanaprotthāpyamānadvitīyajāgaraṇādhikṛteṣu gulmakapuruṣeṣu niścalapatatrigaṇādhyāsitaśākhākulāyeṣu vitapiṣu sthāṇum apy ālokya purataḥ puruṣa iti śaṅkamānaḥ surabhivarṇakānuliptaḥ sa viṭaḥ prathamajaladharanīlapaṭāvaguṇṭhitaśarīro vāmakakṣāvalambitaniśitakaravālaḥ saha tena suhṛdā pratyāsanne 'rdharātre samupagamya dūtyupadiṣṭenopāyena punardarśanāyeti suhṛdam āmantrya pramadavanaṃ prāviśat | atha tam āgacchantam ālokya gṛhītasaviśeṣamaṇḍanānupamā cintayāmāsa | niyatam avatarann ayam anayā vaṭaśākhayānena mayūreṇa dṛṣṭaḥ | kadācid ayam imaṃ vṛttāntam āgatāya rājñe nivedayed iti | tad enaṃ śikhinaṃ viṣasaṃpṛktenāhāreṇābhāvam eva neṣyāmīti vicintya |
