children.translated_text: 'So be it,' and when that persuasive messenger had bowed and departed, on paths made difficult to discern by the concealing darkness of the dark fortnight, at tethering-posts where the breathing of sleeping elephants could be heard, with guardsmen of the second watch being roused by those of the first, amid trees whose still branches served as roosts for motionless flocks of birds, suspecting even a tree-stump ahead to be a man — that rake, anointed with fragrant unguent, his body wrapped in a cloth dark as a fresh rain-cloud, a sharp sword hanging at his left side, together with his friend, approaching at the close of midnight, following the method instructed by the messenger, bidding farewell to his friend with 'till we meet again,' entered the pleasure garden. Then <s>Anupamā</s>, having adorned herself with special ornaments, seeing him coming, thought: 'Surely this one descending by this banyan branch has been seen by this peacock. Perhaps he will report this incident to the king when he returns.' Thinking: 'I shall bring this peacock to destruction with poison-mixed food,' she —
to the peacock, poison-mixed
food and water, she —
she gave [herself], not being in control of herself,
driven by both passion and fear.
Free from the fear of family honor, desiring pleasure,
deluded by a fortune that is the enemy of merit,
what impropriety does not the unrestrained person,
shameless, devoted to passion, commit?

children.text: sa ca mayūrādhipatiḥ kiṃcit tiktam āhāram udakaṃ cāsvādya niyatam anupamayānena puruṣeṇa saha saṃgamam abhilaṣantyā jātaśaṅkayā mahyaṃ viṣaṃ dattaṃ | tad idam atra prāptakālam |
children.translated_text: And that lord of peacocks, tasting some bitter food and water, [thought]: 'Certainly she, desiring union with that man of incomparable charm, has given me poison out of suspicion. Now this is the opportune moment:' —
'So long as these two, man and woman, their minds blinded by passion,
have not yet attained the state of marriage,
I shall endeavor to lead them both to dispassion,
delivering a discourse on <s>dharma</s> that destroys the evil path!'

children.text: iti vicintya sa mahātmā taṃ viṭam ājuhāva | mahātmann ihopaviśya matsaṃkathayā vinodyātmānaṃ yathābhipretam anuṣṭhāsyasīti | sa ca viṭaḥ kutūhalavaśād upagamya mayūrādhipatisamīpe samupaviveśa | sāpi ca rājñī kiṃcit tam ālokya sasādhvasā tūṣṇīm evāvatasthe | tato bodhisattvas tayor upaviṣṭayoḥ purastād iti vairāgyasaṃbandhinīṃ kathām akarot |
children.translated_text: Thinking thus, that great-souled one summoned that paramour: 'Great sir, sit here and, having dispelled your mind with my discourse, you shall do as you wish.' And that paramour, driven by curiosity, approached and sat down near the lord of peacocks. And the queen, seeing him somewhat, remained standing in silence, alarmed. Then the <s>Bodhisattva</s>, in the presence of both seated ones, delivered the following discourse on dispassion:
'Ah, the moon-like face, charming with the familiarity of laughter-moonlight!
The pair of breasts, lofty and beautiful, with a playful forward movement!
Of a man thus deluded, contemplating the beauty of another's wife,
due to the absence of discernment, the Flower-armed one [<s>Kāma</s>] enters within.'
'She will restrain my hand in private as it loosens the waist-knot,
her face lowered with the modesty of a first trembling' —
thus, for the sake of union with a woman, the mind of the one blinded by manifold imaginings
is daily emaciated by the bodiless one [<s>Kāma</s>], who watches for vulnerabilities in the body.

children.text: āgacchet punar adya sā gurubhayāt tasyāḥ kuto 'bhyāgamaḥ
children.translated_text: 'Will she come again today? From fear of elders, how can she come?

children.text: śarvaryām athavāham eva cakitaṃ gacchāmi supte jane
children.translated_text: Or rather, at night, when people sleep, shall I go myself, trembling?

children.text: dūtyāpy adya ciraṃ kṛtaṃ kim u manas tasyā nivṛttaṃ bhaved
children.translated_text: Even the messenger has been gone long — could her mind have turned?'

children.text: ity ārūḍhavikalpanākuladhiyaḥ kiṃ tat sukhaṃ kāminaḥ
children.translated_text: Thus, of the lover whose mind is agitated with mounting speculations — where is happiness?
'From imagination
the fire of the bodiless one [<s>Kāma</s>] arises; from that, torment is born;

children.text: saṃtāpād aratiḥ smṛteḥ pramathanī smṛtyā vinā hrīḥ kutaḥ
children.translated_text: from torment, discontent that destroys memory; without memory, whence is shame?
From the breaking of shame, the humiliation of being talked about; of the two [man and woman], pierced by afflictions,

children.text: syātām ādhimatoḥ kadā nu sukhinī strīpuṃsayoś cetasī
children.translated_text: when will the minds of the man and woman, racked by anxiety, ever be happy?'

children.text: akṣāṇāṃ vaśam āgataḥ sukham iti vyāmohitaś cintayā
children.translated_text: 'Having come under the power of the senses, the person deluded by thought
thinks "this is happiness"; afflicted by desire, he covets another's wife, devoid of shame.',
'An iron woman, seething with sparks and flames of fire,

children.text: soḍhuṃ śakṣyati tāṃ kathaṃ nu narake prādurbhavadvepathuḥ
children.translated_text: embracing him — how will he endure her in hell, trembling?'

children.text: iti paradārāsaṅgaṃ bahudoṣam avetya dhairyam ālambya /
children.translated_text: Thus, having recognized the manifold faults of attachment to another's wife, taking hold of fortitude,
regarding [her] as a sister, the wise one should turn away from that.

children.text:
tad evam alpasya nāma sukhasya hetor anekānalajvālāsahasrāliṅgyamānavikūṇitākṣāṇām aśubhakarmakāriṇām ārtanādakaruṇam tīkṣṇakrakacapāṭyamānaśirasāṃ cāpareṣāṃ
rudhiradhārokṣitajvalitabhūtalam krūrayamapuruṣodgūrṇalohamudgarābhighātavicūrṇyamānapuruṣaśarīrāsthidhvānabhīṣaṇam ayaḥśālmalīkaṇṭakaparibhidyamānair aparaiś ca muhur abhinisvanadbhir upacitaparyantaṃ narakam icchanty amedhasaḥ patitum ity aho mahad etad ajñānam | athāsau viṭas tena mayūrādhipatinā narakakathāṃ varṇyamānām ākarṇya saṃvignamanā vinivartitaparadārābhilāṣa uvāca |
children.translated_text: For thus, for the sake of a mere trifle of pleasure, the foolish wish to fall into a hell filled to the brim with thousands of fire-flames, where those who perform evil deeds are embraced [by flames], their eyes contorted, uttering cries of anguish, pitifully — and others whose heads are being sawn by sharp saws, [into a hell] whose ground is terrifying with the sound of bones being pulverized as human bodies are smashed by iron maces hurled by cruel servants of <s>Yama</s>, and where others are being pierced by the thorns of the iron silk-cotton tree and crying out repeatedly — ah, this is great ignorance! Then that paramour, hearing the description of hell being narrated by the lord of peacocks, his mind filled with alarm, his desire for another's wife turned away, spoke:
'Ah, hearing this description of hell from you,
so terrifying at every turn,
I seem to behold the fierce flames
and the rising roar of the hell-fire!'
'Therefore, from today onward, to the stealing of another's wife,
which robs the minds of people blinded by passion
and blocks the door to a good rebirth —
homage! [i.e., I renounce it forever!]'
'Through the clear elucidation
of the paths of good and evil,
I behold you, the instructor,
as my teacher.'
'And this queen of the king,
whose vow to her husband is unbroken —
free from the darkness of passion,
I regard her as a sister.'

children.text: athānupamā tasya bhaginīti vacanam upaśrutya parāṃ vrīḍām upagatā tāṃ ca bodhisattvadharmadeśanām avadhārya saṃvignamatir idam uvāca | mayā khalu mandabhāgyayā narakagāminyā kāmarāgavaśagayāsmai mayūrākṛtaye maharṣaye viṣasaṃpṛktam annam udakaṃ ca viśrāṇitaṃ tat katham idānīṃ kartavyam iti | tāṃ ca vipratisāravatīm ālokya bodhisattvo dhīrayāmāsa ||
children.translated_text: Then <s>Anupamā</s>, hearing his word 'sister,' became overcome with supreme shame, and having reflected upon that <s>Dharma</s>-teaching of the <s>Bodhisattva</s>, her mind alarmed, she spoke thus: 'Indeed, by me, the ill-fortuned one, bound for hell, overcome by the power of sensual desire, poisoned food and water were served to this sage in peacock-form. What is now to be done?' And seeing her full of remorse, the <s>Bodhisattva</s> reassured her:
'My body is always consecrated
by the spell of <s>maitrī</s> (loving-kindness);
it undergoes no transformation
even from the poison <s>hālāhala</s>.'
'O queen, do not entertain the fear
born of [having caused] harm to me.',
'Nor shall I speak of any
such thing to the king.'

children.text: athānupamā tadvacanam ākarṇya paraṃ paritoṣam upajagāma | so 'pi ca viṭas taṃ mayūrādhipatim abhivādya vinivṛttaparadāravyasanas tenaiva nyagrodhena svanilayam agāt | atha prabhātasamaye brahmadattaḥ samāpayya svarājyakaraṇīyam āgamya praviśya ca svabhavanaṃ prāg eva mayūrādhipatim agāt | parasparakuśalavārttāṃ ca nṛpatimayūrādhipatī papracchatuḥ | athānyasminn ahani rājānaṃ śikhipatir evam uvāca |
children.translated_text: Then <s>Anupamā</s>, hearing his words, attained supreme satisfaction. And that paramour too, having saluted the lord of peacocks, his addiction to other men's wives eliminated, returned to his own dwelling by that very banyan tree. Then at dawn, <s>Brahmadatta</s>, having completed the business of his kingdom, came and entered his own palace and went to the lord of peacocks as before. The king and the lord of peacocks inquired after each other's welfare. Then on another day, the lord of the peacocks spoke thus to the king:
'My peacock-flock, their minds sorrowful from the grief of separation from me,

children.text: na pibati vāri phalaṃ na cāpi bhuṅkte
children.translated_text: neither drinks water nor eats fruit;
even in the rainy season, they have ceased dancing —
the peacock-flock has surely fallen into distress.'
'Therefore, O best of men, protect this
entire earth, with your senses and enemies conquered!
And I, with your permission, shall go to the <s>Himavat</s>, bright as the moon,
for the protection of the peacocks.'
As he spoke thus — the flock-leader,
with neck [gleaming like] sapphire,
bearing the burden of his long, beautiful tail —
the king reluctantly permitted him to depart from the excellent city.
Watched by the king-lord with an eager heart
and by the city-folk,
the noble peacock took to the cloud-covered sky
for the welfare of the peacocks.
Then, beholding in the sky the enchanting peacock
languid with the burden of his extended train,
the harem women released, overcome by longing,
tear-drops from their eyes.
In the intense separation from the beloved, which shatters the mind's resolve,
the tears that arise when the mind and eyes are overwhelmed —
that is surely embodied suffering, which, from the heat of the fire of anxiety,
melts and flows in people who are attached.
Then, seeing from afar that bull among peacocks
traveling through the sky, with trembling plumage on his neck,
the peacocks, with fluttering wing-tips, trusting,
came forth to meet him, uttering sweet, melodious cries.
When the peacock arrived there from the king's side —
that virtuous one, like a dear friend whose every wish has been fulfilled —
the <s>Himavat</s> mountain manifested towering delight,
with the sprouting of grass-hairs [of horripilation] and the laughter of spreading snow.

children.text:
bodhisattvo 'pi ca sametya tan mayūrayūthaṃ ciravirahaparyutsukaṃ pakṣābhyām āliṅgya samāśvāsayāmāsa |
tad evam ātmani nirapekṣeṇa tena bhagavatā bodhisattvabhūtena prāṇāḥ prāṇātyayāt paripālitā iti vicintya sugatibhavanadvāraprakāśini pradīpabhūte śīle bhavadbhir ādaraḥ karaṇīya iti |
children.translated_text:
And the <s>Bodhisattva</s>, meeting that peacock-flock, long yearning from separation, embraced [them] with his wings and consoled them.
Thus, reflecting that the Blessed One, being a <s>Bodhisattva</s>, heedless of himself, protected lives from mortal danger, one should have regard for moral conduct (<s>śīla</s>), which is a lamp illuminating the door to the mansion of good rebirth.
|| Thus the <s>Mayūra Jātaka</s> (Peacock Birth-Story). ||
19. <s>Hastin</s> (The Elephant)

children.text: jānāti kṣāntiphalaṃ ya eva rāgādiśāntim anvicchan /
children.translated_text: He alone who knows the fruit of patience (<s>kṣānti</s>) and who desires the pacification of passion and the like,

children.text: kurute sa eva dhīraḥ praharaty api vairiṇi kṣāntim //
children.translated_text: that resolute one alone practices patience even toward an enemy who strikes him.
Thus it is heard:

children.text: vividhatarukusumagandhādhivāsitadigantarāle revāsalilakṣālitavipulāntarīyaśilātale pavanacalitaveṇuvanapalāśasalasalāśabdasaṃtrāsotkarṇacalitamṛgakule kvacid analaprasūtabhayotpatitaśakunigaṇe kvacid ucchritaśikharasthitadhavalabalāhakacchāyāśyāmīkṛtanitambe kvacid ibhayūthabhajyamānaśallakīgandhasurabhīkṛtanikuñje kvacit pulindījanasamuccīyamānapatitaviralamayūracandrake candrakiraṇavimalasalilaprasravaṇe 'nyatra tāpasakanyakāgaṇānīyamānalatākusumasamudbhrāntālikulopagīte śukaharitaśādvalaramaṇīyavasudhātale vindhyabhūbhṛti śarajjaladharākṛtibṛhaddehaḥ śeṣabhujagānurūpakaraḥ kamalābhitāmrapuṣkaraḥ kṣuṇṇābhinavamustāsurabhimadalekhāśyāmakapolaḥ susaṃsthitanakhapādaḥ kaladhautaracitakumbhākṛtikumbhaḥ kṣamāṅkuśavinivāritāmārgaprasthitiḥ sthitir iva sarvaguṇānāṃ ṣaḍdanto gandhahastī bodhisattvo gajayūthādhipatir babhūva |
children.translated_text: On the <s>Vindhya</s> mountain — in a region whose horizon-spaces were perfumed by the fragrance of diverse tree-blossoms, whose broad interior rock-surfaces were washed by the waters of the <s>Revā</s> [<s>Narmadā</s>], where herds of deer pricked up their ears and stirred at the rustling sound of bamboo-forest leaves shaken by the wind, where somewhere flocks of birds had taken flight in fear from a fire, where somewhere the slopes were darkened by the shadow of white clouds resting on high peaks, where somewhere the groves were perfumed by the scent of <s>śallakī</s> trees broken by herds of elephants, where somewhere the <s>Pulindī</s> women were gathering fallen, scattered peacock-feathers, where crystal-clear water springs flowed, and elsewhere garland-flowers brought by groups of ascetic maidens were sung over by swarms of bewildered bees — on that mountain of lovely green-parrot-colored sward, there was the <s>Bodhisattva</s>, a six-tusked <s>gandha</s>-elephant, lord of the elephant-herd: with a body vast as an autumn cloud, with a trunk proportioned like [that of] the serpent <s>Śeṣa</s>, with ear-lobes reddish-coppery like lotuses, with cheeks dark with musk-streaks fragrant from crushing fresh <s>mustā</s> grass, with well-formed nails and feet, with frontal globes shaped like golden-crafted vessels, whose wandering from the wrong path was restrained by the goad of patience — the repository, as it were, of all virtues.
That herd-lord shone, white as moonbeams,
with teeth pale as pearls, with broad, full frontal globes —
like the great accumulated laughter of <s>Paśupati</s> [<s>Śiva</s>]
at the time of his cosmic dance, which dispelled the darkness of night.
The trees, releasing flowers struck by the wind,
their stamens yellow with pollen-dust,
seemed to praise that elephant-lord, white as the Snow Mountain,
with devotion, through the sound of bees.
Forsaking from afar the flowers of trees
and the lotuses with laughing petals,
the bees slowly alighted with delight
upon his cheeks anointed with rut-water.
Constantly adorned with full, plump cheeks,
perfuming the horizon-spaces all around —
that herd-lord did not ward off the bees
slowly drinking the rut-juice, with the flaps of his ears.
The bees took from him
that charming, unbroken, abundant [rut-juice]
like supplicants [receiving]
the gift of the lord of generosity.

children.text: tena ca yūthapatinā samāśrito vindhyagiriḥ kanakagirer apy ātmānam abhyadhikam ivāmanyata | tac ca gajayūthaṃ samyak tena paripālyamānaṃ rājanvad iva rājyam anudivasam avardhata |
children.translated_text: And the <s>Vindhya</s> mountain, sheltered by that herd-lord, considered itself superior even to the Golden Mountain [<s>Meru</s>]. And that elephant-herd, well-protected by him, grew day by day like a kingdom [ruled by] a good king.
That one of noble nature had two
beloved she-elephants:
<s>Bhadrā</s> and <s>Subhadrā</s> —
dear to the beloved one [who was] dear to patience.

children.text: atha kadācid anilacalitapatākakuṭilavidyullatāparisphuraṇasaṃmīlitavipulākṣyāḥ salilabharagurujaladharagarjitasaṃtrāsapravepitāṅghryāḥ tanubhujalatotkṣeponnatataragurupayodharāyāḥ khaḍgaprabhāvabhāsitadakṣiṇabhujaṃ kalpatarukusumam ājighrantaṃ dayitam āliṅgantyāḥ patitakarṇotpalāyāḥ śithilakeśapāśacchannāṃsadeśāyāḥ pavanacalitam uttarīyam avarundhatyāḥ sphuritābharaṇamaṇikiraṇāvabhāsitaśarīrayaṣṭer nabhasā gacchantyā vidyādharyāḥ kisalayasukumārāt pāṇeḥ paribhraṣṭam abhinavam āmodādhivāsitadigantarālam alikulaparigītaṃ kanakasūcīsadṛśakesaraṃ rathacakrapramāṇaṃ haritālakapilamakarandam aravindaṃ mānasasaraḥsaṃbhūtaṃ tasya gajapater ekākinas tatrācalavare viharataḥ purastāt papāta | tac ca kamalam ādāya sa evam acintayat | bhadrāyāḥ subhadrāyāś ca me patnyor yā prathamam āgamiṣyati tasyai prasādam ahaṃ dāsyāmi |
children.translated_text: Then once, a <s>Vidyādharī</s> (celestial woman), her wide eyes closing at the flashing of crooked lightning-creepers on wind-tossed banners, her feet trembling with fright at the thundering of rain-clouds heavy with water, her slender vine-like arms raised and her heavy breasts elevated, her right arm illuminated by the splendor of a sword, inhaling the flower of a wish-fulfilling tree, embracing her beloved, her ear-lotus having fallen, the region of her shoulders covered by loose tresses, restraining her upper garment blown by the wind, her body-frame illuminated by the rays of sparkling ornament-gems, as she was traveling through the sky — from her sprout-tender hand there fell a lotus, newly fragrant, its horizon-spaces perfumed, sung over by swarms of bees, with stamens like golden needles, as large as a chariot-wheel, with orpiment-tawny nectar, born from Lake <s>Mānasa</s>, before that lord of elephants as he wandered alone on that excellent mountain. Taking that lotus, he thought: 'Of my two wives, <s>Bhadrā</s> and <s>Subhadrā</s>, whichever comes first, to her I shall give this gift.'
'With bees swarming and agitated within,
its fragrant filaments scattering pollen-stamens,
this great lotus, with its laughing cluster of beautiful petals —
I shall give it with delight!'

children.text: atha subhadrāyai prathamam āgatāyai tat kanakamayam ambhoruhaṃ sa gajapatiḥ prāyacchat | sāpi ca tad āghrāya sabahumānaṃ śirasi niveśayāmāsa | paścāc ca bhadrā samupagamya tat subhadrāyāḥ kumbhamadhyāvasthitam aravindam ālokya niyatam idam ambhoruham asyai sapatnyai mām avamanyānena yūthapatinā dattam iti vicintya parām īrṣyām āgamya taṃ dviradapatim apahāyānyatra vijahāra |
children.translated_text: Then, to <s>Subhadrā</s> who had come first, that lord of elephants presented the golden lotus. And she, having reverently smelled it, placed it upon her head. Afterward, <s>Bhadrā</s>, approaching and seeing that lotus resting upon the vessel of <s>Subhadrā</s>, thought: 'Surely this lotus was given to that rival wife by this herd-leader, treating me with contempt!' And having arrived at extreme jealousy, she abandoned that elephant-lord and went elsewhere.

children.text: sā yatra dṛṣṭam ahani dviradena tena
children.translated_text: On the day she saw the sweet-scented, blooming lotus
given by that elephant to her rival wife,
there, consumed by jealousy, she ate no grass,
drank no water, her form wasting away even from thirst.
What sensible person would,
with the oblation of false imaginings,
feed the blazing flame of jealousy
for the burning of oneself?
Happy do those resolute ones sleep,
they do not travel the wrong path,
in the house of whose mind
the serpent of jealousy does not dwell.

children.text: atha bhadrā vindhyaśilātale tarucchāyāpihitavinibaddhaparyaṅkadhyānaniścalanayanam ālikhitam iva mattacakoravilocanaraktacīvaraprāvṛtāṅgaṃ pratyekabuddham ālokya sarasaḥ kusumāny ānīyārcayāmāsa |
children.translated_text: Then <s>Bhadrā</s>, on the rock-surface of the <s>Vindhya</s> [mountain], seeing a <s>Pratyekabuddha</s> — with legs crossed in meditation in the shade of a tree, his eyes motionless as if painted, his body wrapped in a red-ochre robe [red] as the eye of an intoxicated <s>cakora</s> bird — brought flowers from a lake and worshipped him.

children.text: kṣiptābhir ūrdhvam atha vāśitayā sa bhāsvāṃs
children.translated_text: Then the radiant sage, showered upward
with rows of night-lotuses by that she-elephant, shone
with his body illuminated by their transient radiance —
like a twilight cloud above, adorned by stars.

children.text: atha sā hastinī vindhyācalataṭam āruhya yad asmāt pratyekabuddhārcanakuśalamūlāt phalaṃ tenāham asya gandhahastino vadhāya rājamahiṣī syām iti vicintyātmānaṃ mumoca | tasyāś ca śarīrabhāraparibhagnataruśākhāyāḥ patanaśabdam ākarṇya |
children.translated_text: Then that she-elephant, having ascended the slope of the <s>Vindhya</s> mountain, thought: 'May the fruit of this root of merit from worshipping the <s>Pratyekabuddha</s> be that I become a chief queen for the destruction of that scent-elephant!' Having resolved thus, she cast herself down. And hearing the sound of her fall, which broke the tree-branches under the weight of her body:
Peacocks flew up, their moon-spots trembling;
the sleeping tiger opened its eyes;
from fright, dropping the mouthful of grass, from afar,
the deer-herds, ears pricked up, became agitated.

children.text: sā ca kālaṃ kṛtvānyatarasya rājño jātismarā duhitā babhūva | kiṃcidudbhidyamānastanamukulāṃ ca tāṃ trivalīsopānamālādhirohaṇajātakhedeneva navayauvanaśilpinā samanmatham upacīyamānaśarīralāvaṇyāṃ prārabdhalajjāhasitavilāsām alikulaśyāmakeśapāśāṃ kanakacchedāvadātāṃ śriyam iva mūrtimatīṃ pitā kasmaicid eva nṛpataye prāyacchat | sā ca taṃ rājānam ananyastrīsadṛśair abalāguṇair apahṛtendriyaṃ kṛtvā kadācic candanānuliptastanagātrī niśvāsaparikuñcitādharapuṭā jvaritām ivātmānaṃ darśayāmāsa | yadā ca bhiṣagbhiś cikitsyamānāpi tathaiva jvaracchadmanā pariceṣṭate sma tadā tasyā bhartā bhṛśam aratim ājagāma | sā cainam uvāca |
children.translated_text: And having died, she was reborn as the daughter of a certain king, remembering her past life. And when her breast-buds were just beginning to swell, and her bodily charm was increasing — as if the craftsman of fresh youth were weary from climbing the staircase-garland of the three folds [of skin on her belly] — with the dawning of bashful, smiling coquetry, with tresses dark as a swarm of bees, fair as the cutting of gold, like <s>Śrī</s> (the goddess of fortune) embodied — her father gave her to a certain king. And she, having captivated that king's senses with feminine virtues unmatched by any other woman, once, with her breasts and body anointed with sandalwood, with her lip-fold curled from sighing, displayed herself as if feverish. And when, though being treated by physicians, she continued to behave thus under the pretense of fever, her husband became greatly distressed. And she said to him:
'This fever of mine is not quelled
by <s>haricandana</s> (sandalwood), nor by cloud-cool breezes,
nor by the crystal-pure
net of rays of the moon.'
'On <s>Vindhya</s> mountain there is a lord of elephants,
white as a rain-cloud, with six mighty tusks;'
'upon his great tusks,
white as lotus-stalks, there are pearls, O lord of the earth.'
'If my body were anointed with those [pearls],
ground fine, pure as water-drops —'
'and if a bed were made for me from those tusks,
then this burning fever would be calmed.'

children.text: atha sa rājā niyatam anayā devyā jātismarayā jātyantare śruto dṛṣṭo vā vindhyavanavāsī gandhahastīti niścayam upetya vyādham āhūyāvocat |asti vindhyācale ṣaḍdanto gandhahastī | yadi tasya dantān āneṣyasi tato 'haṃ bhavantaṃ mahatārthena yojayiṣyāmīti | vyādha uvāca | yathā śakṣyāmi tathā kariṣyāmīti | devy uvāca | aham upāyaṃ jānāmi yathāsau gandhahastī viśrambham āyātīti |
children.translated_text: Then that king, [thinking] 'Surely this queen, remembering her past life, has heard of or seen the scent-elephant dwelling in the <s>Vindhya</s> forest,' having reached this certainty, summoned a hunter and said: 'There is a six-tusked scent-elephant on <s>Vindhya</s> mountain. If you bring his tusks, I shall reward you with great wealth.' The hunter said: 'I shall do as I am able.' The queen said: 'I know a stratagem by which that scent-elephant will approach with trust.'
'Seeing a mendicant, peaceful,
wearing ochre-colored robes —'
'like an intelligent, good pupil,
the elephant bows and worships.'
'Therefore, having properly donned
the two ochre-colored garments, you should'
'strike him with an arrow
smeared with poison, upon a vital spot.'

children.text: sa ca tatheti pratiśrutya kāṣāyavasanasaṃbhṛtāṅgaḥ saśaraṃ dhanur ādāya vindhyācalam agamat | atha tam acalavanāntare saṃcarantam ālokya tad gajayūthaṃ sāśaṅkam ibhādhipataye nivedayāmāsa |
children.translated_text: And having agreed, he, his body clothed in ochre garments, taking a bow with arrows, went to <s>Vindhya</s> mountain. Then, seeing him moving about in that mountain forest, the elephant herd apprehensively reported to the lord of elephants:
'Someone in ochre garments,
with eyes tawny as sparks,
with a body [sturdy] as an iron pillar —
is seen as if frightening the creatures.'

children.text: bodhisattva uvāca | na khalu kāṣāyavāsaḥ śaṅkanīyam | paśyantu bhavantaḥ |
children.translated_text: The <s>Bodhisattva</s> said: 'Surely one who wears ochre robes should not be viewed with suspicion. Behold, good ones:'
'Modesty, the indicator of the path of peace,
the banner of sages, the cause of destroying pride —'
'if a person's body-ornament is a garment dyed with ochre,
that robe is a cause of trust in people.'

children.text: atha tasya yūthasya nātidūre 'vasthitaḥ sa vyādhas taruṇātmānam āvṛtya dhanur āropayāmāsa |
children.translated_text: Then, stationed not far from that herd, the hunter, having concealed himself behind a tree, raised his bow.
As he fitted upon the string, for the destruction of the elephant-king,
an arrow with a keen blade, upon a bowstring made of sinew-essence,
<s>Vindhya</s> seemed to try to stop him, with the branch-hands
and leaf-fingers of the trees, shaken by the wind.
The hunter struck the lord of elephants — his eyes half-closed in rut,
his hand placed upon his ear, rubbing his ichor-smeared cheek
against a tree — the one who knew the path of virtue —
struck him nearby, upon the temporal boss.
Then the elephant-lord embraced the hunter
— his bow and upper garment fallen, being pursued angrily by the elephant herd —
consoling the fear-stricken one
as if he were his own son.
'Here is the enemy who has committed an offense —
and alas, here is the compassion of the elephant-lord!'
Thus, in the minds of the mountain-cave-dwelling deities,
astonishment surely arose.
When the lord of elephants was pierced by the sharp arrow there,
the elephant herd, shaking its faces slightly marked with blood-drops,
released the half-chewed, fragrant <s>śallakī</s>
leaves, overcome by great grief.
<s>Subhadrā</s>, the chief she-elephant,
then drew out that arrow, grasping it
with her trunk slightly bent,
by force — the quivering [arrow] from her lord, like patience [drawing out] anger.
Grieving, she sprinkled the arrow-wound
of that elephant-lord, smeared with a trace of blood,
with trunk-spray resembling
a severed pearl-necklace string.
'Who will perfume me with rut-ichor when I enter the water thirsty?'
— thus, with the sound of clear whirling waves,
the <s>Narmadā</s> [river]
cried out in great anguish, as if in mourning.
'O lord of elephants, is the pain born of the arrow-wound
growing thinner today?'
— thus, flitting about restlessly upon his cheeks,
rows of bees seemed to gently inquire.
With clouds gray from spreading dark <s>aguru</s> (aloe) smoke,
their bellies marked with trembling lightning-rings,
<s>Vāsava</s> [<s>Indra</s>] covered the scorching forehead-heating sun
for the comfort of that [elephant].
A breeze, cool from contact with the clear, fresh water of the <s>Revā</s> [<s>Narmadā</s>],
fragrant with blooming flowers of many kinds,
arriving like a friend, fanned the lord of elephants
who had been pierced by the arrow.

children.text: atha gajapatir yadi kathaṃcid antakālaṃ kariṣyāmi tad idaṃ gajayūtham anāthatāṃ yāsyatīti vicintya satyādhiṣṭhānam iti cakāra ||
children.translated_text: Then the elephant-lord thought: 'If somehow I meet my end, this elephant herd will become orphaned.' Having reflected thus, he made a declaration of truth (<s>satyādhiṣṭhāna</s>):
'As there is love in me
even toward this hunter who has done harm —'
'by this truth today,
may the poison in me come to destruction!'

children.text: atha satyādhiṣṭhānaprabhāvāt sadya evāpagataśaramūrcchāvedanaḥ sa gajapatir abhūt | taṃ ca tathā svāsthyam āgatam ālokya sa vyādhaḥ praṇamya taṃ rājamahiṣīvṛttāntam ākhyāyābhyuvāca |
children.translated_text: And by the power of the declaration of truth, immediately the elephant-lord was freed from the wound's swooning pain and the arrow's venom. And seeing him thus restored to health, the hunter, bowing, related the account of the chief queen and spoke:
'For the sake of your tusks, O lord of elephants,
by a cruel one — though you are gentle-minded —'
'you have been struck, O you who have destroyed hatred,
by me, an unworthy [vessel], with an arrow.'
Hearing those words of the hunter,
the lord of elephants
extracted his own tusks
with his trunk, without pain.
That trunk of his, with the flow of blood tied [stanched],
bore the beauty
of a white lotus garland
with a <s>bandhūka</s> flower-wreath attached.
By that very declaration of truth,
the tusks of that lord of elephants
sprouted again in an instant,
white as conch-shell cuttings.
Astonished at the re-emergence of the tusks
of the elephant-lord of white-cloud luster,
the hunter, taking the tusks from the forest,
went to the house of the king.

children.text: atha dantāvalokanapramuditamanāḥ sa rājā taṃ lubdhakaṃ yathāpratipannenārthena yojayāmāsa | sāpi ca rājñī taṃ chadmajvaram apāsya tāni viṣāṇāni dṛṣṭvā jātapaścāttāpā tam īrṣyāvṛttāntam anyajanmānubhūtaṃ patye nivedya bāṣpasalilavyāptanayanotpalā tat tad vilalāpa |
children.translated_text: Then the king, his mind delighted at the sight of the tusks, rewarded that hunter with the wealth as promised. And the queen, abandoning her pretended fever and seeing those tusks, was seized by remorse; having confided to her husband the account of her jealousy experienced in her former birth, with her lotus-eyes flooded with tears, she lamented thus:
'Alas, shame upon jealousy, the destroyer of the side of virtue!
By me, deluded and dull-minded by it,
that herd-lord dwelling in the forest, of tranquil mind like an ascetic,
was driven to the abode of <s>Yama</s> (Death)!'
'That elephant-herd, protected for ages by that great-souled one,
which could not be harassed by other elephants —'
'without that tusker now, thrown into confusion —
how will that elephant-herd fare?'
'The bees, thirsty for his constant rut-ichor,
that used to swarm repeatedly upon his cheeks —'
'without him, those bees, confused,
will after a long time resort to the lotus-pool forest.'
'That tree whose bark was repeatedly polished
by the cheek-rubbing of that elephant-lord —'
'fragrant with a trace of his rut for a long time,
surely <s>Subhadrā</s> will not abandon that tree.'
'O Earth, adorned with the girdle of the ocean-shore,
with a garment of soft, heaving turf —'
'do you bear me, the slayer of the chief lord?

children.text: kṣite vidāraṃ na dadāsi kiṃ nu me
children.translated_text: Why do you not open a chasm for me?'

children.text: atha tāṃ rājñīṃ tathā vilāpaparāṃ sa vyādho dhīrayāmāsa | mā devi śokaṃ kārṣīḥ | satyādhiṣṭhānamāhātmyena sa mahātmā punarudbhūtamanoharamahāviṣāṇaḥ samapagataśaraviṣavegaḥ sattvopakārāya prāṇān bibhrat karoty eva tasya mahato gajayūthasyādhipatyam iti ||
children.translated_text: Then the hunter consoled that queen in her supreme lamentation: 'Do not grieve, O queen! By the power of his declaration of truth, that great-souled one, with magnificent new tusks having re-emerged, his arrow-poison having completely subsided, continues to protect his life for the benefit of beings, and exercises lordship over that great elephant herd.'
Then, hearing those words from him,
the chief queen became joyful again;
and the king too was filled with wonder,
repeatedly reflecting on the compassion of the elephant-lord.

children.text: tad evaṃ kṣāntiphalam abhilaṣantaḥ karuṇātmakāḥ śastreṇāpi praharati vairiṇi satyām api śaktau kṣamanta eva mahātmāna ity avadhārya kṣamāyām ādaraḥ karaṇīya iti ||
children.translated_text: Thus, reflecting that the great-souled ones who desire the fruit of forbearance and are compassionate by nature, even when an enemy strikes with a weapon, even when they have the power [to retaliate], practice forgiveness alone — one should cultivate regard for forbearance.
|| The <s>Hastijātaka</s>, the Nineteenth ||
20. <s>Candra</s>
Like a snake with its fangs removed, even one who is angry practices forbearance when without power;

children.text: sati sāmarthye nojjhati yaḥ kṣāntiṃ sa kṣamī jñeyaḥ //
children.translated_text: he who, possessing capability, does not abandon forbearance — he should be known as truly forbearing.

children.text:
tadyathānuśrūyate
parākramanītiprabhāvavijitānyarājasāmantaḥ prabhūtahastyaśvakośasaṃpadupetas tejasvī dhīraḥ śuśrūṣādibhiḥ prajñāguṇair adhiṣṭhitas trivargānukūlaprakṛtiḥ prakṛtidakṣiṇo dakṣiṇāpathādhipatiḥ kaliṅgarājo nāma rājā babhūva |
children.translated_text: Thus it is heard in tradition: There was a king named <s>Kaliṅgarāja</s>, lord of the southern region — whose rival kings and vassals were conquered by the power of valor, strategy, and might, who was endowed with abundant wealth of elephants, horses, and treasury, who was spirited and resolute, who was possessed of the intellectual qualities of obedience and the like, whose subjects were favorably disposed toward the three aims [of life], who was gracious to his subjects.
The armies of that mighty king, who had conquered enemies by the valor of his arms,
[flooded] the enemy's territory,
advancing like the waters of the ocean upon the shore,
whose surging, towering growth had intensified.
His elephants, with their mutual kettle-drums sounding,
spreading their wrath widely,
at marching time came under the control
of the goad-bearers only with difficulty.

children.text: tasyaivaṃvidhabalodayasya narapateḥ sapatnair akhaṇḍitamānasya khaṇḍadhāro nāma dvijātir amātyo babhūva | sa ca rājā kulasaṃtativicchedabhīruḥ kadācid anekān devatāviśeṣāṃs tanayārtham upayācate sma | tataḥ khaṇḍadhāras taṃ rājānam uvāca | praviśatu devo 'ntaḥpuram ahaṃ devasya putrārthaṃ devatāṃ samupāsiṣye rājyaṃ ca pratipālayiṣyāmīti | tatheti ca rājābhidhāyāntaḥpuraṃ praviśya viṣayaparāyaṇo babhūva | khaṇḍadhāro 'pi ca svanāmāṅkaṃ sarvaparicchedajātaṃ rājyam anuśaśāsa | kaliṅgarājo 'pi ca vividhanṛttagītāvalokanaśravaṇāpahṛtahṛdayaḥ surapatir ivāpsarogaṇaparivṛto 'varodhanajanamadhyagato vijahāra |
children.translated_text: That king of such formidable rising power, whose honor was unbroken by his rivals, had a <s>brāhmaṇa</s> minister named <s>Khaṇḍadhāra</s>. The king, fearing the extinction of his family lineage, once prayed to various deities for a son. Then <s>Khaṇḍadhāra</s> said to the king: 'Let Your Majesty enter the inner quarters; I shall worship the deity for a son for Your Majesty and shall administer the kingdom.' The king said 'So be it,' entered the inner quarters, and became devoted to sensual pleasures. And <s>Khaṇḍadhāra</s> administered the kingdom — all the possessions of which bore the stamp of his own name. And the <s>Kaliṅga</s> king, his heart captivated by beholding various dances, songs, and spectacles, like <s>Indra</s> surrounded by troupes of <s>apsarases</s>, sported amid the women of the inner quarters.
Upon the charming cheeks — pale as moist <s>madhūka</s> blossoms,
seeming to emanate the radiance of the moon —
of a certain woman whose gaze was fixed upon a mirror,
he drew leaf-ornament designs.
He beheld another, with still, wide eyes,
the tip of her lower lip slightly moved by a smile,
concealing a startled bee with a [blue] lotus
from among [the bees] resting on a fresh blue lotus.
Approaching another, who sat turned away
gazing at a charming painted canvas, with soundless steps,
the king covered her eyes
with both his hands.
One who shook her hand saying 'Enough!' —
her voice failing from shyness, her words indistinct,
concealing her breasts with a fine cloth —
he seized, together with the trembling-limbed messenger-woman.

children.text: tvam eva me bhāvini jīvitaṃ paraṃ
children.translated_text: 'You alone are my supreme life, O lovely one!
Cast your glance upon me, O you of charming laughter!' —
thus speaking, he somehow appeased
a certain woman who stood with face downcast.
To one playfully scratching the mosaic floor
with her foot adorned by slightly tinkling anklets,

children.text: karṇe jagāda kim api pramadāṃ hasantīṃ
children.translated_text: laughing, he whispered something in her ear,
while being targeted by the arrow-glances of other women.

children.text:
atha tasya narapater evam akhaṇḍaviṣayasukhānubhāvinas tāḥ śuddhāntamattakāśinyo
vividhamṛduhasitakathākrodherṣyābhrūbhaṅgamanoharair vilāsair atīva hṛdayam ācikṣipuḥ ||
children.translated_text: Thus, as that king experienced unbroken sensual pleasures, those women of the inner chambers, radiant like the intoxicated moon, utterly captivated his heart with their graces — charming with various soft laughter, sweet conversation, feigned anger, jealous frowning, and coquetry.
Women whose brows are raised and arched during the time of playful jest,
whose moon-faces are enveloped by the moonlight of smiles,
whose bodies display curving lines of hair along the three creases [of the belly] —

children.text: na mano haranti vada kasya yoṣitaḥ
children.translated_text: tell me, whose mind do they not steal?
With the gleaming beauty of flashing rows of teeth
seeming to scatter lunar radiance all around,
fragrant with <s>lavalī</s> (clove) — whose mind do they not steal,
the intoxicating, adorning words of the women-folk?
Faces like moons, gazes arrested at the ears [i.e., wide-reaching sidelong glances],
tresses with the luster of a <s>koyal</s> (cuckoo) throat,
breasts resembling ripe palm-fruits —

children.text: na manoharaṃ kim iva nāma yoṣitām
children.translated_text: is there anything about women that is not captivating?

children.text: na gatās ta eva laghutāṃ jagattraye
children.translated_text: Those alone in the triple world have not attained degradation,

children.text: sukhinas ta eva sudhiyas ta eva ca
children.translated_text: those alone are happy, those alone are truly wise,
who have not resorted to the poison-creeper forests of coquettes,
packed with the serpents of manifold faults!

children.text: atha kāle gacchati devy āpannasattvā babhūva |
children.translated_text: Then, in time, the chief queen became pregnant.
As the embryo in her, that treasure of virtues,
grew day by day,
her breasts, with milk gathering at their tips,
took on a dark complexion.
Placing her tender, sprout-soft hands
upon her knees,
upon seeing her husband, she somehow
rose from her seat.
'Will she give birth today? Or tomorrow?' —
thus, with curiosity,
the king, desiring a son, looked at her
affectionately, again and again.

children.text: atha viśuddhe 'hani sākṣṇāṃ nidhim iva svaprabhayāvabhāsitanṛpatibhavanāntaram amarakumārākāram akhilabhuvanālaṃkārabhūtaṃ tanayam asūta |
children.translated_text: Then, on an auspicious day, she gave birth to a son — like a treasury of the stars, his own radiance illuminating the interior of the royal palace, resembling a divine prince, an ornament of the entire world.
Since with the radiance of his body
he surpassed the moon's brilliance,
the name <s>Candra</s> (Moon) was given to him
by his kinsmen.

children.text: anyāsām api triṃśanmātrāṇāṃ rājñīnāṃ tanayā jajñire | athāṣṭavarṣadeśīyāṃś candreṇa kumāreṇa saha kumārān kṣatravidyāgrahaṇāya kasmaicid gurave nivedayāmāsa | sarvāṃś ca tān kumārān mṛgayādivyasanaparāyaṇān anekaiḥ kalāguṇais tejasā bhujabalena ca candraḥ kumāro 'tiśiṣye |
children.translated_text: The other queens too — about thirty in number — bore sons. Then the king entrusted the princes, about eight years old, together with Prince <s>Candra</s>, to a certain guru for the study of the martial arts. Among all those princes, who were devoted to pastimes such as hunting, Prince <s>Candra</s> surpassed them all in many arts and qualities, in brilliance, and in the strength of his arms.

children.text: jāyante guṇabāndhavāḥ sumatayaḥ ślāghyaṃ garimṇāṃ padaṃ
children.translated_text: 'Wise ones with kindred virtues are born as a laudable station of distinction;

children.text: rūḍhaṃ lāghavadoṣa eva mahatāṃ keṣāṃcid ā janmanaḥ
children.translated_text: the very fault of frivolity has taken deep root in certain great ones from birth itself;

children.text: dṛśyante hi narā mahaty api kule jātāḥ samānāḥ śunā
children.translated_text: for men born even in great families are seen to be equal to dogs —
does not a snail also arise from the ocean that abounds with excellent gems?'
'The blueness is indeed the same
in a peacock's moon-crest and in a sapphire;
but that which belongs to a gem is praiseworthy —
for excellence always [depends on] its locus.'
'Virtues are not always present in a person
merely because of [outward] form;
glass, even though bearing the form of a sapphire,
does not possess its qualities.'

children.text: atha sa rājā bodhisattvaṃ yauvarājye 'bhiṣicya tebhyo 'pi ca kumārebhyaḥ kiṃcid deśam adāt | atha ca candro manujādhipānumataḥ saha bhrātṛbhiḥ svadeśaṃ gatvā khaṇḍadhāranāmāṅkāni dṛṣṭvovāca | sarvathā nāmamātreṇāsmatpitā rājā khaṇḍadhāra evātrādhipatir iti | kumārā ūcuḥ | nanv apanīyedaṃ khaṇḍadhāranāma svāni svāni svadeśe nāmāni vayaṃ sarvopakaraṇeṣu lekhayāmaḥ | tatheti ca pratipanne candreṇa prathamaṃ candranāmāropya paścād ātmīyāni nāmāni te lekhayāmāsuḥ | tac ca tathā nirvṛttaṃ vijñāya khaṇḍadhāraḥ paraṃ kopam āgamya brāhmaṇān saṃnipātya rahasy avocat | apahṛtam anena me rājaputreṇādhipatyam | tad idam atra prāptakālaṃ kenacid upāṃśunā candraḥ prāṇair viyojanīya iti | paśyantu bhavantaḥ |
children.translated_text: Then the king, having consecrated the <s>Bodhisattva</s> as heir-apparent and having given some territory to those other princes as well — <s>Candra</s>, with the king's permission, having gone with his brothers to their own territory and seeing [everything] stamped with the name <s>Khaṇḍadhāra</s>, said: 'In every way, our father is king in name only; <s>Khaṇḍadhāra</s> alone is the ruler here.' The princes said: 'Let us remove this name of <s>Khaṇḍadhāra</s> and inscribe our own names on all the equipment in our own territory.' When <s>Candra</s> agreed, they first inscribed the name <s>Candra</s>, and afterward their own names. Learning that this had been done, <s>Khaṇḍadhāra</s> became extremely angry, assembled the <s>brāhmaṇas</s>, and said to them in secret: 'This prince has usurped my authority! Therefore, the time has come — <s>Candra</s> must somehow be secretly deprived of his life-breaths. Consider —'

children.text: laghīyaḥ prājyaṃ vā phalam abhimataṃ prāptumanasā
children.translated_text: 'Whether the fruit one desires is small or great,

children.text: nirīheṇa sthātuṃ kṣaṇam api na yuktaṃ matimatā
children.translated_text: it is not proper for a wise person to remain inactive even for a moment;

children.text: kulālo daṇḍena bhramayati na cec cakram aniśaṃ
children.translated_text: if a potter does not constantly revolve the wheel with his stick,

children.text: śarāvaḥ kumbho vā na hi bhavati satyām api mṛdi
children.translated_text: neither pot nor saucer comes into being, even though there be good clay.'

children.text: brāhmaṇā ūcuḥ | tvam evopāyam atra vastuni śakto 'dhigantum iti | khaṇḍadhāra uvāca | yady evaṃ tato yadi kathaṃcid ayaṃ rājā svapnaṃ bhavatām agrato nivedayet tato yuṣmābhir vaktavyaṃ deva khaṇḍadhāraḥ svapnaphalābhijñaḥ | sa eṣa praṣṭavya iti | tatheti ca brāhmaṇāḥ pratipedire | atha kadācit sa rājā svapnadarśanodvignahṛdayas tebhyo brāhmaṇebhyaḥ svapnaṃ nivedayāmāsa | brāhmaṇaiś ca khaṇḍadhāraḥ svapnādhyāyavedīti nirdiṣṭaḥ | tataḥ sa rājā khaṇḍadhāram āhūya svapnam iti nivedayāmāsa |
children.translated_text: The <s>brāhmaṇas</s> said: 'You alone are capable of devising a stratagem in this matter.' <s>Khaṇḍadhāra</s> said: 'If so, then if somehow the king were to report a dream to you, then you should say: "O lord, <s>Khaṇḍadhāra</s> is expert in the meaning of dreams; let him be consulted."' The <s>brāhmaṇas</s> agreed. Then one day, the king, his heart troubled by a dream-vision, reported the dream to those <s>brāhmaṇas</s>. The <s>brāhmaṇas</s> declared that <s>Khaṇḍadhāra</s> was a knower of dream-interpretation. The king then summoned <s>Khaṇḍadhāra</s> and reported the dream.

children.text: svapne kilādya puram etad aśeṣam antrair
children.translated_text: 'In my dream today, this entire city was apparently
enwrapped in entrails, its people pale and wretched;
and I, bound and my body compressed by an evil-natured one,
was cast upon the cremation ground, crowded with corpses.'

children.text: tad asya tāvat svapnasya guravaḥ phalam ākhyātum arhantīti | khaṇḍadhāra uvāca | deva kaṣṭaḥ khalu svapnasya vipāko dṛśyate |
children.translated_text: 'Then let the masters announce the fruit of this dream.' <s>Khaṇḍadhāra</s> said: 'O lord, indeed, a terrible ripening of this dream is foreseen —'
'Either the dream indicates a fall from
your great kingdom,
or else you will reach your destined end
within two months.'
Hearing those words, the king,
that lord of the earth, his beauty and splendor departed,
overcome by the dread that 'I must die,' was terrified —
he found no pleasure in the garden, nor in the house.
Death, when merely thought of, by its very nature
produces dejection of mind even from afar;
how much more so when death is imminent,
terrible to behold like a serpent with raised hood?

children.text: atha sa rājā khaṇḍadhāram uvāca | bhavet punaḥ kaścid upāyo yenāhaṃ rājyaparibhraṃśaṃ na prāpnuyām akālamaraṇaṃ veti | khaṇḍadhāra uvāca | tena khalu devaḥ śrotum arhaty upāyam iti | saha candreṇa kumāreṇa sarvakumārā yajñakarmaṇy ālabdhavyā anye ca catuṣpadāḥ prāṇinaḥ |
children.translated_text: Then the king said to <s>Khaṇḍadhāra</s>: 'Is there any remedy by which I might not suffer the fall from my kingdom or an untimely death?' <s>Khaṇḍadhāra</s> said: 'Then let Your Majesty hear the remedy: together with Prince <s>Candra</s>, all the princes are to be sacrificed in a ritual offering, as well as other four-footed creatures.'
'O king, if you will descend into a vast pool
filled with their blood, red as a parrot's beak,

children.text: bhūpāla yady avatariṣyasi tan na rājyād
children.translated_text: upon the sacrificial ground — then you will not suffer the fall
from your kingdom, nor come under the power of the lord of the dead!'

children.text: atha sa rājā punar api me jīvataḥ putrā guṇavattarā bhaviṣyantīti vicintya tān kumārān nigaḍabaddhān ānīya khaṇḍadhāram uvāca | prārabhyatām ādhvaraṃ karmeti |
children.translated_text: Then the king, thinking 'While I live, I will have yet more virtuous sons,' had the princes brought in shackles and said to <s>Khaṇḍadhāra</s>: 'Let the sacrificial ritual begin!'
Then, when the princes were in deep despair
and the ritual of the seven-threaded sacrifice was underway,
that treacherous minister, disturbed at [the absence of] the king's eldest son,
said to the sovereign:
'O moon among men, if <s>Candra</s>, born of your body,
does not come, overpowered by force,
then this sacrificial arrangement will be ruinous to good fortune,
and will not bear the greater fruit.'

children.text: rājovāca | gurujanabhaktaḥ khalu candraḥ kumāras tan na mamājñāṃ laṅghayiṣyati | dūtam asmai praheṣyāmīti | tatheti ca pratipanne khaṇḍadhāreṇa sa rājā dūtam āhūyovāca | gaccha yatra tatrāvasthitaṃ candraṃ brūhi śīghraṃ bhavatā matsakāśam āgantavyam iti | tatheti sa ca dūtaḥ parigṛhītarājaśāsano bodhisattvasakāśam ājagāma | sa ca mahātmā saparijanaḥ surabhimāsaprārabdhasahakāramañjarīkam atimuktakāśokatilakagandhādhivāsitalatāmaṇḍapam akhaṇḍaśobhaṃ vilāsavasatim iva vasantalakṣmyāḥ kiṃcid udyānaṃ praviśyātmānaṃ vinodayāmāsa | pratīhāranivedito 'bhyanujñātapraveśaś ca dūtaḥ pratatabāṣpakaṇavarṣiṇā mukhena praṇamya candraṃ katham api tam anekasattvavināśāyopacaritam adhvaravṛttāntam ākhyāya tāṃ rājājñāṃ nivedayāmāsa | tato bodhisattvaṃ suhṛdo bāndhavāś caivam ūcuḥ | sarvam idaṃ tava nāśāya durātmanaḥ khaṇḍadhārasya cchandaviceṣṭitam | mahādhūrtasya yater iva śāntā ca śarīrakriyā rākṣasasyeva cāśuddham antaḥkaraṇam | aho durātmanāṃ caritāni sarvathā |
children.translated_text: The king said: '<s>Candra</s> the prince is devoted to his elders; he will not transgress my command. I shall send a messenger to him.' When <s>Khaṇḍadhāra</s> agreed, the king summoned a messenger and said: 'Go — wherever <s>Candra</s> may be, tell him he must come to my presence quickly.' The messenger, having received the royal decree, came to the <s>Bodhisattva</s>'s presence. That great soul, together with his retinue, had entered a certain garden — where mango blossoms had begun to sprout in the fragrant month, with <s>atimuktaka</s>, <s>aśoka</s>, and <s>tilaka</s> trees scenting the creeper-pavilions — a bower of unbroken beauty, like the pleasure-dwelling of the goddess of spring — and was diverting himself. The messenger, announced by the chamberlain and permitted to enter, with a face showering incessant drops of tears, prostrating before <s>Candra</s>, somehow narrated the entire account of the sacrifice contrived for the destruction of many beings, and conveyed the king's command. Then the friends and kinsmen of the <s>Bodhisattva</s> spoke thus: 'All this is the scheming of the wicked <s>Khaṇḍadhāra</s> for your destruction. The great impostor — his bodily conduct is outwardly serene like an ascetic's, but his inner heart is impure like a <s>rākṣasa</s>'s! Ah, the conduct of the wicked, in every way —'
'Even when the wicked one has a tranquil appearance but a savage mind,
he is not to be trusted even in the slightest;

children.text: bako hi tiṣṭhann api niścalas taṭe
children.translated_text: does not the heron, even standing motionless on the bank,
kill the shimmering fish?'
'It brings despair even upon the steadfast of those who depend on him,
generates confusion, inflicts inner suffering —
like the poison of a snake reaching through its bite, extremely intense —
the conduct of the wicked is unworthy of association, unbearable!'

children.text: tad ājñāpayatu kumāro yāvad enaṃ durātmānaṃ rakṣovṛttim aphalabrāhmaṇanāmānaṃ khaṇḍadhārakaṃ baddhvānayāmaḥ paretanāthavaśaṃ vā prāpayāma iti | bodhisattva uvāca | satyaṃ mamāpi khaṇḍadhāraṃ prati kiṃcid abhyutthitaḥ kopa āsīt | sa tu me hutavaha iva saliladhārayā kṣamayopaśāntiṃ nītaḥ | yadi cāsmatprāṇair guravaś cirajīvino bhavanti nanu kṛtārthā vayam iti tad alam atrabhavatāṃ khaṇḍadhāraṃ prati kopena yāsyāmy evāham | atha sa dūto vismayād ity avocat | aho mahad āścaryaṃ sarvathā kumāraḥ paramārthakṣamī | kutaḥ |
children.translated_text: 'Then let the prince command, so that we may bind and bring this wicked one of <s>rākṣasa</s> conduct, bearing the fruitless name of a <s>brāhmaṇa</s>, <s>Khaṇḍadhāra</s>, or deliver him to the power of the lord of the dead!' The <s>Bodhisattva</s> said: 'Indeed, some anger had arisen in me toward <s>Khaṇḍadhāra</s>; but it was led to subsidence by forbearance (<s>kṣamā</s>), like fire by a stream of water. And if by [the sacrifice of] my life-breaths my elders become long-lived, then surely we have accomplished our purpose! Therefore, let there be no anger on your part toward <s>Khaṇḍadhāra</s> — I shall indeed go.' Then the messenger spoke in wonder: 'What a great marvel! In every way the prince is one of supreme forbearance! For —'
'One in whom the wisdom of forbearance (<s>kṣānti-vidyā</s>) restrains
the serpent of anger rising to destroy enemies —
he has attained the highest good, among those of pure intentions,
he who has gained illumination is the foremost among those who possess forbearance.'

children.text: atha bodhisattvo bāṣpasalilakaṇamucā svaparijanenānugamyamāno rathavaram āruhya yajñamadhyagataṃ pitaram āgamya covāca |
children.translated_text: Then the <s>Bodhisattva</s>, followed by his retinue shedding tear-drops, ascended the foremost chariot, went to his father who was in the midst of the sacrifice, and said:
'If I have been abandoned by my father
who seeks to save his own life,
then let this body of mine be put to use
as a sacrificial animal in the sacrifice!'
When the king was saying
'I have abandoned you, O son!' —
tears fell upon <s>Candra</s>'s [face],
with pain.
'When, even after standing for a long time,
one must go into the domain of death —',
'then who would wish to prolong life
by the destruction of another?'

children.text: atha khaṇḍadhāras tān ṛtvija uvāca | śṛṇvantūpādhyāyāḥ prathamāhutau pātyamānāyāṃ candraḥ kumāraḥ prāg ānaddhavyaḥ paścād ime kumārā iti |
children.translated_text: Then <s>Khaṇḍadhāra</s> said to those priests: 'Listen, O preceptors! When the first oblation is being offered, let Prince <s>Candra</s> be bound first as the victim, and afterwards these princes.' And —
The princes, of delicate limbs,
looked up with raised necks
at <s>Khaṇḍadhāra</s>
as deer [look upon] a tiger.

children.text: atha te kumārāḥ kṛtāñjalayo bodhisattvam iti vijñāpayāmāsuḥ |
children.translated_text: Then those princes, with folded hands, entreated the <s>Bodhisattva</s> thus:
'While you stand, O brother, lover of the world,
great-souled, eldest, of lofty mind —',
'how will this merciless <s>Khaṇḍadhāra</s>
lead us like animals to the abode of <s>Yama</s>?'

children.text: atha teṣāṃ bhrātṝṇāṃ vacanam ākarṇya duḥkhāyamānahṛdayo bodhisattvo maitrīsamanvitaṃ samādhim ālalambe |
children.translated_text: Then the <s>Bodhisattva</s>, hearing the words of his brothers, his heart pained, entered a meditation suffused with loving-kindness (<s>maitrī</s>).
Through the meditation of that one of purified mind,
composed and concentrated,
the fetters — dark as serpents — of the princes,
their minds amazed, shattered asunder!

children.text: nigaḍasphuṭanavismite ca tasmin rājani kim idam iti ca jātavimarśe tatra khaṇḍadhārake |
children.translated_text: And while the king was astonished at the shattering of the fetters, and while <s>Khaṇḍadhāra</s> was deliberating 'What is this?' —
a cloud arose, heavy with water,
covering the sky, dark as the throat of <s>Śiva</s>,
with the flashing frown of lightning,
and roared loudly, like an enraged <s>rākṣasa</s>!
Felling the peaks of mountains
with broken trees released by the birds,
with resounding, trembling rock surfaces —
the wind blew, friend of fire, with furious force!
Then that dense mass of clouds released
a dense volley, a compact mass of stones!
The sound of <s>praṇava</s> (Oṃ) of the twice-born [priests],
their minds greatly agitated, fell silent in the midst of the sacrifice.
Reddening with its radiance the bellies of the clouds,
heavy with water —
the sun quickly set, as if unable
to witness the calamity of the king.
The golden pots, placed on the sacrificial ground,
as if struck by the angry [gods],
shattered by stones swiftly falling from the sky,
rolled about, broken and ringing.
The sacrificial fire subsided, as if from fear,
its sparks trembling and scattered all around,
its network of pale smoke loosened and fallen,
struck by stones falling from the sky.
The tusks of the elephants, bound in heavy iron casings,
their soft [flesh] compacted from the impact at the banks,
struck by stones, ringing,
released sparks with flashing luster.
The peacock fell from the dwelling-pole;
the rooster crowed discordantly in fear;
and the tame deer, struck by stones, their eyes rolling,
entered the interior of the houses.
A serpent, desiring to drink the cool cloud-wind,
half-emerged from a broad anthill,
quickly spreading its hood with a hiss,
struck by stones, re-entered [the anthill].
But the stones, falling furiously, avoided the <s>Bodhisattva</s>
together with the princes from afar!
The king, together with <s>Khaṇḍadhāra</s>,
set out for the palace, crowded with frightened people.
Halfway along the road — illuminated by the flash of lightning —
as the king and his minister went,
a thunderbolt split their heads,
their hair smeared with drops of fallen brain-matter.
The queen, hearing with tear-filled [eyes] that the king,
whose commands were honored by [other] kings, was dead —
from the weight of extreme sorrow, due to her tender-mindedness,
she suddenly gave up her life.
Then the palace of the king, its interior abandoned by the frightened people,
its door-panels burst open —
struck by stones, immediately collapsed,
producing a sound from the breaking of golden pillars.

children.text: mṛtau bhavetām atha kiṃ nu jīvitau
children.translated_text: 'Are they now dead or alive —
the wicked-hearted king and <s>Khaṇḍadhāra</s>?' —
thus, the rain-clouds, with their flashing
lightning-eyes, seemed to look around on all sides, as if in anger.

children.text: atha prabhātasamaye bodhisattvaḥ pitror agnisaṃskāraṃ kṛtvā dattanivāpasalilāñjaliḥ saṃvignamatir aho sūktam idaṃ buddhānāṃ bhagavatām utpannapradhvaṃsinaḥ sarvabhāvā iti vicintya tān bhrātṝn uvāca |
children.translated_text: Then at dawn, the <s>Bodhisattva</s>, having performed the fire-funeral of his parents, having offered handfuls of water and food-offerings, with a mind stirred with urgency — 'Ah, well said is this by the Blessed Buddhas: all conditioned things are subject to arising and destruction!' — reflecting thus, he said to his brothers:
'She who watered me, the tree of her son,
with the water of affection for my growth —',
'without having obtained the fruit from me,
where has my mother gone?'
'My father, the protector of the earth,
having protected the earth —',
'where has he gone, together with <s>Khaṇḍadhāra</s>,',
'whose <s>dharma</s> was broken?'
'This mansion of the master, with its splendors now only to be remembered,
its pillars and arches fallen —',
'the <s>śālabhañjikā</s> statues, having fallen,
seem to be mourning.'
'These painted walls, now dust-colored,
cracked from the impact of the violent hail,',
'their bricks fallen away,
seem to mourn for themselves.'
'Is this a music-hall
or a dwelling-house?',
'The parts of the ruined mansion
are conjectured only with difficulty.'
'Here, in this place, stood the splendid
house of that king' —',
'thus the people, with longing, from grief,
will tell others.'
'This palace-garden of the king too,
stripped of splendor by the stone-impact,',
'its parrots and cuckoos dead,
seems to be meditating [in mourning].'
'Awaiting the downfall of those
whose hopes of pleasure are unfulfilled —',
'the word "thus" ("iti"), meaning "it is finished,"
stands as if with longing.'
'For men whose tasks are unfinished,',
'[concerning] "he will do," "he does,"',
'and "he did" — impermanence brings about',
'the word "thus" ("iti"), meaning "finished."'
'"Even while I yet stand, the sky
is called eternal" —',
'thus, Impermanence stands',
'looking upward, as if in anger.'
'Those whose conduct is not dependent on others,
who have found tranquility of mind,',
'who have cast off attachment to kinsmen,',
'dwell happily, free from clinging.'

children.text: saṃkalpād viṣayābhilāṣiṇi jane tṛṣṇā karoty āspadaṃ
children.translated_text: 'From intention, craving establishes its foothold in people who desire sense-objects;
one whose mind is bound by craving joins the impure service of folded hands [subservience];',

children.text: sevārtaḥ param ārirādhayiṣayā nighno bhavaty andhavan
children.translated_text: 'one afflicted by service, out of desire to gratify another, becomes violent, walking blindly;',
'the violent one is oppressed by the afflictions of humiliation in the succession of sufferings.'

children.text: kṛcchrāl labdham api krameṇa bhavati prabhraṃśi bhūyaḥ sukhaṃ
children.translated_text: 'Even pleasure obtained with difficulty gradually falls away;

children.text: tadbhraṃśe paritāpam eti puruṣaś cittānalaṃ jvālayan
children.translated_text: when it falls, a man attains torment, kindling the fire of the mind.',
'The cause that generates the continuity of this suffering is the treacherous, ensnaring [craving];',

children.text: te 'tyantaṃ sukhino manaḥsu nihitā yaiḥ samyag alpecchatā
children.translated_text: 'those who have firmly placed contentment with little in their minds are supremely happy.'
'Therefore I, abandoning the kingdom,
thorny with many calamities,',
'for the sake of peace, shall go to the ascetic forest',
'which is the abode on the path of tranquility.'
Then, having consecrated his next-born brother, devoted to ritual,
[amid] the blessings raised by twice-born ones,
abandoning prosperity for the increase of austerity,
he of steadfast mind departed for the forest.

children.text: tad evaṃ tena bhagavatā bodhisattvabhūtenāpakāriṇy api kṣamā na śithilīkṛteti vicintya śreyogaveṣibhiḥ kṣāntibalair bhavitavyam iti ||
children.translated_text: Thus, reflecting that the Blessed One, being a <s>Bodhisattva</s>, did not relax his patience (<s>kṣamā</s>) even toward one who wronged him — those who seek well-being should possess the strength of patience.
|| Thus ends the tenth [birth-story], the <s>Candra Jātaka</s>. ||
22. <s>Mṛga</s> (The Deer)

children.text: na vinā vīryāt tanv api phalam īpsitam āpyate jagadbhūtyai /
children.translated_text: Without effort, not even a slight desired fruit is obtained for the welfare of the world;
thus, disregarding weariness, the fortunate ones exert themselves.

children.text:
tadyathānuśrūyate
kvacid amalasalilavāhinyā vetasapaṅktiśyāmatīralekhayā madgukulānugamyamānacakitamīnakulākulāmbhastalayā prasāritadukūladhavalapulinayā nimnagayā parikṣiptabhūdharapārśve kvacid dāvānalārdhadagdhapariṇatāmalakākṣabadarākīrṇavasudhātale marakatasūcīharitadarbhāṅkuropacite kvacid varāhāvataraṇasaṃtrāsapariplutadarduraparimucyamānapalvalataṭānte 'nyatra mṛgapiśitādhmātaprasuptaśārdūlādhyāsitaguhāmukhe vividhavallīvalayapariveṣṭitanimnakuṭilalekhāṅkitataruskandhe ghanapalāśavaṃśīvanarodhāndhakāranikuñje gahanāntare bodhisattvo mṛgayūthādhipatir babhūva | tena ca mahātmanā rājyam iva sadvṛttena narapatinānupālyamānaṃ hariṇayūtham akutobhayaṃ mahatīṃ vṛddhim agamat |
children.translated_text: As it is traditionally heard: Somewhere, beside a mountain encompassed by a river carrying pure water, with a line of green banks bordered by rows of <s>vetasa</s> reeds, with waters made turbulent by frightened fish-schools pursued by groups of cormorants, with white sandbars stretched out like spread <s>dukūla</s> cloth; somewhere, on ground strewn with half-burnt, ripened <s>āmalaka</s>, <s>akṣa</s>, and <s>badara</s> from a forest fire, planted with darbha-grass shoots green as emerald needles; somewhere, at the edge of pools whose banks were splashed by frogs leaping in terror from a boar's descent; elsewhere, at the mouths of caves occupied by tigers, gorged and sleeping on deer-flesh; with tree-trunks inscribed with curved, winding lines of manifold creeper-garlands, in dark dense bowers of thick-leaved bamboo-forest groves — in the depths of this wilderness, the <s>Bodhisattva</s> was the lord of a deer-herd. And that great-souled one, protecting the deer-herd as if it were a kingdom ruled by a good-conduct king, brought it, free from any fear, to great growth.
That deer, of the color of <s>Hara</s>'s [<s>Śiva</s>'s] blue throat on its back,
possessing the being of <s>Hari</s> [<s>Viṣṇu</s>], eating green grass,
who knew the right and wrong paths — those deer
followed him like good pupils follow their teacher.

children.text: atha kadācit priyamṛgayasya tan mṛgayūthaṃ vyādhasakāśāt kasyacid avanipateḥ śrutipatham ājagāma | sa ca rājā gṛhītadhanvā turagavarādhirohī sainyaparivṛtas tad vanam āgamya dūrāt taṃ mṛgayūtham ālokayāmāsa |
children.translated_text: Now once, through a certain hunter, the news of that deer-herd reached the ears of a certain king who was fond of hunting. And that king, having taken his bow, mounted upon a fine horse, surrounded by his army, came to that forest and from afar surveyed the deer-herd.
That black antelope, abandoning his cud-chewing, standing upright with raised head,
anxious about the fall of arrows upon the deer,
wishing to lead [them away], beheld the king
at the head of his army, come within arrow-range.
Seeing that army, intent on killing,
with bows strung, producing the sound of jingling bridles —
surrounded by deer with eyes rolling in fear,
that herd-lord reflected firmly thus:
'A king protects the welfare-seeking subjects,
in whom no fear has arisen, through [his] auspicious nature.',
'Without considering his own exertion,',
'he is a true protector who protects even in adversity.'
'How can I bear to watch these deer —
their eyes rolling in terror-stricken bewilderment,',
'their ground sprinkled with dripping blood,
their bodies quivering, fallen before me, struck by arrows?'
'Before the sport-hunting ones strike these deer',
'with sharpened arrows,',
'let me, with my strength, make the effort
to protect these fearful, rolling-eyed ones!'

children.text: idam vanam anena sainyena sarvataḥ parikṣiptaṃ tat katamayā diśā mṛgayūthaṃ nirvāhayāmīti samantato 'valokyācintayat | bhavatu labdha upāyaḥ | imāṃ girisaritam ullaṅghya svasti mṛgebhyaḥ syād iti tarkayāmi | na caikena krameṇaite hariṇāḥ śakyanta etāṃ śīghrasalilavāhinīṃ samudrapatnīṃ ullaṅghitum iti | tad idam atra prāptam asyāḥ sarito madhyāvasthitasya mama pṛṣṭhe kramaṃ dattvā sukham ete mṛgā yāsyantīti vicintya kvacit taṭataruśikhāpraskhalitasalilāyāḥ paribhramadāvartamadhyabhrāntaviśīrṇaphenasaṅghāyās tasyāḥ kṣitidharasarito madhyam avagāhya sthirayitvātmānaṃ sa mahātmā tān mṛgān uvāca |
children.translated_text: 'This forest is encircled on all sides by this army. By which direction shall I lead out the deer-herd?' — thus looking around on all sides, he reflected: 'So be it — a plan has been found! I reckon that by crossing over this mountain-river, safety for the deer will be [achieved]. But these deer cannot cross this swift-flowing wife of the ocean by a single crossing.' 'Therefore, this is the appropriate [thing here] — let the deer easily go by placing their step on my back as I stand in the middle of this river!' — having reflected thus, plunging into the middle of that mountain-river — whose water stumbled off the treetops of the bank-side trees and whose scattered foam-masses whirled in circling eddies — and steadying himself, the great-souled one said to the deer:
'Leaping from this bank
and placing your step on my back,',
'go swiftly, your fear gone,
O flock-members, from this danger!'
'This body of mine is worthless
because it is destined for arrows, and because of [its] lack of <s>dharma</s>;',
'through saving you,
it shall at long last obtain something of substance.'
'When the body is averse to helping others,
it is then an inauspicious thing;',
'but when it supports the welfare of others,',
'then this body is a jewel.'
'If I am able to save you from fear,
pursued by the king's soldiers —',
'then today on this earth, this title',
'"lord of the herd" would be fruitful for me.'

children.text: āgamyatāṃ tad adhunā nanu tāvad eva
children.translated_text: 'Come then, right now — quickly,

children.text: yuṣmāsu yāvad iṣavo na patanti śātāḥ
children.translated_text: before the sharp arrows fall upon you!',
'Climbing upon my back, which has become a bridge
over the mountain-river's water, cross over from that army-fear!'

children.text: atha te hariṇā maraṇabhītā yūthapatipṛṣṭhe kramaṃ dattvā nadīsalilam ullaṅghya dvitīyaṃ kūlam upagantum ārebhire |
children.translated_text: Then those deer, frightened of death, placing their step on the herd-lord's back, began to cross over the river-water and reach the other bank.
The more violently the deer, their eyes rolling in fright,
fell upon his back —
the more that lord of the deer-herd
forced his hooves firmly into steadfastness.
Then blood [flowed] from the torn flesh of the deer-lord's [back] —
from his back, scored and split by hooves, gushed [blood].
Seeing the deer-herd safely reaching the mountain-edge from afar,
he disregarded his pain and took hold of joy alone.
Of those whose beings have been protected
by stratagem or by strength,
the succession of inner joy
blocks the suffering of the great.

children.text: atha sa rājā hariṇanistaraṇāya saritsalilamadhyasaṃkramībhūtātmānaṃ yūthapatim ālokya vismayam āgamya śarāsaneṣu śarān saṃdadhānaṃ senājanam uvāca | yaḥ khalu kaścin mṛgam āhanyāt so 'smaddrohīti |
children.translated_text: Then that king, seeing the herd-leader who had made himself a bridge in the midst of the river's water for the deer to cross, was filled with wonder and said to the army-men who were nocking arrows to their bows: 'Whoever kills a deer is a traitor to me!'
Then, hearing the command
of that sovereign,
those people immediately unstrung
the bowstrings from their bows.

children.text: bodhisattvo 'pi ca kiṃ nu nistīrṇāḥ sarve mṛgāḥ syur na veti paścād ālokayann apaśyad ekam atīva bhayacañcalākṣam atikrāntaṃ yūtham ālokayantam asāmarthyād anutsahamāṇaṃ kramaṃ dātuṃ katamayā diśā gacchāmīti dolāyamānahṛdayaṃ hariṇaśāvakam ālokya ca paramāṃ karuṇām ālalambe |
children.translated_text: And the <s>Bodhisattva</s>, looking back to see whether all the deer had crossed safely, saw a deer-fawn — its eyes excessively agitated with fear, looking toward the herd that had passed, unable from weakness to take a step, its heart swaying [in indecision] as to 'which direction shall I go?' — and upon seeing it, he took hold of supreme compassion.
'Abandon your fear! For the <s>Bodhisattva</s>
will not forsake you, a young one, alone!'
The flowering trees, as if by the sounds of bees,
seemed to console him thus.

children.text: atha yūthapatiḥ pratyuttīrya tasmāt salilāt taṃ mṛgaśāvakam uvāca |
children.translated_text: Then the herd-leader, having crossed back from that water, said to the deer-fawn:
'Climb upon my back with your limbs
and release the agony of [fear of] death!
I shall carry you from this bank
to the other shore of the river.'
'He who has undertaken the exertion of valor
to rescue the world from the ocean of existence —
how shall he not rescue you,
a single one, from the waters of a river?'
Then, mounted by that deer-fawn,
that valorous one,
relying on compassion,
plunged into the wave-garlanded river.
'These wounds on your back —
do they not cause you deep pain?' —
saying this, as it were, the river, with wave-hands,
touched him as he emerged.

children.text: atha yūthādhipatis taṃ mṛgaśāvakam uttārya tasyāḥ saritaḥ praharṣaviśālalocanayā mātrā saṃyojayāmāsa |
children.translated_text: Then the herd-leader, having carried the deer-fawn across, reunited it with its mother, whose eyes were wide with joy.
Then the thirsty deer-fawn,
placing both knees on the ground,
quickly seized the teats of its mother,
from which milk had begun to flow.
And she, turning her face around,
toward his face moving with the suckling,
licked him repeatedly with affection
with the quivering tip of her tongue.
Then the <s>Bodhisattva</s>, his bodily exertion depleted from fatigue and the pain of the hoof-wounds,
somehow finding the path of the deer, marked with hoof-prints on the turf,
confused, slowly settling down on the ground, stained with blood,
rested for a moment, that one burdened with accumulated fatigue.
'To this state, O child, you have been brought by me,
your pitiless birth-mother, in truth!' —
thus, seeing his wounded body, from the anguish of compassion,
[his mother] wept bitterly, gazing at him.
And that king, having crossed the river with his retinue, dismounting from his horse, approached that great-souled one with an astonished mind. The herd-leader, seeing the king, spoke:

children.text: sa ca rājā tāṃ saritam uttīrya saparijanas turagād avatīrya vismitamanās taṃ mahātmānam upasasāda | sa yūthādhipatī rājānam ālokyābravīt |
children.translated_text: 'That I did not rise
upon seeing you, who deserve to be received with honor —
that is not disrespect on my part;
I am overcome by fatigue.'
Then that king, sitting down with amazement, having inquired about [the herd-leader's] welfare, spoke these gratifying words to the herd-leader:

children.text: atha sa rājā savismayam upaviśya kuśalaṃ pṛṣṭvā yūthapatim iti saṃrādhayann uvāca |
children.translated_text: 'By the shameless, who with weapons raised are intent on slaying others,
whose mind-eyes are sealed by the darkness of desire for pleasures,
you, O deer-sage who knows <s>dharma</s>, accompanied by compassion,
are to be worshipped by such human-animals as myself!'
'A king protects his servants, fearless in time of battle,
desiring the protection of his own self;
but by your statecraft, skilled in protecting your own herd,
the statecraft of all kings has been surpassed in every way!'
'What is remarkable if many servants

children.text: citraṃ kim atra bahavo yadi bhūmipālaṃ
children.translated_text: protect a king who has entered the battle-field?
That these many deer were protected by you,
a single deer — that is truly wondrous here!'

children.text: yat pālitāḥ khalu tad adbhutam etad atra

children.translated_text: 'O deer, this deer-state of yours,
endowed with manifold virtues and compassion,
seems to mock this human-state of mine,
which is devoid of qualities, light from lack of compassion, by the gain of its distinction!'
Thus having honored the herd-leader, the king asked: 'What station do you aspire to with this valor so skilled in helping others?' The <s>Bodhisattva</s> said: 'Hear, O great king!'

children.text: ity abhisaṃrādhya sa rājā yūthapatim apṛcchat | kīdṛśaṃ punar anena paropakārapaṭunā vīryeṇa bhavān padam abhilaṣati | bodhisattva uvāca |śrūyatāṃ mahārāja |
children.translated_text: 'To attain Buddhahood —
this is my vigor, O best of the vigorous!
As far as it is able, even in the state of a deer,
it does not flag.'
'Just as these deer, agitated with fear,
were rescued by me from the river-waters of terrifying current,
so may I rescue the world, beset by many afflictions,
from the ocean of the suffering of existence!'
'And, O great king, even a powerful person who turns his back on vigor cannot attain the desired goal. See:'

children.text: na ca mahārāja śakyate vīryaparāṅmukhena balavatāpy abhilaṣitaṃ padam abhigantum | paśya |
children.translated_text: 'Even with allies, a person
does not attain success through laziness —
like a ball, wet with water,
that has slipped from the hand to the ground.'
'Moreover:'
'Even by a wise one with lazy mind,
the lofty station that is the abode of happiness cannot be attained;
a vessel not rowed by those holding oars
does not reach the far shore of the ocean, even after a long time.'

children.text: cirād api vrajati na pāram ambudheḥ

children.translated_text: The king said: 'Well spoken by the lord of the deer-herd! For indeed:'
'Even one born in a lineage of pure fame, of renowned prosperity,
even one who has attained the foremost position in assemblies through the wisdom of a scholar —
through laziness, a man's wish never attains its fruit even once;

children.text: ālasyān na manorathaḥ sakṛd api prāpnoti puṃsaḥ phalaṃ
children.translated_text: an arrow, even though well-aimed with virtue, does not hit its mark without the archer's effort.'

children.text: lakṣyaṃ naiti guṇārpito 'pi viśikhaḥ kṣeptuḥ prayatnād vinā

children.translated_text: 'Therefore, by you who rely on vigor, the state of Buddhahood can surely be attained.'

children.text: tad itthaṃ vīryāvalambinā bhavatā śakyam adhigantuṃ bauddhaṃ padam iti |
ye śāntaṃ padam ārurukṣava iha kleśair abhinnāśayās
children.translated_text: 'Those people of merit who, desiring the peaceful state here, with minds unbroken by afflictions,

children.text: tvattaḥ prāk kṛtinaḥ kṛtapraṇidhayo bodhau ghaṭante janāḥ
children.translated_text: who have made vows toward enlightenment before you, strive [on the path] —'

children.text: teṣāṃ vartmani vājinām iva pariśrāntyā śanair dhāvatām
children.translated_text: 'on their path, like horses gradually running with weariness,
you, like a thoroughbred freed from the fear of fatigue, will be the foremost.'
'Bearing the aggregate of bodily radiances free of darkness, as a serving attendant [bears a lamp],
proclaiming the <s>Dharma</s> repeatedly to people eager for <s>Dharma</s>-discourse,
with the bonds of afflictions cut, honored by the wise who possess the wealth of virtues —

children.text: tvāṃ buddhatvam upāgataṃ gatabhavaṃ drakṣyanti dhanyā janāḥ
children.translated_text: the fortunate shall behold you, having attained Buddhahood, gone beyond existence!'

children.text: iti sa rājā bodhisattvam abhisaṃrādhyovāca | aho bhavantam evaṃ dharmābhimukham ālokya mamāpi dharmābhilāṣa utpannaḥ |
children.translated_text: Then that king, saying 'Ah, my heart has been delighted by this <s>Dharma</s>-teaching of yours!', attained supreme joy.
'Then teach, O great-minded one,
the <s>Dharma</s>, O best among knowers of <s>Dharma</s>!
By practicing which, pure [<s>Dharma</s>],
I would not go to an evil rebirth.'

children.text: bodhisattva uvāca | yady evam ataḥ śrotum arhati mahārājaḥ |
children.translated_text: The <s>Bodhisattva</s> said: 'If so, then may the great king hear:'
'Turning away from wrongdoing
and engaging in what is virtuous —
this is the essence of <s>Dharma</s>,
rightly declared by those of renowned wisdom.'
'Even when this truth is elucidated,
with good and evil made manifest —
he who goes by the wrong path
is blind even while possessing eyes.'
'Therefore, with the lamp of wisdom
having surveyed the great path,
undertake those actions that are to be practiced
for the destruction of afflictions!'
'O lord of the earth, with ignorance destroyed,
protect the earth through <s>dharma</s>!
People are always alarmed
by a king of harsh punishment.'
'If you have any desire for fame —
white as the breaking of a lotus stalk,
illuminating the world — or a wish
to obtain the desired fruit, then bear the pure ornament of virtues!'

children.text: atha sa narapatir aho bhavato 'nayā dharmadeśanayā prahlāditam idaṃ me hṛdayam ity abhidhāya parāṃ prītim ājagāma |
children.translated_text: Then that king, saying 'Ah, my heart has been delighted by this <s>Dharma</s>-teaching of yours,' attained supreme joy.
Then, of that herd-leader,
by the grievous pain arising from the hoof-wounds,
that had afflicted him,
both eyes closed.
Then the king, having built for him
a pyre of sandalwood logs,
performed the fire-obsequies
for that meritorious, nobly-born one.
Then, when that deer, of nature purified by compassion,
had gone to heaven, like a dear friend,
the king, having mourned for a long time,
swiftly returned to the city, his mind distraught.
When that deer died — by the forest-deities,
whose eyes were like those of doe-eyed women,
skilled in benefiting beings, endowed with virtue,
their activities ceased as if for a known kinsman —
unbroken tears were shed, with a luster like pearls.
Then the earth trembled, with its mountain-peaks shaking;
the ocean-waves were swollen by the gale-wind;
