and from the sky fell a shower of <s>mandāra</s> flowers,
variegated with wandering bees, scattering fragrance.

children.text: nirvāṇakāle ca bhagavatā bhikṣūnāṃ purastād idaṃ jātakam abhyadhāyi |

children.translated_text: And at the time of [His] <s>nirvāṇa</s>, the Blessed One narrated this <s>jātaka</s> before the monks:
'The herd-leader of the deer
in that forest was I at that time;
and this wandering ascetic <s>Subhadra</s>
was the deer-fawn.'

children.text: bhagavataś ca prāk parinirvṛte tatra subhadre parivrājake bhikṣavaḥ papracchuḥ | kāni punaḥ karmāṇi subhadreṇa kṛtāni yat sarvaśrāvakebhyaḥ paścād arhatphalaṃ prāpya prathamam eva ca bhagavataḥ parinirvṛta iti | bhagavān āha |

children.translated_text: And after the Blessed One had first passed into <s>nirvāṇa</s>, the monks asked about that wandering ascetic <s>Subhadra</s>: 'What deeds did <s>Subhadra</s> perform that, [though] the last of all disciples to attain the fruit of <s>arhat</s>-ship, he was the first to pass into <s>nirvāṇa</s> before the Blessed One?' The Blessed One said:
'There was a <s>Buddha</s> named <s>Kāśyapa</s>,
who had crossed the ocean of the knowable;
a monk named <s>Aśoka</s>
was the nephew of that Protector.'
'The supreme light is easily obtainable for me
since my uncle is the <s>Sugata</s>' —
thinking thus, <s>Aśoka</s>
did not exert himself for liberation.
'Then, when <s>Aśoka</s> had gone to another land,
<s>Kāśyapa</s>, the best of the meritorious,
who had gone beyond rebirth,
set his mind upon <s>nirvāṇa</s>.'
'Then, when the monk <s>Aśoka</s> was standing beneath an <s>aśoka</s> tree,
stricken with grief,
a tree-deity dwelling in that great tree
shed tears, with a luster like pearls.'
'As she was reflecting "Today it shall come to pass" —
the <s>nirvāṇa</s> of the <s>Jina</s> — she, unquiet,
her hot tear fell upon the body
of the son of <s>Pārāśarin</s> [<s>Aśoka</s>, that tree-deity's [tear].'
'This sky is cloudless — whence then
has this water fallen upon my body?'
Speaking thus, looking upward,
he saw that deity weeping.
He asked her, pitiably grieving:
'Why do you weep, O deity, stricken with sorrow?'
And she, her speech faltering in her throat,
somehow managed to tell the monk:
'The great sage <s>Kāśyapa</s>, compassionate, working for the world's good,
self-controlled, his fuel of latent tendencies burned —
giving sorrow to beings, he will now pass into <s>nirvāṇa</s> —
therefore I weep, pitifully!'
'When that sage-lamp, unshaken by the moths of disputants' words,
who illuminated the true path and the false —
when that sage-lamp is extinguished in <s>nirvāṇa</s>,
darkness will pervade the three worlds!'
Hearing this speech of the tree-deity,
he fell to the ground as if struck in a vital spot by a sharp arrow,
his eyes closed;
and after a long time, having risen, he lamented.
The tree-deity, concerned, asked him:

children.text: sa mātulo me bhagavān iti vyathāṃ
children.translated_text: 'Tell me, O monk, why do you weep so?'

children.text: kathaṃ na yāsyāmi sa cedam abravīt
children.translated_text: 'That Blessed One is my uncle!' — he said —
'How shall I not feel anguish?'
'The enchanting flower of words from the <s>Jina</s>-tree,
only a little was gathered by me, the negligent one;
the fruit that destroys the chain of afflictions of the three worlds —
that was not obtained by me, the dull-witted one!'
'This [ignorance], which has taken shelter in the mansion of my mind,
terrible, blocking the path to liberation —
why did you not shatter it and go to liberation
with the word-rays of the <s>Tathāgata</s>-moon, O darkness?'

children.text: atha sā devatā taṃ bhikṣum idam avocat | alam alam ativiṣādena | yāvan na nirvāṇam upagacchati sa bhagavāṃs tāvad eva bhavantaṃ mantraprabhāvād ākāśena neṣyāmīti | anukampitaḥ syām ahaṃ bhavatyety uktavati tatra tathāgatabhāgineye sā devatā tasmād aśokān mantraparijaptāni kusumāny ādāya mamainam aśokakusumāñjalim īkṣamāṇo nabhasā gacchantīm mām anugacchety uvāca |

children.translated_text: Then he followed that deity through the sky.
his eyes fixed upon an offering of <s>aśoka</s> flowers,
and quickly coming into the presence of the <s>Tathāgata</s>,
spoke, shedding tears again and again:
'O lord of sages, this heedless, childish one, whose raft of understanding has departed,
submerged in the great ocean of ignorance,
me, tormented by the great waves of suffering —
how can you go, without in an instant having rescued [me]?'
Speaking thus, with stammering syllables,
shedding tears, with eyes clouded,
the <s>Jina</s> (Victorious One), turning him from the wrong path for immediate liberation,
led him by the purified path.

children.text: athārhatphalabhāginaṃ bhāgineyaṃ kṛtvā sakalaṃ ca lokaṃ vacanāṃśubhiḥ prakāśya kāśyapaḥ samyaksaṃbuddhaḥ parinirvavau | parinirvṛte ca tatra bhagavati śokavaśīkṛteṣu surāsurakinnaramahoragayakṣamanuṣyeṣu nabhasaḥ paripatati mandārakusumavarṣe sā devatā śokavaśād iti tat tad vilapitum ārebhe |
children.translated_text: Then, having made his nephew a partaker of the fruit of <s>arhatship</s>, and having illuminated the entire world with the rays of his words, <s>Kāśyapa</s> the perfectly enlightened <s>Buddha</s> (<s>samyaksaṃbuddha</s>) passed into <s>parinirvāṇa</s>. And when the Blessed One had passed away, while gods, <s>asuras</s>, <s>kinnaras</s>, great serpents, <s>yakṣas</s>, and humans were overcome by grief, and a rain of <s>mandāra</s> flowers was falling from the sky, that deity, overcome by grief, began to lament thus:
'Seated upon the lion-throne,
releasing flower-words [of the Dharma] —'
'whose teaching of the <s>Dharma</s> will this world,
seeking the <s>Dharma</s>, listen to?'
'With you, O Lord, the supreme light,
having set like the sun —'
'this world has been closed off
by an irresistible darkness.'
'Now that you have gone to peace,
by the restless <s>Manobhava</s> (Cupid),
surely the bow has been raised again
to delude the world!'
'With the sage gone to peace, we, shelterless,
where shall we rest, our passions aroused?'
'By the virtues thus following the path of the knowable,
O lord of sages, it is as if a cry [is uttered] without you!'
'Relying on your aspiration (<s>praṇidhi</s>) toward enlightenment, wandering in the three worlds
for the sake of beings, firm of mind — I never abandoned you;'

children.text: parityajya tvaṃ māṃ kim iti jananīṃ vatsala gataḥ
children.translated_text: 'O affectionate one, why have you gone, forsaking me, your mother?

children.text: prayāte tvayy evaṃ ruditam iva dīnaṃ karuṇayā
children.translated_text: When you departed thus, even compassion seemed to weep pitifully.'

children.text:
atha sa bhikṣur abhyadhāt | alam alaṃ devate viṣādena na kvacid iyam anityatā na praharati yatredṛśasyāpi bhagavato vajragurusārasyābhāva
iti | atha sā devatā kathaṃcid ātmānaṃ dhīrayitvā praṇidhim iti cakāra |
children.translated_text: Then that monk said: 'Enough, enough, O deity, with despair! This impermanence strikes everywhere — where even for such a one as the Blessed One, firm as a diamond, there is absence.' Then that deity, having somehow steeled herself, made this aspiration (<s>praṇidhi</s>):
'As by coming to me, this monk
has attained the fruit —'
'so may I then become the last disciple
of <s>Śākyamuni</s>!'
'Having attained the fruit of <s>arhatship</s>
at the time of the sage's <s>nirvāṇa</s> —'
'therefore, may I pass into <s>parinirvāṇa</s> before [him],
unable to bear the grief!'

children.text: atha bhagavāṃs teṣāṃ bhikṣūṇāṃ purastād idaṃ varṇayitvā punar uvāca |
children.translated_text: Then the Blessed One, having narrated this before those monks, said further:
'That forest-deity who dwelt
in the <s>aśoka</s> tree —'
'is this wandering ascetic <s>Subhadra</s>,
of auspicious mind and great wisdom.'
'By the power of his aspiration,
he attained the status of my disciple;'
'and first, before my <s>nirvāṇa</s>,
he himself attained <s>nirvṛti</s> (final liberation).'
This wonderful <s>jātaka</s>,
properly revealed by <s>Śākyamuni</s>,
should be recounted by one of sweet speech
for the pacification of the minds of the learned.
Having made known his supreme vows for the purpose of benefiting others,
the bond of heroic effort is not loosened even in calamity;
reflecting thus, to attain the ultimate end
in the work of the world's welfare, let there be no indolence!
|| Thus ends the <s>Mṛgajātaka</s> ||
24. <s>Mūlikajātaka</s>
Those who are soft-hearted with compassion do not neglect even an enemy afflicted with disease, being friends of the world;
how much less one who is a continuous companion from birth!

children.text:
tadyathānuśrūyate
samadhigatavedavedāṅgatihāsaḥ paramārthajñaḥ paramārthābhilāṣī sarvasattvānukampī mūliko nāma brāḥmaṇo bodhisattvo babhūva |
sa ca mahātmā vyādhimatāṃ vyādhipraśamanāya himavanmandarapariyātrasahyavindhyavanāntarāṇy oṣadhinimittaṃ vicacāra |
children.translated_text: Thus it is heard in tradition: There was a brāhmaṇa named <s>Mūlika</s>, a <s>Bodhisattva</s>, who had mastered the <s>Vedas</s>, <s>Vedāṅgas</s>, and <s>Itihāsas</s>, who knew the supreme truth, who aspired to the supreme truth, who was compassionate toward all beings. And that great-souled one, to cure the diseases of the sick, wandered through the forests of the <s>Himavat</s>, <s>Mandara</s>, <s>Pariyātra</s>, <s>Sahya</s>, and <s>Vindhya</s> [mountains] in search of medicinal herbs.
Then, observing the dense sandalwood forests entwined with serpents
in the summer season,
with the web of his hair at the front matted and worn from slipping on the peaks,
he once wandered to <s>Malaya</s>, the abode of <s>siddhas</s> (perfected ones).
Seeing fresh peppercorns at the cave-mouths
bitten by the beaks of <s>hārīta</s> birds like bits of lightning,
smelling the breeze-stirred fragrance of flowers,
that resolute one sat upon a rock to rest from fatigue.

children.text:
kṛtapariśramavinodaś ca samutthāya mahauṣadhīnāṃ khanitreṇa mūlāni cakhāna |
baddhvā ca mahāntam auṣadhabhāraṃ gacchāmy adhunāuṣadhapradānena janam anāmayaṃ kariṣyāmīti vicintya malayāt pratiṣṭhamāno gāḍhaglāniparipāṇḍutanuśarīram upāntanihitakamaṇḍalupātraṃ pariṇatatṛṇasaṃstaropaviṣṭam agratoniṣaṇṇahariṇamithunam abhinavasaṃdhyāsadṛśacīvaraprāvṛtāṅgam upaśāntendriyaṃ pratyekabuddham adrākṣīt ||
children.translated_text: And having rested, rising and digging the roots of great medicinal herbs with a spade, and having bound a great bundle of herbs, thinking 'I shall now go and make the people free from disease through the gift of medicines,' as he was setting forth from <s>Malaya</s>, he beheld a <s>Pratyekabuddha</s> — body pale and thin from severe weakness, with his water-vessel placed nearby, seated upon a mat of withered grass, with a pair of deer sitting quietly before him, his body wrapped in a robe the color of a fresh sunset, his senses calmed.
Then, seeing that tranquil one, following the path of humility,
having set down from his shoulders the great burden of roots,
as if pouring forth the burden of devotion and faith from afar,
he bowed with his head, touching the dust of the ground.
[...lacuna...] HJm_24.5
And that brāhmaṇa asked him thus:
'I see the noble one's body wasted with illness.'
The <s>Pratyekabuddha</s> spoke to him with a voice
made faint by the overpowering onset of disease:
'This body, like an anthill,
produced by a succession of karmic actions,
causing affliction to the world, is inhabited by
numerous disease-serpents.'
'And when this lioness of old age
attacks the body of the proud one,
then the elephant of his mind, its sense-faculties gone, abandons
its pride from despair.'
'Thereafter, death, an enemy without cause,
breaks the body-hut;'
'and when that is broken, in an instant
all activities of a person cease.'
'By these three enemies — death, old age, and disease —
set in motion by <s>karma</s>, a person is assailed;'
'this existence, arising from the fire of unending afflictions (<s>kleśas</s>),

children.text: bhavo yam āryair ata eva neṣyate
children.translated_text: is therefore not desired by the noble ones.'
'Having reflected thus, you who are skilled in reflection,
upon these existences, which are fearsome like serpents,
fixing your aspiration upon the path of tranquility,
mount the chariot made of heroic effort!'

children.text: atha bodhisattvaḥ aho subhāṣitam ity abhidhāya taṃ pratyekajinam abhimantryābravīt |
children.translated_text: Then the <s>Bodhisattva</s>, exclaiming 'Ah, well spoken!' and addressing that <s>Pratyekajina</s>, said:
'The attainment of the jewel of well-spoken words,
which cleaves the darkness of ignorance —'
'is found nowhere else than in the clear, deep
ocean of the saintly, whose waters are understanding.'
'The heroic effort of a person urged by a good person toward the <s>Dharma</s>
progresses with ever-greater sharpness —'
'like a vessel on the ocean, driven by the wind,
with a skilled helmsman stationed [at the helm].'

children.text: tato 'haṃ bhadantaṃ tāvat paricariṣyāmi yāvad asmād glānyān mahākāntārād iva samuttīrṇa ity abhidhāya gaganamadhyapratyāsanne sphuradaṅśumaṇḍale vivasvati tarucchāyānilīneṣu śvāsavaśaparisphuratprakāśajihvātāluṣu śvetāpāṅgeṣu palvalasalilāvataraṇasamutsukeṣu sajalajaladharanīleṣu vanamahiṣayūtheṣu surabhiśiśiracandanataruviṭapān sutarāṃ pariveṣṭayatsu bhujageṣu tīkṣṇatarātapāliṅganasaṃtaptapāṃsunikareṣu pathikajanavimucyamāneṣv adhvasu malayatarugṛhapativiśrāṇitaṃ paripākamṛdusurabhivividhaphalapiṇḍapātam ānīya |
children.translated_text: Saying 'Therefore I shall attend upon the venerable one until [he] has, as it were, crossed over from this great wilderness of illness,' in midday when the sun's blazing disk was near the middle of the sky, when the herds of wild buffaloes — dark as rain-clouds full of water — were hidden in the shade of trees, their tongues and palates flickering visibly from panting breath, their eyes white-cornered, eager to descend into pool-waters, when serpents coiled even more tightly around the cool, fragrant branches of sandalwood trees, when the roads were deserted by travelers [fleeing] the heaps of dust scorched by the embrace of the fierce heat — he brought the alms-food of various ripe, fragrant, soft fruits, distributed as if by the householder of the <s>Malaya</s> trees, and
with <s>palāśa</s> leaves, he made a great
sun-shade from a <s>palāśa</s> tree
and held it over the <s>Pratyekabuddha</s>
for the cooling of the heat.
A merchant skilled in means,
who does not heed fatigue,
wandering the four directions,
obtains abundant profit.
The <s>Bodhisattva</s>, reflecting thus,
in order to perform service to him,
regarded neither hunger nor fierce heat
nor fatigue.
'If one does not attend upon the wise, the world's teachers,
one never obtains well-spoken [wisdom];'
'he who goes to the jewel-land for wealth
is endowed with the prosperity of special gems.'
Thus, attending upon that noble-conducted one,
that one of resolute spirit, for the accumulation of the fruit of merit,
with faith increasing day by day,
considered the gain of [this] birth fruitful indeed.

children.text: atha sa pratyekajino bodhisattvasya dviguṇataraprasādajananārtham ambaratalam utpatya tat tat prātihāryam adarśayat ||
children.translated_text: Then that <s>Pratyekajina</s>, in order to generate even greater faith in the <s>Bodhisattva</s>, flying up into the sky, displayed various miracles:
With his body surrounded by radiating beams of light,
he spread across the spotless sky as if upon water;
and he shone, resembling a golden mountain,
that self-controlled one, seated upon a lotus-seat in the midst [of the sky].
Again and again he entered the earth, splitting it open,
and slowly rose again like the sun;
and by the power of yoga he brought forth multiplicity,
simultaneously [producing] water and fire from his arms.
With a hand lotus-like, with trembling nail-luster,
he touched the sun;
he attained multiplicity, free from the fear of birth,
like the sun [reflected] in waters, his body pure.
Beholding him thus, of great miraculous power,
radiant like the cool-rayed [moon],
for a long time with both eyes held still,
that foremost of brāhmaṇas proclaimed his joy.
Beholding that <s>Pratyekabuddha</s> of even more wondrous power
through miraculous display, with firm faith,
the <s>vidyādharas</s> (knowledge-bearers), traveling through the sky, released
flowers with their interiors golden from stamen-pollen.

children.text: atha bodhisattvaḥ kṣititalavinihitajānuḥ pramodāpūryamāṇahṛdayaḥ śirasi viniveśitāñjalis taṃ pratyekajinaṃ prabhāsvarair vacanamaṇibhir abhyarcayām āsa ||
children.translated_text: Then the <s>Bodhisattva</s>, with knees placed upon the ground, his heart overflowing with joy, with joined palms placed upon his head, worshipped that <s>Pratyekajina</s> with luminous word-jewels:
'Beholding this miraculous body
of yours —'
'even <s>Brahmā</s> would be amazed —
how much more an ordinary person like me!'
'By you, of blazing splendor,
who have displayed these miracles —'
'this sky that you occupy
appears as if having two suns.'
'This wondrous majesty of miraculous power
belongs to yogins such as you —'
'those who are skilled in the accomplishment
of blessing others — it manifests fittingly.'
'The moon does not shine for its own sake,
the forehead-ornament of the eastern [quarter];'
'the risings of great ones of pure mind
are solely for the sake of others.'
'Had I not come to this <s>Malaya</s>,
dark with sandalwood trees —'
'I would not have gained the merit arising from attending upon you,
the seed of the path to liberation.'
'Desiring to bestow grace upon me, you bear
this body of no small power and weight,
standing in the <s>Malaya</s> mountain forest —
surely under the pretext of having destroyed afflictions, with your illness.'
'Oceans bear radiant gems; clouds bear water white as crystal cuttings;
trees bear great abundance of fruit;'
'and those like you [bear] long life —
all for the sake of others.'
'By weaving with the threads of words a garland of praise of your virtues,
the fruit of the root of merit that I have obtained —'
'by that, having attained the station of wisdom, the state of the Ten-Powered [<s>Buddha</s>],
may I become the cause of the destruction of existence for this world!'

children.text:
atha sa pratyekabuddhaḥ tasya brāhamaṇasya buddhatvāya praṇidhim ākarṇya pramuditamanās tatraivāntaradhīyata |
bodhisattvo 'pi ca mahāntam iva lābham adhigamya
children.translated_text: Then that <s>Pratyekabuddha</s>, hearing the <s>Bodhisattva</s>'s aspiration toward Buddhahood, with a delighted mind, vanished right there. And the <s>Bodhisattva</s> too, as if having attained a great gain,
having placed the dust from the feet of the <s>Pratyekabuddha</s>
upon his head, with body-hair standing on end from faith,
taking his herbs from the interior of the <s>Malaya</s> mountain forest,
went among the people to remove the world's illness.

children.text: tad evaṃ sa bhagavān bodhisattvabhūtaḥ sakalalokasya kleśavyādhim apahartukāmaḥ karuṇāprotsāhitavīryabalaḥ svakhedam agaṇayitvā glānam pratyekabuddhaṃ paricacārety ataḥ kuśalaphalam abhilaṣatā kulaputreṇa glānaparicaryāyān nānādareṇa bhavitavyam iti ||
children.translated_text: Thus, reflecting that the Blessed One who was a <s>Bodhisattva</s>, desiring to remove the disease of afflictions of the entire world, with heroic effort spurred by compassion, without regarding his own fatigue, attended upon the ailing <s>Pratyekabuddha</s> — therefore, a son of good family who desires the fruit of merit should act with diligent care in attending upon the sick.
|| The <s>Mūlikajātaka</s>, the Twenty-fourth ||
26. <s>Jājvalijātaka</s>
Even one who has gained illumination by the light of the lamp of <s>dhyāna</s> (meditation) does not go to <s>nirvāṇa</s>,
because, desiring to attain enlightenment (<s>bodhi</s>), that is for the sake of continued benefit to beings.

children.text:
tadyathānuśrūyate |
samadhigatavedatattvo vividhaśāstrābhyāsavimalamatir anekāsu vidvatsadaḥsu prasṛtakīrtiḥ svasamayavyāpāraparāyaṇo gṛhāśramam adhyāvasan kadā cit bodhisattvo jājvalī nāma brāhmaṇo babhūva |
sa ca mahātmā viditagārhasthyadoṣaḥ praśamasukhābhilāṣī paripūrṇavibhave 'pi bhavane ratim alabhamānaḥ kadā cid evam acintayat ||
children.translated_text:
Thus it is heard:
The <s>Bodhisattva</s> was once a <s>brāhmaṇa</s> named <s>Jājvalī</s>, who had mastered the essence of the <s>Vedas</s>, whose intellect was purified by the study of various <s>śāstras</s>, whose fame had spread in many assemblies of the learned, who was devoted to the practices of his own tradition, and who dwelt in the householder's stage of life.
That great soul, having recognized the faults of household life and desiring the happiness of tranquility, finding no delight even in his abundantly prosperous home, one day reflected thus:
'When there is wealth, pride arises;
when there is that [pride], how can tranquility exist?
In the absence of tranquility, one who has lost shame
undertakes impure actions.'
'Now the suffering of contact with the unpleasant,
now the distress at the time of separation from the dear;
for those whose minds are wearied by the pursuit of wealth —
if their desires are unfulfilled, then despair.'
'For householders, who are always agitated,
whose minds are bound by affection for their own people,
who harbor the fruitless conceit of happiness —

children.text: tanur apy asti na nirvṛtir gṛheṣu
children.translated_text: there is not even the slightest cessation of suffering at home.'
'Therefore, casting aside this terrible bondage
called "household," swiftly, desiring my own [spiritual] welfare,
for the growth of austerities, I shall take refuge
in the forest's edge, the abode of tranquility.'

children.text: iti sa cintayitvā mahātmā parityajya gṛhavāsaṃ stimitasalilavāhinyā kusumitataṭataruśobhitayā śāstrābhyāsanirmalayeva prajñayā nimnagayālaṅkṛtabhūdharaikadeśe visrabdhahariṇagaṇadaśanadaṣṭaśādvalaramaṇīye nalinīvananilīnakalahaṃsakādambacakravākopaśobhite yogimano'nukūle kva cid atimahati vanāntare kṛṣṇājinaśabalīkṛtavakṣaḥsthalaḥ sthānaviśeṣalābhaparituṣṭayeva brāhmyā śriyāliṅgitamūrtir mūrtimān iva saṃtoṣaḥ kaṃ cid viṭapinam āśritya yogābaddhamanās tapaś caritum ārebhe ||
children.translated_text: Having thus reflected, that great soul, abandoning the household life, at a certain spot on a mountain adorned by a river — with its still-flowing waters and banks beautified by blossoming trees, like pure wisdom cleansed by the study of <s>śāstras</s> — a place delightful with grass nibbled by trusting herds of deer, graced by <s>haṃsa</s> geese, <s>kādamba</s> geese, and <s>cakravāka</s> ducks hidden in lotus-groves, agreeable to the minds of yogis — in a certain vast forest-interior, his chest mottled with a black deerskin, his form embraced by the <s>brāhmaṇa</s>'s glory as if contented with having obtained a special station, like contentment itself embodied — leaning against a certain tree, his mind absorbed in <s>yoga</s>, he began to practice austerities.
The tree under which that twice-born one of noble mind dwelt,
whose mind was single-pointed in meditation, whose senses were conquered,
who was happy with the gain of contentment and endowed with compassion —

children.text: mene mudeva sa tarus tarutāṃ kṛtārthām
children.translated_text: that tree itself considered its tree-hood fulfilled, as if with delight.
Spreading a bed of grass,
his gaze fixed upon the tip of his nose,
that foremost among meditators meditated
upon the object of meditation, with single-pointed mind.
The toil accumulated on the path of the <s>vīrya-pāramitā</s> (perfection of energy),
as if [a burden] borne by a vehicle,
the <s>dhyāna-pāramitā</s> (perfection of meditation)
now gave rest to that steadfast one.
Withdrawn from desires and unwholesome
states (<s>dharmas</s>), abiding separately,
with investigation and examination (<s>savitarka-savicāra</s>),
purified in self,
having tasted the pleasure of rapture and bliss (<s>prīti-sukha</s>),
having savored the nectar of peace,
he attained the first <s>dhyāna</s> (meditation),
meditating for the attainment of the path.
Then, free from investigation and examination (<s>avitarka-avicāra</s>),
skilled in discernment,
through inner serenity (<s>adhyātma-saṃprasāda</s>),
he entered the second <s>dhyāna</s>.
Then, gradually becoming dispassionate toward rapture (<s>prīti</s>),
mindful, equanimous,
the steadfast one, tasting bodily bliss,
attained the third <s>dhyāna</s>.
And purified by equanimity (<s>upekṣā</s>),
through the abandonment of pleasure and pain,
and through dispassion toward rapture,
he then reached the fourth <s>dhyāna</s>.

children.text: evam asāv utpāditacaturdhyāno mūrtivatyeva karuṇayāliṅgitamūrtir upaśamaparāyaṇas tatra vane tiraścām api bandhur iva viśrambhahetur āsīt ||
children.translated_text: Thus, having developed the four <s>dhyānas</s>, his form embraced by compassion as though it were embodied, devoted to tranquility, he became in that forest a friend even to animals, as it were — a cause of trust.
Deer, pigeons, peacocks, <s>cakora</s> partridges,
those various wild beasts of benign temperament —
having roamed about, like disciples at the forest's edge,
they came to his vicinity and rested.

children.text: atha tasya mahātmanaḥ kadā cid ābaddhaparyaṅkasya caraṇasamīpāvasthitamṛgamithunasya dhyānaniścalanayanasya pratyāsannaprasavā kapotī tṛṇāni tanūni ca dāruśakalāni cañcvādāya vinibaddhajaṭākalāpamaulau śirasi nilīya kiñcinnimnamadhyakulāyaṃ racayitvā tatrāṇḍāni muktvā tṛṇabījāśvatthaphalādyāhārakāṅkṣiṇī nabhaḥ samutpatya vanāntareṣu vihṛtya punaḥ punar āgamya ca tāny aṇḍāny avaṣṭabhyāvatasthe ||
children.translated_text: Then one day, while that great soul sat cross-legged, with a pair of deer standing near his feet and his eyes motionless in meditation, a pigeon-hen near the time of laying, taking fine straws and small twigs of wood in her beak, nestled upon his head in the crown of matted locks, fashioned a slightly hollowed nest there, laid her eggs, and, desiring food — grass-seeds, <s>aśvattha</s>-fruits, and the like — flew up into the sky, roaming among the forests, and returning again and again, she settled upon those eggs.
Then, in that little nest — clustered with the pigeon-hen's fine feathers,
its warmth gathered from the pressing of her body —
the pigeon chicks, their bodies tinged with pink,
broke through the eggs and emerged.
Then the pigeon-hen, seeing those chicks
with beak-tips repeatedly opened wide from hunger,
without considering her own great hunger,
nourished them with grains of <s>priyaṅgu</s> (millet) and <s>nīvāra</s> (wild rice).
Those little pigeons, their feathers growing strong,
seeing their mother who had obtained a seed,
with tips of their small wings fluttering, stretched out
their beaks repeatedly, uttering cries.
Then, at the conclusion of his meditation, when that sage
with senses subdued wished to go to the forest for firewood and fruits,
seeing the pigeon-hen, carrying grass and tree-fruits,
nestling upon his head where the nest was, he remained still.

children.text:
atha bodhisattvo niyatam atra mama jaṭābhāre viracitatṛṇakāṣṭhaśakalālayā prasūteyaṃ kapotī |
yadi cāham utthāya samidhāṃ kandamūlaphalānāṃ cāharaṇāya gamiṣyāmi tato niyatam eṣā tapasvinī sthānam idam āgamya ||
children.translated_text: Then the <s>Bodhisattva</s> [reflected]: 'Surely this pigeon-hen has built a nest of grass and wood-fragments in the tangle of my matted hair and has given birth. If I rise and go to gather firewood, roots, and fruits, then surely this poor creature, coming to this place —'
'not finding these pigeon-chicks today,
with their reddish palates openly displayed,
she will hide in the trees and again and again
fly up into the sky and wander about in grief.'
'Ah! The impression (<s>vāsanā</s>) accumulated through a hundred births
persists and is followed —
even in animals, in regard to their offspring,
this deep-rooted attachment is well established!'
'If there were no offspring,
nor friend, nor kinsman,
one would be free; in the absence of a sense of "mine,"
whence would attachment arise, being seedless?'
'When attachment does not exist,
anxieties do not envelop the mind;
in the absence of anxieties, one who is unattached
abides happily, endowed with tranquility.'
'Having produced sufferings labeled "offspring,"
deluded by afflictions,
the foolish person comes to weariness,
tormented by remorse.'
'Just as an unwilling ox is yoked by force
by a stronger cartman,
so is a person of wrong understanding driven
by good and bad <s>karma</s> in the ocean of existence.'
'Therefore, until the pigeon-chicks in the nest upon my matted hair
have grown their wings,
I shall remain here, perfectly motionless,
my mind and body satisfied by the nectar of meditation.'

children.text:
iti vicintya bodhisattvaḥ kapotaśāvakānukampayā kṣudham avigaṇayya punaḥ paryaṅkam ābadhya dhyānasukhenātmānaṃ prīṇayām āsa |
pravirūḍhapakṣeṣu kapotaśāvakeṣu mātrā saha gaganaṃ utplutya gateṣu tatsamīpanivāsinī devatā samupagamya bodhisattvam ālokya vismayasamadhyāsitamatir aho mahātmano 'sya maharṣeḥ sattveṣv anukampā yat prāktanāt dhyānād utthāya kapotakaparirakṣaṇāya punar api dhyānenātmānaṃ niścalīkṛtyāyam avasthitaḥ || na caiṣa mahātmā gateṣv apy eteṣu kapotakeṣu kulāyam imaṃ śirastaḥ samapaneṣyati |
tad aham evāsya jaṭāmukuṭaviracitam enaṃ kapotālayam apaneṣyāmīti vicintya ||
children.translated_text:
Having reflected thus, the <s>Bodhisattva</s>, out of compassion for the pigeon chicks, disregarding his hunger, once again assumed the cross-legged posture and delighted himself with the bliss of meditation.
When the pigeon-chicks, their wings fully grown, flew up into the sky together with their mother and departed, a nearby deity approached, and beholding the <s>Bodhisattva</s>, her mind pervaded with astonishment, [thought]: 'What compassion for beings this great-souled sage has! Having arisen from his former meditation, he remained again motionless through meditation for the protection of the pigeon family! And this great soul will not remove even now this nest from his head, even though the pigeons have departed. Therefore I myself shall remove this pigeon-dwelling fashioned in his matted-hair crown.' Having reflected thus —
She removed that nest from the head of the best of sages —
with some egg-shell fragments scattered within —
slowly, slowly,
with her pair of hands, tender as sprouts.

children.text: gatāyām ca tasyāṃ devatāyāṃ bodhisattvo dhyānāc cittam apanīya śiraso laghutvam avetyaivaṃ cintayām āsa ||
children.translated_text: And when that deity had departed, the <s>Bodhisattva</s>, withdrawing his mind from meditation, perceiving the lightness of his head, reflected thus:
'When the pigeon-chicks, their wings fully grown,
had departed with their mother to the forest's edge,
surely by someone filled with devotion
their nest was removed from my head.'

children.text: iti vicintyotthāya sa mahātmā samitkuśakusumaphalāny ānīya kṛtābhiṣekaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Having reflected thus, the great soul arose, brought firewood, <s>kuśa</s> grass, flowers, and fruits, and having performed his ablutions —
Having offered oblations into the fire blazing with leaping flames at midday,
and having consumed the unpasted, fragrant-bound fruit,
his gaze fixed upon the tip of his nose, beneath the tree,
he began <s>yoga</s> once again, with single-pointed mind.

children.text: tad evam dhyānavilokitatattvaḥ kṣamo 'pi nirvāṇam upagantuṃ sa bhagavān bodhisattvabhūto lokahitāya bahūpadrave 'pi saṃsāre paribhrāntavān iti vicintya buddhe bhagavati paraḥ prasāda utpādanīya iti ||
children.translated_text: Thus, he who had realized the truth through meditation, though capable of entering <s>nirvāṇa</s>, that Blessed One — being a <s>Bodhisattva</s> — wandered in <s>saṃsāra</s>, fraught with many dangers, for the welfare of the world. Reflecting upon this, supreme faith should be generated in the Blessed <s>Buddha</s>. ||
|| The <s>Jājvali</s> <s>Jātaka</s>, the sixth ||
32. Lion

children.text: tṛṇam api rakṣanti budhā yatnena mahīyasānyanikṣiptam /
children.translated_text: The wise protect even a blade of grass placed with care by the great ones;
how much more so, untiringly, a deposit of living beings, [they] whose guru is wisdom?

children.text:
tadyathānuśrūyate
dhautarajatastambhānurūpasatuhinaśikharāgraskhalanaparijarjarīkṛtajaladharasya muktācūrṇanikaradhavalaprāleyoparivyādhagaṇānusṛtacamarakhuramārgasya haravṛṣabhaviṣāṇollekhaviṣamīkṛtavividhakukṣer anekabhūrjasaraladevadārunamerupadmakavanaśyāmanikuñjasya prasṛtanirjharasalilakṣālitamūlabhūmeḥ kṣaṇadāsamayajvalitamahauṣadhitvāt kṛtapradīpasahasrasyeva vidyādharamithunaparibhogasurabhīkṛtamānasasarastīraparyantalatāgṛhakāntarasya kvacit kesaritalaprahāravinipātitabhītaprasphuritanyaṅkucaraṇakṣepotkhātatṛṇasya kvacid umācaraṇatalālaktakāṇkitaśādvalaśyāmabhūmer anyatra śakunituṇḍakhaṇḍitapariṇatataruphalākīrṇopavanāntarasya pavanavitanyamānoccāvacakusumagandhasurabheḥ surabhimāsaprārabdhaviṭapimukulāṅkurasya kuraravinipātaśabdabhītaśakunikulavimucyamānagaṅgātīrasalilasya salīlakinnaramithunagītaśravaṇaniścalamṛgakulasya tuṅgaśikharatayā kṣīrasāgarasyevoccatām upagatasya himagirer ekadeśe sādaram iva tarubhiḥ kusumārcitadvāraśilātalāṃ
haritatṛṇāṅkurodbhedaśyāmaparyantāṃ vikacakamalena sarasābhyalaṃkṛtasamīpām anatimahatīṃ guhām adhyāvasann atibahalaharidrāsalilābhiṣiktadukūlasūtraparipiṅgakesaraniruddhakandharaḥ kisalayasukumāralolatarajihvaḥ kiṃcitparimlānātimuktakakusumarāśiparipāṇḍuvigrahaḥ śaśikalākoṭikuṭilatīkṣṇadaṃṣṭraḥ pṛthūraskaḥ pīvaraprakoṣṭhaḥ pratanumadhyaḥ sphuritakhadirāṅgārakapilanayanayugalaḥ śyenatuṇḍavṛjinanakhāṅkuraḥ śyāmaprāntavāladhir alaṃkāra iva tuhinagirer aninditāṅgo nāma kadācid anuttrāsitadviradamṛgo mṛgādhipatir bodhisattvo babhūva |
children.translated_text:
Thus it is heard:
On the <s>Himālaya</s> — whose peaks resembled pillars of polished silver, whose clouds were shattered to fragments by sliding from the frost-covered summits, whose snow-surfaces were white as heaps of pearl-dust, with trails of <s>camara</s>-yak hooves followed by hunters, whose various mountain-flanks were furrowed by the scratching of <s>Śiva</s>'s bull's horns, with dark bowers of many birch, pine, <s>devadāru</s>, and <s>meru</s>-pine (<s>padmaka</s>) forests, whose soil at the base was washed by flowing waterfall-waters, which seemed to have a thousand lamps lit because of the blazing great herbs at nighttime, with fragrant hermitage-bowers on the shore of <s>Mānasa</s> lake made fragrant by the enjoyments of <s>Vidyādhara</s> couples, where in some places the grass was uprooted by the panicking kicks of startled <s>nyaṅku</s> deer struck by lion-paw blows, where elsewhere the green ground was marked with lac-dye from <s>Umā</s>'s foot-soles, where in other places the garden-interiors were strewn with ripe tree-fruits cut by the beaks of birds, fragrant with the scent of high and low flowers spread by the wind, with tree-buds beginning to sprout in the fragrant month [spring], with flocks of birds on the <s>Gaṅgā</s>'s banks releasing their waters, startled by the swooping sound of <s>kurara</s> birds, with deer-herds motionless from listening to the songs of playful <s>Kinnara</s> couples — on one side of that <s>Himālaya</s>, which by its lofty peaks had attained the height, as it were, of the Milk Ocean — dwelling in a not-too-large cave whose rock-floor at the entrance was reverently adorned, as it were, with flowers by the trees, whose surroundings were dark-green with the sprouting of tender green grass, and whose vicinity was adorned with a lake of blooming lotuses — there was the <s>Bodhisattva</s>, born as a king of beasts named <s>Anindita</s> (the Blameless). His mane was confined at the neck with threads of silk yellowish as if dyed in copious turmeric-water, his tongue tender and rolling like a shoot, his body pale like a heap of slightly withered <s>atimuktaka</s> flowers, his fangs sharp and curved like the tips of the moon's crescent, his chest broad, his forearms sturdy, his waist slender, his pair of eyes tawny like sparkling <s>khadira</s>-wood embers, his claw-buds curved like a hawk's beak, his tail-end dark-tipped — an ornament, as it were, of the Snow Mountain, a lion-king who never frightened deer or elephants.
Then, recognizing his innate benevolence,
like that of a sage whose mind is kindly toward all beings,
the naturally gentle, beautiful-eyed deer
followed him with delight, as if he were a kinsman.
Endowed with tranquility, his mane covered with bark-garments,
followed by deer, the lion-ascetic —
slowly emerging from within the cave-hermitage,
ate the ripe fruits of the trees.
Roaming in the forest for the enjoyment of fruits,
with playful gait and beautiful waving mane,
he was awaited like a guest by the great trees,
like generous householders fond of guests.
Emerging from the cave at winter's end,
from his exceedingly great yawning, [his mouth] shining like a visible palm,
the sun slowly spread before him
fresh warmth, as an offering of body-pleasure.
'This is the lord of beasts on this mountain,
mighty in valor like <s>Tārkṣya</s> (<s>Garuḍa</s>) among birds' —
as if thinking thus, overcome with reverence,
the night held a moon-parasol above him.
At the river where he stood on the bank
and drank the clear, cool water by moonlight,
that [river] seemed to consider herself fulfilled,
and clearly seemed to laugh with her rows of foam.
The <s>Himālaya</s>, by that one of pure mind —
sheltered by the great-souled lion,
it considered itself even greater
than the Golden Mountain, as if rejoicing.
'Where is this fearsomeness as a beast of prey toward the world,
and where is this supreme compassion toward the deer?' —

children.text: iti munim iva taṃ sthitaṃ himādrau
children.translated_text: thus, even the enemies of deer bowed to that king of beasts
dwelling on the <s>Himālaya</s>, as to a sage.

children.text: atha kadācit tasya mṛgapater avanipater iva salīlam āsannakusumitalatānartakīkisalayāṅgulisamāhanyamānamadhukaraśreṇivīṇāśabdaramaṇīye prasṛtanirjharamṛdaṅgadhvanipravartitamayūralāsake guhādvāre samupaviṣṭasya purastān niṣpīditālaktakagulikāparipāṭalamukham abhinavāmalakīphalānurūpanayanam āttapariṇatodumbarābhyāṃ śāvakābhyām adhyāsitaskandhaṃ phalarasārdramalinakarāṅgulīkaṃ vānaramithunam abhipraṇamyovāca |
children.translated_text: Now, once, as that lord of beasts — like a king — sat at the entrance of his cave, delightful with the sound of vīṇā-like humming of bee-rows being clapped together by the leaf-sprout-fingers of nearby blossoming creeper-dancers, with cascading waterfall-drum-sounds setting peacocks to dance — before him, a pair of monkeys appeared: their faces reddened as if by pressed lacquer-pellets, their eyes matching fresh <s>āmalakī</s> fruits, their shoulders mounted by two young ones bearing ripened <s>udumbara</s> [fig] fruits, their finger-tips wet and stained by fruit-juice — and, bowing down, they spoke:
'Ah, the conduct of your speech, body, and mind
is blameless!',
'Therefore, "<s>Aninditāṅga</s>" ("Of Blameless Limbs")',
'is remembered as a name befitting your qualities.'
'Ah, your generosity, patience, valor,
depth, compassion, and the rest —',
'your virtues, O best among the virtuous,',
'surpass even those of sages!'
'Ah, by your pure conduct,
O one of pure mind —',
'even the minds of the cruel',
'have been brought to supreme gentleness!'
'Blessed is this blessed <s>Himavān</s>,
with its rock-surfaces covered in snow —',
'which has been sheltered by you,',
'of steadfast nature!'
'Therefore, O fearsome one, these two little ones,',
'timid at the sight of serpents —',
'placing them with you, we two',
'shall go into the forest, seeking fruits.'
'Until we return quickly',
'from the forest-interior with fruits,',
'these two, of restless bodies,',
'are to be guarded by you.'
'Monkey-nature and restlessness —',
'these two are simultaneous.',
'Therefore, the mischief caused by these two',
'should be endured by you for a moment.'
'Even the greatest sufferings,
for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of others,',
'are endured indeed by the wise',
'who are indifferent to their own comfort.'
'He who wishes to remove the fear',
'of those of extremely timid minds —',
'how would he not endure',
'the mind-tormenting affliction [they cause]?'
Thus addressed by that monkey-pair
to protect their offspring,
the lion, though able to protect others like a king,
was thrown into momentary perplexity and pondered.

children.text: śakyate hi mahān api kanakarāśir anyanikṣipto 'bhirakṣitum | katham imau capalaprakṛtī vānaraśiśū rakṣaṇīyāv iti | atha vā yena mayā sakalam eva saṃsārabhayāj jagat paripālanīyaṃ so 'ham etau na paripālayiṣyāmīti na tu yuktam idaṃ mayā vitarkayitum iti sa mahātmā viniścitya tat pravaṅgamithunam uvāca |
children.translated_text: 'Indeed, even a great heap of gold deposited by another can be guarded. But how are these two monkey-infants, restless by nature, to be protected?' But then — 'I who must protect the entire world from the fear of <s>saṃsāra</s> — that I should not protect these two — it is not right for me to reason thus.' Having resolved this, the great-souled one said to the monkey-pair:
'Then go, plunging into this snowy mountain
that seems to scratch the midst of the sky with its lofty trees!',
'Bring back sweet fruits quickly!',
'I shall lovingly protect this pair of little ones.'

children.text: atha tat kapimithunaṃ bodhisattvasamīpe tat putrakadvayaṃ vinikṣipya sāntvayitvā ca tvaritataragamanaṃ phalopanayanāya himavadvanāntarāṇi paribabhrāma | aciragatayoś ca tayoḥ kapyos tasmin mahātmani kesariṇi pitarīva tau kapiśāvau premābabandhatuḥ | aninditāṇgaś ca tābhyāṃ pariṇatisvādūni śithiladaśanaprāntagṛhītāni phalāni prāyacchat | tau ca prakṛticapalatayā tasya mahātmanas tāṃ tāṃ viheṭhanāṃ cakratuḥ |
children.translated_text: Then that monkey-pair, depositing their two offspring near the <s>Bodhisattva</s>, consoling them, roamed most swiftly through the forest-interiors of the <s>Himavat</s> to bring back fruits. And though the two monkey-parents had gone only a short while, the two monkey-infants formed an attachment to that great-souled lion, as to a father. And <s>Aninditāṅga</s> gave them fruits, deliciously ripe, lightly held at the tips of his loose teeth. And the two, from their innate restlessness, caused him various kinds of annoyance:
In the beautiful forest at the edge of the cave's courtyard,
when <s>Hari</s> [the lion] wished to sleep in the pleasant cool breeze —
those two monkey-infants, with their chattering,
repeatedly destroyed his moment's pleasure of sleep.
When his eyes had slightly closed in drowsiness,
they poked at the two eyes
with their fingers —
[his eyes] with pupils tawny as sparks.
When he sat comfortably,
standing nearby without alarm,
they repeatedly pulled
the tip of his tail.
Hanging from his mane and again and again
climbing onto his back,
from their innate restlessness,
they leaped up and fell down far [from him].
Even when there were abundant
fruits placed before them,
they threw fruit
into his face as he was about to eat.
Thus, all that misbehavior
of the two monkey-infants
he endured, because of his compassionate and virtuous mind,
as if they were his own sons.
For those of equal mind toward all,
indifferent to pleasure and pain,
the virtuous ones who bear all burdens —
their mind is never vexed anywhere.

children.text: atha kadācid atiparuṣavipulapakṣasaṃghātaḥ kuṭilakarkaśanakhāgraḥ prakṛtiraudranayanaḥ kvacid alabdhapiśitāhāraḥ paribhramya gaganatalaṃ niśātakṣuratīkṣṇatuṇḍaḥ kṣurako nāma gṛdhraḥ saśabdavegaḥ sahasāvapatya tau bodhisattvasamīpavartinau phalāsvādena calitadhavalatanudantapaṅktī vānaraśiśū bhayavivṛtavikṛtamukhakau virasataravyāhṛtī caraṇābhyām ādāya tvaritataram antarīkṣam utpatya himagiriśikhare vyalīyata | bodhisattvo 'pi ca kaṣṭaṃ kaṣṭam ity abhidhāya yady aham enaṃ gṛdhraṃ parākrameṇābhidraveyaṃ punar ayam utpatyānyatra viṣamatare śikhare nilīya pravagaśiśudvayam idam vipādayet | sarvathā nedaṃ kapiśiśudvayaṃ mayā śakyate draṣṭum |
children.translated_text: Now, once, a vulture named <s>Kṣuraka</s> ('Razor') — with a mass of extremely rough, broad feathers, crooked and harsh-tipped claws, naturally fierce eyes, having found no flesh-food anywhere, having roamed the expanse of the sky, with a beak sharp as a whetted razor — suddenly swooped down with a rush of sound and, seizing the two monkey-infants — who were near the <s>Bodhisattva</s>, their rows of white, thin teeth exposed from tasting fruit, their mouths distorted and ugly from fear, their cries discordant — in his talons, he swiftly flew up into the sky and alighted on a peak of the snowy mountain. And the <s>Bodhisattva</s>, exclaiming 'Alas, alas!', [thought]: 'If I were to rush at this vulture with my might, he would fly up again and alight on some other, more precipitous peak and destroy this pair of monkey-young. By no means can I bear to see these two monkey-infants —'
'their eyes agitated with intensifying pain,
their palate-cavities visible from discordant cries,',
'their belly-fur moist with flowing blood,
their flesh being torn by the hungry hawk!'
'When the flesh of this pair of monkey-infants',
'has been thoroughly torn by this vulture,',
'and their parents come bringing fruits,',
'what shall I be able to say before them today?'

children.text: pātuṃ gatau capalakau saraso jalaṃ nu
children.translated_text: 'Have the two restless ones gone to drink water from a lake?

children.text: vṛkṣaṃ phalārtham abhiruhya nu kiṃ niviṣṭau
children.translated_text: Or have they climbed a tree for fruit and settled there?',

children.text: syātām imāṃ kim atha vādriguhāṃ praviṣṭau
children.translated_text: 'Or could they have entered this mountain-cave?',
'Or have they been killed here by some serpent?'

children.text: tūṣṇīṃ sthito mṛgapate kim adhomukhas tvam
children.translated_text: 'Why do you stand silently, O lord of beasts, with downcast face?',

children.text: ācakṣva tāv iha śiśū kva gatau bhavetām
children.translated_text: 'Tell us — where might these two little ones have gone?'
'How shall I hear the faltering words',
'of those two parents, with pitiable eyes?'
'Perceiving, after a long time, the absence',
'of their offspring, with teeth white as <s>kunda</s> [jasmine],',
'they will approach and, from grief, will make',
'quivering movements like a fish pulled out by a hook!'
'Therefore, I think this is the appropriate thing here:',
'Before this vulture, with his beak shaped like a tiger's claw-tip,',
'tears out the entrails from the belly of the two frightened monkey-infants —',
'let me go to the peak-edge of the snowy mountain, stand facing him,',

children.text: sāntvenainam upāyapūrvakam ahaṃ neṣyāmi dharmyāṃ sthitim
children.translated_text: 'and with gentle words, skillfully, lead him to the righteous path!'

children.text: iti vicintya sa mahātmā gṛdhrasamīpam āgamyovāca | bho śakunivara mama haste pitṛbhyām etau śāvakau nikṣiptau tan na yuktaṃ bhavato vivṛtadaśanadīnamukhakau virasasvarau vipādayitum enāv iti |
children.translated_text: Having reflected thus, the great-souled one, approaching the vulture, said: 'O excellent bird, these two young ones were deposited in my care by their parents. Therefore it is not right for you to destroy them — with their teeth bared pitiably, their mouths ugly, their voices discordant!'
'Surely you too have or once had',
'offspring of your own!',
'The affection that you have for them,',
'another has the same!'
'Therefore, taking compassion as your support,',
'do not kill the monkey-infants!',
'There is no ultimate satisfaction [in eating them] —',
'even after eating them, you will still be wretched.'
'Shame on the life of that one,',
'shame on such self-love,',
'who nourishes this quarrelsome body',
'by harming others!'
'From ignorance, attachment arises',
'even toward the faulty body.',
'For its nourishment, the ignorant one performs',
'causal actions leading to bad rebirth.'
'He who sees all things as empty',
'because of the absence of self and mine —',
'the darkness of false conceptualization',
'does not obstruct his mind.'
'When, in the absence of darkness,',
'the skilled one reaches the truth —',
'then, turning away from good and evil,',
'he reaches liberation.'
'There is no flesh-eater on earth more',
'cruel than a lion — this is well known on earth.',
'Yet I, even having taken birth in the terrible womb of a lion,',
'do not desire this unrighteous killing of living beings!'
'A deer here in the deep forest inhabited by the lord of beasts,',
'killed by an enemy of deer [i.e., a predator], or dead on its own —',
'O best of birds, wandering the sky, spotting it,',
'you may swiftly come and eat its flesh!'
'Therefore, enduring even this great hunger,',
'which burns the body like a flame of fire —',
'do not commit such unwholesome action',
'that leads to falling into hell, having abandoned heedlessness!'
'The hell-fires — terrifying with the cracking and popping sounds of the splitting of the joints, bones, and sinews of the beings within,',
'spreading heaps of sparks, terrifying with their tall flames dark-red,',
'with wavering garlands of flame, as described by the sages —',

children.text: kurvanty ādhiṃ janasya śravaṇam api gatāḥ kiṃ punaḥ saṃspṛśantaḥ
children.translated_text: 'they cause anguish to people even when merely heard about — how much more when they touch!'
'Beholding on a painted wall even a depicted hell-being being cooked',
'in an iron pot — his eyes squinting from the pain, loudly wailing,',

children.text: ālokyālekhyabhittau likhitam api naraṃ nārakaṃ pacyamānaṃ
children.translated_text: 'his face and throat overflowing with boiling, bubbling oil,',

children.text: hiṃsro 'pi krūrabhāvāt ka iva na viramed durgatiprāptihetoḥ
children.translated_text: 'who, even the violent, from their cruel nature, would not desist from the cause of reaching bad rebirth?'
'He who, having heard of the sufferings of bad rebirth,',
'does not desist from unwholesome deeds —',
'he is merely wearing the disguise of a human',
'or has a heart of stone.'

children.text: atha sa gṛdhro bodhisattvadharmadeśanāprasāditamatir abhipraṇamyovāca | mṛgapate prakāśitam idam bhavatā bālalakṣaṇam | paṇḍitalakṣaṇam idānīṃ vyākhyātum arhasīti | atha bodhisattvaḥ prasannamanasam enam avetyovāca | yady evam ataḥ śrūyatāṃ paṇḍitalakṣaṇam iti |
children.translated_text: Then that vulture, his mind calmed by the <s>Bodhisattva</s>'s teaching of the <s>Dharma</s>, bowed down and said: 'O lord of beasts, the characteristic of a fool has been illuminated by you. Now please explain the characteristic of a wise man.' Then the <s>Bodhisattva</s>, perceiving him to be of a receptive mind, said: 'If so, then hear the characteristic of a wise man:'

children.text: alābhe lābhe vā suhṛdi hitavāci dviṣati vā
children.translated_text: 'He who, whether in loss or gain, whether toward a friend who speaks beneficially or toward an enemy,',

children.text: stutau nindāyāṃ vā mahati vibhave vā vipadi vā
children.translated_text: 'whether in praise or blame, in great prosperity or in adversity,',
'undergoes no perturbation, standing with a mind purified by tranquility —',

children.text: sthitaḥ sa prājñānām upari saviteva dyutimatām
children.translated_text: 'he stands above the wise, like the sun above the luminaries.'

children.text: athavā kim anena bhavataḥ paṇḍitalakṣaṇaśravaṇena | vimucyetām etau kapiśāvakāv ātmānam evāhaṃ te pradāsyāmīti |
children.translated_text: 'But what use is this hearing about the characteristic of a wise man for you? Release these two monkey-infants — I shall give my own self to you!'

children.text: tvam addhi māṃsaṃ piba śoṇitaṃ ca
children.translated_text: 'Eat my flesh and drink my blood,',
'and pluck out the eyes of me, who am motionless!' —
Having spoken thus, with eyes closed,
he remained for a long time, his body without the slightest tremor.
A divine drum then filled the horizon-edges with its sound,
resounding in the midst of the city of the lord of the gods;
and the <s>siddhas</s>, standing in the sky with bowed heads,

children.text: siṃhaṃ sthitā nabhasi tuṣṭuvire ca siddhāḥ
children.translated_text: praised the lion who had given his body to the vulture.
The earth trembled, its golden mountains shaken;
the host of gods, together with <s>Indra</s>, was amazed;
with praises uttered even by the lords of serpents,
showers of flowers were cast upon him.
Then, near the lion's cave,
the bird placed the two monkey-infants —
their bodies wounded by claws, motionless,
their eyes closed from the swoon of fear.
And slowly approaching the <s>Bodhisattva</s>,
that excellent vulture roused him.
Standing before him with humble demeanor,
he spoke this praise with devotion:
'Where is this soaring compassion of yours —
and where is this lion-nature, fearsome to the world?',
'For some special reason, long ago,',
'you, some sage, assumed the form of a beast-lord!'
'He alone whose mind rests on wisdom,',
'equal in sorrow and joy —',
'he alone purchases, at the price of his life,',
'another who has fallen into calamity!'
'If there were not such as you —',
'firm bridges of the virtuous —',
'beings would drown in the fathomless,',
'vast ocean of suffering!'
'Having heard this auspicious',
'teaching of the <s>Dharma</s> from you,',
'from this day forth I shall practice',
'compassion even toward enemies!'

children.text: pṛcchāmi ca bhavantaṃ kiṃ punar anena tapasā padam abhilaṣasīti | bodhisattva uvāca |
children.translated_text: 'And I ask you: what station do you aspire to by this austerity?' The <s>Bodhisattva</s> said:
'The weariness of revolving in beginningless <s>saṃsāra</s> —'
is struck by successive waves of suffering from afflictions;
to rescue this world from the ocean of existence —
this is my devotion toward the state of a <s>Tathāgata</s>.'

children.text: gṛdhra uvāca | īdṛṅ mahāprajñasya bhavato na durlabhaṃ bauddhaṃ padaṃ sarvathā |
children.translated_text: The vulture said: 'For one of your great wisdom, the state of Buddhahood is certainly not hard to attain:'
'By those whose minds are revealed through the scriptures, who comprehend profound, inaccessible actions of the good and the bad,
who are devoted to the work of others' welfare,
who understand the words of the <s>Tathāgatas</s> that break existence, [words] of virtuous women —'

children.text: mohacchedi bhave bhave bhavatu no yuṣmadvidhaiḥ saṃgatam
children.translated_text: 'may we have the company of those like you, which cuts through delusion, in birth after birth!'
'Near the cave, I had placed
those two monkey-infants;
therefore, O virtuous one, you should now
permit me to depart.'

children.text: bodhisattva uvāca | aho paṭuvijñāno 'si yat tvayāyam asmadupadeśo gṛhītaḥ |
children.translated_text: The <s>Bodhisattva</s> said: 'Ah, you are of keen discernment, since you have grasped this teaching of mine!'

children.text: bodhyaṃ bandhugirā sphuṭīkṛtam api sthūlaṃ na gṛhṇāti yaḥ
children.translated_text: 'He who does not grasp even the plain [teaching] made clear by a kinsman's words, [seeking] what is to be awakened to —

children.text: sūkṣme vastuni tasya śāstraviṣaye vyarthaṃ matiḥ khidyate
children.translated_text: his mind labors in vain over subtle matters, the domain of the scriptures.',

children.text: draṣṭuṃ yasya na śaktir asti bhavanadvāraṃ prakāśe sati
children.translated_text: 'He who has no ability to see the door of a house when there is light —

children.text: cchidraṃ sūkṣmataraṃ sa jātatimiraḥ sūcyāḥ kathaṃ drakṣyati
children.translated_text: how shall he, afflicted by darkness, see the finer hole of a needle?'
'Even with a teacher present, the negligent
fool does not abandon the perversity of his mind;
even when repeatedly straightened,
a dog's tail returns to crookedness.'
'One who is instructed in the path by clear scriptures,
whose mind is not inferior, does not go astray —
like a great elephant, keenly good-minded, well-bodied,
[guided] by skilled mahouts.'
'This aggregate of senses, well-controlled,
does not cause disturbance for the wise person;
a serpent whose hood is firmly grasped

children.text: na hi śaknoty aparāddhum aṇv api
children.translated_text: cannot offend even slightly.'
'Power and position bestow deeply
the fruit of harm upon evil people;
orpiment, when poured inside a serpent's
mouth, makes the poison more intense.'
'Desire, through negligence, casts into ruin
a person who has been conquered by the enemies that are the senses —
like a flame, beautiful as molten gold,
[casts into ruin] a moth fluttering in the fire.'
'Attachment to sense-objects topples the unwise
person from the path of his own <s>dharma</s> —
like ripeness [topples] a fruit from the top of a tree,
whose stalk-root is held by a loosened bond.'
'If poison-trees, venomous serpents, weapons, and fires
were not naturally harmful,
what comparison could there be, in equal measure,
with an evil person of turbid, fierce mind?'
'An evil person who is angry without cause, hot-spoken,
whose gaze is made crooked by furrowed brows —
like an anthill from whose many openings fierce serpents emerge —
creates excessive fear.'
'Whetted firmly on the grinding-stone of anger,
raised with delight for the injury of others —

children.text: dunoti kaṃ nāma na gocaraṃ gataṃ
children.translated_text: whom that has come within range does not the shameless villain wound
with the sword-edge of his speech?'
'Villains, armored with deceit, long
hard to restrain, stationed amid the army of the senses,
pitiless and hurtful even toward good people,
bring down speech like a sword's edge.'
'The wise should never trust an evil person,
even when of humble dress, even when of pleasant speech;
does not the peacock, even with beautiful body and sweet voice,
devour writhing serpents?'
'If one desires the nourishment of the family of the mind
or the long-term growth of the queen that is wisdom,
then, when the rain-cloud of a wise person appears,
let the seed of good qualities be sown within oneself!'
'A self-possessed man whose mind is purified by long association with the good
does not seek the company of the wicked;
a bee that frequents charming blue-lotus flowers
never settles upon a corpse.'
'Just as delight arises for a warrior gone to battle,
an archer whose arrows have not failed —
so too for the wise one whose enemy of faults has been struck down
by the far-reaching arrows of virtues.'
'Having obtained the perfectly pure, irremovable, unartificial
ornament of virtues, honored by noble people —
a person does not feel wonder
even at the ornaments of the best of gods.'
'One who seeks ultimate happiness
or the arising of virtues,
having therefore abandoned evil company,
should resort to a virtuous friend.'
'The company of ignoble people never pleases
a virtuous person —
like a dark-colored garment [does not please]
one who has bathed in sacred waters.'
'Through association with the wise, who are destroyers of darkness and eliminators of the world's sin,

children.text: krūro 'pi prakṛtiṃ vihāya malinām ālambate bhadratām
children.translated_text: even a cruel person, abandoning his stained nature, takes hold of goodness;

children.text: yat tṛṣṇāglapito 'pi necchati janaḥ pātuṃ tad eva kṣaṇād
children.translated_text: the water of the lord of waters [the ocean], which even a thirsty person does not wish to drink —

children.text: ujjhaty ambudharodarasthitam apāṃ patyuḥ payaḥ kṣāratām
children.translated_text: that very water, when situated in the belly of a cloud, instantly abandons its saltiness.'

children.text: tad gamyatām yathāsukham iti bodhisattvenābhihitaḥ sa pakṣī taṃ mahātmānaṃ pradakṣiṇīkṛtya gaganatalam utpatya paribhraman dadarśa rudhirābhiraktanakhamukhaśmaśruṇā vyāghreṇopayujyamānamāṃsam upacitamedaḥpīvaraskandham abhinavamustāsvādanasurabhīkṛtavadanāntarālam avanitalotkiraṇamalinakuṭiladaṃṣṭrādvayam īṣatpaṅkopadigdhaśarīram anatidūrāvasthitagṛdhramaṇḍalaparivṛtam upāntatarunilīnamukharavāyasagaṇāvalokyamānaṃ varāhataruṇam | ālokya caivam acintayad yāvad ayaṃ vyāghraḥ kṛtāhāraparyāptir bhūtvā svanilayaṃ gacchati tāvad aham ekānte tiṣṭhāmīti sthitvā ca krameṇa |
children.translated_text: Having been told by the <s>Bodhisattva</s>, 'Go as you wish,' that bird, having circumambulated the great-souled one, flew up into the sky and, wandering about, saw a young boar — whose shoulder-hump was built up with accumulated fat, whose mouth-interior was made fragrant by the taste of fresh <s>mustā</s> grass, with a pair of curved tusks soiled by digging the earth's surface, its body slightly smeared with mud, surrounded at a distance by a circle of vultures, watched by a flock of crows concealed in nearby undergrowth — being eaten by a tiger, its flesh being consumed, its nails, snout, and whiskers stained with blood. Seeing this, [the vulture] thought: 'Until this tiger, having eaten his fill, departs to his own lair, I shall wait apart.' And having waited, gradually —
When the tiger, content and having obtained satisfaction,
playfully went to his own dwelling by chance,
the hawk too, having consumed a piece of the boar-flesh, nourished with fat,
swiftly returned to his own lair.
And the lord of beasts too, when the sun, with its crown-ornament reddened like <s>kiṃśuka</s> flowers,
stood upon the summit of the Golden Mountain with blazing rays,
when the birds had settled in their nests in the clusters of tree-branches,
his soft mane-tips stirring, went to his own dwelling.

children.text: dṛṣṭvā ca tau kṣurakanakhavibhinnatanū tanūbhūtaceṣṭau mūrcchāvaśavinimīlitanayanau kapiśiśū duḥkhāyamānahṛdayo bhavatu salilābhiṣekeṇānayor mūrcchāpanodaṃ kariṣyāmīti vicintya |
children.translated_text: And seeing the two monkey-infants — their bodies torn by sharp vulture-claws, their movements weakened, their eyes closed in a faint — with a grieving heart, [the lion] thought: 'Let me revive them from their faint by sprinkling water.' Thinking thus,
a lake whose waters were blocked by bank-dwelling [plants],
continuously surrounded by trees [red] like coral sprouts,
slowly he entered, the lotus-dwelling, with its yellowish stamens
tinged [by his approach].
And having plunged into that great lake,
quickly emerging, with dripping mane,
he came repeatedly to the cave's vicinity,
the turf bent by the placing of his paws.
Then, upon the two monkey-infants
whose bodies were wounded by the sharp vulture-claws,
that lion swiftly shook his mane,
streaming with water, above them.
The two monkey-infants, sprinkled with water from the lion's mane,
regaining consciousness as the heavy faint departed,
opened their eyes,
their mouths gaping upward, quivering.
Trembling with fear of the vulture, their bodies agitated and anxious,
the two stood, having come to the feet of the lord of beasts;
and he, with a tongue charming as a swaying sprout,
licked them both repeatedly with affection.
Taking a ripe fruit fallen from its stalk,
soothing his two [charges] again and again with love, as if they were his own children,
entering his own cave, glimmering with firefly-lights,

children.text: suṣvāpa tau sa parirabhya sukhaṃ niśāyām
children.translated_text: he slept happily at night, embracing them both.

children.text: krameṇa ca parimlānamālatīkusumaśekharaparidhūsaraniśākaraparimucyamānapaścimadigbhāgāyāṃ svavasatisthānotthitamātrahariṇadaśanādaśyamānatṛṇāṅkurāyāṃ pūrvasaṃdhyāsaṃrajyamānasāgarasalilāyāṃ praviralībhavannakṣatragaṇāyāṃ kamalavanaprabodharamaṇīyatarasalilāśayāyāṃ taruviṭapāvataraṇacalitaśikhikalāpamanoharataravanāntarāyām apagatāyāṃ rātrau guhāsamīpatarulatākusumaparyantasaṃcāriṇībhir alikulāvalībhiḥ sādaram upagīyamāna ivāninditakarmāninditāṅgaḥ |
children.translated_text: And gradually, as the night departed — when the <s>mālatī</s> flower garland-crown of the moon was fading and growing dusty as the western quarter released [the moon]; when the grass-shoots were being nibbled by deer risen from their resting places; when the ocean-waters were reddened by the glow of the morning twilight; when the clusters of stars were thinning; when the water-reservoirs were even more delightful as the lotus-gardens awakened; when the forest-interiors were even more charming as the peacock-plumes stirred with the birds descending from tree-branches — [the lion], with blameless deeds and blameless body, seemed to be sung over with respect by swarms of bees moving among the flowers of the creepers on the trees near the cave.
As the sun entered the eastern quarter
like a golden vessel,
slowly, accompanied by the monkey-infants,
with his mane trembling and hanging, he went out.
Then the monkey-couple, having obtained fruit, greedy for fruit,
eager to see their children,
swiftly came
to the dwelling of the lord of beasts.
When they arrived, the lion, the rise of his pride and rut subsided,
soft-footed, soft-spoken, accompanied by compassion,
having received their salutation, that knower of the world
spoke to them, beginning with an inquiry about their welfare.
He then related in sequence
everything that had happened regarding the monkey-infants,
and finally told of
their seizure by the vulture.
Then, hearing the past calamity
of their children, with grief,
the two monkeys touched
the vulture-wounded limbs of those two.
And they spoke these words,
deeply tender, joined with praise, to the lord of beasts:
'By you who protected our children,
we too have been well-protected!'
'Extending the Ganges-stream of <s>Dharma</s>-discourse,
marked by the peaks of virtues,
covered with the snow of fame —
you are a mobile <s>Himālaya</s>!'
'Those innumerable virtues of yours
that do not fit within the body —
I believe, having attained the state of a mane,
they stand outside!'

children.text: stimitam udadheḥ kṣubhṇāty ambhaḥ patatripatiḥ patañ
children.translated_text: 'The lord of birds [<s>Garuḍa</s>], falling, disturbs the calm waters of the ocean;
the radiance of the moon, covered by a mass of clouds, does not spread.',

children.text: tava punar aghavyucchedinyāṃ sthitau sthitam anyatāṃ
children.translated_text: 'But your pure mind, steadfast in the destruction of sin,

children.text: na tu gamayituṃ cetaḥ śuddhaṃ rajastamasī kṣame
children.translated_text: is not capable of being led astray by <s>rajas</s> and <s>tamas</s>.'
'By the exceedingly great merit you have acquired
in protecting these two children of ours,
may you obtain
the desired fruit!'
'Then take these two children,
carefully protected by you with effort,
and go to our own dwelling
in the forest-interior, surrounded by many kinsmen.'

children.text: tena proktau yātam ity utsukau tau
children.translated_text: Told by him 'Go!', those two, eager,
having made a salutation to that virtuous one with devotion,
with children mounted on their backs, from the peaceful abode,
slowly, slowly departed for the forest-interior.
Of the parents departing, the two [infants] mounted on the middle of their backs,
clinging tightly to the mass of shoulder-fur,
turning their eyes slightly, eager,
again and again beheld the lord of beasts.
Having entrusted that deposit — the essence of all deposits —
that one whose domain was essential wisdom,
as if having set down a burden from his shoulders onto the ground,
attained a greater joy from the cutting off of weariness.
'There is nothing more difficult
than holding the deposit of living beings;
and from the return of that very [deposit],
there is no other happiness for people.'

children.text: tad evaṃ tena bhagavatā tiryaggatāv api vartamānena suciram abhirakṣitaḥ prāṇinikṣepaḥ | tadavasthenāpi ca prajñāparicayaḥ kṛta iti vicintya
children.translated_text: Thus the Blessed One, even while existing in an animal birth, long protected the deposit of living beings. And even in that state, he cultivated the practice of wisdom. Reflecting thus —
'That deposit of <s>Dharma</s>
deposited well by that Protector —
should be guarded by you
who desire supreme happiness!'
|| Thus the <s>Siṃha Jātaka</s> (Lion Birth-Story). ||
35. <s>Śākyasiṃha</s> (Lion of the <s>Śākyas</s>)

children.text: vijahati divyam api sukhaṃ tribhuvanahitakāmyayā mahātmānaḥ /
children.translated_text: Great souls abandon even divine happiness out of desire for the welfare of the three worlds;

children.text: paraduḥkhaṃ hi garīyo duḥkhayati dayāvatāṃ cetaḥ //
children.translated_text: for the suffering of others is heavier — it grieves the minds of the compassionate.

children.text:
tadyathānuśrūyate
sakalapāramitādhigamāt pratyāsannabodhiḥ svaprabhayāvabhāsitāṅgaḥ kadācid bodhisattvas tuṣitabhavane samudapādi | sa ca mahātmā tannivāsināṃ devānāṃ dharmyayā kathayā sanmārgam abhiprakāśyaivam acintayat | kṛtayuge hi dharmaparāyaṇo lokaḥ sukham avatāryate satpatham | asmiṃs tu kaliyuge madamānalobharāgadveṣamohavaśīkṛtāḥ prāṇinaḥ sukhalavamohitātmāno durgatiparāyaṇāḥ | tan mayā yuktaṃ bodhim avagamya saṃsārāj jagad uddhartum iti | madhyadeśe ca śraddhāviśuddhamanā lokaḥ | yaś caiṣa śuddhodanaḥ kapilavastuni mahānagare narapatir ayam atīva saccaritena maharṣīn apy atiśete | tad asyaivāgramahiṣyā māyāyāḥ kukṣau janmaparigrahaṃ kariṣyāmīti vicintya niśi suptāyāḥ svapne |
children.translated_text: Thus it is heard in tradition: The <s>Bodhisattva</s>, who was near to enlightenment through the attainment of all the perfections (<s>pāramitās</s>), his body illuminated by his own radiance, was once born in the <s>Tuṣita</s> heaven. And that great-souled one, having illuminated the right path for the gods dwelling there through a discourse on the <s>Dharma</s>, reflected thus: 'In the <s>Kṛtayuga</s> (golden age), the world, devoted to <s>dharma</s>, is easily led to the right path. But in this <s>Kaliyuga</s>, beings, overpowered by intoxication, pride, greed, passion, hatred, and delusion, deceived by a morsel of happiness, are destined for bad rebirths. Therefore it is proper for me, having realized enlightenment, to rescue the world from <s>saṃsāra</s>.' 'In the Middle Country, the people have minds purified by faith. And this <s>Śuddhodana</s>, the king of the great city <s>Kapilavastu</s>, surpasses even the great sages by his excellent conduct. I shall take birth in the womb of his chief queen <s>Māyā</s>.' Having resolved thus, while she was sleeping at night, in a dream —
assuming the form of an elephant, white as the Himalaya, with six great tusks,
its face perfumed by [the fragrance of] generosity,
he entered the womb of the queen
of King <s>Śuddhodana</s>, the lord of the earth, for the destruction of the world's suffering.

children.text: atha devī mahāmāyā rājñe taṃ svapnaṃ nivedayāmāsa | deva svapne kila mamādya śaradambudharāvadātaḥ ṣaḍdanto gajendro dakṣiṇaṃ kukṣiṃ bhittvodaraṃ praviṣṭa iti | tataḥ sa rājā taṃ svapnaṃ svapnaphalavidāṃ dvijātīnāṃ purastād varṇayāmāsa | te ca brāhmaṇās tam ūcuḥ | mahārāja cakravartī te putro bhaviṣyatīti | sa ca rājā pratītamanās tān dvijātīn satkṛtya visasarja |
children.translated_text: Then Queen <s>Mahāmāyā</s> reported that dream to the king: 'Sire, in my dream today, an elephant-lord, white as an autumn cloud, with six tusks, pierced my right side and entered my womb.' Then the king described that dream before brāhmaṇas who were skilled in interpreting the fruits of dreams. And those brāhmaṇas said to him: 'Great king, a universal monarch (<s>cakravartin</s>) will be born to you as a son.' And the king, with a gladdened mind, honored those brāhmaṇas and dismissed them.
Then the queen, with her inner-palace attendants,
once went to <s>Lumbinī</s>
with the king's permission,
having developed the finest pregnancy-cravings.
As the queen was grasping a branch
bending with the weight of blossoms,
the <s>Bodhisattva</s>, splitting her side, swiftly
emerged.
The just-born one was then gently received
by the delighted Thousand-eyed one [<s>Indra</s>], golden as a sacrificial post;
and upon his head, together with showers of <s>mandāra</s> flowers,
two streams of water fell from the spotless sky.
Placed upon the ground by <s>Balabhid</s> (<s>Indra</s>), the sole lord of the world,
the resolute one, having taken seven steps upon the earth in sequence,
spoke this most wondrous, serene utterance:

children.text: janmedam antyam iti me tamasām abhāvāt
children.translated_text: 'This is my last birth, for there is no more darkness [of ignorance].'
And his radiance, surpassing the luster of the cool-rayed [moon],
illuminating the earth from that tranquil-souled one,
split the darkness in the fearsome dark hells —
impenetrable even by the powerful rays of the sun and moon.

children.text: ayam ayam mahātmā dharmarājo 'bhiṣikta iti pramuditamanobhir amaraiś cāmbaratale dundubhayo 'bhijaghnire | śibikām cādhiruhya devī bodhisattvam ādāya svabhavanam agamat | athātyadbhutavismitamanāḥ śuddhodanaḥ sarvabandhanamokṣaṃ kārayitvā samucchritadhvajapatākavicitravipaṇimārgam atisurabhigandhodakokṣitavasudhātalam abhinavakusumopahāraśabalarathyāntaraṃ kapilavastunagaram akārayat |
children.translated_text: 'This, this great-souled one — the king of <s>Dharma</s> — has been consecrated!' — with delighted minds, the immortals struck the kettledrums in the firmament. And the queen, mounting a palanquin and taking the <s>Bodhisattva</s>, went to her own dwelling. Then <s>Śuddhodana</s>, his mind filled with extreme wonder, having ordered the release of all prisoners, had the city of <s>Kapilavastu</s> decorated — with marketplace streets resplendent with raised banner-pennants, the earth's surface sprinkled with exceedingly fragrant perfumed water, the streets dappled with fresh flower-offerings.
From the sky, the king heard — the people [too heard] — [a sage] descending,
his shoulder-area covered with a dappled deer-skin,
bearing a pile of flame-like matted locks,
dark-hued, a repository of deeds that are not dark [i.e., pure].

children.text: atha sa rājābhyutthāya taṃ maharṣiṃ viditabodhisattvajanmānaṃ praviśantam abhigamyābhivādyārghapradānādinā ca satkāreṇa satkṛtya kṛtāsanaparigrahaṃ cainaṃ kuśalaṃ pṛṣṭvā dhātryaṅkagataṃ bodhisattvaṃ darśayann uvāca | bhagavan dṛśyatāṃ tāvad ayaṃ me tanayaḥ kiṃ dīrghāyuḥ syād iti | athāsito bodhisattvam ālokya caivam acintayat |
children.translated_text: Then the king, rising, went to welcome that great sage who knew of the <s>Bodhisattva</s>'s birth, entering [the palace]; having honored him with respectful greetings, offerings of water and the like, and having inquired about his welfare as he took his seat, the king, showing the <s>Bodhisattva</s> seated on the nurse's lap, said: 'Venerable sir, pray behold this son of mine — will he be long-lived?' Then <s>Asita</s>, beholding the <s>Bodhisattva</s>, thought thus:
'As this one is adorned, as if with ornaments,
by clear auspicious marks —'
'so will he become a <s>Buddha</s>
for the removal of the world's suffering.'
'When this one shall become a <s>Buddha</s>,
I shall then go to death;'
'those who will hear the discourse on <s>Dharma</s> from him —
those embodied beings are blessed!'
As that great sage of pure mind
thus reflected,
his two eyes, with their lashes bent downward,
became filled with tears.

children.text:
atha śuddhodanaḥ sāśrunayanam asitam avalokya sasaṃbhramam uvā-
ca | niyatam ayam alpāyuḥ | tena bhagavān sāśrulocanaḥ samvṛttaḥ | kaṣṭam avikasitam eva me tanayakamalam idam antakadviradapatir unmūlayiṣyati | asito 'bravīt | alam alaṃ mahārāja śokena | aham ātmānam anuśocāmi | yadāyaṃ viṣayān utsṛjya jarāmaraṇagrastān dehino 'valokya saṃvignamanās tapovanaṃ gatvā buddho bhaviṣyati tadāhaṃ pañcatvam upayāsyāmīty ato mama śokena sāśrum idaṃ cakṣuḥ kṛtam ity abhidhāya gate tasmin maharṣau siddhārtha iti nāma bodhisattvasya kṛtvācireṇaiva kālena gurusakāśād adhigatasarvavijñānasya tasya sadṛśāt kulād yaśodharāṃ nāma varayitvā vadhūm ānināya | katham ayaṃ jarāmaraṇarogānabhijña eva me tanayaḥ syād iti vicintya śuddhodano 'ntarbhavana evāntaḥpuramadhyavartinam avicchinnanṛttagītāvalokanaśravaṇaparāyaṇaṃ bodhisattvaṃ kārayāmāsa | sa ca yaśodharāyāṃ rāhulaṃ nāma tanayaṃ janayitvā kadācid gītopanibaddhāni pramadavanāni śrutvā bahirniṣkramaṇāya buddhiṃ kṛtvā pitrābhyanujñāto rathavaram adhiruhya kṛtaśobhāṃ kapilavastuvīthīm ālokayan paricacāra |
children.translated_text: Then <s>Śuddhodana</s>, seeing <s>Asita</s> with tearful eyes, spoke in alarm: 'Surely this one will be short-lived! That is why the venerable one has become tearful. Alas, before it even blossoms, the lord of elephants that is death will uproot this lotus-son of mine!' <s>Asita</s> said: 'Enough, enough, great king, with grief! I grieve for myself. When this one, having renounced the sense-objects, seeing embodied beings seized by old age and death, with a stirred mind going to the ascetic grove, shall become a <s>Buddha</s> — then I shall meet my end. Therefore my eye has been made tearful with grief.' Having said this, when that great sage had departed, the king, having named the <s>Bodhisattva</s> '<s>Siddhārtha</s>,' and in a short time [when the boy had] acquired all knowledge from his teachers, brought from a family equal to his own a bride named <s>Yaśodharā</s>. Thinking 'How may this son of mine remain ignorant of old age, death, and disease?' <s>Śuddhodana</s> kept the <s>Bodhisattva</s> within the inner apartments of the palace, in the midst of the women's quarters, devoted to the uninterrupted enjoyment of seeing and hearing dance and song. And he, having begotten a son named <s>Rāhula</s> by <s>Yaśodharā</s>, once hearing songs about the pleasure-gardens, having formed the intention to go outside, and permitted by his father, mounted an excellent chariot and, viewing the beautified streets of <s>Kapilavastu</s>, made his rounds.
Then, hearing from the attendants about him — delightful to the eyes,
like <s>Manobhava</s> (Cupid) in person, with ears elongated like [lotus]-eyes —
of the city-women, whose minds were eager to see him,
the behavior became manifold.

children.text: atha kācid asamāptamaṇḍanārdratilakābhyalaṃkṛtalalāṭamadhyā śravaṇaparicyutakuvalayotthāyāñjitaikavilocanā gṛhītaśalākena kamalānukāriṇā hastena paśyainam anaṅgānukāriṇam kumāraṃ gacchantam iti sakhyai darśayāmāsa | kācit punar aho bhāgyavatī yaśodharā yāsya dharmacāriṇīti vicintya ciram enaṃ stimitanayanāpaśyat | aparā punaḥ karadvayāvalambitagavākṣastambhaśālabhañjikeva bhṛśam aśobhata | kim evaṃ rājaputradarśanakutūhalād atitvaritaṃ gacchasi | samutkṣipainam ardhabaddhaṃ stanataṭāt patantaṃ hāram ayaṃ tvam aho capaleti bruvāṇaḥ kupito gurujanaḥ paśyati | kim iti nirvrīḍāsīti kācid aparām upālabdhavatī | kācit punar gurupayodharaikadeśe saṃsparśenārdhāpāvṛtaṃ kapāṭam anujagrāheva | naikākinyās tavaiva kumāradarśanakutūhalaṃ dīyatām tāvad antaram aham api kutūhalavatī rājaputraṃ draṣṭukāmā kācid ity abhāṣata |
children.translated_text: One woman, with her ornamentation unfinished, her forehead adorned with a still-wet tilaka, with one eye painted with collyrium from a blue lotus fallen from her ear, showed him to her friend with a hand lotus-like holding the applicator-stick: 'Look at this prince going by, who resembles Cupid!' Another, thinking 'Ah, how fortunate is <s>Yaśodharā</s>, who is this one's companion in <s>dharma</s>!' gazed at him for a long time with motionless eyes. Another, with both hands resting on the window-pillar, shone like a bracket-figure. 'Why do you go so hastily in your curiosity to see the prince? Pick up this half-strung necklace falling from the surface of your breast! You are, oh, fickle one!' — thus the angry elders spoke and watched. 'Why are you so shameless?' one reproached another. Another, with one side of her heavy breast pressing against [it], seemed to hold back a half-opened door. 'The curiosity of seeing the prince is not for you alone — give some space! I too am curious and wish to see the prince!' — said another.
From the movements of those [women]
eager to see the prince,
the sounds of girdles and anklets
resounded in the dwellings.
